Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by 'Ali bin Abi Talhah, said it means: "We bring forth a more beneficial ruling, that is also easier for you." Qatadah: "We replace it by an Ayah more facilitating, permitting, commanding, or prohibiting." As-Suddi: "We bring forth a better Ayah, or similar to that which was repealed."

So "better" here does not mean better *in itself*, as though revelation could be improved upon. Ibn Kathir is explicit that "better" relates to the benefit provided for the one it addresses. The measure is you: what serves the servant at this point in his formation. And when the replacement is merely "its like," you are told plainly that you have lost nothing.

## Why a perfect Lawgiver changes a law

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers the single most clarifying passage on this subject. Making laws and repealing them is a well-known practice in human governments, and it happens for two reasons: either the lawmakers did not understand the situation properly when they made the law and must change it once they realise their mistake, or the law suited the situation at the time but unforeseen changes altered that situation. Both of these forms are out of the question where Allah is the Lawgiver.

But there is a third form. A lawmaker may make a law knowing full well that circumstances are going to change in such a way that the law will no longer suit the new situation; so when the situation changes as he already knew it would, he changes the law and promulgates the new one he had in mind from the very start. Maʿārif gives the illustration of a physician: he prescribes a medicine in view of the patient's present condition, knowing that after two days the condition will have changed and will require a different medicine. He could easily hand over written instructions for the whole course of treatment at the outset — but that would put too much burden on the already feeble patient, and there would be the danger of harm through a possible error or misunderstanding.

This third form, Maʿārif says, is the only kind of abrogation that can occur, and has been occurring, in divine injunctions and divine books. Every new Shari'ah and every new revealed Book has abrogated many injunctions of the one before it; and within a single Shari'ah too, a law would be in force for a time until Divine Wisdom chose to abrogate it and promulgate another in its place. Maʿārif cites here a hadith reported by Muslim: **"There has never been a prophethood which did not abrogate some injunctions."** The error, on this reading, was to confuse divine abrogation with the two forms of repeal that belong to man-made laws — to hear "the law changed" and assume someone had been mistaken.

Ibn Kathir makes the same case from their own scripture and history. The sound mind does not deny that there could be naskh in Allah's commandments, for He decides what He wills just as He does what He wills; and naskh did occur in the previous Books and Laws. Allah allowed Adam to marry his daughters to his sons and later forbade it; allowed Nuh to eat from all kinds of animals after they left the ark, then prohibited some types of food; allowed Israel and his children to have two sisters married to one man, then prohibited it later in the Torah; commanded Ibrahim to slaughter his son, then repealed the command before it was implemented; commanded the Children of Israel to kill those who had worshipped the calf, then repealed that command so that they were not all exterminated. There are many other instances, Ibn Kathir says, that they themselves admit have occurred and yet ignore.

## Ayah 107: the argument moves to ownership

Having answered the objection, the passage now goes underneath it. **"Know you not that it is Allah to Whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth? And besides Allah you have neither any protector or guardian nor any helper."**

Ibn Kathir draws out the force of this. Allah directed His servants to the fact that He alone is the Owner of His creatures and does with them as He wills. His is the supreme authority and all creation is His; and just as He created them as He wills, He brings happiness to whom He wills and misery to whom He wills, health to whom He wills and ailment to whom He wills, success to whom He wills and failure to whom He wills. He judges between His servants as He wills, allows what He wills and disallows what He wills. There is no opponent for His judgment, and no one can question Him about what He does, while they shall be questioned.

Imam Abu Ja'far bin Jarir phrases the ayah as direct address to the Prophet ﷺ: "Do you not know, O Muhammad, that I alone own the heavens and the earth and that I decide whatever I will in them? I forbid whatever I will, change and repeal whatever I will of My previous rulings, whenever I will. I also uphold whatever I will." Ibn Jarir adds that although Allah directed this statement of His greatness towards His Prophet ﷺ, He also rejected the lies of those who denied that the rulings of the Torah could undergo naskh — the same denial that led them to reject the prophethood of 'Isa and of Muhammad ﷺ, because they disliked what the two brought from Allah, including changes to some rulings of the Torah made at Allah's command. The subjects in Allah's kingdom are His creation, and they are required to hear and obey His commands and prohibitions.

Ibn Kathir also names a purpose in abrogation that is easy to miss: **Allah tests His servants and their obedience to His Messengers by the naskh.** He commands a matter containing a benefit which He knows of, and then, out of His wisdom, prohibits it — and it is here that perfect obedience is realised, in adhering to His commands, following His Messengers, believing whatever they convey, implementing their commands and avoiding what they prohibit.

**"No protector and no helper."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the two words as two distinct mercies. As friend and protector, Allah keeps men's good in view while laying down the injunctions themselves. As helper, He protects those who obey His commandments against the hostility of their foes. And Maʿārif adds a sober qualification: if the obedient are to receive blessings in the other world greater than the harm they suffer in this one, then the apparent domination of their foes does not really matter.

## How much of the Qur'an is abrogated? The scholars differ

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces a real disagreement here, and it turns almost entirely on how the word *naskh* is being used.

The 'Ulama' of the **early period of Islam** used *naskh* in a general and comprehensive sense: it covered not only the total repeal of an injunction and its replacement by another (fixing the Ka'bah as the qiblah instead of Baytul-Maqdis), but also the retention of an injunction with certain conditions, provisions or exceptions added to it. That is why the scholars of that earlier period indicated some **five hundred** verses as abrogated.

**Later scholars** narrowed the term: only a change that cannot in any way be brought into consonance with an earlier injunction is to be called naskh. This greatly reduces the count — according to al-Suyuti, there are only about **twenty** such verses.

**Shah Waliyyullah**, seeking to bring the abrogated injunctions into consonance with the earlier ones, reduced the number to **five** — the cases where the later injunctions could not be made to correspond with the earlier without far-fetched interpretations. Maʿārif calls this effort highly commendable, and gives the principle behind it: the basic postulate behind an injunction is its permanence, and abrogation goes against that postulate, so it is not proper to posit abrogation in a verse laying down an injunction which can, in some justifiable manner, be shown to be still valid.

But Maʿārif then guards that door firmly. This effort to reduce the number does not, and cannot in the least, imply that the presence of abrogation is some shortcoming or defect in the Qur'an or in Islam which the 'Ulama' have spent fourteen hundred years trying to remove, with the ultimate inspiration coming to Shah Waliyyullah and a few geniuses now awaited to bring the number down to zero. To take that approach is no service to Islam or to the Qur'an; it cannot obliterate the profound investigations of the Companions, their Successors and the scholars of the generations after them, and it cannot stop the recriminations of Islam's enemies. All it would do is furnish a weapon to present-day traducers of Islam, who would say that what the 'Ulama' of the Ummah have maintained for fourteen hundred years has finally proved wrong. If that door is opened, Maʿārif warns, it would let in all kinds of disorders and every injunction of the Shari'ah would come under suspicion.

## The one dissenting view, and how it was answered

Some among the Mu'tazilah — the view is attributed to **Abu Muslim al-Isfahani** — conceded that abrogation is rationally possible in the case of divine injunctions and cannot be denied on any rational ground, but held that it never actually occurred in the Qur'an: no verse abrogating (*nāsikh*), no verse abrogated (*mansūkh*). Maʿārif quotes *Ruh al-Maʿani*: the people belonging to all the Shari'ahs are unanimous in accepting both the validity of abrogation and its actual occurrence; only the Jews — with the exception of their 'Isawiyyah sect — denied its very possibility, and only Abu Muslim al-Isfahani denied its occurrence. The 'Ulama' in general have always rejected this opinion and refuted the argument, and Imam Razi, in his commentary, exposed its hollowness in detail.

Maʿārif also addresses recent writings that attempt to revive Abu Muslim's argument, and the attempt hangs on a single word. Such writers assume that the Arabic *mā* at the start of ayah 106 is not a relative or adverbial pronoun meaning "whenever" or "whichever," but a conjunction meaning "if" introducing a conditional clause — so they render the phrase "if We abrogate a verse" and treat it as a supposition or imaginary situation, like the phrases introduced by *law*: "If there were in the sky and the earth another god beside Allah" (21:22), "If the All-Merciful had a son" (43:81). On that basis they argue that abrogation is possible but never actually happened. Maʿārif answers that such writers do not show an intimate knowledge of Arabic grammar, for there is a great deal of difference between a condition suggested by *mā* and the imaginary situation introduced by *law*. And beyond the grammar: it is on the basis of this very ayah that the blessed Companions affirmed the occurrence of abrogation and cited many instances of it, as did their Successors and all the authentic commentators. Even Shah Waliyyullah, in reducing the number of abrogated verses, never thought of denying the fact of abrogation.

## Why this matters to a believer

Imam al-Qurtubi's verdict, as Maʿārif reports it: "It is essential to understand the question of abrogation, and great benefits flow from such an understanding, which no scholar can dispense with, and no one can deny abrogation except the ignorant and the dull-headed."

Al-Qurtubi relates an incident that makes the point unforgettable. Sayyidna 'Ali, the fourth Khalifah, saw a man preaching in the mosque and asked the people what he was doing. Told that he was preaching, 'Ali said he was doing nothing of the sort — he was only announcing to the people that he was such and such a man, son of such and such, and asking them to recognise and remember him. Then he called the man to his side and asked: do you know which injunctions have been abrogated and which have abrogated the earlier ones? When the man confessed that he did not, the Khalifah turned him out of the mosque and ordered him never to preach there.

Two things to carry away. First, **trust rests on the Lawgiver, not on the permanence of a particular ruling.** Everything He reveals to His prophets is good; He alone knows the wisdom in His choices, He knows what is good for men at a particular time, and He makes these changes for their good. Second, **do not speak about Allah's law from an incomplete grasp of it** — 'Ali's rebuke was not to a heretic but to a man who had simply not done the work. And the closing words of ayah 107 tell you where to stand while you learn: no protector besides Allah and no helper besides Him — the One who legislates with your good in view, and who defends those who obey Him.

passages.title: Questioning the Messenger, and how to meet hostility
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat turn from the long argument with the People of the Book toward the young Muslim community itself, and they answer a single practical question: when people around you demand signs, mock, and scheme to pull you out of your faith, what should you actually do? Ayah 108 warns against a certain kind of questioning; ayah 109 exposes the envy behind the hostility and orders forbearance; ayah 110 tells the believer where to put his energy instead.

## The two kinds of questions

Ayah 108 opens by asking whether you want to question your Messenger ﷺ the way Musa (Moses), peace be upon him, was questioned before. Ibn Kathir supplies the reference in a brief gloss on the ayah itself: *"as Musa was asked before (i.e. show us openly our Lord)."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills the scene in — the forefathers of those being addressed "had asked Sayyidna Musa (Moses عليہ السلام) to help them to see Allah openly with their physical eyes" — and it is Maʿārif ul Qurʼān that names what was really going on: in such cases their intention "had never been to seek guidance or to satisfy their doubts or to strengthen their faith, but only to cast aspersions on a prophet, or to question the wisdom of Allah." That was not a request for guidance. It was defiance dressed up as a question.

Ibn Kathir gives the occasion in which this ayah came down. Muhammad bin Ishaq reported from Muhammad bin Abi Muhammad, from 'Ikrimah or Sa'id, from Ibn 'Abbas, that Rafi' bin Huraymilah or Wahb bin Zayd said: "O Muhammad! Bring us a Book sent down from heaven and which we could read, and make some rivers flow for us, then we will follow you and believe in you." Allah sent down this ayah in answer. Note the shape of the demand: it is framed as an offer of belief, but the price keeps moving. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records another such demand — that the whole Qur'an be brought down at once, as the Torah had been — and says that hostility to the Prophet ﷺ had become so habitual to them that they were "always making insolent demands."

Because the motive was mockery rather than inquiry, the ayah treats this behaviour not as mere rudeness but as kufr — disbelief. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says plainly that the verse "indicts this behavior as Kufr (infidelity)." Ibn Kathir describes the same posture: Allah criticized those who question the Messenger ﷺ "just for the purpose of being difficult, just as the Children of Israel asked Musa out of stubbornness, rejection and rebellion."

So the ayah is not closing the door on learning. What it closes is the question asked in order to corner, to test, to embarrass — and behind that, the assumption that Allah owes His creation an explanation before He is obeyed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws this out: "there is a raison d'être for everything Allah does, but divine wisdom alone knows what that is, and the creature has no right to determine the precise mode of his Creator's acts" — he should not even ask the why and wherefore of a divine action, but accept it and submit himself to the Divine Will.

## The believers' share of the warning

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that if the address in ayah 108 is taken as directed at the Muslims, it means they are being warned against making improper demands on the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir reads it in exactly this direction, and here the passage becomes searching for anyone who takes their faith seriously. He explains that Allah forbade the believers from asking the Prophet ﷺ numerous questions about matters that had not yet occurred — the hypothetical, the not-yet-real — and links it to Allah's words in 5:101: *"O you who believe! Ask not about things which, if made plain to you, may cause you trouble. But if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be made plain to you."*

His comment on that verse is the key: if you ask about a matter after it is revealed, it will be duly explained to you; so do not ask about things that have not yet occurred, "for they might become prohibited, due to your questions." Revelation was live. A question could pull down a ruling that would then bind the whole community.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites the following here:

- Narrated in the Sahih: *"The greatest criminal among the Muslims is the one who asks if a thing is prohibited, which is not prohibited, and it becomes prohibited because of his asking about it."*
- The Two Sahihs recorded from Al-Mughirah bin Shu'bah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade saying "It was said" and "He said," and wasting money, and asking many questions.
- Muslim recorded that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"Leave me as I leave you; those before you were only destroyed because of their excessive questioning and disputing with their Prophets. Therefore, when I command you with a matter, adhere to it as much as you can, and when I forbid from something, avoid it."*

Ibn Kathir supplies the setting of that last hadith, and it is the clearest illustration in the whole passage. The Prophet ﷺ had told the Companions that Allah had ordered them to perform Hajj. A man asked, "Every year, O Messenger of Allah?" The Prophet ﷺ did not answer him. The man repeated the question three times. Then he ﷺ said: *"No. Had I said yes, it would have been ordained, and you would not have been able to implement it."* One question, pressed three times, came close to fixing upon the community an obligation that — by the Prophet's own words ﷺ — they would not have been able to carry.

Ibn Kathir also mentions that when the Prophet ﷺ was asked about a husband who finds another man with his wife — where exposing it means exposing a major incident, and staying quiet about it means being quiet about a major matter — he ﷺ did not like such questions; later Allah revealed the ruling of *mulāʿanah*, the ruling that governs precisely that case (see 24:6–9). And he quotes Anas bin Malik: "We were forbidden from asking the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about things. So we were delighted when a bedouin man would come and ask him while we listened."

**"Whoever changes faith for disbelief."** Ibn Kathir glosses this as: whoever prefers disbelief to faith. And *"he has gone astray from the right way"* means, in his words, "he has strayed from the straight path, to the path of ignorance and misguidance." This, he says, is the case of those who deviated from accepting the Prophets and obeying them, and of those who kept asking their Prophets unnecessary questions in defiance and disbelief. He connects it to 14:28–29, about those "who have changed the blessings of Allah into disbelief... and caused their people to dwell in the house of destruction." Abu Al-'Aliyah summed the exchange up in four words: "They exchanged comfort for hardship." That is the bargain — trading something priceless for something worthless, and thinking you have gained.

## Ayah 109: naming the real motive

Now the passage turns to what lies underneath the hostility. Many of the People of the Book, the ayah says, *wish* they could turn you back into disbelievers after you have believed — and the reason given is *ḥasad*, envy, "from their own selves."

Ibn Kathir opens the ayah by describing the situation it addresses: Allah warned His believing servants against following the ways of the People of the Book, who publicly and secretly harbour enmity and hatred for the believers, and who envy them "while they recognize the virtue of the believers and their Prophet ﷺ."

He then reports an occasion for this ayah: Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from 'Abdullah bin Ka'b bin Malik that Ka'b bin Al-Ashraf, who was a Jew and a poet, used to criticize the Prophet ﷺ in his poems, and Allah revealed this ayah concerning his affair.

The diagnosis is devastating. Ad-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas: an unlettered Messenger came to the People of the Scriptures confirming what they already had in their own Books about the Messengers and the signs of Allah, and believing in all of it just as they believed in it — "yet, they rejected the Prophet out of disbelief, envy and transgression." Ibn Kathir adds that Allah had made the truth plain to them, "such that they were not ignorant of any of it, yet their envy made them deny the Prophet ﷺ."

Two early comments open up the phrasing:

- **"From their own selves"** — Ar-Rabi' bin Anas said this means "of their making." The envy is not something the believers provoked; it is generated inside the envier. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point: the hostility "arises not from anything the Muslims do, but spontaneously from within themselves."
- **"After the truth has become manifest to them"** — Abu Al-'Aliyah said this means: after it became clear that Muhammad ﷺ is the Messenger of Allah, "whom they find written of in the Torah and the Injil. They denied him in disbelief and transgression because he was not one of them." Qatadah and Ar-Rabi' bin Anas said the same. The obstacle was never the evidence. It was that the gift had gone to someone else.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the texture of daily life in Madinah: some of the Jews, "pretending to be the well-wishers of the Muslims, were always inventing new stratagems to make them turn away from Islam," and repeated failure did not stop them. So the ayah is also a warning about counsel that arrives wearing the face of friendship.

**"But forgive and overlook."** The response commanded is neither retaliation nor argument. The Arabic pairs two verbs — *ʿafw* and *ṣafḥ*, rendered "forgive and overlook" — and Ibn Kathir notes the parallel in 3:186: *"And you shall certainly hear much that will grieve you from those who received the Scripture before you and from those who ascribe partners to Allah."* Injury was expected; patience was the answer. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to call the Muslims' anger justifiable — the ayah does not pretend no wrong was done — but they were told not to give way to it.

Ibn Kathir records, from Ibn Abi Hatim, Usamah bin Zayd saying that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions used to forgive the disbelievers and the People of the Book just as Allah commanded here, and that he ﷺ was patient with them as Allah ordered him, until Allah allowed fighting them. Ibn Kathir comments on this report with a scholar's honesty: the chain of narration is Sahih, but he did not see its wordings in the six collections of Hadith, although the basis of it is in the Two Sahihs, narrated from Usamah bin Zayd.

**"Till Allah brings His command."** This is the hinge of the ayah, and the classical commentators read it as a deliberate signal that the situation was temporary. Ibn Kathir reports, through Ali bin Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, that this instruction to forgive and overlook was abrogated by the verses of fighting in Surah At-Tawbah (9:5 and 9:29), and that Abu Al-'Aliyah, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas, Qatadah and As-Suddi said the same — what the commentators call "the Ayah of the sword." Ibn Kathir notes that the wording *"till Allah brings His command"* itself gives further support to that reading, since it points forward to a command still to come.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the same development without the language of abrogation: the command to show forbearance "was proper to the situations of the Muslims at that time," and the ayah indicates that Allah was soon going to lay down a law for the preservation of peace and order on the earth — which came later as the injunction regarding jihad, applied to the mischief-makers so that disorder would be prevented and peace and order would prevail; those who persisted were killed, forced into exile, or made to pay jizyah (which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains as "a special levy on non-Muslims who live under the protection of the Islamic state and which absolves them from military service"). Both readings agree on what the reader most needs to see: the forbearance commanded here was a real command for a real moment, and a further command was expressly promised.

**"Verily, Allah is able to do all things."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this closing phrase as consolation aimed straight at the Muslims' anxiety. They were conscious of their own weakness and of the strength of their foe, and could have wondered how they would ever be able to act upon the new law. So they are reminded that Allah's power "extends over everything, small or big, ordinary or extraordinary."

## Ayah 110: what to do while you wait

Told to restrain themselves, the believers might have felt idle. Ayah 110 answers immediately: *establish the prayer, give the zakah, and whatever good you send forward for yourselves you will find it with Allah.*

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah encouraged the believers to busy themselves in performing deeds that would bring them benefit and reward on the Day of Resurrection — such as prayer and paying zakah — and that in this way they will gain Allah's aid in this life and on a Day when the witnesses testify, "the Day when their excuses will be of no profit to the Zalimin (wrongdoers)" (40:52).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a reassurance the community needed: the Muslims should not suppose that, until they could take part in jihad, mere prayers and worship would not bring them the spiritual merit they desired. They shall "receive a full reward in the other world for each and every good deed they perform... and not a particle of one's good deeds shall be lost." When the new law came down, participation in it would simply be added to the good deeds they had already been performing.

**"You will find it with Allah."** The image is of sending something on ahead. The deed does not vanish when it leaves your hand; it is deposited, kept, and waiting for you at the destination. And the ayah closes: *"Certainly, Allah is the Seer of what you do."* Ibn Kathir explains this as meaning that He is never unaware of the deeds of any person, nor will these deeds be lost by Him; whether the deeds are righteous or evil, Allah will award each according to what he or she deserves based on their deeds. Nothing slips past Him, and nothing is mislaid.

## Living it

Read together, the three ayat form one instruction. **Ayah 108:** guard your tongue with the sacred — do not use questions as weapons, and do not make your submission conditional on Allah first justifying Himself to you. **Ayah 109:** when hostility comes, understand it. Much of it is envy that arises from within the other person rather than from anything you did — and seeing that is what makes forgiving and overlooking possible rather than merely difficult. **Ayah 110:** having restrained yourself, do not then sit still. Turn that energy into prayer, into giving, into any good you can send on ahead — because the One who sees the injury also sees the deed, and not a particle of it is lost.

passages.title: Rival claims to Paradise refuted
passages.tafsir:
Two communities each insisted that Paradise was reserved for them alone — and in the same breath told each other that the other had nothing at all. In these three ayat Allah asks the claimants for evidence, replaces group identity with a clear and universal criterion for who is actually saved, and then shows how empty the claim is by letting the two sides refute each other in front of us.

What holds the passage together is a single movement: **a claim (111), the true standard that replaces it (112), and the exposure of that claim's hollowness in the claimants' own mouths (113).**

## The claim, and the words that dismantle it

Ayah 111 quotes them: "None shall enter Paradise unless he be a Jew or a Christian." Ibn Kathir notes that Allah is here making their confusion plain, and that this is of a piece with other claims the Qur'an records from them — as in Surat al-Ma'idah, "We are the children of Allah and His loved ones" (5:18) — a claim Allah refuted by informing them that they will in fact be punished for their sins. It also follows on from the claim mentioned earlier in this surah, that the Fire would not touch them for more than a few days before they were placed in Paradise. Allah rebuked that too.

Then comes the verdict on all of it, in two words: **tilka amāniyyuhum** — "these are their own desires." Ibn Kathir introduces the phrase as Allah's word about a baseless claim, and Abu al-'Aliyah explained it exactly so: "These are wishes that they wished Allah would answer, without basis." Qatadah and ar-Rabi' bin Anas said the same. Notice what that does. The Qur'an is not calling their claim a weak argument; it is calling it a wish. Wishing does not become true by being wished, however confidently.

**"Produce your burhān, if you are truthful."** Abu al-'Aliyah, Mujahid, as-Suddi and ar-Rabi' bin Anas all glossed *burhān* as "your proof." Qatadah put it as: bring the evidence that supports your statement. Notice how the Prophet ﷺ is instructed to respond — not with a counter-claim of the same kind, but with a demand for evidence. A community that cannot produce a burhān for its claim about the next world has said nothing, however loudly it says it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens the diagnosis: both groups had forgotten what religion actually is — adherence to true and authentic doctrines, and the performance of good deeds as laid down by the Shari'ah — and had quietly identified it with **a mere affiliation to a racial or social community**. Each claimed the exclusive right to Paradise without any argument to substantiate it. That substitution — belonging in place of obeying — is the disease this passage treats.

## The standard that actually decides

Ayah 112 answers with a single word — **"Yes!"** — and then, instead of naming a community, names a criterion, in the most open language imaginable:

**"Whoever submits his face to Allah, and he is a muhsin — his reward is with his Lord."**

Two expressions carry the whole verse.

**Aslama wajhahu.** Literally, "surrendered his face," which the translators render as submitting *himself* to Allah. Ibn Kathir explains the phrase as "whoever performs deeds in sincerity, for Allah alone without partners," and cites the parallel: "So if they dispute with you say: I have submitted myself to Allah, and so have those who follow me" (3:20). Abu al-'Aliyah and ar-Rabi' said *aslama wajhahu lillah* means "whoever is sincere with Allah." Sa'id bin Jubayr broke it into its two halves: *aslama* — he is sincere; *wajhahu* — in his religion.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out two principles that together make up the essence of religion, and attaches a word of the ayah to each. The first principle is that **one should obey Allah in one's belief as well as in one's actions** — and it is to this principle, it says, that the Qur'an's word *aslama* belongs, a word which signifies total submission to Allah.

**Wa huwa muhsin.** Ibn Kathir glosses this second condition with striking economy: *and he is a muhsin* means **following the Messenger ﷺ**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attaches to this second word its second principle: **this obedience should not arise from expediency; one should surrender oneself to the divine commandments in all sincerity** — and *muhsin*, it explains, signifies "one who performs good deeds" according to the Shari'ah.

So the ayah names two conditions, and Ibn Kathir states the resulting rule plainly:

> There are two conditions for deeds to be accepted: the deed must be performed for Allah's sake alone, and conform to the Shari'ah.

## The two ways a deed dies

Ibn Kathir then works through both failure modes, and this is the heart of the passage's practical teaching.

**Sincere but unauthorised.** A deed offered genuinely for Allah, but in a form He never legislated, is not accepted. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Whoever performs a deed that does not conform with our matter — it will be rejected."* Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith was recorded by Muslim. On this basis he says the good deeds of the priests and rabbis will not be accepted even if performed sincerely for Allah alone, because they do not conform with the method of the Messenger ﷺ, who was sent for all mankind. He gathers the Qur'an's own images for such wasted effort: deeds turned into "scattered floating particles of dust" (25:23); deeds "like a mirage in a desert — the thirsty one thinks it to be water, until he comes up to it and finds it to be nothing" (24:39); and faces on that Day "labouring, weary," yet entering a hot blazing Fire (88:2–5). Effort is not the issue. Direction is.

**Correct but insincere.** The reverse also fails: a deed that conforms outwardly to the Shari'ah but was not done sincerely for Allah alone is likewise rejected — the case of the hypocrites and of those who do their deeds to show off. Ibn Kathir cites "the hypocrites... when they stand up for the prayer, they stand with laziness, to be seen by people" (4:142), and "woe unto those performers of prayer... those who do good deeds only to be seen" (107:4–7). Hence the summarising ayah he quotes: "Whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him work righteousness and associate none as a partner in the worship of his Lord" (18:110).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point from the other side: it is not enough to have a sincere intention to obey Allah and then invent, according to one's own fancy, the modes and forms of that obedience. It is absolutely essential that the forms of worship be no other than those which Allah Himself has appointed through the agency of His prophets — which, since the revelation of the Qur'an, can only mean accepting and following the Islamic Shari'ah.

## How wide the door is — and where the argument lands

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the breadth of ayah 112. The Qur'an dismisses the two rival claims as mere fancy and self-delusion, and declares that other people too will go to Paradise: those who in their own time followed the Shari'ah of their own prophet, and — now that the Qur'an has abrogated all the earlier Divine Books — those who follow the Islamic Shari'ah. Ayah 112 lays down a general principle in this respect, one accepted by the followers of all the Divine Books.

The argument then closes back on the claimants of ayah 111. Having laid down the two principles whose acceptance makes one worthy of Paradise, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, the Qur'an suggests that they should now try to find out **who is really acting upon them**. Someone who keeps following an injunction after it has been abrogated cannot be described as obedient; after an abrogation, obedience consists in acting upon the new injunction which replaced the earlier one. On that reasoning the condition is fulfilled by those who have accepted the last Prophet ﷺ and his Shari'ah. And the condition of sincerity in obedience, it adds, excludes the hypocrites as well.

## "No fear, nor shall they grieve"

The reward has three parts. **"Their reward is with their Lord"** — Ibn Kathir says this guaranteed them the rewards and safety from what they fear and should avoid. Then the two negations, which he reads as covering the whole span of a person's anxiety: **no fear** in the future, and **no grief** about what they abandoned in the past. Sa'id bin Jubayr read it slightly differently: no fear in the Hereafter, and no grief about their imminent death. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that on the Day of Judgment the angels will give them good tidings.

Between the two readings, the phrase covers everything a soul can dread: the future it cannot see, the past it cannot undo, and the death standing in between.

## Ayah 113: what actually happened

Ibn Kathir preserves the occasion behind this ayah. Muhammad bin Ishaq reported that Ibn 'Abbas said: when a delegation of Christians from Najran came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the Jewish rabbis came and began arguing with them before him. Rafi' bin Huraymilah said, "You do not follow anything," reiterating his disbelief in Jesus and the Injil. Then a Christian man from the Najran delegation said to the Jews, "Rather, *you* do not follow anything," reiterating his rejection of Musa's prophethood and his disbelief in the Torah. So Allah revealed this ayah.

Picture the scene: two scriptural communities standing before the Prophet ﷺ, each one so intent on defeating the other that it denies exactly what the other had claimed for itself in ayah 111. Ibn Kathir sums up what Allah is exposing here — the disputes, hatred and stubbornness that the People of the Book had towards each other. Allah does not need to argue with them in this ayah. He quotes them.

**"Though they both recite the Scripture."** This is the sting in the ayah. Ibn Kathir explains that each party read, in its own Book, the affirmation of what it claimed to reject: the Jews disbelieve in Jesus although they have the Torah, in which Allah took their covenant by the tongue of Musa to believe in him; and the Gospel contains Jesus' assertion that Musa's prophethood and the Torah came from Allah. Yet each party disbelieved in what the other party had. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point — the Jews read the Torah and the Christians read the Evangel, and they could easily have seen that the two Books confirm each other. Each side was rejecting what its own Book affirmed.

**"Like unto their word said those who know not."** Ibn Kathir records a real difference among the early authorities over who these are:

- **Ar-Rabi' bin Anas and Qatadah**: the Christians, who said similar statements to the Jews.
- **'Ata'** — when Ibn Jurayj asked him — nations that existed before the Jews and the Christians, and before the Torah and the Gospel.
- **As-Suddi**: the Arabs, who said that Muhammad ﷺ was not following anything.

Ibn Kathir then reports that Abu Ja'far bin Jarir chose the view that this ayah is **general**, since there is no evidence that specifically supports any one of these explanations — and that interpreting it in a general way is better, closing with "Allah knows best." That is worth pausing on: where the sources genuinely differ and nothing settles the matter, the sound instinct is to leave the wording as wide as Allah left it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a bitter consequence of the quarrel: each party used to assert, in its malice, that the religion of the other was baseless — and this gave an excuse to the mushrikin (those who associate partners with Allah), who, in spite of their ignorance, began to say the same of both religions. When people of scripture tear each other down, those watching conclude that scripture itself is worthless.

## "Allah will judge between them"

The passage ends by lifting the dispute out of human hands entirely. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah will gather them all on the Day of Return and judge justly between them, for He is never unjust with anyone, even as little as the weight of an atom. He connects it to Surat al-Hajj — "those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Majus, and those who associate partners with Allah: truly Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection; verily Allah is over all things a Witness" (22:17) — and to "Our Lord will assemble us all together, then He will judge between us with truth, and He is the Just Judge, the Knower of the true state of affairs" (34:26).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a fine distinction here. The question is not actually still open: it has already been settled on the basis of what Allah has revealed in His Books and on the basis of rational argument. What the Day of Judgment adds is the decision **of the visible kind** — those who follow the Truth sent to Paradise, those who go after falsehood cast down. The judgment is not a discovery; it is a disclosure.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ends where the passage most needs to land — and it is not on other communities:

> These verses provide a warning to the Muslims as well, lest they too should delude themselves like the Jews and the Christians, and suppose that merely because they belong to the social community of Muslims... they can dispense with the need to obey Allah and to follow the Shari'ah, and yet receive the rewards Allah has promised.

The claim of ayah 111 is not a historical curiosity; it is a permanently available temptation. Anyone can slide from *I submit to Allah* into *I belong to the group that submits to Allah* — and the second costs nothing. Ayah 112 is worded so as to make that slide impossible: it never names a community. It names a person, described by what he does — *whoever surrenders his face*, *and he is a muhsin*.

So the passage leaves a believer with three concrete questions. **Is this deed truly for Allah alone, or is there an audience in it?** **Is it done the way He legislated through His Messenger ﷺ, or the way I preferred?** And **am I resting on belonging, or on obeying?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers the last directly: even Muslims have no right to hope for these rewards until and unless they submit themselves totally, in thought and deed both, to the commandments of Allah and His Prophet ﷺ.

The consolation is that the promise is as personal as the demand. Whoever does this has his reward *with his Lord* — not with a community, not contingent on anyone's approval — and upon such there shall be no fear, nor shall they grieve.

passages.title: Barring Allah's houses; east and west are His
passages.tafsir:
**Two ayat, one movement of thought.** Ayah 114 asks a question with no possible answer: who could be more unjust than someone who bars Allah's houses against Allah's own name being remembered in them, and works to leave them in ruins? Ayah 115 then speaks to the people on the wrong side of that locked door — the ones shut out of the sanctuary they loved — and tells them that the east and the west both belong to Allah, so wherever they turn, there is the Face of Allah. The first ayah names the crime; the second quietly announces that the crime cannot reach its target. You can lock a man out of a building. You cannot lock him out of his Lord.

## Who was doing the barring

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets these ayat against three incidents involving the three groups then hostile to Islam, each of which was, in one way or another, guilty of keeping people from worshipping Allah in a mosque and thus of "laying it waste":

- **The Jews of Madinah**, when Allah turned the Muslims from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Kaʿbah in prayer, raised every kind of objection and tried to seed doubts that — had they taken root — would have led to rejecting the Prophet ﷺ and abandoning the prescribed Salah altogether, and so to emptying the Prophet's ﷺ own mosque.
- **The Romans** had once invaded Jerusalem and the ignorant among them polluted Bayt al-Maqdis, which prevented people from praying there. The Christians looked on the Romans as their forebears, and the humiliation of the Jews pleased them; in refusing to condemn the deed, they shared indirectly in the ruin of that mosque.
- **The idolaters of Makkah**, at Hudaybiyyah, would not let the Prophet ﷺ enter Makkah or perform Hajj.

Maʿārif notes that ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas held that ayah 114 refers to the second of these — the desecration of Bayt al-Maqdis — and that Ibn Jarir accepted this view, while Ibn Kathir follows Ibn Zayd in preferring the third, Hudaybiyyah, as the occasion of revelation. Ibn Kathir also records, through Ibn Abi Hatim, a report from Ibn ʿAbbas that the Quraysh prevented the Prophet ﷺ from praying at the Kaʿbah in Al-Masjid Al-Haram, and that Allah then revealed this ayah. The scholars differed; the Qur'an itself, as Maʿārif observes, deliberately speaks in the general plural — *the mosques of Allah* — laying down a permanent law for all peoples covering every form of desecration and every way of hindering the remembrance of Allah.

**The scene at Hudaybiyyah.** Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Zayd that this ayah concerns the Quraysh idolaters who stopped the Prophet ﷺ from entering Makkah, so that he slaughtered the sacrificial animal at Dhi-Tuwa. He then made peace with them and said to them that no one before had ever barred people from the House — a man would see the killer of his father and brother there and still not turn him away. Their answer was flat: whoever killed our fathers at Badr shall never enter it while one of us is alive. Read against that exchange, the question of ayah 114 lands like a verdict.

## "And strive for their ruin"

Ibn Kathir explains *saʿā fī kharābihā* — striving for their ruin — as preventing those who would fill the mosques with Allah's remembrance, and those who come to the House for Hajj and ʿUmrah. And then the line that reframes the whole subject: **maintaining the mosques is not a matter of beautifying them.** It means remembering Allah in them, establishing His Sharīʿah there, and purifying them of the filth of shirk. If, he argues, the very believers described in Sūrah al-Tawbah — "The Masjids of Allah shall be maintained only by those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, perform the Salah, give the Zakah, and fear none but Allah" (9:18) — are the ones being kept out, then what worse ruin could there be?

Maʿārif draws the same distinction and presses it further. A mosque is *flourishing* not through its architecture or ornament but only when it is full of men who come to pray and to remember Allah. Maʿārif relates that the Prophet ﷺ foretold that as the Day of Judgment draws near the mosques of the Muslims would be beautifully designed and decorated and apparently full, yet in reality deserted, because few would come to them to pray. And it recalls the counsel of the fourth Khalīfah, ʿAlī: of six deeds that befit a man, three belong to settled life — to read the Qur'an, to populate the mosques, and to gather friends who wish to serve Allah and His faith; and three to travel — to spend on needy companions of the road, to be polite to everyone, and to be cheerful with fellow travellers within the limits of the Sharīʿah. "Populating" a mosque, he explains, means entering it in humility with the fear of Allah in the heart, and then praying, reciting, or making dhikr.

## What ayah 114 asks of us

Maʿārif derives several practical rulings from this ayah:

**Every mosque is sacred.** To desecrate any mosque in any way is as forbidden as desecrating Bayt al-Maqdis, Al-Masjid al-Haram, or the mosque of the Prophet ﷺ. Those three do hold a higher rank and deserve special reverence — Maʿārif notes that one prayer in Al-Masjid al-Haram equals a hundred thousand elsewhere, and one in the Prophet's ﷺ mosque or in Bayt al-Maqdis equals fifty thousand — and to travel far to pray in these three is meritorious and makes one worthy of a special *barakah*, that is, a special blessing; while the Prophet ﷺ forbade undertaking a long journey to pray in any other mosque believing that to be meritorious. But rank is not the same as sanctity: the small mosque down the road is Allah's house exactly as those are.

**Obstruction takes subtle forms.** The obvious form is barring someone from entering, praying, or reciting the Qur'an. A less obvious form is producing noise inside the mosque or playing music nearby so that people are disturbed in their prayer or dhikr. Even reciting the Qur'an or making dhikr *loudly* in a way that disturbs those praying nawāfil (supererogatory, voluntary prayers), reading quietly, or making silent dhikr (remembrance of Allah) falls under the same sin — which is why the fuqahā' (the masters of Islamic jurisprudence) have forbidden it. If no one else is present, one may recite or make dhikr aloud. On the same principle, begging or collecting donations — even for a religious cause — while people are praying or in dhikr is forbidden.

**Ruining a mosque includes emptying it.** Not only demolition, but creating any condition that leaves a mosque deserted, or that makes it hard for those present to reach a state of humility. And as Maʿārif points out, if the ayah came down at Hudaybiyyah, then "laying waste" plainly includes a mosque that still stands but is not allowed to be used for what it was built for: Salah and the remembrance of Allah.

## "Except in fear" — a promise hidden inside a rebuke

The second half of ayah 114 says it was not fitting that such people should enter Allah's mosques except in fear. Ibn Kathir gives two readings. As a ruling: do not let the disbelievers enter the mosques except under the terms of a truce or treaty — and indeed, when the Prophet ﷺ conquered Makkah, he had it announced at Mina that after that year no idolater would perform Hajj and no one would circle the House naked, except those with a treaty, which would run to its term. This accords with "Verily, the Mushrikūn are impure, so let them not come near Al-Masjid Al-Haram after this year" (9:28).

It was also said, Ibn Kathir reports, that the ayah carries **good news**: that Allah would give the Muslims charge of Al-Masjid Al-Haram and of all the mosques, and humble the idolaters — so that soon no idolater would enter the House except in fear of being seized or killed, unless he accepted Islam. Allah fulfilled that promise. Maʿārif makes the same observation: the prediction came true, the groups who tried to lay waste the mosques were soon humiliated and came under Muslim rule.

Notice how exact the requital is. Ibn Kathir points out that the punishment came in a form matching the deed: **just as they prevented the believers from entering Al-Masjid Al-Haram, they were prevented from entering it; just as they expelled the believers from Makkah, they were themselves expelled.** The disgrace in this world is that reversal. The great torment in the Hereafter, he says, is for having violated the sanctity of the House — setting idols around it, calling on other than Allah, circling it naked.

**From the Sunnah.** Because ayah 114 pairs disgrace in this world with torment in the next, Ibn Kathir cites here the supplication recorded by Imam Ahmad from Busr bin Artah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say: *"O Allah! Make our end better in all affairs, and save us from disgrace in this life and the torment of the Hereafter."* Ibn Kathir grades this hadith Hasan.

## Ayah 115: the doors they cannot lock

Ibn Kathir says plainly that this ruling **brought comfort to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions**, who had been driven out of Makkah and cut off from Al-Masjid Al-Haram. In Makkah the Prophet ﷺ used to pray facing Bayt Al-Maqdis with the Kaʿbah between him and that direction; after the Hijrah he faced Bayt Al-Maqdis for sixteen or seventeen months, and then Allah directed him to the Kaʿbah.

ʿAli bin Abi Talha reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that the first part of the Qur'an to be abrogated concerned the qiblah. On arriving in Madinah, which the Jews inhabited, the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to face Bayt Al-Maqdis, which pleased them, and he did so for some ten months. But he loved the qiblah of Ibrahim, and would look up to the sky and supplicate — until Allah revealed, "Verily, We have seen the turning of your face towards the heaven… turn your faces in that direction" (2:144). The Jews were disturbed and asked what had made them change the qiblah they used to face. It was then, in this report, that Allah revealed that the east and the west belong to Him, and that wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah.

So the ayah works on two fronts at once, as Maʿārif puts it: **an answer to the objection, and a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions.** Its argument is this: had Allah been confined to one direction, a single fixed orientation would have been necessary in order to worship Him at all. But He is beyond every limitation — Lord of the east, the west, and every conceivable direction. Wherever a man turns, he finds Allah "facing" him: that is, ready to accept his prayer and pour out His bounties on him. It follows that neither Bayt al-Maqdis nor the Kaʿbah has any inherent, inalienable superiority; either acquires its privileged position **only by divine ordination**. What matters is obeying Allah's command — and if He, being free of all limits, has nonetheless fixed a direction, that is because He is Omniscient and knows what is best for a given people in a given situation.

Maʿārif adds a reason we can perceive: if a worshipper had to choose a direction afresh each time he prayed, it would only scatter his attention, and if a congregation each faced a different way the effect would be absurd. A single fixed orientation gives the individual concentration and gives the group a shared sense of purpose. This, Maʿārif says, answers the charge sometimes levelled that Muslims worship the Kaʿbah — turning towards it is not worship of it.

## How the scholars read "wherever you turn"

The commentators offer several complementary readings, and Ibn Kathir reports them all:

- **Ikrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas:** it means Allah's direction is wherever you face, east or west.
- **Mujahid:** it means wherever you may be, you have a qiblah to face — the Kaʿbah.
- **Ibn Jarir** reports the view of others that the ayah came down before the command to face the Kaʿbah, permitting one praying voluntary prayers to face east or west as he wishes while travelling, when in fear, and when facing the enemy. Ibn ʿUmar used to pray facing whichever way his mount was headed, saying the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did the same, and citing this ayah. Ibn Kathir notes this hadith was collected by Muslim, At-Tirmidhi, An-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Marduwyah, and that its origin is in the Two Sahihs from Ibn ʿUmar and ʿAmr bin Rabiʿah without mention of the ayah. Al-Bukhari recorded in his Sahih from Nafiʿ that when Ibn ʿUmar was asked about prayer in times of fear he would describe it and then say: when the fear is worse than that, pray standing or riding, whether facing the qiblah or not — and Nafiʿ thought Ibn ʿUmar traced this to the Prophet ﷺ.
- It was also said the ayah concerns **those who cannot determine the qiblah** in darkness or under cloud and so pray, by mistake, in another direction.

**Where this lands in practice.** Maʿārif spells out the fiqh: for supererogatory prayers (nawāfil) offered while travelling on a horse or camel — where turning to the qiblah is genuinely difficult — one may face the direction of travel and pray by gestures of the head and arms. Some commentators hold that ayah 115 lays down precisely this rule. But the concession applies to that kind of travel; in a train, ship, or aeroplane, where facing the qiblah is not difficult, one must still orient properly even for nawāfil. If the vehicle changes direction mid-prayer and there is no room to readjust, one may finish as one is. Likewise, if one does not know the qiblah and cannot determine it because of darkness or another valid reason, and no one can inform him, he acts on his best judgement and the direction he chooses **is** his qiblah — and if he later discovers he was wrong, his prayer still stands and need not be repeated.

Ibn Kathir also records here, from Al-Hafiz Ibn Marduwyah, that Abu Hurayrah reported the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"What is between the east and the west is the Qiblah for the people of Al-Madinah, Ash-Sham and ʿIraq."* At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah recorded it with the wording: *"What is between the east and the west is a Qiblah."*

## "Allah is Wāsiʿ, ʿAlīm"

The ayah closes on two names. Ibn Jarir explains that Allah being *Wāsiʿ* — all-encompassing, sufficient — means He encompasses all His creation, providing for their needs out of His generosity and favour; and *ʿAlīm* means He knows their deeds, nothing escapes His watch, He is unaware of nothing, and His knowledge encompasses everything. Placed at the end of a passage about people barred from a mosque, the two names say: your provision is not in their hands, and your situation is not outside His sight.

**A word of restraint about "the Face of Allah."** Ibn Kathir, in rendering the ayah, is careful to keep alongside it that Allah is high above, over His Throne. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sounds a deliberate note of caution here: wisdom lies in not trying to investigate unnecessarily into the meaning of such statements. Just as it is not at all possible for a creature to comprehend fully the Being (Dhāt — the divine Essence, Allah as He is in Himself) of Allah, it is equally impossible to comprehend the essential reality of His Attributes (Sifāt — the qualities Allah has told us of Himself). All that man is required to do, Maʿārif says, is to hold a general faith in the realities of the divine order; there is no obligation on him to look into the particulars of a sphere that lies wholly beyond human reach.

## Living it

Read together, the two ayat put a duty and a consolation into the same hand.

**The duty:** guard the houses of Allah — and understand that guarding them means filling them, not decorating them. Every barrier counts, including the small ones we erect casually: noise, a raised voice over someone's silent dhikr, a collection tin passed round while a man is praying, anything that makes it harder for a worshipper to reach humility. The severity of the language in ayah 114 — *who is more unjust?* — is a measure of how seriously the Qur'an takes obstruction of worship.

**The consolation:** ayah 115 brought comfort to men who had been physically shut out of the holiest mosque on earth. Its answer to them was not that the mosque did not matter — it plainly did — but that Allah is not confined to it. The east and the west are His. Turn where you will and He is there, receiving. The Kaʿbah is our direction because Allah appointed it, not because Allah is limited to any one direction; and when circumstance takes even that direction from you — on a moving mount, under a clouded sky, in a moment of fear — the door is still open. Turn as best you can, and He is facing you.

passages.title: "Allah has taken a son" answered
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat answer the single most persistent falsehood ever spoken about Allah — that He has taken a son — and then answer the demand of those who refuse to believe until Allah speaks to them face to face. What holds the passage together is one theme: everything other than Allah is owned, made, and answerable to Him, so nothing other than Him can be His child, and no creature is in a position to set the terms on which it will believe.

## Who was saying it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene: as the Qurʼan reports in some other verses, some of the Jews called the Prophet ʿUzayr (Ezra) ʿalayhi al-salām — "peace be upon him" — the son of Allah; the Christians said this of Sayyidnā ʿĪsā (Jesus) ʿalayhi al-salām, and most of them still do; and the mushrikīn (idolaters) of Makkah considered the angels to be Allah's daughters. Ibn Kathir says the same — this ayah and what follows refute the Christians and those like them among the Jews and the Arab idolaters, who claimed that the angels are Allah's daughters. So ayah 116 is not aimed at one community. It gathers three different versions of the same error and answers them at once.

## "Glory be to Him" — the first answer is not an argument

Before any reasoning, the ayah says **subḥānahu**. Ibn Kathir explains it simply: He is holier and more perfect than such a claim. Tasbīḥ means declaring Allah free of every defect and of everything unbefitting Him. The Qurʼan's opening move is to place the claim outside the realm of what may even be entertained about Allah — the way a slander against someone you love is answered first by recoiling from it, and only then by refuting it.

## "Nay — to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth"

Then comes the argument, and it turns on ownership. Ibn Kathir writes that the truth is not as the disbelievers claimed; rather Allah's is the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and whatever and whoever is in, on and between them. He is the Supreme Authority, the Creator, Provider and Sustainer who decides all the affairs of the creation as He wills. All creatures are Allah's servants and are owned by Him.

And that is the knife-edge of the argument: **how could one of them be His son?** The son of any being is born out of two comparable beings. Allah has no equal or rival sharing His grace and greatness — so how can He have a son when He has no wife? Ibn Kathir supports this with Allah's words, "He is the Originator of the heavens and the earth. How can He have children when He has no wife? He created all things and He is the Knower of everything" (6:101); with the passage of Sūrah Maryam in which the heavens are almost torn, the earth is split asunder and the mountains fall in ruins at the ascription of a son to the Most Gracious, ending with "there is none in the heavens and the earth but comes unto the Most Gracious as a servant" (19:88–95); and with Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ: "He begets not, nor was He begotten, and there is none comparable to Him" (112).

Notice how the categories are sealed off. Everything in existence falls under "to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth." Whatever falls under that heading is owned. What is owned is a servant. A servant is not a son.

## The reasoning of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the same point through pure reason, and it is worth following slowly. If Allah could have offspring, that offspring would belong either to the same genus (kind) as the father does, or to a different genus. If it belongs to a different genus, that obviously is a defect — and Allah, in order to be Allah, must be free of all defects, as reason itself requires and as ayah 116 affirms with *subḥānahu*. If the offspring belongs to the same genus, that too is a contradiction in terms, for Allah has no equal and no existent can belong to the same genus as He does.

The reason given is this: Allah alone is the Necessary Being (*al-Dhāt al-Wājib*), and hence necessarily carries within Himself the Attributes of Perfection which are peculiar to Him alone and which cannot exist in anyone other than Allah. If we deny a necessary attribute to a certain being, we automatically deny the existence of that being. So no one other than Allah can be a necessary being; and insofar as "necessity" is itself the essence of the Ultimate Reality, anyone other than Allah cannot share that Reality with Him. To claim that anyone other than Allah can belong to the same genus is a plain and simple contradiction in terms.

Maʿārif then shows how the two ayat demonstrate that the Attributes of Perfection are peculiar to Allah alone, in four steps: **first**, all that exists in heaven or earth belongs to Allah; **second**, everything is also subservient to Him — in the sense that no one can interfere with His omnipotence, for example His power to create and to destroy, even if some men may be lax in obeying the injunctions of the Sharīʿah; **third**, He is the Creator and the Inventor of the skies and of the earth; **fourth**, His power of creation is so mighty that He needs no instruments and no helpers — all He does is say "Be," and the thing becomes what He wishes it to be. These four qualities are not to be found in anyone other than Allah. And, Maʿārif notes pointedly, even those who attributed offspring to Him believed in this truth. Their own creed refutes their claim.

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir cites, in the tafsir of this ayah, that **Al-Bukhari** recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah said, 'The son of Adam has denied Me, and that is not his right. He has insulted Me, and that is not his right. As for the denial of Me, he claimed that I am unable to bring him back as he used to be. As for his insulting Me, he claimed that I have a son. All praise is due to Me, it is unbefitting that I should have a wife or a son.'"

Sit with what the claim is called: an **insult**. Not merely a theological mistake, but an affront directed at Allah Himself.

And then, recorded in the **Two Ṣaḥīḥs**, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No one is more patient when hearing an insult than Allah. They attribute a son to Him, yet He still gives them sustenance and health."

This is one of the most staggering sentences in the Sunnah. The same breath that utters the insult is a breath Allah is giving. The health and the provision of the one saying it — all from Him, uninterrupted. It should make a believer slower to demand instant retribution for anything, and quicker to recognise how much of Allah's forbearance he is himself living on.

## "And all are *qānitūn* to Him"

The word **qānitūn** comes from *qunūt*, and Ibn Kathir gathers the sayings of the early authorities on it:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās** (on *qānitīn* in 2:238): they pray to Him.
- **ʿIkrimah** and **Abū Mālik**: bound to Him in servitude to Him.
- **Saʿīd bin Jubayr**: *qānitūn* is sincerity.
- **Ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas**: standing up before Him on the Day of Resurrection.
- **As-Suddī**: obedient on the Day of Resurrection.
- **Mujāhid**: obedient — He says "Be a human," and he becomes a human; "Be a donkey," and it becomes a donkey. And: the obedience of the disbeliever occurs when his shadow prostrates, while he hates that.

Ibn Kathir says Mujāhid's statement — which Ibn Jarīr preferred — combines all the meanings: *qunūt* is obedience and submission to Allah. And he draws out a crucial distinction: there are **two categories of qunūt, the legislated and the destined**. The legislated is the obedience Allah has commanded and which a person chooses to give. The destined is the submission no creature can escape — hence Allah's words, "And unto Allah alone falls in prostration whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly, and so do their shadows in the mornings and the late afternoons" (13:15).

This is why the ayah answers the claim of sonship so completely. Even the one who denies Allah is, at the level of his own existence, submitting to Him. His shadow bows while he refuses to. A universe in which nothing can fail to submit is a universe with no room in it for a partner or a child.

## Ayah 117: *Badīʿ* — the Originator

**Badīʿ as-samāwāti wal-arḍ.** Ibn Kathir explains it as: He created them when nothing resembling them existed — no pattern to copy, no precedent to follow. Mujāhid and As-Suddī said that this is the linguistic meaning, for all new matters are called a *bidʿah*. (Ibn Kathir pauses here on the word: **Muslim** recorded the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saying that every innovation in religion is a *bidʿah* — and Ibn Kathir distinguishes that religious sense from the linguistic sense, in which ʿUmar bin al-Khaṭṭāb, on gathering the Muslims to pray Tarāwīḥ in congregation — which was also an earlier practice of the Prophet ﷺ — said, "What a good *bidʿah* this is.")

Then Ibn Kathir quotes **Ibn Jarīr**'s summary of both ayat, and calls it "very good and correct": Allah is far more glorious than to have had a son, for He is the Owner of everything in the heavens and the earth; all testify to His Oneness and to their submissiveness to Him; He is their Creator and Maker, who shaped the creatures in their current shapes without created precedence. And Allah bears witness that ʿĪsā ʿalayhi al-salām — the very one some claimed to be Allah's son — is himself among those who testify to Allah's Oneness. Allah created the heavens and the earth out of nothing and without precedent; likewise, He created ʿĪsā the Messiah ʿalayhi al-salām with His power and without a father.

That is the hinge of the whole passage. Ayah 117 names Allah *Badīʿ*: the One who makes without a template. On Ibn Jarīr's reading, the birth without a father is not a mark of divine parentage at all — it stands in the same line as the making of the heavens and the earth themselves, brought about by the power of the One who originates without precedent.

## "When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be' — and it is"

Ibn Kathir: this demonstrates His perfectly complete ability and tremendous authority — if He decides a matter, He merely orders it, "Be," and it comes into existence. He brings the parallels: 36:82, 16:40, and "Our commandment is but one, as the twinkling of an eye" (54:50). And he closes with 3:59: "Verily, the likeness of ʿĪsā before Allah is the likeness of Ādam. He created him from dust, then said to him, 'Be' — and he was." Allah informed us that He created ʿĪsā ʿalayhi al-salām by merely saying "Be," and he was, as Allah willed.

**Where the scholars differed.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records — following Maulānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānavī's *Bayān al-Qurʼān*, and with his own warning that no good comes of unnecessarily meddling with such delicate questions, especially if the purpose is no more than to seek a new sensation — that there is a difference of approach between the two groups of the Mutakallimīn (the masters of ʿilm al-kalām, dialectical theology) over *Kun fa yakūn*. According to the **Ashʿarī** group, it is a metaphorical or allegorical expression: the phrase does not signify that Allah actually addressed an existent and commanded it "to be," but is an allegorical illustration of His omnipotence, suggesting that there is no interval between an act of will on His part and its realization. The commentator al-Bayḍāwī adopted this view. According to the **Māturīdī** group, the phrase literally means what it says. Maʿārif notes the difficulty this raises — a command is given only to an existent, yet what does not exist cannot be addressed, and what already exists needs no command — and resolves it by observing that this command does not belong to the order of *tashrīʿ* (legislation), which requires the addressee to exist in fact and to possess understanding; it belongs to the order of *takwīn* (creation), which is concerned with giving existence to non-existents. Maʿārif sets both out as the approaches of the Mutakallimīn without ruling one of them out.

**One practical consequence** Maʿārif draws from these two ayat: if Allah has chosen to assign certain tasks to certain angels — sending down rain, bringing the creatures their nourishment — or has chosen to employ causes, materials or physical forces to produce certain effects, He has done so in His wisdom. It is therefore neither permissible nor proper that men should look upon those angels, causes or forces as being effective agents in themselves, or turn to them for help in their need. Means are real; they are not powers.

Maʿārif also relays the commentator al-Bayḍāwī's remark that, Allah being the First Cause of things, the earlier Sharīʿahs had allowed the use of the title "Father" for Him — but the ignorant misunderstood and distorted the sense of "Fatherhood" so badly that to entertain such a belief or to apply this title to Allah has now been declared to be an act of infidelity (*kufr*, that is, unbelief). As this can lead to all kinds of doctrinal disorders, it is no longer permissible to employ that word or a similar expression with reference to Allah.

## Ayah 118: "If only Allah would speak to us"

Ibn Kathir reports that Muḥammad bin Isḥāq related from Ibn ʿAbbās that Rāfiʿ bin Ḥuraymilah said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "O Muhammad! If you were truly a Messenger from Allah, as you claim, then ask Allah to speak to us directly, so that we hear His Speech." And Allah revealed this ayah. Ibn Kathir also records that Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas, Qatādah and As-Suddī said the words in the ayah were actually the statement of the Arab disbelievers, with "those before them" being the Jews and the Christians — and he supports the idolaters' involvement with 6:124, 17:90–93, 25:21 and 74:52, recording their demands to receive the like of what the Messengers received, for a spring to gush forth from the earth, for angels to be sent down or to see their Lord, and for pages spread out.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the two demands precisely. First: that Allah Himself should speak to them — either directly, as He speaks to the angels, or through the angels, as He speaks to the prophets — and should Himself proclaim His injunctions to them, so as to make the intervention of a new prophet unnecessary; or should at least announce that He had sent Sayyidnā Muhammad ﷺ as a prophet, making it easy for them to have faith in him. Second, failing that: that Allah should send them a sign or proof in confirmation of his prophethood.

Maʿārif observes that the first demand was, on the face of it, silly enough: with all the grossness of their minds and hearts they had the audacity to place themselves on the level of angels and prophets — and so the Holy Qurʼan dismisses it as unworthy of a reply. In answer to the other demand, Allah reminds them that He has sent not one but a number of clear signs and proofs to confirm and establish the prophethood of Sayyidnā Muhammad ﷺ. But such signs can help only those who sincerely wish to know the truth and to attain certitude; as for those who are not in search of the truth but enjoy being stuck in their malice and obstinacy, there is no help for them.

## "Their hearts are alike"

This is the ayah's diagnosis, and it is devastating in its simplicity. Ibn Kathir: the hearts of the Arab idolaters are just like the hearts of those before them, containing disbelief, stubbornness and injustice. He cites, "Likewise, no Messenger came to those before them but they said, 'A sorcerer or a madman!' Have they transmitted this saying to one another?" (51:52–53). He also notes that the People of the Scripture asked the Prophet ﷺ to cause a book to descend upon them from heaven, and that they had asked Mūsā ʿalayhi al-salām for even greater than that: "Show us Allah in public" (4:153), and "O Mūsā! We shall never believe in you until we see Allah plainly" (2:55).

Maʿārif traces the demand to the same root: Allah puts it down as no more than a foolish custom unthinkingly practised by ignorant people even in the earlier ages, and the verse traces its origin to a distortion of the heart, in respect of which all ignorant people, past or present, are alike — hence the parrot-like repetition of the same demand throughout the ages. The objection is not new, and it was never really a question. It is a posture that each generation of the unwilling inherits without knowing it is quoting.

Maʿārif also answers a difficulty the reader may feel: the Jews and the Christians were People of the Book, and some of them were men of learning — so why does Allah call them ignorant? Because although Allah had sent so large a number of clear signs and definite proofs to establish the prophethood of Sayyidnā Muhammad ﷺ, they persisted in their denial. That is the mentality and the conduct of the ignorant. Ignorance here is not an empty head; it is a closed one.

## "We have made the signs plain for a people who have certainty"

Ibn Kathir: We made the arguments clear, proving the truth of the Messengers, with no need of more questions or proofs, for those who believe, follow the Messengers and comprehend what Allah sent them with. As for those whose hearts and hearing Allah has stamped and whose eyes have been sealed, He describes them: "Truly, those against whom the Word of your Lord has been justified will not believe — even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful torment" (10:96–97).

## Living with these ayat

**Guard how you speak of Allah.** The hadith recorded by Al-Bukhari calls a false statement about Allah an insult, not a debating point. That should shape the care with which a believer talks about his Lord — and the reflex of saying *subḥānahu* when he hears otherwise.

**Learn from His forbearance.** No one is more patient when hearing an insult than Allah: they attribute a son to Him, and He still gives them sustenance and health. Whatever patience you are being asked for today is smaller than that.

**Do not treat means as powers.** Rain, provision, angels, causes, physical forces — all are employed by Him in His wisdom, and none is an effective agent in itself. Need turns you to Allah, not to the channel.

**Stop waiting for the sign that will finally settle it.** Ayah 118 shows that the signs and proofs are already many and clear; what they cannot supply is the willingness to be convinced. The signs, Allah says, are made plain — for a people who believe with certainty.

passages.title: Follow the truth, not their community's approval
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These three ayat answer a question that was weighing on the Prophet's ﷺ heart: *why will they not accept?* Allah first defines his job so that he stops carrying a burden that was never his (ayah 119), then closes off the one route by which their approval could ever be won — abandoning the truth (ayah 120), and finally shows that the sincere among the People of the Book *do* respond, because they read their own Book honestly (ayah 121). The thread holding the three together is a single principle: **the messenger's duty is to convey the truth faithfully, not to secure the applause of a community that has already decided.**

---

## The consolation behind ayah 119

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the link back to the previous ayah. The implication of verse 118 was that those who persisted in their denial of the Prophet ﷺ did so out of sheer malice and ignorance, and could not be expected to reform themselves. But since he had been sent as the mercy for all the worlds, the thought of their being incorrigible was likely to make him sad on their account.

So ayah 119 is offered as consolation. Notice what Allah does *not* say. He does not say "they will believe eventually." He redefines the assignment: *"Verily, We have sent you (O Muhammad ﷺ) with the truth (Islam), a bringer of glad tidings … and a warner…"* Ibn Kathir unpacks both halves — glad tidings **for those who believe in what you brought, that they will enter Paradise**; a warning **for those who disbelieve in what you brought, that they will enter the Hellfire**. Two functions, and both are about *delivery*. Neither is about results. Maʿārif puts the same point as a twofold function: to give glad tidings to those who accept the truth, and warnings of dire punishment to those who deny.

**"And you will not be asked about the dwellers of the blazing Fire."** Ibn Kathir explains this plainly: it means, *"We shall not ask you about the disbelief of those who rejected you."* He then lines up the Qur'an's own parallels, because this is one of its recurring reassurances to the Prophet ﷺ:

- *"Your duty is only to convey (the Message) and on Us is the reckoning."* (13:40)
- *"So remind them (O Muhammad ﷺ) — you are only one who reminds. You are not a dictator over them."* (88:21–22)
- *"We know best what they say. And you (O Muhammad ﷺ) are not the one to force them (to belief). But warn by the Qur'an him who fears My threat."* (50:45)

Ibn Kathir adds that there are many other similar ayat. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the whole verse: Allah assures him that he will not be held responsible or taken to account for those who willingly pursue the way to Hell. All that he is required to do is to keep performing his own function, and not to worry as to who accepts the truth and who does not.

That is a heavy weight lifted. And it is worth sitting with, because the anxiety it addresses — *I told them and they still refuse; have I failed?* — is not unique to prophets.

## The Prophet ﷺ as the Torah described him

Ibn Kathir attaches a remarkable narration here.
