Imam Ahmad recorded ʿAtāʾ bin Yasār saying that he met ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr bin al-ʿĀṣ and said to him, "Tell me about the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the Torah." He replied, "Yes, by Allah, he is described by the Torah with the same characteristics that he is described with in the Qur'an with":

> "O Prophet! We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good news, a warner, and as safe refuge for the unlettered people. You are My servant and Messenger. I have called you the Mutawakkil (who depends and relies on Allah for each and everything). You are not harsh, nor hard, nor obnoxious in the bazaars. He does not reward the evil deed with an evil deed. Rather, he forgives and pardons. Allah will not bring his life to an end, until he straightens the wicked's religion by his hands so that the people proclaim: There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah. By his hands, Allah will open blind eyes, deaf ears and sealed hearts."

Ibn Kathir notes that this was recorded by al-Bukhari only. (*Mutawakkil*, as the narration itself explains, means the one who depends and relies on Allah for each and everything.)

Two things are worth catching. First, the same pairing appears there as in ayah 119 — *a bringer of good news* and *a warner* — which is precisely the point: this description was already in their scripture. Second, look at the character sketch: not harsh, not hard, not obnoxious in the bazaars, forgiving and pardoning rather than repaying evil with evil. Ayah 119 does not tell the Prophet ﷺ to become severe with those who reject him. It tells him to stop carrying their outcome. Those are different things.

---

## Ayah 120: the door that will never open

*"Never will the Jews nor the Christians be pleased with you (O Muhammad ﷺ) till you follow their religion."*

Ibn Jarir explains the meaning: the Jews and the Christians will never be happy with you, O Muhammad — **therefore, do not seek what pleases or appeases them, and stick to what pleases Allah by calling them to the truth that Allah sent you with.** The verse is not merely a description of them; it carries an instruction about where to aim.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *why* the door stays shut. The Prophet ﷺ, anxious to save as many men as possible from misguidance and damnation, took great pains to convince the deniers, and was specially lenient and gentle with the People of the Book. Allah now informs him that their denial is not due to a lack of convincing arguments and proofs. It is motivated by **pride and self-satisfaction**: each of the two groups believes its own religion to be the only genuine religion, so there is no likelihood of pleasing either of them until and unless the Prophet ﷺ accepts their religion.

Maʿārif is careful and fair here: the religions of the Jews and the Christians, no doubt, were once genuine and had been instituted by Allah. But each had since distorted its religion out of shape; moreover, in sending down Islam as the final Sharīʿah, Allah had abrogated all the earlier ones. So Islam had by now become the only Sharīʿah acceptable to Allah — and in that sense the only genuine and veritable guidance possible in this last of all the ages.

## A word worth pausing on: *ahwāʾ*

The verse first speaks of their *religion* — and then, in the warning clause, of their *ahwāʾ*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the shift: it is on account of the present distorted state of the earlier religions, and especially because of their having been abrogated by divine commandment, that verse 120 equates them with *Ahwāʾ* — the plural of *hawā*, that is to say, personal desires, or individual opinions and baseless conjectures.

And this explains the deadlock exactly. Since the deniers are not willing to extricate themselves from their desires and fancies, it is not possible to please them without accepting their opinions — a thing which a Messenger of Allah can never do.

**"Say: 'Verily, the guidance of Allah — that is the (only) guidance.'"** Ibn Jarir explains: say, O Muhammad ﷺ, the guidance of Allah that He sent me with is the true guidance, meaning the straight, perfect and comprehensive religion. Maʿārif adds the tone in which it is to be said: should they affect a more friendly stance towards him, Allah asks him to say to them in plain and simple words that the only guidance worth the name is that which comes from Allah — and He has already made it clear enough that Islam is now the only form of guidance acceptable to Him. Qatādah said of this sentence that it is "a true argument that Allah taught Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions and which they used against the people of misguidance."

## The warning clause — and why it never applied to him

*"And if you (O Muhammad ﷺ) were to follow their desires after what you have received of Knowledge (i.e. the Qur'an), then you would have against Allah neither any Walī (protector or guardian) nor any helper."*

Maʿārif treats this as a supposition made purely for the sake of supposing. Other verses of the Qur'an definitely establish the fact that Allah is pleased, and will always remain pleased, with the Holy Prophet ﷺ — and thus he can never be the object of divine wrath. Since divine wrath necessarily follows upon the acceptance of baseless fancies, it is logically impossible for him to follow the opinions of the Jews and the Christians, as divine pleasure and divine wrath cannot be combined with each other. The translator's note in Maʿārif adds a further layer: the warning is apparently addressed to the Holy Prophet ﷺ, but is really intended for the deniers, the purpose being to make them realize the dire consequences of their vanity — and the very indirectness of the address shows the contempt in which Allah holds them. The purport of the verse, Maʿārif concludes, is to advise the Prophet ﷺ not to worry too much about them.

## Why this ayah is about us

Ibn Kathir states it directly: this ayah carries **a stern warning for the Muslim Ummah** against imitating the ways and methods of the Jews and Christians, after they have acquired knowledge of the Qur'an and Sunnah — may Allah grant us refuge from this behavior. Although the speech in this ayah was directed at the Messenger ﷺ, its ruling applies to his entire Ummah.

The condition in the ayah is worth noticing: *after what you have received of Knowledge*. The gravity is not in being influenced while ignorant; it is in knowing and then bending anyway, because a community's approval is more comfortable than its displeasure.

Ibn Kathir places a hadith here. Qatādah said, "We were told that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say":

> "There will always be a group of my Ummah fighting upon the truth, having the upper hand, not harmed by their opponents, until the decree of Allah (the Last Hour) comes."

Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith was collected in the Ṣaḥīḥ and narrated from ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr. Set beside ayah 120, its comfort is precise: *disapproval is not the same as defeat*. The group standing on the truth is not promised popularity — it is promised that opposition will not harm it.

---

## Ayah 121: and yet, some do respond

Verse 120 dealt with the hopeless condition of the opponents of Islam among the People of the Book. Now, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, the present verse turns — in the usual manner of the Holy Qur'an — to the other aspect, and speaks of those Jews and Christians who were honest and just, and, having recognised the truth, affirmed the Prophet ﷺ and accepted Islam.

*"Those to whom We gave the Book recite it as it should be recited — they are the ones who believe therein."*

**Who are "those to whom We gave the Book"?** The commentators differed, and Ibn Kathir reports the difference rather than settling it:

- ʿAbd al-Razzāq said, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah: "They are the Jews and Christians." This is the opinion of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam, and it was also chosen by Ibn Jarīr.
- Saʿīd reported from Qatādah: "They are the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the same split. Its own commentary is based on a report from Ibn ʿAbbās, according to whom this verse was revealed on the occasion of the arrival of forty Christians from Abyssinia who had accepted Islam — while other commentators believe that "those to whom We have given the Book" are the Companions and "the Book" is the Qur'an.

## *Ḥaqqa tilāwatihi* — reciting it as it should be recited

The heart of ayah 121 is this phrase, and the early authorities defined it in complementary ways.

- **Ibn Masʿūd** (reported by Abū al-ʿĀliyah): "By He in Whose Hand is my soul! The right *Tilāwah* is allowing what it makes lawful, prohibiting what it makes unlawful, reciting it as it was revealed by Allah, not changing the words from their places, and not interpreting it with other than its actual interpretation."
- **Ibn ʿAbbās** (as-Suddī, from Abū Mālik), said about this ayah: "They make lawful what it allows and they prohibit what it makes unlawful, and they do not alter its wordings."
- **ʿUmar bin al-Khaṭṭāb**: "They are those who when they recite an Ayah that mentions mercy, they ask Allah for it, and when they recite an Ayah that mentions torment, they seek refuge with Allah from it." Ibn Kathir adds that this meaning was attributed to the Prophet ﷺ, for when he used to recite an ayah of mercy, he invoked Allah for mercy, and when he recited an ayah of torment, he sought refuge from it with Allah.

*(In Ibn Masʿūd's oath, "By He in Whose Hand is my soul," we affirm the Hand of Allah as Allah and His Messenger ﷺ affirmed it — without likening it to anything in creation and without emptying it of meaning.)*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the strands together: these people have distorted neither the words nor the meanings, nor have they tried to misinterpret or conceal the prophecies about the coming of the Prophet ﷺ. In other words, they have used their **intellect** in trying to understand the meanings, and their **will** in accepting the truth and in following it. And Maʿārif's footnote adds a further layer to the phrase — enunciating each word correctly and clearly, keeping the fear and love of Allah present in one's heart while reading, and also the resolve to follow divine guidance and to obey divine commandments. That footnote also reports, citing Ibn Abī Ḥātim, that ʿUmar said reading the Qur'an while observing the rights of its recitation requires that when one comes to a description of Paradise, one should pray to Allah for granting one this abode, and when one finds a description of Hell, one should seek Allah's protection from it.

## "They are the ones who believe therein"

Ibn Kathir treats this clause as the explanation of the one before it: "Those among the People of the Book who perfectly adhered to the Books that were revealed to the previous Prophets, will believe in what I have sent you with, O Muhammad!" Honest reading leads there. He supports this with a run of ayat — *"And if only they had acted according to the Tawrah, the Injil, and what has (now) been sent down to them from their Lord…"* (5:66); *"O People of the Scripture! You have nothing (as regards guidance) till you act according to the Tawrah, the Injil, and what has (now) been sent down to you from your Lord"* (5:68); *"Those who follow the Messenger, the Prophet who can neither read nor write, whom they find written with them in the Tawrah and the Injil"* (7:157); and *"Verily, those who were given knowledge before it, when it is recited to them, fall down on their faces in humble prostration"* (17:107–108).

On 5:68 Ibn Kathir comments: if you adhere to the Torah and the Gospel in the correct manner, believe in them as you should, and believe in the news they carry about Muhammad's prophethood, his description and the command to follow, aid and support him, then this will direct you to adhere to truth and righteousness in this life and the Hereafter.

Maʿārif makes the same point from the other end: in accepting the Qur'an, these believers are actually affirming their own Books too and acting upon them, insofar as their Books explicitly foretell the coming of the Last Prophet and of the last Book of Allah.

**"And whoever disbelieves in it, those are they who are the losers."** Ibn Kathir pairs this with *"But those of the sects (Jews, Christians and all the other non-Muslim nations) that reject it (the Qur'an), the Fire will be their promised meeting place"* (11:17), and cites what is recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ, that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "By He in Whose Hand is my soul! There is no member of this Ummah (mankind and Jinns), Jew or a Christian, who hears of me, yet does not believe in me, but will enter the Fire."

Maʿārif frames the loss in terms of the ayah's own logic: those who persist in their denial are bound to suffer the greatest loss, for they have refused to believe in the Last Revelation, and have, in fact, not shown much of a belief in their own Books, and not followed the guidance provided by them in this matter.

---

## Living it

**Do your part and release the rest.** The Prophet ﷺ himself was told he would not be asked about the dwellers of the blazing Fire. If that was said to him, then the anxiety a believer feels over a relative or friend who will not listen is misplaced as *guilt*, however right it is as *concern*. Convey, and leave the reckoning to Allah — "your duty is only to convey the Message, and on Us is the reckoning."

**Do not build your religion around being liked.** Ayah 120 removes approval as a goal. Ibn Jarīr's phrasing is the practical rule: do not seek what pleases or appeases them; stick to what pleases Allah by calling them to the truth. And Ibn Kathir's note that the ruling extends to the whole Ummah means the danger is live for us — especially, as the ayah specifies, *after knowledge has come to us*.

**Recite the Book as it should be recited.** Taking Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿUmar together, that means: recite it as it was revealed by Allah and do not change the words from their places; do not interpret it with other than its actual interpretation; treat what it makes lawful as lawful and what it makes unlawful as unlawful; and let it move you as you go — asking Allah for the mercy it mentions, seeking refuge from the torment it mentions, as the Prophet ﷺ did. Ayah 121 makes this the dividing line between those who end up believing and those who end up losing everything, so the standard of recitation it sets is not a refinement for specialists. It is the whole point of having a Book at all.

passages.title: The closing call to the Children of Israel
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat close the long address to the Children of Israel that has occupied much of this sūrah. They gather everything that came before into a single pair of sentences: **remember what Allah gave you** — and **fear a Day when no one will be able to stand in for you**. Mercy in one hand, warning in the other.

## A statement repeated, and why

Ibn Kathir notes that a similar ayah was mentioned at the *beginning* of this sūrah. Here it returns at the end. That repetition is not accidental, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes it the key to the whole passage.

A large section of this sūrah, ending with the previous ayah, has been dealing with different aspects of the conduct of the Israelites in the course of their history. That entire account, Maʿārif explains, *began* with the statement that is now *repeated* at the end in these two ayat. The statement is "of a general and principal kind," and the ayat that come in between the beginning and the end are, as Maʿārif puts it, a detailed demonstration of it. The particular episodes are the demonstration; these two ayat are the principle.

Maʿārif then draws out the reasoning behind the design, in terms any teacher or writer will recognise. What a discussion aims at is the affirmation of certain basic and general principles. Being succinct, such principles are easily kept alive in the mind; being comprehensive and readily applicable to particular situations, they make it easy to remember the details too. So in the art of writing and speaking, Maʿārif says, it is considered one of the most effective means of carrying conviction that before starting a long analytical discussion one should define the basic ideas very briefly and clearly, and that in concluding the argument one should repeat those ideas by way of a summary. The repetition here is of this very nature, and its purpose is "to make the two ideas sink deep into their minds."

So when you reach ayah 122 and feel you have heard this before, that recognition is the point. The Qur'an is closing a circle, and asking that the whole argument settle into the heart as two things a person can carry: *what you were given*, and *the Day you are heading toward*.

## Ayah 122 — "Remember My favour"

The ayah opens with the same call that has punctuated this whole section: **yā banī Isrāʾīl** — O Children of Israel. Then the command: **udhkurū** — remember. And what is to be remembered is **niʿmatī allatī anʿamtu ʿalaykum** — "My favour which I bestowed upon you."

Notice how the phrasing folds back on itself. The noun *niʿmah* (favour, blessing) is followed by a verb built from the same letters, *anʿamtu* (I bestowed). The favour and the Giver of the favour are named in the same breath. It is not a blessing they simply *have*; it is a blessing *He gave them*. Then, in Ibn Kathir's rendering: "and that I preferred you over the nations."

Ibn Kathir opens up what that favour actually included. Allah, he says, commanded them to remember their daily life and their religious affairs and how He blessed them — the whole texture of their existence, worldly and sacred alike. But he singles out one favour in particular, and it is the one that turns this closing appeal into something urgent.

## The favour they were warned not to conceal

Ibn Kathir reads the repetition here as serving one purpose above all: **to emphasise the importance of following the Ummī Prophet and Messenger ﷺ.**

Why address that to *them*? Because, as Ibn Kathir explains, this Prophet ﷺ is described for the People of the Scriptures in their Books — by his characteristics, by his name, by the good news about him, and by the description of his Ummah. That description, Ibn Kathir says, is among the favours that Allah granted them. And Allah warned them against **concealing this information**.

That reframes ayah 122. "Remember My favour" is not only a general invitation to gratitude. It carries a pointed edge: *the description of the final Messenger was placed in your own Books. That was a gift. You were warned not to bury it.*

## Envy, and what it costs

Ibn Kathir then names the obstacle directly. They should not envy their cousins, the Arabs, for what Allah has given them — the Final Messenger of Allah ﷺ being an Arab. And envy, he says, should not incite them to oppose or deny the Prophet ﷺ, or to refrain from following him.

That is worth sitting with, because of what it identifies as standing in the way. Ibn Kathir does not present a counter-argument that had to be answered. He names an emotion — envy at a favour given to someone else — and warns that it must not be allowed to drive a person into opposition, denial, or refusal to follow.

And there is a sober irony in the pairing. The ayah says "I preferred you over the nations," and the very next thing Ibn Kathir warns against is resentment at what Allah has given to others. A favour received and a favour begrudged sit side by side in the same passage.

## Ayah 123 — the Day when the doors are shut

Then comes the turn: **wa-ttaqū yawman**. Ibn Kathir's rendering is "And fear the Day (of Judgement)"; the translation given with the ayah puts it as "And guard yourselves against the Day." Fear and guarding — the same command approached from two sides.

And in Ibn Kathir's rendering, the Day is described by four closures, one after another:

- **no person shall avail another** — *lā tajzī nafsun ʿan nafsin shayʾan*, no soul will discharge anything on behalf of another soul, not in the smallest thing;
- **nor shall compensation be accepted from him** — nothing can be paid in exchange;
- **nor shall intercession be of use to him** — no intercession will avail;
- **nor shall they be helped** — and no help arrives.

Read them together and you see the architecture. Each closure shuts a different door that people instinctively reach for. *Someone else will carry it for me.* No. *I will pay my way out.* No. *Someone will speak for me.* No. *Something, somehow, will come to my rescue.* No. The ayah works through every exit in turn and seals it — and the final clause, "nor shall they be helped," sweeps up whatever the first three might have left standing.

Note the wording of the first clause especially. The Arabic sets *nafs* against *nafs* — soul against soul, the same word on both sides. The ayah does not name any particular kind of person who will fail to help. It uses the most general term available, twice, and Ibn Kathir's rendering keeps that generality: *no person* shall avail *another*.

## The two ayat as one movement

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the double effect of this closing statement with real precision. On the one hand, it **encourages** the Israelites to come back to the Straight Path by reminding them of the blessings which Allah has bestowed on them. On the other hand, it **warns** them of the consequences of their lapses by depicting the Day of Judgement.

That is the shape of the passage: an appeal made from both sides. Ayah 122 works on the heart through memory and gratitude — *look at what He gave you*. Ayah 123 works on the heart through fear and accountability — *look at where you are going*. Held together, the two do what neither does alone: gratitude without accountability drifts into complacency; fear without gratitude curdles into despair. Together, they turn a person around.

And crucially, this is a **call back**, not a dismissal. Maʿārif's word is that it "encourages the Israelites to come back to the Straight Path." After the long account of history that fills this section, the door is left open. The closing note of the address is an invitation.

## Living it

The address is to the Children of Israel, but the summons is one any reader can feel the weight of.

**Remember the favour as a favour.** Ayah 122 pairs *niʿmah* with *anʿamtu* — the gift named together with the Giver. Blessings that we come to see as simply ours, as entitlements rather than gifts, quietly stop producing gratitude. The practice the ayah commands is active: *udhkurū* — remember, in your daily life and your religious affairs alike, as Ibn Kathir describes.

**Do not let envy decide what you accept.** This is the most transferable line in Ibn Kathir's comment: envy should not incite a person to oppose, to deny, or to refrain from following. Envy is not an argument, and it was never meant to function as one. Wherever we find ourselves resisting something because of who was favoured with it rather than because of what it is, that warning is speaking to us.

**Live as someone who will stand alone.** The four denials of ayah 123 quietly reorder priorities. If no person can avail another, if no compensation is accepted, if no intercession is of use, and if no help arrives — then whatever is going to be of use on that Day has to be built now, by you. That is not a bleak thought. It is a clarifying one. It tells you exactly where your effort belongs.

**And notice that the warning is placed at the end of an appeal, not instead of one.** These two ayat close a large section of the sūrah, and they close it by opening a door: *remember, and be careful — because the call is to come back.*

passages.title: Abraham tested and appointed a leader for mankind
passages.tafsir:
## What this ayah is about

One verse, but it carries the whole argument: Allah put Ibrahim (peace be upon him) through a series of trials, Ibrahim came through them completely, and Allah's reward was to make him **an Imam — a leader for mankind to follow**. When Ibrahim then asked that this station also be given to some of his descendants, Allah granted it, but attached a permanent condition. In Ibn Kathir's rendering, Allah replied: **"My covenant (prophethood) includes not Zalimin (polytheists and wrongdoers)."** Leadership in religion is earned by obedience under trial, and forfeited by injustice — it is not inherited by blood.

## Why this story appears here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the preceding section of Sūrat al-Baqarah has been dealing directly with the conduct of the Jews through their history and their hostility to Islam. Part of what drove that hostility was pride of lineage: they were proud of being the children of Yaʿqūb and of Ibrahim, and believed that, as the chosen people, they had the exclusive privilege of leading humanity — so prophethood could not possibly be conferred on someone outside their race.

The Qur'an now refutes that line of thought, but indirectly, by telling the story of Ibrahim and his elder son Ismāʿīl (peace be upon them). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists what this section is establishing: that only one who is *not* unjust, not a transgressor, and who has successfully passed the trial Allah imposed on him can guide humanity; that the Kaʿbah, towards which Muslims turn in prayer, had actually been built by Ibrahim, so the Muslims' qiblah is his qiblah; that the way of Islam is the way of Ibrahim and the Muslims alone are his real followers; that Ibrahim himself prayed for the Last Prophet to be sent to humanity; and that Ibrahim had two sons, Ismāʿīl and Isḥāq, so that the superiority enjoyed by the children of Isḥāq in their own time has now been transferred to the children of Ismāʿīl.

Ibn Kathir reads the opening imperative the same way. The verse means: *O Muhammad, remind the idolaters and the People of the Scriptures, who pretend to be followers of the religion of Ibrahim while in reality they do not follow it, of the commands and prohibitions that Allah tested Ibrahim with* — while you and your followers are the true followers of his religion. Ibn Kathir gathers the verses that hammer this in, including: "Ibrahim was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a true Muslim Hanifan... Verily, among mankind who have the best claim to Ibrahim are those who followed him, and this Prophet and those who have believed" (3:67-68).

## "When his Lord tested him" — why *Rabb*?

An obvious question, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises it directly: the purpose of a trial is to test a man's aptitude and worthiness for a certain function — but Allah is all-knowing and knows every existent inside out. So what was the purpose of this trial?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān finds the clue in the word the verse chooses. Out of all the divine names, this verse says **his *Rabb*** tested him. *Rabb* indicates a specific divine attribute — that of making a thing attain the state of its perfection **gradually and stage by stage**. So the trial was not the punishment for a crime, nor was it intended to uncover a hidden aptitude. It was a manifestation of that divine action: a necessary part of "nurturing" the prophet and making him reveal his inherent qualities to the world, so that he might be led stage by stage to the final station already chosen for him by his Lord. Although it is divine knowledge and will that choose a man for prophethood, he is not allowed to assume that station until his aptitude and worthiness have openly shown themselves for all men and angels to witness — exactly as happened earlier in this sūrah in the trial of Ādam before the angels.

There is a second delicacy of the Arabic worth feeling. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Arabic text places the object — *Ibrāhīm* — **before** the subject *Rabbuhu* ("his Lord"), a word order that indicates Ibrahim's glorious position among the prophets.

## The *kalimāt*: what were the "words"?

The Qur'an says he was tested "with *kalimāt*" — literally "words." Ibn Kathir explains that here it means **laws, commandments and prohibitions**. He shows how flexible the word is across the Qur'an: sometimes "words" refers to what Allah has willed (as in 66:12, where Maryam "testified to the truth of the Words of her Lord"), sometimes to Allah's Law (as in 6:115, "And the Word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and in justice" — meaning His legislation), and sometimes to truthful news or a just commandment or prohibition, which is the sense here.

**Which** commands? Ibn Kathir records a difference of opinion, with several views attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās himself:

- **The rites of Hajj.** ʿAbdur-Razzāq said that Ibn ʿAbbās said, "Allah tested him with the rituals (of Hajj)." Abu Isḥāq reported the same.
- **The disciplines of bodily purity.** ʿAbdur-Razzāq also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that it means *ṭahārah* — purity and ablution: five on the head and five on the body. As for the head: cutting the mustache, rinsing the mouth, inhaling and discarding water, using the *siwāk*, and parting the hair. As for the body: trimming the nails, shaving the pubic hair, circumcision, plucking under the arm, and washing with water after answering the call of nature. Ibn Abi Ḥātim said a similar statement was reported from Saʿīd bin al-Musayyib, Mujāhid, ash-Shaʿbī, an-Nakhaʿī, Abu Ṣāliḥ, Abu al-Jald and others.
- **The great ordeals of his life.** Muhammad bin Isḥāq reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said the words Ibrahim was tested with, and implemented, were: abandoning his disbelieving people when Allah commanded him to; disputing with Nimrod, king of Babylon, about Allah; being patient when he was thrown into the fire, although this was extremely traumatic; migrating from his homeland when Allah commanded him to; patience with the monetary and material demands of hosting guests by Allah's command; and Allah's order for him to slaughter his son. When Allah had tested him with these and he was ready for the major test, Allah said to him, "Submit (be a Muslim)!" — and he said, "I have submitted myself to the Lord of all that exists" (2:131), although this meant defying and standing apart from the people.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the blessed Companions and their immediate successors differed over the number too — according to some, ten; according to others, thirty — but basically there is no opposition among these views, since all the injunctions mentioned in this context were, in one way or another, meant to serve as trials and tests. This, it says, is what great commentators like Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Kathir believe to be the truth of the matter.

One thing is clear either way. These trials were **not like academic tests**, nor were they intended to gauge mental capacities or the grasp of mere theories. The purpose was to test readiness in obeying Allah and steadfastness in submitting to divine commandments. Which helps us see that what really has value in the eyes of Allah is not theoretical hair-splitting, but actual deeds, within and without.

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir connects the purity report to two hadiths. Imam Muslim narrated from ʿĀ'ishah that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said: **"Ten are among the *Fiṭrah*"** — trimming the mustache, growing the beard, using the *siwāk*, inhaling and then exhaling water in ablution, cutting the nails, washing between the fingers, plucking the underarm hair, shaving the pubic hair, washing with water after answering the call of nature, "and I forgot the tenth, I think it was" rinsing the mouth.

The Two Ṣaḥīḥs recorded Abu Hurayrah saying that the Prophet ﷺ said: **"Five are among the acts of *Fiṭrah*: circumcision, shaving the pubic hair, trimming the mustache, cutting the nails and plucking the underarm hair."** (This is the wording with Muslim.)

*Fiṭrah*, as Ibn Kathir glosses it, means instinct — the natural constitution Allah made human beings on. The point is quietly beautiful: the same habits of bodily dignity that were part of Ibrahim's testing were later commanded to this ummah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that these ten characteristics of the *Fiṭrah*, concerned with the cleanliness and purification of the body, have been made permanent injunctions for all the later communities of believers too, and the Last Prophet ﷺ insistently commanded his followers to fulfil them.

## The trials, told properly

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān walks through the more important ones, noting that since Allah intended to raise Ibrahim to a specially exalted station among the prophets and to confer on him the title **Khalīlullāh** — the Friend of Allah — he was made to go through very severe trials.

**The fire.** Not only his people but his own family were sunk deep in idol-worship. Against their creed and customs he was given "al-Dīn al-Ḥanīf," the Pure Religion, and was asked to go out to his people and bring them back to the Straight Path. Unflinchingly he obeyed, setting out to wage war against idol-worship and to call people to the unalloyed worship of the One God. This drew upon him the fury of his people and of their king Nimrod, who finally decided to burn him alive. Seeking nothing but the pleasure of his Lord, he gladly let himself be thrown onto the pyre. Then came the command: **"O fire, be coolness and safety for Ibrahim"** (21:69). As one can see, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, the command was given to fire *as such*, not to any particular fire — so all fire, wherever it was present in the world, grew cold, and Nimrod's fire with it. And note the second word: excessive cold is equally painful and killing — there is a region of extreme cold in Hell itself, called *Zamharīr* — so in commanding the fire to grow cold, Allah in His grace added *salāman*, "be safe."

**The migration.** He was asked to leave his homeland and migrate to Syria with his family, then commanded to leave even that country — which he readily did, accompanied by his wife Hājar and his infant son Ismāʿīl, and led by the archangel Jibrāʾīl. Whenever they passed through a fertile land, Ibrahim would wish to be allowed to settle there, but the archangel would inform him that Allah did not want him to — until they reached the barren desert destined to become the site of Makkah.

**The abandonment in the desert.** Then began a new trial, much harder for a man to bear: he was ordered to leave his wife and son in the desert and go back to Syria. "The Friend of Allah" had so annihilated his own will and desire, and was so anxious to obey his Lord, that he did not allow even a moment to lapse between the command and its execution — he started on his journey without informing his wife. When she noticed he was going away, she called after him and received no reply; not even when she demanded why he was forsaking them in such a vast and lonely desert. But she was, after all, the wife of "the Friend of Allah," and could now see for herself how matters stood. So she asked whether he had received a divine command. Only then did Ibrahim reply that it was so. And having understood the situation, she calmly remarked, **"Alright. Go. The Lord who has commanded you to part from us shall Himself look after us, and not let us be destroyed."**

She sat back in the desert, full of trust and peace, with the infant on her lap. But as time passed, thirst — her own and especially that of her suckling son — compelled her to leave him and go in search of water. She climbed up and down the hills of Ṣafā and Marwah, and after seven attempts had to come back unsuccessfully. It is to commemorate this event that running seven times between the two hills has been made an obligatory part of the rites of Hajj and ʿUmrah. As she returned to her son, the mercy of Allah descended in the form of the archangel Jibrāʾīl, who made a spring of fresh water spout forth from the parched ground — the spring now called Zamzam. In a day or two the water began to draw animals, and the sight of animals brought men to the place; by and by the provisions necessary for human life became regularly available, and the future city of Makkah began to take shape.

**The sacrifice.** The infant grew up and was soon able to take on the usual functions of human life, and under divine permission Ibrahim came now and then to see how his wife and son were doing. It is now that Allah chose to submit him to the greatest of all possible trials. The son had grown up in such unpromising circumstances, deprived of constant fatherly care and affection — and now the father received the command to slaughter him with his own hand. The Qur'an records the exchange: "My son, I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you. Now, say, what do you think?" — "My father, do as you have been bidden; you shall find me, if Allah so wills, one of the patients" (37:102).

He took his son to the wilderness of Minā and fulfilled, so far as he himself was concerned, the divine commandment. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to something precise in the wording: in his dream he had not seen the *accomplishment* of the slaughter, but only the *act* of slaughtering — and that much he did perform. Revelation came to him in the form of a dream picturing the act, perhaps for this very reason: Allah did not want to give him a verbal command to sacrifice his son. Hence Allah commended him for having **"confirmed the dream"** (37:105). In recompense for this total submission to the divine will, Allah sent down a ram from heaven to be sacrificed in place of Ismāʿīl — and the annual sacrifice has been made a regular form of worship in commemoration of the way of Ibrahim.

## "Which he fulfilled"

*Fa-atammahunna* — "which he fulfilled." Ibn Kathir says this indicates that Ibrahim implemented **all** of Allah's orders, and points to the Qur'an's own verdict elsewhere: **"And of Ibrahim who fulfilled (or conveyed) all that Allah ordered him to do or convey"** (53:37) — meaning, he was truthful and he was obedient to Allah's legislation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same verse: **"And Ibrahim who paid his debt in full."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also reports that Ibn Kathir related from Ibn ʿAbbās that thirty elements make up the whole of Islam: ten mentioned in Sūrah 9 (9:112 — those who repent, worship, praise, keep a fast, bow and prostrate, invite others to good and forbid evil, and keep within the bounds fixed by Allah), ten in Sūrah 23 (23:1–11 — humility in prayer, turning away from idle activities, keenness to purify themselves, guarding chastity, preserving what has been entrusted to them and their covenant, and regularity in prayer), and ten in Sūrah 33 (33:35 — the paired list of submitting, believing, obedient, truthful, patient, humble, charitable, fasting, chaste, and abundantly remembering men and women). These formed a part of Ibrahim's trials, and he fulfilled these conditions with equal faithfulness.

## The reward: *Imām*

"Verily, I am going to make you an Imam (a leader) for mankind." Ibn Kathir says this was **as a reward** for Ibrahim's good deeds — for adhering to the commandments and avoiding the prohibitions. This is why Allah made him a role model for the people, and an Imam whose conduct and path are imitated and followed.

Lexically, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, *imām* signifies "leader or chief or guide." Since this verse concerns Ibrahim, the word means above all **"a prophet"** — though it includes the general sense of "leadership" too, as also the title "Patriarch" that Jews and Christians have given him. Prophethood cannot be won through personal effort; all the same, a prophet has to display his perfection in those thirty qualities, and even people of a lower scale must possess them in their own degree to be worthy of leadership in a general sense. The Qur'an makes the principle plain elsewhere: **"And from among them We appointed some as leaders to guide men by Our command, when they were patient (in restraining themselves from disobedience), and had a sure faith in Our commandments"** (32:24). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this verse as a résumé of the thirty qualities in two words — *ṣabr* (patience), which refers to the perfection of actual practice, and *yaqīn* (sure faith, certitude), which refers to the perfection of knowledge.

## "And from my offspring" — and the limit Allah set

Having been made an Imam, Ibrahim asked Allah that Imams thereafter be chosen from his offspring. Allah accepted his supplication — Ibn Kathir's proof is Allah's statement in Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt, "And We ordained among his offspring prophethood and the Book" (29:27); every prophet Allah sent after Ibrahim was from among his offspring, and every Book Allah revealed was revealed to them. **But** Allah told him at the same time that there would be unjust people among his offspring who would not benefit from Allah's promise: **"My covenant (prophethood) includes not Zalimin (polytheists and wrongdoers)."**

So Allah was telling him, in the same breath, two things: that there will be unjust people among his descendants, and that they will not benefit from Allah's promise, nor be entrusted with anything, even though they are among the children of Allah's Khalīl. They will neither become Imams nor be imitated. And there will also be those who do good among the children of Ibrahim — and these are the ones who will benefit from Ibrahim's supplication.

Ibn Jarīr said this ayah indicated that **the unjust shall not be Imams for the people**. Ibn Khuwayz Mindād al-Mālikī drew the ruling out further: "The unjust person does not qualify to be a Khalīfah, a ruler, one who gives religious verdicts, a witness, or even a narrator of hadiths."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the reasoning: to hold this station is, in a way, to be a vicegerent of Allah, and hence this rank cannot be given to a rebel. It follows that Muslims, insofar as they have a choice in the matter, **should not appoint as their ruler or representative a man who is a rebel against Allah or disobedient to Him**.

## A point of creed

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a further conclusion from the word *ẓālim* ("unjust"). In its reading, the word shows very explicitly that **each and every prophet is totally sinless, before becoming a prophet as much as after**. Certain words in the Qur'an which seem to suggest the contrary — for example, in the case of Ādam — have on this view been employed not in a literal or technical sense but only metaphorically; and to interpret such expressions in the sense of technical "sin," the commentary warns, constitutes a very grave doctrinal error, and insistence on such an interpretation opens the way to further errors.

It is worth being clear about what is being reported here: this is the conclusion Maʿārif ul Qurʼān itself draws from the word *ẓālim*, stated in its own emphatic terms. The protection of the prophets from sin (*ʿiṣmah*) is affirmed across Ahl al-Sunnah; the precise scope of that protection before prophethood is a question the scholars have discussed, and our source bundle here preserves only this one commentator's formulation of it, not a survey of the positions. Take it, then, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's considered view — argued from this verse — rather than as a summary of everything the scholars have said on the matter.

## Living it

The verse leaves a believer with a plain shape for life. **Allah's tests are not verdicts against you; they are the work of your *Rabb*, bringing you stage by stage to the station He intends for you.** What is being measured is not how well you argue — these were never academic tests — but readiness to obey, and steadfastness when obedience costs your homeland, your comfort, or your dearest attachment. Notice, too, how the sources place the small beside the enormous: trimming the nails and using the *siwāk* sit in the same discussion of Ibrahim's trials as the fire and the sacrifice, because both are simply Allah's command taken seriously.

And the closing clause should stay with us. Honour with Allah does not run in the blood. Being among the children of Allah's Khalīl secured nothing for the wrongdoer; those with the best claim to Ibrahim are the ones who followed him. Whatever standing we want with Allah, this ayah says there is only one road to it: passing the test.

passages.title: The House made a sanctuary, and the prayer for Mecca
passages.tafsir:
**These two ayat are about the Kaʿbah** — what Allah made it *for*, and the prayer Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said over the city that grew around it. In ayah 125 Allah speaks about the House: He made it a place people return to and a place of safety, appointed the Station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer, and charged Ibrahim and Ismaʿil to keep His House pure for those who circle it, retreat in it, and bow and prostrate in it. In ayah 126 we hear Ibrahim's own voice, asking his Lord to make this place a secure city and to feed its people with fruits — and Allah answers him mid-prayer. One idea holds them together: **the House is Allah's, its sanctity is Allah's doing, and everything good about Makkah is an answered supplication.**

## Why this comes up here

The Jews of that time, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, denied the Prophet ﷺ on the assumption that prophethood could not go outside their own clan, mocked the Muslims for turning towards the Kaʿbah in prayer, and treated the Hajj as no more than a custom of ignorant Arabs. The previous ayah answered the first claim — the covenant does not reach the wrongdoers, even among Ibrahim's own progeny. This ayah answers the other two: the Kaʿbah was built under divine commandment by Ibrahim himself, with Ismaʿil helping. Facing it in prayer and making pilgrimage to it are not Arab folklore but divine institutions — and the Prophet ﷺ, a descendant of Ibrahim and Ismaʿil, is reviving the Abrahamic way, which the Jews too must follow.

## "Mathābah" — the word that explains the crowds

**Mathābah**, the key word of ayah 125, comes from the root *thāba*, "to come back" — a place one returns to, again and again. Allah did not merely call the House a place to visit; He built the returning into the noun. Al-Qurtubi reports Mujahid saying that one never has enough of the Kaʿbah: every visit sends a person home with a greater longing to return and see it again. Some scholars have said this is itself a sign that a Hajj has been accepted. Makkah offers no beautiful landscape, no easy access, no worldly comforts, and yet millions are drawn to it every year; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls that pull "nothing short of a miracle." Ibrahim's prayer in Sūrah Ibrāhīm names the mechanism: *"make the hearts of men tender towards them"* (14:37). Hearts, not roads.

Note also that the House was found, not founded. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that every ayah of the Qurʼān on this subject either says the site was indicated by Allah Himself or gives the command to keep the House clean — none of them suggests a new House in a new place. Ibrahim and Ismaʿil were not the original founders; they raised a new building on foundations that were already there, the earlier structure having been destroyed at the Deluge of Nuh (peace be upon him), or raised into the heavens, leaving the foundations buried in the ground. Recounting a hadith reported by Al-Bukhari, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that when the two began digging, those earlier foundations became visible, and it was on them that they began to raise the walls. Who founded it first, and when, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to say, no fully authenticated hadith settles.

## Hajar in the valley

The most illuminating thing in the sources is a long narration Al-Bukhari records from Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibrahim brought Ismaʿil and his mother to the area of the House and left them by a tree above where Zamzam now is — an uninhabited place with no water source — with a bag of dates and a skin of water. As he turned to go she followed him: "O Ibrahim! To whom are you leaving us in this barren valley that is not inhabited?" He gave no answer. She asked again and again. Then she asked the only question that mattered: "Has Allah commanded you to do this?" He said, "Yes." She said: **"I am satisfied that Allah will never abandon us."** He walked until they could not see him, faced the House, raised his hands and supplicated: *"O our Lord! I have made some of my offspring dwell in an uncultivable valley by Your Sacred House…"* (14:37).

The water ran out. Mother and child grew thirsty, and she could not bear the sight of his face, so she climbed the nearest mountain, aṣ-Ṣafā, and looked out for anyone — in vain. She came down into the valley, raised her garment and ran the way an exhausted person runs, up to al-Marwah. In vain again. Seven times, back and forth — and the Prophet ﷺ said, in this narration, that this is why people make that trip between aṣ-Ṣafā and al-Marwah. At al-Marwah she heard a voice, listened for it again, and said, "I have heard you. Do you have relief?" She found the angel digging where Zamzam now is, and the water gushed out. As she scooped it into her water-skin, the Prophet ﷺ said, "May Allah grant His mercy to the mother of Ismaʿil; had she left the water alone, it would have been flowing on the surface of the earth." The angel told her: "Do not fear abandonment. There shall be a House for Allah built here by this boy and his father. **Allah does not abandon His people.**"

Then people of Jurhum, camping at the bottom of the valley, saw birds and reasoned that birds mean water — and a settlement began. Years later Ibrahim found his grown son behind the Zamzam well, mending his arrows. Ibrahim said, "Your Lord has ordered me to do something." Ismaʿil said, "Obey your Lord." — "Will you help me?" — "Yes, I will help you." They rose and began to raise the foundations of the House, Ibrahim building and Ismaʿil handing him the stones, both going around it praying — and what they prayed as they built is the subject of the ayah that follows. That valley, that woman, that infant and that certainty are the ground ayat 125–126 describe.

## The Station of Ibrahim

Ayah 125 commands that the Maqām Ibrāhīm be taken as a place of prayer. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains it is the stone Ibrahim stood on while building the Kaʿbah, which miraculously acquired the print of his foot (Al-Bukhari); the Companion Anas said he saw the mark himself. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that the Ḥaram as a whole is the "Station of Ibrahim" — probably meaning the two rakʿahs this ayah enjoins after ṭawāf may be prayed anywhere within the Ḥaram, and most of the jurists accept this. The Prophet ﷺ showed how the command is carried out: on his last Hajj, after ṭawāf, he reached the Station, recited this very ayah, and prayed two rakʿahs on the other side of the stone with his face turned towards the Kaʿbah (Sahih Muslim). Al-Jassas and Mulla ʿAli al-Qari hold those two rakʿahs *wājib* (necessary); praying them behind the Station is Sunnah.

## "Purify My House"

The command is to purify the House *for* three groups: those making ṭawāf, those in iʿtikāf (retreat for worship), and those bowing and prostrating. Saʿid bin Jubayr understood the first as those who do not live in Makkah and the second as the people living around the Sacred House; Qatadah and Ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas said the same. As for *purify* — Al-Hasan Al-Basri said Allah ordered them to purify it from all filth and impurities, of which none should ever touch it. Saʿid bin Jubayr reported that Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Purify it from the idols." Mujahid and Saʿid bin Jubayr widened it: "From the idols, sexual activity, false witness, and sins of all kinds." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds both halves — outward, physical dirt, and the inner filth of disbelief (kufr) and association (shirk), along with greed, lust, envy, pride, vanity and hypocrisy.

Because Allah called it **"My House,"** the ruling reaches every masjid, since all masjids are houses of Allah: *"In houses which Allah has ordered to be raised, in them His Name is remembered…"* (24:36). Al-Qurtubi reports that ʿUmar once heard a man shout in the mosque and rebuked him for forgetting where he was; and the Prophet ﷺ taught that the masjids are established for the very purpose they were built for — the worship of Allah alone. Note too Ibrahim's own response to the command: he understood the House had to be kept clean of shirk and kufr as much as of dirt, and that people might one day drift, out of sheer ignorance, into worshipping the Kaʿbah itself — so rather than trusting his own resolve he asked Allah, *"and keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols"* (14:35). He turned to Allah even for the ability to obey Allah.

## A city where blood is not shed

"And a place of security." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that "the House" means not the Kaʿbah alone but the whole surrounding sanctuary, the Ḥaram — the Qurʼān uses "Kaʿbah" for the wider precinct elsewhere, as in *"an offering to reach the Kaʿbah"* (5:95), which cannot mean inside the building, since such a sacrifice is not offered there. So the whole Ḥaram is a place of peace: bloodshed and revenge are forbidden within it (Ibn al-ʿArabi). This remnant of Ibrahim's way survived even the Age of Ignorance — a man would come upon his brother's or father's killer inside the Ḥaram and not touch him.

The sanctity, though, is older than Ibrahim. Some reports say Ibrahim made Makkah a sanctuary, others that Allah made it one when He created the heavens and earth; Ibn Kathir says there is no contradiction — **Ibrahim was conveying a decree Allah had already made.** At-Tabari narrated from Jabir bin ʿAbdullah that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"Ibrahim made Allah's House a Sacred Area and a safe refuge. I have made what is between the two sides of Al-Madinah a Sacred Area; its game should not be hunted, and its trees should not be cut"* — An-Nasaʼi and Muslim also recorded it. And the Two Sahihs record from ʿAbdullah bin ʿAbbas: *"Allah has made this city a sanctuary the Day He created the heavens and earth… It was not legal for anyone to fight in it before me, and it was legal for me for a few hours of one day… None is allowed to uproot its thorny shrubs, or to chase its game, nor should any of its trees be cut"* — and when Al-ʿAbbas asked an exception for lemon-grass, the Prophet ﷺ granted it. Al-Bukhari and Muslim also record Abu Shurayh Al-ʿAdawi reporting the address of the day that followed the victory of Makkah: *"Allah, not the people, made Makkah a sanctuary… today its sanctity is valid as it was before."* And Muslim records from Jabir: *"No one is allowed to carry weapons in Makkah."*

**But the Ḥaram shelters no criminal.** There is consensus, report Al-Jassas and Al-Qurtubi, that whoever commits a crime inside the precincts carrying a fixed punishment (ḥadd) or liability to retaliation (qiṣāṣ) is duly punished; the jurists differed only over the man who offends outside and then flees in. Some would have him punished as prescribed; Imam Abu Hanifah held that out of regard for the sanctity of the place he is not punished inside the Ḥaram, but is forced to come out, and the punishment is carried out then — otherwise the Ḥaram would become an easy refuge for every kind of criminal.

## The prayer of ayah 126

Ibrahim's prayer opens with one word: **Rabb**, which lexically signifies the One who gives nurture. That form of address is itself a lesson in how to ask: it draws Allah's mercy and grace upon the one praying (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān).

He asks two things: that this place be made a secure *city*, and that its people be provided with fruits. Note the wording — here it is *baladan*, "a city," indefinite, because the place was still desert and he was asking that a city grow in it; in Sūrah Ibrāhīm (14:35) the same prayer uses *al-balad*, "the city," definite — a later prayer, when the city already stood. Ibn Kathir places the Sūrah Ibrāhīm supplication after the House was built and its people lived around it, after the birth of Ishaq, thirteen years Ismaʿil's junior — which is why that prayer ends *"All praise be to Allah, who has given me in old age Ismaʿil and Ishaq. Verily my Lord is indeed the Hearer of invocations"* (14:39).

Both requests were granted, visibly. Makkah became a place of security — *"Whosoever enters it, he attains security"* (3:97); *"Have they not seen that We have made a secure sanctuary, while men are being snatched away from all around them?"* (29:67). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that no disbeliever has ever been able to conquer or dominate it — the Qurʼān itself tells of the People of the Elephant, destroyed for venturing to invade Makkah — and that even the birds and animals inside the Ḥaram show no fear of people, since hunting there is forbidden.

The fruits came too — but from elsewhere. The surrounding land was uncultivable, so Allah made the neighbouring city of Ṭāʼif fertile and productive in fruits, and its fruit came to Makkah. And note: Ibrahim did *not* pray for Makkah's own soil to be made fertile, and Allah would have granted that just as easily. He asked instead that fruit be brought in, so that his descendants should not be unduly absorbed in agriculture — his purpose in founding the settlement was *"that they may be steadfast in the prayers"* (14:37); he wanted their essential function to be protecting the House of Allah and engaging in worship. And *"the fruits of all kinds of things are drawn towards it"* (28:57) says the fruits of all *things*, not of trees — so the word covers the products of every craft and industry, everything needed to sustain human life. Makkah has neither agriculture nor industry, yet enjoys the benefits of both as fully as any prosperous city in the world.

## Ibrahim's rectitude, and Allah's answer

The request for fruit carries a clause: *"…such of them as believe in Allah and the Last Day."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as a window into Ibrahim's scrupulousness. In ayah 124 he had prayed for his descendants without distinguishing the faithful from the unjust, and Allah had answered that His covenant does not reach the wrongdoers. Now, praying only for worldly prosperity, that earlier proviso came back to his mind, and he at once narrowed the request to the faithful. That is what fear of Allah does to a heart.

Allah's reply comes immediately, inside the same ayah: *"As for him who disbelieves, I shall leave him in contentment for a while, then I shall compel him to the torment of the Fire — and worst indeed is that destination."* Ibn Jarir reports that Ubayy bin Kaʿb said these are Allah's words, not Ibrahim's; Mujahid and ʿIkrimah said the same. And Ibn Abi Hatim narrated that Ibn ʿAbbas gave the sense: Ibrahim asked Allah to grant sustenance for the believers only, but Allah revealed that He would provide for the disbelievers just as He provides for the believers — **"Would I create something and not sustain and provide for?"** — allowing them a little delight, then forcing them to the torment of the Fire. Ibn ʿAbbas then recited: *"On each — these as well as those — We bestow from the bounties of your Lord"* (17:20).

This is easy to misread: **worldly provision is not a verdict.** The ayah shows, says Ibn Kathir, that Allah gives the disbelievers respite and then seizes them in a manner compatible with His greatness and ability: *"And many a township did I give respite while it was given to wrongdoing. Then I seized it"* (22:48). The Two Sahihs record: *"No one is more patient than Allah when hearing abuse. They attribute a son to Him, while He grants them sustenance and health."* And the Sahih also records: *"Allah gives respite to the unjust person, until when He seizes him, He never lets go of him."* Worldly prosperity, then, is given to the disbelievers too; in the other world the faithful alone prosper.

## Living it

**Ask Allah for the strength to obey Allah.** Ibrahim was commanded to keep the House pure of shirk and immediately prayed to be kept from idols himself. Obedience is requested, not supplied.

**Do not read prosperity as approval.** Allah feeds those who deny Him. The measure of a life is its destination, not its comfort.

**And notice what Hajar said.** "Has Allah commanded you to do this?" — "Yes." — "Then I am satisfied that Allah will never abandon us." Zamzam still runs.

passages.title: Raising the foundations: the prayer of Abraham and Ishmael
passages.tafsir:
## One prayer, spoken over stone

These three ayat are a single, continuous supplication made while the work was still in progress. Ibrahim and his son Isma'il are raising the foundations of the Ka'bah, and as they build they ask: accept this from us (ayah 127); make the two of us submissive to You, raise a submissive nation from our offspring, show us our rites, and turn to us in mercy (ayah 128); and send among them a Messenger from themselves, who will recite Your verses, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them (ayah 129).

What holds the passage together is that the last request is the summit of the first. A House is only stone until there is a people who worship rightly inside it, and a people are only a crowd until Allah raises a Prophet among them. Ibn Kathir reads ayah 129 this way: Ibrahim's supplication for the people of the Sacred Area "was perfected by invoking Allah to send a Messenger from his offspring."

## The scene behind "when they were raising the foundations"

Ayah 127 opens mid-action, and the sources fill in decades of backstory. Al-Bukhari recorded from Ibn 'Abbas that Ibrahim brought Isma'il and his mother to the area of the House and left them beside a tree above where Zamzam now is — Makkah then uninhabited, with no water source — leaving only a bag of dates and a water-skin. As he turned to go she followed him: "O Ibrahim! To whom are you leaving us in this barren valley that is not inhabited?" He did not reply. She repeated the question several times. Then came the question that changed everything: "Has Allah commanded you to do this?" He said, "Yes." She said, "I am satisfied that Allah will never abandon us."

The rest of that narration is the origin of the pilgrimage itself: the water running out; her running between As-Safa and Al-Marwah seven times looking for help — Ibn 'Abbas reports the Prophet ﷺ saying, "This is why the people make the trip between As-Safa and Al-Marwah"; the angel digging where Zamzam now exists, the water gushing out, and the angel telling her, "Do not fear abandonment. There shall be a House for Allah built here by this boy and his father. Allah does not abandon His people."

Then the tribe of Jurhum settled by the water, Isma'il grew up among them and learned Arabic from them, and his mother died. Years later Ibrahim came back and found his son behind the Zamzam well, next to a tree, mending his arrows. They greeted each other, just as a father and son greet each other. Ibrahim said, "O Isma'il, your Lord has ordered me to do something." Isma'il said, "Obey your Lord." Ibrahim asked, "Will you help me?" He said, "Yes, I will help you." Then: "Allah has commanded me to build a house for Him there." So both of them rose and started to raise the foundations of the House — Ibrahim building, Isma'il handing him the stones — building it part by part, "going around it and saying, 'Our Lord! Accept this from us. Verily, You are the Hearer, the Knower.'"

Hold that against ayah 127: this prayer was not composed in a quiet room. It was repeated, course after course, by an old man and his son with their hands in the work.

## A prayer said over and over

The narration in Al-Bukhari shows the two of them repeating these words as they went around the building, part by part — not one act of building with one prayer at the end, but continuous labour with a continuous prayer running through it.

The wording of the ayah itself moves straight from the building to the words spoken, which is why translators supply "(saying)" in brackets. Ibn Kathir mentions, on the authority of Al-Qurtubi, that Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud used to recite the ayah with the added words *wa yaqulan* — "and the two of them were saying: Our Lord! Accept this from us." Ibn Kathir notes that what follows in ayah 128 further testifies to this sense, since the next words are plainly speech.

## The fear of the accepted

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what is most striking in ayah 127. In obedience to Allah, Ibrahim had left the fertile land of Syria and settled his wife and child in a barren desert, and was now taking up the labour of building the House of Allah — a moment when a man who had borne such hardships might normally be expected to feel satisfied with himself. Instead, "the Friend of Allah" — al-Khalil, the intimate friend — recognised the Majesty of Allah, and knew that no creature can possibly worship or obey his Creator as is His due, but only within his own limited powers. So in performing the hardest or greatest of tasks one should not be proud of the attainment, but should in all humility pray that the little effort one was capable of be accepted — an effort itself made only by the grace of Allah.

Ibn Kathir makes the same point bluntly: "The Prophets Ibrahim and Isma'il were performing a good deed, yet they asked Allah to accept this good deed from them." He records, through Ibn Abi Hatim, that Wuhayb bin Al-Ward once recited this ayah, cried, and said: "O Khalil of Ar-Rahman!" — O intimate friend of the Most Gracious — "You raise the foundations of the House of Ar-Rahman, yet you are afraid that He will not accept it from you?" This, says Ibn Kathir, is the behaviour of the sincere believers, whom Allah describes as those "who give that which they give" while "their hearts are full of fear" (23:60) — afraid that these good deeds might not be accepted of them.

Notice the two names chosen to close the request: **as-Samiʿ al-ʿAlim**, the Hearer, the Knower. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pairs them precisely: Allah hears all prayers, and knows the intentions of His creatures. He hears the words rising from the building; He knows the heart behind them.

## Ayah 128: four requests

**"Make us submissive to You."** Ibn Jarir explains their meaning: "Make us submit to Your command and obedience and not associate anyone with You in obedience or worship." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Ibrahim here prays for himself and his son together — and presses on the strangeness of the request, since a man who has all his life been performing exemplary deeds of obedience prays to *be made* obedient. It is so, it says, "because the more one grows in one's knowledge of Divine Majesty, the more one comes to realize that one is not being faithful and obedient as is due." Guidance is not a possession one banks; it is asked for again on the day one is at one's best. 'Ikrimah comments on this request, and on the one that follows for their offspring, that Allah said: "I shall do that."

**"And from our offspring a nation submissive to You."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that men of Allah who never hesitate to sacrifice themselves and their children in the way of Allah nonetheless love them deeply — they simply know what the proper requirements of parental love are. Average people suppose their children's well-being lies in physical health and comfort alone; those who have received the favour of Allah show much greater solicitude for their children's spiritual well-being, and are more anxious about the next world than this one. So, it says, "the great prophet prayed to Allah to make a group from among his descendants fully obedient to Him" — not a claim on every descendant, but on a company drawn from among them. Citing al-Bahr al-Muhit, it adds a further benefit: when people of standing and their descendants keep to the right path, they are held in esteem and their conduct inspires others to reform. And this prayer was answered: even in the Age of Ignorance, when Arabia in particular was lost in the darkness of idol-worship and shirk (associating partners with Allah), there still remained men of Ibrahim's line who had faith in the One Allah — Zayd ibn 'Amr bin Nufayl and Quss ibn Sa'idah; and it is also reported that 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, the grandfather of the Prophet ﷺ, shunned idol-worship and shirk.

Ibn Kathir notes that this type of supplication is allowed, because loving to have offspring who worship Allah alone without partners is a sign of complete love of Allah (25:74) — and cites Muslim's narration from Abu Hurayrah: "When the son of Adam dies, his deeds end except for three deeds: an ongoing charity, a knowledge that is being benefited from and a righteous son who supplicates for him."

**"And show us our manasik."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *manasik* (the plural of *mansik*): it signifies both the different actions involved in performing the Hajj and the different places where those rites are performed — 'Arafah, Muzdalifah, Mina — and both meanings are intended here. The verb employed is *arina*, "show us"; seeing is done through the eyes and also through the heart, so the locations of the rites were shown to Ibrahim through the angel Jibril and the injunctions regarding Hajj were explained in detail.

Ibn Kathir records, through Sa'id bin Mansur, the statement of Mujahid — a statement of that early scholar, not a prophetic report — on how the request was answered. Jibril came down, took Ibrahim to the House and said, "Raise its foundations"; then held his hand and led him to As-Safa — "This is among the rituals of Allah" — and to Al-Marwah, and on to Mina. At the 'Aqabah they found Iblis standing next to a tree, and Jibril said, "Say Takbir and throw at him," and Ibrahim said the Takbir and threw; and again at the middle Jamrah. Iblis sought to add some evil acts to the rituals of Hajj, but was unable to succeed. Then Jibril led him to Al-Mash'ar Al-Haram and 'Arafat and asked three times, "Have you *'arafta* — known, learned — what I showed you?" and Ibrahim said, "Yes I did." Similar statements were reported from Abu Mijlaz and Qatadah.

**"And turn to us in mercy."** Two prophets, in the midst of an act of pure obedience, ask Allah to accept their repentance — and seal it with *at-Tawwab ar-Rahim*, the One who accepts repentance, the Most Merciful. It is the same instinct as ayah 127: the closer they come, the less they lean on what they have done.

## Ayah 129: the request that became the Prophet ﷺ

Ibn Kathir writes that this accepted supplication "conformed with Allah's appointed destiny that Muhammad ﷺ be sent as a Messenger among the Ummiyyin and to all non-Arabs, among the Jinns and mankind" — a mission reaching far beyond the people of that one valley — and that "Ibrahim was the first person to mention the Prophet ﷺ to the people." The announcement then runs forward to 'Isa, who told the Children of Israel he was "giving glad tidings of a Messenger to come after me, whose name shall be Ahmad" (61:6). Ibn Kathir cites the Prophet's ﷺ own answer when he was asked how his prophethood began: "I am the supplication of my father Ibrahim, the good news of Jesus the son of Mary, and my mother saw a light that radiated from her which illuminated the castles of Ash-Sham." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports this from Imam Ahmad's *Musnad*, adding that Allah had chosen him as the Last Prophet at a time when Adam's clay was still being prepared.

That detail raises a question the sources answer directly. If the Prophet ﷺ was written as the Final Prophet when Adam was still clay, what did Ibrahim's prayer accomplish? Ibn Kathir answers in this very context: **Allah accepted Ibrahim's supplication although He had full knowledge beforehand that it would occur by His decree.** He draws the same parallel with Makkah's sanctity — Allah made it a sanctuary the day He created the heavens and the earth, and Ibrahim's making it a sanctuary was his conveying of Allah's decree, so the two sets of reports do not contradict. Supplication is not a rival to the decree; it is written into it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks why Ibrahim requested a Messenger *minhum*, "from among them", and gives two reasons: the appearance of a prophet from among them would in itself be an honour and a blessing; and because he is one of their own, they would be thoroughly familiar with his past and present and with his ways, and so find it easy to trust him and to profit from his guidance. It adds — citing Ibn Jarir and Ibn Kathir — that according to a hadith, in accepting this prayer Allah promised that this prophet would be sent in the last of all ages.

That second reason was borne out before revelation ever came. Ibn Kathir quotes Ibn Ishaq's *Sīrah*: when the Prophet ﷺ was thirty-five, Quraysh gathered to rebuild the Ka'bah, and on reaching the foundations that Ibrahim built they uncovered green stones lying above each other, just like a pile of spears; when a man placed a shovel between two of them to pull them up, all of Makkah shook, so they left them. A dispute over who would set the Black Stone then erupted and almost led to violence, until the oldest man of Quraysh, Abu Umayyah bin Al-Mughirah, proposed that the first man to enter the House be their mediator. Seeing who it was, they proclaimed: "This is Al-Amin (the Honest one). We all accept him; This is Muhammad." He had a garment spread on the ground, placed the stone on it, had each of the leaders hold a side and lift it together, then carried the stone himself and set it in its position. As Ibn Ishaq notes, Quraysh used to call him Al-Amin even before the revelation came to him.

**The three functions asked for.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that these same words are repeated in Surah Al 'Imran and Surah Al-Jumu'ah, both of which speak of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ — which shows who was prayed for. It examines the three:

- *Yatlu* — "recites". From *tilawah*, which lexically signifies "to follow, to obey"; Imam al-Raghib al-Isfahani says in his *Mufradat al-Qur'an* that the word cannot, in current idiom, be applied to the reading of any book other than the Word of Allah. Because reciting is mentioned *separately* from teaching, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues that the very words of the Qur'an — not merely their meanings — are an inalienable part of what was intended: recitation is an act of worship in its own right, which is why a translation, however accurate, is not entitled to be called "the Qur'an".
- *Yu'allimuhum al-Kitab wa'l-Hikmah* — "teaches them the Book and wisdom". Ibn Kathir reports that *al-Kitab* means the Qur'an and *al-Hikmah* means the Sunnah, as Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Muqatil bin Hayyan and Abu Malik asserted; it was also said to mean comprehension in the religion, "and both meanings are correct." That teaching is listed separately is the proof, argues Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, that knowing Arabic is not by itself enough to understand the Qur'an — otherwise Abu Jahl and Abu Lahab would have been counted among its greatest commentators. Understanding comes through the Prophet's ﷺ teaching: "So that you should explain to men what We have revealed for them" (16:44).
- *Yuzakkihim* — "purifies them". 'Ali bin Abi Talhah reported that Ibn 'Abbas said this means "with the obedience of Allah." *Tazkiyah*, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, denotes purifying from all kinds of filth, internal as well as external: false beliefs such as kufr (rejection of faith) and shirk on one side, and pride, vanity, malice, jealousy and love of worldly things on the other. Listing it separately shows that even a proper understanding of the principles does not by itself make one perfect in them; they must be put into practice.

The ayah closes with **al-'Aziz al-Hakim** — the Mighty, the Wise. Ibn Kathir: Allah is able to do anything and nothing escapes His ability; and He is Wise in His decisions and His actions, and puts everything in its rightful place due to His perfect knowledge, wisdom and justice. Only the Mighty could grant a request this large; only the Wise would appoint the age in which it was answered.

## Living it

**Pray while you work, not only after it.** The supplication of ayah 127 was said with stone in hand, going around the House as the walls went up.

**Fear for your best deeds, not only your worst.** If Ibrahim, raising the House of Allah under direct command, still begged that it be accepted, then the deed you are quietly pleased with is the one to hand back to Allah in fear.

**Pray for the faith of those who come after you.** The request of ayah 128 was answered down the generations, and the request of ayah 129 is why there is a Book to recite and a Prophet ﷺ to learn it from. Whoever recites the Qur'an today is standing inside the answer to a prayer made beside those foundations.

passages.title: The religion of Abraham is pure submission
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat make a single argument: the religion of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is not a tribal inheritance or an ancestral label — it is *islām*, the willing surrender of oneself to Allah alone. It moves from a rhetorical question exposing the folly of abandoning that way (ayah 130), to the moment Ibrahim himself embraced it (131), to the counsel he and Ya'qub left their sons (132), to Ya'qub's deathbed (133), and closes by cutting away the one thing the listeners were leaning on: descent from great men (134). Ibn Kathir reads it as refuting "the disbelievers' innovations of associating others with Allah in defiance of the religion of Ibrahim, the leader of the upright."

## Ayah 130 — "Who would turn away from the religion of Ibrahim?"

The verb is *yarghabu 'an*: Ibn Kathir glosses turning from Ibrahim's *millah* as one who "abandons his path, way and method." Not a technical disagreement — walking off a road.

And the answer is savage in its brevity: *illā man safiha nafsah* — "except him who fools himself." Ibn Kathir explains this as one "who commits injustice against himself by deviating from the truth, to wickedness," and presses on: such a person defies the path of the man Allah chose to be a true leader from his youth until Allah chose him to be His *Khalīl* (intimate friend), and who is among the successful in the Hereafter. "Is there anything more insane than deviating from this path…? Is there more injustice than this?" He anchors the charge in Allah's own words, *"Verily, joining others in worship with Allah is a great Zulm (wrong) indeed"* (31:13).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the Arabic can be carried into English three ways: such a man is stupid in himself; or he has besotted himself and allowed himself to become stupid; or he is ignorant of his own self. All three land in the same place — the loss is not Ibrahim's, it is the deserter's. Only someone who has lost his understanding can turn from this way, Maʿārif adds, because this alone is the religion of "Nature" — *fitrah*, the sound original disposition Allah created in every human being — which no one can deny so long as his nature remains intact.

**Why Ibrahim is the measure.** Ibn Kathir stacks up the evidence that Ibrahim never wavered: he "always singled out Allah in worship, with sincerity," and "he did not commit Shirk, even for an instant." He disowned every deity worshipped besides Allah and defied his whole people — *"O my people! I am indeed free from all that you join as partners (in worship with Allah). Verily, I have turned my face towards Him Who has created the heavens and the earth Hanifa (Islamic Monotheism), and I am not of Al-Mushrikin"* (6:78-79). That parenthesis is the source's own gloss: to be *ḥanīf* is to lean away from every rival object of worship and towards Allah alone, and *al-mushrikīn* are precisely those who assign Him partners. Even his prayer for his father rested on a promise, and when it became clear his father was an enemy of Allah, "he dissociated himself from him" (9:114).
