Allah's own verdict — *"We gave him good in this world, and in the Hereafter he shall be of the righteous"* (16:120-122) — is the same pairing of two worlds that ayah 130 repeats.

**The occasion.** Abu Al-'Aliyah and Qatadah said this ayah was revealed about the Jews "who invented a practice that did not come from Allah and that defied the religion of Ibrahim." Ibn Kathir cites as testimony: *"Ibrahim was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a true Muslim Hanifa (to worship none but Allah alone) and he was not of Al-Mushrikin. Verily, among mankind who have the best claim to Ibrahim are those who followed him, and this Prophet (Muhammad ﷺ) and those who have believed"* (3:67-68).

**His honour in this world.** Maʿārif fills in what "We chose him in this world" meant on the ground. Nimrod with all his might failed to impress him; he accepted gladly to be thrown into the fire rather than give up the worship of the One God, and the Lord of the worlds changed the fire into a garden for him — so that believers and non-believers alike finally came to recognise his uprightness and his unalloyed faith. The associators of Arabia were, after all, his own progeny; despite their idol-worship they always held him in great esteem and even claimed to be his followers, and certain remnants of his religion were still present among them — the Hajj, the annual sacrifice of animals, hospitality — though somewhat distorted by their ignorance. These, says Maʿārif, are manifestations of the special divine grace by which *Khalīlullāh*, the Friend of Allah, had been designated the *Imām* of people (2:124). Ayah 130 then adds his exalted station in the Hereafter.

## Ayah 131 — one word, and a whole religion

*"When his Lord said to him: Submit!"* The command is a single word: **Aslim**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that it comes from the same root as *Islam*, and that it is difficult to find an exact English equivalent, for the word signifies "to obey, to submit oneself, to surrender one's will." Ibn Kathir reads the ayah as Allah commanding Ibrahim to be sincere with Him and to abide and submit to Him — and Ibrahim "perfectly adhered to Allah's command."

Now notice the shape of the reply. You would expect *aslamtu laka*, "I submit myself to You." He does not say that. He says, more elaborately, *aslamtu li-Rabb al-'ālamīn* — "I submit myself to the Lord of the worlds." Maʿārif draws three things out of that choice: it expresses the attitude of respect and awe proper to the occasion; it includes the praise of Allah which the moment of receiving the honour of divine address demanded; and it carries a recognition that in submitting he was only performing the essential duty of a servant towards the Master of All — and doing it for his own benefit. The very essence of Ibrahim's religion sits in that one word, *Islam*: total obedience and willing submission of oneself to Allah. It was to show the world his perfect adherence to this principle that he was made to pass through all the trials before attaining his exalted station. Submission to Allah, Maʿārif says, "is what the world has been created for; it is the end all the prophets and all the divine books have been sent to serve."

**The religion of every prophet.** From this ayah Maʿārif derives that the religion common to all the prophets, the point on which all of them come together, is Islam: beginning with Adam up to the Last Prophet ﷺ, every messenger called men to Islam alone — *"Certainly, in the eyes of Allah the only religion is Islam"* (3:19); *"Whoso desires a religion other than Islam, it shall not be accepted of him"* (3:85). Maʿārif is careful here, and the care matters: every religion the different prophets brought had a divine sanction behind it, was essentially instituted by Allah Himself, and was "accepted" in the sight of Allah in its own time — so each of them, "whether one calls it Judaism or Christianity or something else," must in its essence be Islam, in the general sense of the word: total submission to Allah.

What distinguishes Ibrahim, Maʿārif adds, is that he gave his religion the name of Islam and his followers the name of Muslims. In ayah 128 he prayed that he and his son be kept *muslimayn* — obedient to Allah — and that their progeny be made a *muslimah* nation; in ayah 132 we find him advising his descendants not to die without being sure that they have been Muslims. After him, that distinction of being specifically called Muslims and "the Islamic Ummah" passed, according to his own instruction, to the Ummah of the Prophet ﷺ: *"Be steadfast in the religion of your father, Ibrahim. He named you Muslims before this as well as in this (the Holy Qur'an)"* (22:78). When the Qur'an was revealed, the Jews, the Christians and even the idol-worshippers of Arabia each claimed to be the followers of the Abrahamic religion; the Qur'an and its followers made it evident that in this last phase of human history the religion of the Prophet ﷺ, and this alone, is the religion of Ibrahim, the religion of quintessential "Nature" (*al-fitrah*).

**What submission actually costs.** Maʿārif is blunt: the essence of all the divine books, all the Shariʼahs and the teachings of all the prophets is Islam — "turning away from one's desires in order to obey divine commandments, and giving up individual opinion in order to submit oneself to divine guidance." It grieves over Muslims who reach for whatever interpretation flatters their desires and who "distort the Shari'ah to suit their fancies, and to do it so cleverly that the idols they really worship should appear in the garb of religion." Such men, it says, are trying to be clever with Allah Himself, who knows every particle of the universe and can look into the deepest recesses of the human heart. Real submission comes only by following the Sunnah, the way of the Prophet ﷺ: *"By your Lord, they will never be true Muslims till they make you the judge regarding the disagreements between them, and find in themselves no resistance against your verdict, and surrender themselves in full submission"* (4:65). The perfection of that obedience, submission and love is what Maʿārif calls the Station (*Maqām*) of *'Abdiyyah*, servanthood — the station where Ibrahim received from Allah the title *Khalīlullāh*, the Friend of Allah, and the Last of All the Prophets ﷺ the title *'Abdunā*, "Our Servant." This, Maʿārif says, is the essence of *tawḥīd*, the realization of Allah's oneness: on attaining it, all one's fears and hopes become bound with Allah, and with no one else.

## Ayah 132 — the words they would not let die

*"And this was enjoined by Ibrahim upon his sons, and by Ya'qub."* What is "this"? Ibn Kathir gives two readings. Either Ibrahim commanded his offspring to follow this religion — that is, Islam, for Allah; or — the tender reading — "this" refers to his own words, *"I have submitted myself to the Lord of the 'Alamin."* On that reading, these prophets "loved these words so much that they preserved them until the time of death and advised their children to adhere to them after them," matching *"And he (Ibrahim) made it a Word lasting among his offspring"* (43:28) — the word being, as Ibn Kathir glosses it, *lā ilāha illallāh*, none has the right to be worshipped but Allah alone.

Ibn Kathir argues that Ya'qub was alive in Ibrahim's lifetime, so that he was among those who received the counsel. The glad tidings to Sarah named both Ishaq and, after him, Ya'qub (11:71) — and had Ya'qub not been alive then, there would have been no point in mentioning him specifically. He adds *"And We bestowed on him Ishaq and Ya'qub, and We ordained among his offspring prophethood and the Book"* (29:27) and *"And We bestowed upon him Ishaq, and (a grandson) Ya'qub"* (21:72), and notes that Ya'qub built Bayt al-Maqdis, as earlier books testified — citing from the Two Sahihs that Abu Dharr asked which masjid was built first, and the Prophet ﷺ said al-Masjid al-Harām, then Bayt al-Maqdis, forty years later.

**"Die not except as Muslims."** No one chooses the hour of his death, so the command is really about life. Ibn Kathir: "perform righteous deeds during your lifetime and remain on this path, so that Allah will endow you with the favor of dying upon it. Usually, one dies upon the path that he lived on and is resurrected according to what he died on. Allah, the Most Generous, helps those who seek to do good deeds to remain on the righteous path." Allah's usual way with men, adds Maʿārif, is that when a servant makes up his mind to do good and strives as best he can, Allah helps him and makes the task easy — *"As for him who gives (in charity) and keeps his duty to Allah and fears Him… We will make smooth for him the path of ease"* (92:5-10).

Both commentaries meet the obvious worry. There is an authentic hadith that a man may work the deeds of the people of Paradise until only a span of outstretched arms or a cubit separates him from it, then the Book — the decree — takes precedence, and he does the deeds of the people of the Fire and enters it; and the reverse also happens. (Ibn Kathir calls it authentic without naming a collection; Maʿārif likewise reports it without naming one.) Does that make striving pointless? No: some texts of this hadith carry the proviso "as it appeared to people" — the first man only *appeared* to onlookers to be performing good deeds while in fact he was doing just the opposite, and the second had from the outset been doing what would make him worthy of Paradise, though people thought him a sinner. Whoever has been steadfast in doing good, Maʿārif concludes, should trust the divine promise, rely on Allah's usual way with His creatures, and hope to depart this world in that blessed state.

## Ayah 133 — the last question a dying man asks

*"Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub?"* The challenge is aimed, Ibn Kathir says, at both the Arab pagans among the offspring of Ismaʼil and the disbelievers among the Children of Israel: you were not there. And what Ya'qub asked as death came was not about property or burial but *"What will you worship after me?"* — and his sons answered with a creed: your *Ilāh* and the *Ilāh* of your fathers Ibrahim, Ismaʼil and Ishaq, One *Ilāh*, and to Him we submit. (*Ilāh* is what the source renders as the one worshipped, Allah.)

Two details repay attention. Ismaʼil is called a "father" though he was Ya'qub's uncle; this, says Ibn Kathir, is a figure of speech, and he reports from an-Nahhās, as al-Qurtubi mentioned, that the Arabs call the uncle a father. And *Ilāhan wāhidan*, "One *Ilāh*," Ibn Kathir explains as "we single Him out in divinity and do not associate anything or anyone with Him," with *"to Him we submit"* meaning obedience and submissiveness — of a piece with *"While to Him submitted all creatures in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly"* (3:83).

**Islam is the religion of all the prophets.** From that shared creed at the deathbed Ibn Kathir draws the general rule: "Islam is the religion of all the Prophets, even if their respective laws differed," citing *"And We did not send any Messenger before you but We revealed to him: none has the right to be worshipped but I, so worship Me"* (21:25). He notes there are many other ayat and hadiths on the subject, and gives as an instance the Prophet's ﷺ own image of half-brothers: "We, the Prophets, are brothers with different mothers, but the same religion." (Ibn Kathir reports these words without naming a collection.)

**A point of fiqh, honestly disputed.** Because a grandfather is called "father" here, the ayah is used as evidence that a grandfather counts as a father and inherits, rather than the brothers, when his son dies — as Abu Bakr asserted, according to al-Bukhari, who narrated Abu Bakr's statement from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn az-Zubayr, and al-Bukhari then commented that there are no opposing opinions regarding this subject. It is also the opinion of 'A'ishah the Mother of the believers, al-Hasan al-Basri, Tāwus and 'Atā'. Mālik, ash-Shāfi'i and Ahmad said instead that the inheritance is divided between the grandfather and the brothers — and this was reported to be the opinion of 'Umar, 'Uthmān, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ūd, Zayd ibn Thābit and several scholars among the Salaf and later generations. Maʿārif notes the same deduction from the ayah's wording: Ibn 'Abbas took from it the rule that in matters of inheritance the grandfather is treated like the father.

**Fathers who feared for their sons.** Why were these two prophets so particular about their own children? Because, Maʿārif answers, love for one's progeny and concern for their well-being is in no way incompatible with the station of prophethood or even with that of "the Friend of Allah." The same Ibrahim who was on one occasion not merely willing but happy to sacrifice his son in obedience to Allah's command prayed on another occasion for the well-being of his progeny in this world and the next, and wished, while departing from this world, to offer them what was the greatest blessing in his eyes: Islam. Prophets do love their children. The difference is that ordinary men count the good things of this world worthwhile and try to leave their children as much of them as they can, while in the eyes of the prophets and their genuine followers the only thing that counts is faith and good deeds — and it is that eternal wealth they strive to transmit.

## Ayah 134 — lineage carries no one

*"That was a nation who has passed away"* — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, it existed before your time; "they shall receive the reward of what they earned and you of what you earn." The verdict is plain: "Your relationship to the Prophets or righteous people among your ancestors will not benefit you, unless you perform good deeds that bring about you religious benefit. They have their deeds and you have yours." Hence the hadith he cites: "Whoever was slowed on account of his deeds will not get any faster on account of his family lineage." (Ibn Kathir gives this without naming a collection; Maʿārif reports it likewise.)

Maʿārif draws out both edges. The good deeds of one's forefathers will not suffice you if you have performed none yourself; and you will not have to suffer for your forefathers' misdeeds if your own account is clean — from which it follows that children of associators and disbelievers who die before coming of age will not be punished in the next world on account of their parents' disbelief. The verse also refutes the Jews' claim that, whatever they themselves did, they would enter Paradise on the strength of their forefathers' good deeds — and Maʿārif turns the warning on Muslims who, being descendants of the Prophet ﷺ or of a saint, delude themselves that their sins will go unpunished in consideration of that position: *"Each man shall reap the fruits of his own deeds, and no one shall bear the burden of another"* (6:164). Addressing his own clan, the Prophet ﷺ warned Banu Hashim not to arrive on the Day of Judgment carrying only their trust in being his relations while others bring their good deeds — for on that day, he told them, he could not save them from the wrath of Allah. (Maʿārif reports these words without naming a collection.)

## Living it

**Ask your children Ya'qub's question.** Maʿārif turns these verses into a plain duty on parents: just as they are keen to secure their children's worldly comfort, they should pay equal — if not greater — attention to disciplining their outward and inward conduct according to the Shariʼah. "Is it at all reasonable that one should strain every nerve to protect one's children from the heat of the sun, but leave them exposed to the fire of Hell?" It gives three reasons why one's own family comes first: children, because of their special relationship with the parents, are likelier to accept the counsel thoroughly, and may later be of great help in one's efforts in the service of Islam; if the head of each family takes responsibility for teaching his own household, teaching the families separately amounts finally to teaching society as a whole — *"O believers, guard yourselves and your families against a Fire"* (66:6); and one can observe that when a man's own household does not support what he teaches, his teaching does not succeed so well with others. Even the Prophet ﷺ, sent to the whole of humanity, was commanded to convey the truth first to his own: *"And warn your clan, your nearest kin"* (26:214), and *"And bid your family to offer Salah, and be regular in them yourself"* (20:132) — commandments he ﷺ always fulfilled. Maʿārif traces much of today's indifference to Islam among Muslims to parents who are good Muslims themselves yet leave their children to the social environment to mould, worrying only about how they will do in this world and never about the next.

**And ask it of yourself.** The passage strips away every substitute for personal submission: a revered ancestor, a claimed tradition, a name. What remains is the one word Ibrahim was given — *Aslim* — and the answer he gave back, which his sons would not let die.

passages.title: The believers' creed against sectarian claims
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat answer a claim put to the Prophet ﷺ — that guidance belongs to one community by name — and replace it with something older and larger: the way of Ibrahim, the faith of every prophet, and a creed the believers are told to declare. What holds the passage together is a single movement: the sectarian claim is refused (135), the true creed is recited (136), the test of that creed is stated (137), and its real name is given — the colouring of Allah (138).

## The claim, and who made it

Ibn Kathir records, on the authority of Muhammad bin Ishaq from Ibn 'Abbas, that 'Abdullah bin Suriya Al-A'war said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "The guidance is only what we (Jews) follow. Therefore, follow us, O Muhammad, and you will be rightly guided." The Christians said something similar. Allah then revealed ayah 135.

Notice the shape of the claim. It is not an argument. It is a demand to change labels: *become one of us and you will be guided.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets this against what came just before in the surah, where the religion (*millah*) of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) had already been defined and shown to be, in its present form, Islam. Both groups claimed Ibrahim as their own, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, yet "in spite of their pretension to be his followers, did not in actual fact follow his religion."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful and fair here: each of those two religions was, in its own time and for its own time, a genuine religion. The problem is not that they were never true. It is that in its present form each had become distorted, and each had been abrogated by Allah. So the invitation is backwards — an invitation into a lapsed and altered version of what Islam now carries whole.

## "Rather — the way of Ibrahim, ḥanīf" (ayah 135)

The reply in ayah 135 does not counter one label with another. Say *bal* — "nay, rather" — and then name not a community but a *millah*: the religion of Ibrahim.

The key word is **ḥanīf**. Two explanations are given by the early authorities Ibn Kathir cites, and they complete each other:

- Muhammad bin Ka'b Al-Qurazi and 'Isa bin Jariyah explained *ḥanīf* as being **on the straight path**.
- Abu Qilabah said: "The Ḥanīf is what the Messengers, from beginning to end, believed in."

So *ḥanīf* is not a sect. It is the single unbending direction every messenger faced. Ibn Kathir renders the sense of the reply plainly: "We do not need the Judaism or Christianity that you call us to." And the ayah closes by ruling out the one thing that could corrupt that direction — *and he was not of the idolaters*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why this description of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is the decisive one: he shunned every kind of association (*shirk*), adored nothing but Allah alone, obeyed no one but Him — and for that reason his religion "did not have even a trace of distortion."

## The creed the believers are told to say (ayah 136)

Ayah 135 tells the Prophet ﷺ to say. Ayah 136 tells *you* — the community — to say. The creed is not left as private conviction; it is put into the believers' mouths as declared speech.

**Belief in the revelation, not only in the Revealer.** Ibn Kathir explains that Allah directed His believing servants to believe in what was sent down to them through His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ *and* in what was revealed to the earlier prophets in general — some named here, many others not named at all.

**Al-Asbāṭ.** The ayah names Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub, then *al-Asbāṭ*. Al-Qurtubi is quoted: "Sibt is the group of people or a tribe all belonging to the same ancestors." Abu Al-'Aliyah, Ar-Rabi' and Qatadah said the Asbat are the twelve sons of Ya'qub, each of whom had an *ummah* of people from his descendants — hence the name. Al-Khalil bin Ahmad and others said the Asbat among the Children of Israel are like the tribes among the Children of Isma'il. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān dwells on the blessing in this: in Egypt, Yusuf and his brothers (peace be upon them) made up a group of twelve men; by the time the Israelites left Egypt with Musa (peace be upon him) their numbers ran into thousands — and among that progeny Allah raised a large number of prophets. Ibn Kathir cites Musa's own words to them: *Remember the favour of Allah to you: when He made Prophets among you, made you kings* (5:20), and *And We divided them into twelve tribes* (7:160).

**"We make no distinction between any of them."** This is the hinge of the creed, and it answers the claim of ayah 135 directly. Ibn Kathir says the believers were directed to refrain from differentiating between the prophets and to believe in them all, avoiding what Allah described elsewhere: those who *wish to make distinction between Allah and His Messengers, saying, "We believe in some but reject others," and wish to adopt a way in between. They are in truth disbelievers* (4:150–151).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a needed precision: some prophets may in some ways be superior to others, but it is essential for a Muslim to believe in **all** of them without making any distinction. The "no distinction" is about accepting or rejecting them — not a denial of the ranks Allah Himself gave.

**And their scriptures now?** Ibn Kathir quotes Qatadah: "Allah commanded the believers to believe in Him and in all His Books and Messengers." And Sulayman bin Habib: "We were commanded to believe in the (original) Torah and Injil, but not to implement them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same in doctrinal form: the Sharī'ahs of all the prophets named here were instituted by Allah Himself, but they have now been abrogated, so Muslims follow the Sharī'ah of the Prophet ﷺ, "for this alone is now valid."

## From the Sunnah

**Al-Bukhari** narrated that Abu Hurayrah said: "The People of the Book used to read the Torah in Hebrew and translate it into Arabic for the Muslims. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *Do not believe the People of the Book, nor reject what they say. Rather, say, 'We believe in Allah and in what was sent down to us.'*"

That is ayah 136 turned into a working posture. Faced with a report you cannot verify — from a scripture that was genuine but is now altered — you neither endorse it nor call it a lie. You return to what you *do* know was sent down.

**Muslim, Abu Dawud and An-Nasa'i** recorded that Ibn 'Abbas said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mostly used to recite *We believe in Allah and that which has been sent down to us* (2:136) and *We believe in Allah, and bear witness that we are Muslims* (3:52) in the two voluntary rak'ahs before Fajr. The creed of this passage was not only something the believers were told to declare; it was on the Prophet's own tongue ﷺ in his prayer.

## The measure of true faith (ayah 137)

Ayah 137 is the sharpest line in the passage, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats it as nothing less than a definition of *īmān* (faith): "if they believe in the like of that which you believe, then they are rightly guided."

Read the wording closely. It does not say "if they believe" — it says *if they believe in the like of what you believe*. Faith is measured not by the claim to have it but by its **content and its match**. And who is "you"? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers: the immediate addressees are the Prophet ﷺ and his blessed Companions. Their *īmān* is placed before us as the model, and the ayah is in effect a divine command — that the only faith acceptable to Allah is the one the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions held, and that doctrines deviating from it in the least are neither valid nor acceptable.

Concretely, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: believe in Allah and His attributes, in the angels, in the Books, in the messengers and prophets and their teachings **exactly as** the Prophet ﷺ and the Companions did — adding nothing, subtracting nothing, advancing no interpretations of one's own, distorting no authentic meanings. And do not assign to angels or prophets a station higher or lower than the one the Prophet ﷺ assigned them by word or deed. To this it adds that one must also be sincere and pure in faith, since the contrary would amount to hypocrisy (*nifāq*).

**Two ditches, one road.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows that the ayah cuts both ways at once, because deviation has two opposite forms. Some of the associators of Arabia denied the very existence of angels; others considered them daughters of Allah. Some groups among the Jews refused to obey the prophets and were so hostile to them that they came to assassinate a number of them; while other groups among the Jews and Christians revered the prophets so extravagantly as to identify them with Allah Himself, or to place them on the level of Allah, or to consider them sons of Allah. These, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, are the two extremes of deviation, and in the light of this ayah they are seen to be only two forms of misguidance.

**Where the line falls.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is emphatic that the Sharī'ah makes it obligatory on every Muslim to respect and love the Prophet ﷺ, and that one who falls short in this cannot be said to possess *īmān* in the true sense. But it warns just as firmly that it is misguidance and *shirk* to make him the equal of Allah with respect to an attribute such as knowledge or power. Its definition of *shirk* is drawn from the Qur'an itself — making someone other than Allah His equal with respect to a divine attribute — as indicated by *And when we used to make you equal of the Lord of the worlds* (26:98). So those who hold the Prophet ﷺ to be omniscient and omnipresent as Allah is, while congratulating themselves on showing the love and respect required of a Muslim, are in fact disobeying him and going against his teachings. The love and honour Allah requires is the love and honour his blessed Companions had for him — "neither more nor less than this, for either would be a deviation and a sin."

**Two later distortions, judged by the same ayah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān applies this standard to its own age in two directions. First, to those it names — the Qadianis and the Ahmadis of Lahore — who deny the Qur'an's unambiguous and clear declaration that Muhammad ﷺ is the last of all the prophets, with the Qadianis trying to make room for a new prophet by manufacturing categories such as *buruz* (incarnation) and *zill* (manifestation): the *īmān* of the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions shows no trace of belief in prophets of that kind. Second, to those whose minds are so befogged in modern materialism and so-called "rationalism" that they subject the next world to "crooked interpretations," supposing this to be a service to Islam. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names what is inadmissible: that resurrection will be only "spiritual" and not bodily, that reward and punishment there will be "spiritual" and not physical, or that the "weighing of the deeds" is merely a metaphorical expression. Measured against the *īmān* of the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions, such readings are false and unacceptable.

**"But if they turn away."** Ibn Kathir sets out the two outcomes. If they believe in all of Allah's Books and Messengers without differentiating between any of them, *then they are rightly guided* — they would acquire the truth and be directed to it. But if they turn from truth to falsehood **after proof had been presented to them**, then they are in *shiqāq* — opposition, a standing apart on the far side. This is no longer a case of unclear evidence; it is a chosen posture.

And to that, the answer is not argument but reassurance: *So Allah will suffice you against them.* Ibn Kathir explains it as Allah aiding the believers against them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ not to worry over enemies who remain unconvinced out of sheer obstinacy and malice — Allah will deal with them Himself and protect His prophet, a promise made more explicitly in *And Allah will protect you against these people* (5:67), and one that subsequent events showed fulfilled. The ayah then seals it with two of Allah's names: *He is the Hearer, the Knower*.

## The colouring of Allah (ayah 138)

*Ṣibghata-llāh* — the colouring, or dye, of Allah. Ibn Kathir reports from Ad-Dahhak that Ibn 'Abbas explained it simply as **"the religion of Allah,"** and notes the same explanation reported from Mujahid, Abu Al-'Aliyah, 'Ikrimah, Ibrahim, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak, 'Abdullah bin Kathir, 'Atiyah Al-'Awfi, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas, As-Suddi and other scholars. He places alongside it *the fitrah of Allah* (30:30) — the original disposition Allah made — with its instruction to hold to it.

Why *colour*, though? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the expression carries several levels of meaning, but that the immediate allusion is to a Christian ceremony: on the seventh day after birth an infant was bathed in coloured (probably yellow) water, supposed to be a substitute for circumcision and a sufficient guarantee of the infant's external and internal purification — the fast, indelible dye of the faith. The ayah's retort is quiet: that colour is washed away with the water, leaving no trace outside or inside, and it neither serves the purpose of circumcision nor cleanses a man of physical impurity. The only colouring worth the name, the ayah declares, is the colouring of a genuine and unabrogated religion — the only one that can guarantee physical and spiritual purification, and the only one that shall remain. *And who is better than Allah in colouring?*

Then Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the deeper sense. Just as a colour is openly and clearly visible to the beholder, so the signs of genuine and pure *īmān* should shine through a Muslim's face, movements, habits and behaviour. In this sense the ayah is a commandment: **dye yourselves in the colouring of Allah, outwardly and inwardly** — by offering unalloyed worship to Him alone, by submitting totally to His commandments, and by gladly accepting His will. Which is why the ayah ends *and we are His worshippers*: the colour is not a mark received once, but a life of worship.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also sets ayah 138 beside ayah 135 and draws the conclusion the whole passage has been building toward. Ayah 135 identified Islam with "the religion of Ibrahim"; ayah 138 calls it "the colouring of Allah." Put the two together, it says, and it becomes clear that essentially Islam — or any authentic religion — is the religion of Allah, and that the association of a religion with the name of a prophet can only be symbolic. That dissolves the demand of ayah 135, which was precisely a demand to take on a community's name.

## Living it

Read as one piece, the passage asks five things of a believer — the tenets Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws directly from these ayat: believe in Allah and in the guidance He has sent through the Prophet ﷺ; believe in all the prophets Allah sent from time to time, named and unnamed; make no distinction among them in belief, even while knowing some may in some ways be superior to others; know that the Sharī'ahs of the earlier prophets were instituted by Allah but are now abrogated, so that the Sharī'ah of the Prophet ﷺ alone is followed; and finally, obey Allah alone and submit totally to Him.

And it leaves two habits behind. From the hadith in Al-Bukhari: when you meet a claim from a scripture you cannot verify, neither confirm nor deny it — say, *we believe in Allah and in what was sent down to us*, and stand there. And from what Ibn 'Abbas reported: those same words were among what the Prophet ﷺ mostly recited in the two voluntary rak'ahs before Fajr — the creed of this passage, kept close in his own prayer.

passages.title: Disputing over Allah and over Abraham's faith
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are one closing statement, not three separate notes. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that they "bring to an end the section of the Surah in which certain claims of the Jews and the Christians have been refuted." Two claims in particular: that Ibrahim, Ismaʿil, Ishaq, Yaʿqub (peace be upon them) and the prophets in his lineage were either Jews or Christians, and the claim that they were the chosen people who would have the exclusive privilege of being sent straight to Paradise while Muslims were denied it.

Read together, the three ayat form a single reply the Prophet ﷺ and the believers are told to give — first about Allah, then about the prophets, then about ancestry — and every part of it pulls in one direction: Allah is the Lord of all, so no group holds Him as private property, and no one is carried to safety by the names in his family tree.

## Where we are in the surah

The preceding ayat had already settled the historical point: Maʿārif says they established that the religion of all these prophets was Islam, in the general sense of the term — but that the earlier codes of law (Shariʿahs) have now been abrogated, and the title "Islam" has been given specifically to the religion of Sayyidna Muhammad ﷺ.

Should the Jews and the Christians still continue in their stubbornness to deny, Maʿārif continues, Allah asks the Holy Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims to declare in plain and simple words that Allah, "being the Lord of All, cannot show any special favour to any particular group of His creatures." What follows in these three ayat is that declaration, given to them ready-made.

## The declaration begins: "Would you dispute with us about Allah?"

Ibn Kathir opens his comment by saying that Allah directed His Prophet ﷺ to pre-empt the arguments. The reply is placed in the believers' mouths before the quarrel has run its course.

And Ibn Kathir spells out what the dispute was actually over: **"Do you dispute with us regarding the Oneness of Allah, obedience and submission to Him and in avoiding His prohibitions."** So the disagreement is not an abstract one. It concerns whether Allah alone is worshipped and obeyed.

Ibn Kathir also gathers, around this ayah, the other places where the Qur'an records a dispute of this kind. Two of them concern Ibrahim himself: *"His people disputed with him. He said: 'Do you dispute with me concerning Allah?'"* (6:80), and *"Have you not looked at him who disputed with Ibrahim about his Lord?"* (2:258). The Qur'an is not new to this scene, and neither is the prophetic way of answering it.

**"While He is our Lord and your Lord."** This short clause is the hinge of the whole passage. Ibn Kathir explains it as: "He has full control over us and you, and deserves the worship alone without partners." Maʿārif draws the consequence: a Lordship that covers both parties cannot be claimed by either as a private inheritance. If He is your Lord too, the question is no longer whose ancestors were whose — it is who is actually submitting to Him.

## "For us our deeds, and for you your deeds"

From Lordship the ayah moves straight to accounting, and this is where ayah 139 already begins reaching forward to ayah 141.

Maʿārif: on the Day of Judgment Allah "will assess the Jews and the Christians as well as the Muslims according to what each has believed in and how each has been behaving" — and, it points out, this was "a principle which was accepted by the People of the Book too." The argument is built on ground the other side already stood on.

Ibn Kathir reads the same words as a declaration of separation: "we disown you and what you worship, just as you disown us." He places the clause alongside two other verses where Allah teaches His Messenger ﷺ the same reply — *"For me are my deeds and for you are your deeds! You are innocent of what I do, and I am innocent of what you do!"* (10:41), and *"So if they dispute with you say: 'I have submitted myself to Allah, and so have those who follow me'"* (3:20).

There is a certain dignity in answering this way. It does not shout, and it does not pretend the difference is small. It says plainly: our paths are separate, each of us carries his own file, and no argument will change whose name is on it.

## "And to Him we are purely devoted"

Here the reply turns from what the believers deny to what they are. Maʿārif says ayah 139 "brings out the essential and peculiar characteristic of the Islamic Ummah" — that it has purified itself of all possible admixture of *Shirk* (associating anything with Allah) and devoted itself to Allah externally and internally. Ibn Kathir's gloss is two words: "in worship and submission."

The Arabic word in the text is *Mukhlisun*, the plural of *Mukhlis*. Maʿārif explains that it signifies "one who has purified himself," and that it is allied to the word *Ikhlas*, "the act of purifying oneself." That is the root image behind the term: not a warm feeling, but a substance with the foreign matter taken out of it.

Maʿārif then quotes **Saʿid ibn Jubayr**, according to whom *Ikhlas* consists in three things: worshipping no one but Allah; associating no one with Allah; and doing good deeds only for the sake of obeying Allah, and not for the purpose of winning the admiration of the people. And certain spiritual masters, Maʿārif reports, have said that *Ikhlas* is a deed which can be identified neither by men, nor by angels, nor by Satan — that it is a "secret" between Allah and His servant.

Maʿārif also notes the contrast the ayah is drawing. The Muslims are asked to announce that they recognise no other god but Allah and have purified their religion of all traces of association — "as against the Jews and the Christians who consider Sayyidna ʿUzayr (Ezra) and Sayyidna ʿIsa (Jesus) respectively to be 'the Son of God'," and whose religions have, moreover, been abrogated. "In this respect at least," Maʿārif says, "Muslims have a superiority over them." Notice what that superiority rests on in Maʿārif's account: not blood, but a religion kept clear of association — which is exactly the ground these three ayat are contesting.

### A warning about the word "sincerity"

Maʿārif attaches a long and unusually practical footnote here, because *Ikhlas* is usually rendered into English as "sincerity" — and it doubts that the English word ever carried the full range of meaning the Arabic word carries.

The older sense of "sincerity," Maʿārif says, implied a harmony between external action and inner inclination, along with the tacit assumption that the external action was at least socially acceptable to some degree. In current usage the sense has become "not only perverted but sometimes actually inverted": it now suggests compliance with one's emotions or even one's instincts, and is used to justify and authorise grave wrongs. That, Maʿārif says, is the exact antithesis of *Ikhlas*. One cannot attain even the lowest degree of *Ikhlas* without forming a clear intention to obey the injunctions of the Shariʿah, rather than being guided by instinctual urges and emotional inclinations. The fashionable "sincerity," it warns, reduces a person to "an automaton at the mercy of his reflexes."

Then comes the part that will reach many readers personally. There is another allied notion of "sincerity," Maʿārif says — one that has disturbed the peace of many pious people even in the past, and that has acquired "a devastating intensity" in our own days. It demands fixity and unrelieved continuity in an emotional state, "which is, of course, not possible for man as he is constituted." It so happens with some pious people that once they start seeking this in their enjoined prayers, they find they cannot keep up an unbroken concentration of mind, and are so frightened by the lapse that they sometimes give up praying altogether, believing such worship to be "insincere" and hence invalid.

Maʿārif answers this plainly, and the answer deserves to be read slowly: the only thing the Shariʿah requires from us is **to have the correct intention and attitude when we begin** our prayers or perform any other good deed. That alone is the prerequisite for attaining *Ikhlas*, which "is not a matter of emotions and affective states." Islam requires us to perfect *Ikhlas* as the Shariʿah defines it, not to seek "sincerity" in the Western sense of the term, ancient or modern. (For an elaborate treatment of the subject, Maʿārif refers the reader to *Tarbiyyah al-Salik* by Maulana Ashraf ʿAli Thanavi (رح).)

So a wandering mind in your ṣalāh is not proof that your prayer is worthless. Begin rightly, for Allah alone, and the deed stands.

## "Do you know better, or does Allah?"

With the believers' position stated, the passage turns on the historical claim: **"Or say you that Ibrahim, Ismaʿil, Ishaq, Yaʿqub and Al-Asbāṭ were Jews or Christians?"** *Al-Asbāṭ* appears as "the tribes" in Al-Hasan al-Basri's words below; the translation of the ayah renders it "his descendants"; Maʿārif speaks of the prophets in Yaʿqub's lineage.

Ibn Kathir says Allah then criticised them for the claim that Ibrahim, the Prophets who came after him, and the Asbāṭ were following their religion, whether Judaism or Christianity. And the reply is devastating in its simplicity: **"Say: Do you know better, or does Allah?"** Ibn Kathir's comment: Allah has the best knowledge, and He stated that they were neither Jews nor Christians — as He said elsewhere, *"Ibrahim was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a true Muslim, Hanifa, and he was not of Al-Mushrikin"* (3:67).

Maʿārif frames the same words as the one question that ends the discussion: if the People of the Book, on account of their affiliation with the earlier prophets, keep insisting on their own rectitude, "the Muslims may ask them a basic question — who knows the truth better, Allah or the People of the Book?" Allah has definitely and finally announced the truth in the Last Revelation. There is no appeal above that.

## A testimony held, and hidden

The charge that follows is not merely that they were mistaken.

**Al-Hasan al-Basri**, quoted by Ibn Kathir, says: "They used to recite the Book of Allah He sent to them that stated that the true religion is Islam and that Muhammad ﷺ is the Messenger of Allah. Their Book also stated that Ibrahim, Ismaʿil, Ishaq, Yaʿqub and the tribes were neither Jews, nor Christians. They testified to these facts, yet hid them from the people."

Maʿārif says the same in its own words: the People of the Book themselves know that the religion of the earlier prophets was Islam, "yet they are trying to conceal the truth, and being unjust, in the gravest sense of the term." That phrase — the gravest sense of the term — is worth pausing on. The wrong here is not ignorance. It is holding a testimony that came from Allah and sitting on it.

**"And Allah is not unaware of what you do."** Ibn Kathir calls this "a threat and a warning that His knowledge encompasses every one's deeds, and He shall award each accordingly." Truth can be hidden from people. It cannot be hidden from the One whose knowledge takes in everything a person does. A concealed testimony is already recorded.

## The seal: "That was a nation who has passed away"

Ayah 141 delivers the verdict, and Maʿārif points out that it is a repetition of ayah 134 — the same words at both ends of this whole section. The repetition is not filler; it is a seal on the argument.

**"That was a nation who has passed away"** — Ibn Kathir: meaning, existed before you. **"They shall receive the reward of what they earned, and you of what you earn"** — they bear their deeds while you bear yours. **"And you will not be asked of what they used to do."**

Ibn Kathir draws out the intended blow: "the fact that you are their relatives will not suffice, unless you imitate their good deeds. Further, do not be deceived by the fact that you are their descendants, unless you imitate them in obeying Allah's orders and following His Messengers who were sent as warners and bearers of good news." Maʿārif says it in different words: the ayah "warns them against the consequences of their vanity and pretentiousness, and advises them to take care of themselves rather than relying on ancestral glory."

And Ibn Kathir closes with the principle that decides the case: "whoever disbelieves in even one Prophet, will have disbelieved in all the Messengers" — especially if one disbelieves in the master and Final Messenger from Allah, sent to all mankind and the jinn. So the claim to Ibrahim collapses in the very act of rejecting the Messenger who was sent last. May Allah's peace and blessings be on Muhammad ﷺ and the rest of Allah's Prophets.

## Living it

The passage was revealed against a specific claim, but the disease it treats is universal — and note that the Qur'an aims it here at people who really were descended from prophets. If ancestry could not shelter them, it shelters no one.

**Inherited religion earns nothing.** The closing ayah removes ancestry as a defence in the plainest possible terms. A pious father, a scholarly grandfather, a family known for religion, a community with a proud history — none of it appears on your record. What appears is what you earned. The link to the righteous that counts, Ibn Kathir says, is imitating their good deeds and obeying Allah's orders as they obeyed them.

**Keep the deed clean.** The passage defines the believing community by *Ikhlas* — worshipping no one but Allah, associating no one with Allah, and doing good deeds for the sake of obeying Allah rather than to win people's admiration, as Saʿid ibn Jubayr defined it. Take the reassurance along with the standard: what is required is the correct intention and attitude when you begin, not a sustained emotional glow you cannot manufacture.

**Do not sit on the truth.** Concealing a testimony you hold from Allah is named here as injustice in the gravest sense. Anyone who knows something of the religion and hides it — for reputation, for comfort, for the sake of a group he does not want to disappoint — should read Al-Hasan al-Basri's words slowly.

**Argue like this.** When the Prophet ﷺ is taught how to answer, he is given the shared ground first (He is our Lord and your Lord), then the principle of individual accountability, then a clear statement of who the believers are — and no insult anywhere in it. The question "Do you know better, or does Allah?" is sharp, but it is a question, and it points away from both parties to the One who knows.

passages.title: The objection to the qiblah and the middle community
passages.tafsir:
**Two ayat, one argument.** A community that had prayed towards Jerusalem for sixteen or seventeen months is turned towards the Kaʿbah in Makkah, and the mockers pounce. Ayah 142 records their objection and answers it in a line: direction belongs to Allah, not to a building. Ayah 143 lifts the same episode onto a higher plane — the change was the crowning of this Ummah as a *wasaṭ* community, a sifting of who genuinely follows the Messenger ﷺ, and a reassurance that nothing offered in obedience is ever wasted. What holds the two together is one question: **is worship about a place, or about obedience?**

## What actually happened

Ibn Kathir builds his commentary on the narration of al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib, reported by **Imam al-Bukhari** (and, Ibn Kathir notes, collected by **Muslim** through another chain). The Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed facing Bayt al-Maqdis in Jerusalem for sixteen or seventeen months, "but he wished that he could pray facing the Kaʿbah." The first prayer he offered towards the Kaʿbah was ʿAṣr. One man who had prayed with him then passed a mosque whose worshippers were bowing towards Jerusalem, and called out that he bore witness he had just prayed with the Prophet ﷺ facing Makkah — "hearing that, those people immediately changed their direction towards the House while still as they were," that is, still in rukūʿ.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, drawing on Ibn Kathir, names that congregation as the mosque of the Banū Salamah, and adds a detail related by Nuwaylah bint Muslim: the women who had been in the back row moved, "so that when the orientation had been changed, men were again in the front row and women in the back row."

The news travelled slowly. **Al-Bukhari and Muslim** record from Ibn ʿUmar that the people of Qubāʾ heard only the next morning, during Fajr: a man came and said Qurʾan had been revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanding him to face the Kaʿbah — "therefore, face the Kaʿbah." They had been facing Ash-Shām; they turned. **At-Tirmidhi** adds that they too were bowing when they turned; **Muslim** reports this last narration from Anas.

Sit with that image: worshippers mid-prayer, bent in rukūʿ, receiving a command through a passer-by and swivelling on the spot. Ibn Kathir's comment is exact — these narrations "indicate the perfect obedience the Companions had for Allah and His Messenger ﷺ."

Ibn Kathir draws a legal point from the Qubāʾ story: **an abrogating text binds you only once you know of it.** Companions who prayed ʿAṣr, Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ towards Jerusalem after the revelation had come down were never told to repeat them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, citing Imam al-Jaṣṣāṣ, that a report carried by only one or two people (*khabar al-wāḥid*) was accepted here because every Companion already knew the Prophet ﷺ longed for the Kaʿbah and had been praying for it — so the continuation of Jerusalem as qiblah was already felt to be uncertain rather than settled.

## The word *sufahāʾ* — "the fools"

Ibn Kathir sets the scene: when the change of qiblah occurred, "those inflicted with hypocrisy and mistrust, and the disbelieving Jews, both were led astray from the right guidance and fell into confusion." He identifies the speakers of the objection as the idolaters, the hypocrites and the Jews; elsewhere he glosses "the fools among the people" as the People of the Scripture. Following ʿAli ibn Abi Ṭalḥah's report from Ibn ʿAbbās, he notes the Jews had been delighted when the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to face Jerusalem, and did not like the change. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says some Jews, associators and hypocrites "began to scoff at the Holy Prophet ﷺ and his Companions for being so capricious in the matter of their Qiblah" — as Ibn Kathir renders their words, what is the matter with these people, who face one direction at one time and another at another?

The Qurʾan's word for them is *sufahāʾ*. These sources render it "the fools," "stupid people," those who "have besotted themselves" — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the deliberate echo: earlier in this surah, those who turn away from the religion of Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) were described in just those terms. And it locates their folly precisely: their stupidity "lies in not realizing that the East and the West both belong to Allah Himself, and that He guides whomsoever He likes on the straight path."

## "To Allah belong the east and the west"

Ibn Kathir glosses this with real economy: it means **"the command, the decision and the authority are for Allah Alone."** He links it to two other ayat of this surah — "so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah" (2:115), and "It is not righteousness that you turn your faces towards east or west; but righteousness is the one who believes in Allah" (2:177) — then states the principle: "the best act is to adhere to Allah's commands. Hence, wherever He commands us to face, we should face… if He commands us every day to face different places, we are His servants and under His disposal."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the point to its edge: neither the Kaʿbah nor Bayt al-Maqdis "by itself possesses any exclusive merit in this regard, and it is the divine commandment alone which gives to it the distinction of being the Qiblah." The change may have been meant "to show to the people in a visible form that a Qiblah is not an idol to be worshipped but only a concrete expression of divine commandment, and may hence be changed as and when Allah wills."

And yet Ibn Kathir will not let the Kaʿbah be treated as incidental. Allah's kindness here is immense, he says: "Allah has guided them to the Qiblah of Ibrāhīm — Allah's Khalīl (intimate friend)… the most honorable house of worship on the face of the earth, which was built by Ibrāhīm al-Khalīl in the Name of Allah, the One without a partner." Both are true at once: the honour is real, and it comes entirely from Allah's choosing.

**Why have a fixed qiblah at all?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers: Allah is free of all dimensions, so logically each worshipper could face where he liked — but a shared orientation gives the community a visible form of unity. People have tried to unite around race, colour, homeland, language; all are "arbitrary and accidental," and instead of bringing men together, they divide them. Islam builds on doctrinal unity — the worship of the One — then gives it outward expressions anyone can adopt with equal ease: keeping the ranks straight in congregational prayer, following the movements of the imam, the single form of dress in Ḥajj, and above all the qiblah. Had the choice been left to people it "would in itself have become a cause of dissension."

## Which qiblah came first?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports a genuine difference among the Companions and their Successors. According to **Ibn ʿAbbās** — the view Ibn Kathir says Ibn ʿAbbās and the majority of scholars held — Bayt al-Maqdis was the qiblah from the start; in Makkah the Prophet ﷺ would stand between the Black Stone and the Yemeni corner so that his face was towards Bayt al-Maqdis *and* the House at once, a posture no longer possible in Madinah. **Other Companions** held that the Kaʿbah was the qiblah when the five prayers were made obligatory in Makkah, as it had been for Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl (peace be upon them), that Jerusalem was appointed after the Hijrah, and the Kaʿbah then restored; al-Qurṭubī, relying on Abu ʿAmr, prefers this second view.

Each carries its own wisdom. On the first, Jerusalem distinguished the Muslims from the idolaters of Makkah, and later the Kaʿbah marked them off from the Jews of Madinah. On the second, the Prophet ﷺ adopted the Jews' orientation under divine command to familiarise them with Islam, and when their hostility proved settled, Allah allowed him back to the qiblah of his forefathers. Either way, "the real import of the verse remains the same."

## *Ummah wasaṭ* — the middle community

Ayah 143 does not defend the change; it announces a station. Ibn Kathir explains *wasaṭ* as **"the best and the most honored,"** showing the usage from Arab speech: to say Quraysh is in the *wasaṭ* among the Arab tribes means it is the best of them; the Prophet ﷺ being in the *wasaṭ* of his people means he was from the best sub-tribe; and ʿAṣr, the prayer described as *al-wusṭā*, means the best prayer, "as the authentic collections of Aḥādīth reported."

The Prophet ﷺ himself glossed the word. **Imam Ahmad** reported from Abu Saʿīd that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said Nūḥ will be called on the Day of Resurrection and asked whether he conveyed the message; he will say yes; his people will deny that any warner came; asked who testifies for him, he will answer, "Muhammad and his Ummah." The Prophet ﷺ then said, **"the *wasaṭ* means the *ʿadl* (just)"** — you will be summoned to testify that Nūḥ conveyed, "and I will attest to your testimony" — which is ayah 143's own closing clause. Ibn Kathir notes it was also recorded by **al-Bukhari, at-Tirmidhi, an-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah**. A second narration from Abu Saʿīd al-Khudrī in **Imam Ahmad** widens this to any prophet; asked how it could know, this Ummah answers, "Our Prophet came to us and told us that the Messengers have conveyed."

That is the logic of ayah 143. **Being *wasaṭ* is not a compliment; it is a qualification to testify.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the legal inference: Allah made this Ummah equitable and just, and hence trustworthy, *so that* it may be qualified to bear witness — from which it follows that one who is not *ʿadl*, trustworthy as the Sharīʿah defines it, cannot be accepted as a witness in a court of law. Al-Qurṭubī, it reports, derives from this ayah the authority of *ijmāʿ*, the consensus of the Ummah, as one of the deciding agencies in legislation; al-Tafsīr al-Maẓharī reasons that if a consensus on error were possible, the Ummah could not be characterised as moderate and just at all; and Imam al-Jaṣṣāṣ holds that this trustworthiness is not particular to the Prophet's ﷺ own time but belongs to the Muslims of every age until the Day of Judgement. One caution the same source adds: *ijmāʿ* here is not a referendum by adult franchise, but the agreement of scholars who possess the authority to exercise ijtihād.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also reads *wasaṭ* as **balance**, explaining it through *muʿtadil* and *iʿtidāl* — moderate, equilibrium — words from the same root as *ʿadl*: as bodily health depends on the balance of the body's elements and disease on its disturbance, so in the ethical and spiritual sphere health depends on inner equilibrium and illness arises from intemperance. Earlier communities, it observes, swung between taking their prophets to be sons of Allah and refusing to obey a prophet they had already recognised; between scholars who altered the injunctions and even the text of their scriptures, and ascetics who shut themselves in monastic cells and refused Allah's permitted blessings. This Ummah has loved its Prophet ﷺ enough to sacrifice life and family at his call, yet has never raised him above "the servant of Allah, and His messenger," and has shown "that religion is meant to be put into action in the market-places and the halls of power as much as in the mosques and the contemplative retreats."

## The test, and those who turned on their heels

"And We made the qiblah which you used to face only to test those who followed the Messenger from those who would turn on their heels." Ibn Kathir explains: Allah legislated Jerusalem first and then changed it to the Kaʿbah "so as to find who will follow and obey you and thus face whatever you face." *Turning on one's heels*, he says plainly, means **reverting from one's religion** — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that history bore this out: after this ayah was revealed, those weak in faith and the hypocrites forsook Islam, some even accusing the Prophet ﷺ of having gone back to the ways of his own people.

"Indeed it was heavy" — Ibn Kathir does not minimise this. The change weighed on the heart, "except for whomever Allah has rightly guided their hearts," those certain the Messenger ﷺ is true, and who believe that "Allah does what He wills, decides what He wills, commands His servants with what He wills, abrogates any of His commands that He wills, and that He has the perfect wisdom and the unequivocal proof in all this." The same event that deepens a believer's certainty breeds doubt in a diseased heart — as Allah says of a newly revealed surah, it increases the believers in faith while it adds to the doubt of those with disease in their hearts (9:124–125), and the Qurʾan is "a healing and a mercy to those who believe" while it increases the wrongdoers "in nothing but loss" (17:82). Ibn Kathir adds that those who obeyed without doubt or hesitation were the leaders of the Companions. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the lesson bluntly: rectitude lies in obeying each and every divine commandment unquestioningly, without being too curious about its rationale, "for, those who seek a *raison d'être* usually do so because they wish to deny or denigrate or disobey the Sharīʿah."

## "Allah would never let your faith go to waste"

This is the tenderest line in the passage, and it answers a real worry. In the narration of al-Barāʾ collected by **al-Bukhari**, the Companions said of those who had prayed towards Jerusalem and then died or been martyred: "we did not know what to say about them." Then this line came down.

Ibn Kathir also cites a **separate report of al-Barāʾ transmitted by Muhammad bin Isḥāq**, in which a man from among the Muslims said, "We wish we could know about those among us who died before the Qiblah was changed, and also about our own prayers, that we had performed towards Bayt al-Maqdis" — and this same line was revealed. And Ibn Kathir notes a report in the Ṣaḥīḥ, from Abu Isḥāq as-Sabīʿī from al-Barāʾ, that "the people asked about the matter of those who offered prayers towards Bayt al-Maqdis and died," whereupon Allah revealed it; **at-Tirmidhi** recorded the same from Ibn ʿAbbās and graded it Ṣaḥīḥ.

Ibn Kathir's gloss: "the reward of your prayers towards Bayt al-Maqdis before would not be lost with Allah." Ibn ʿAbbās, reported by Ibn Isḥāq, expands it to cover both directions: "Your prayer towards the first Qiblah and your believing your Prophet and obeying him by facing the second Qiblah; He will grant you the rewards for all these acts."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records two readings of *īmān* here. In its usual sense of *faith*, the ayah reassures the Muslims against those who imagined, when the qiblah changed, that they had forsaken Islam and their faith had come to nothing. Taken — as some early commentators did, on the basis of certain narrations — to mean *the prayer itself*, it declares those Jerusalem-facing prayers valid and already accepted. A further point follows: the command to face Jerusalem is nowhere stated in the Qurʾan; the evidence for it is found only in the Hadith and the Sunnah. So an ayah of the Qurʾan here confirms as valid an injunction known only from Hadith — a fact which, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān comments, "shows the hollowness of the claim that the Holy Qurʾan can be fully understood without the help of the Hadith."

The passage closes on two of Allah's names: *Raʾūf*, full of kindness, and *Raḥīm*, Most Merciful. Ibn Kathir illustrates them with a scene reported in the Ṣaḥīḥ: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw a woman among some captives who had been separated from her child, holding each infant she found close to her chest as she searched — and when she found her own, she embraced him and nursed him. He ﷺ asked, "Do you think that this woman would willingly throw her son in the fire?" They said, "No, O Messenger of Allah!" He said, "By Allah, Allah is more merciful with His servants than this woman with her son."

## Living it

**Obedience does not wait for the rationale.** The Companions turned while bowing. The command came first; the wisdom followed, in ayah 143 itself.

**Nothing offered sincerely is lost.** A person may fear that years of worship rested on something now superseded. Allah settles it: *He would never let your faith go to waste.*

**Being *wasaṭ* is a job, not a badge.** Ibn Kathir says that since Allah made this Ummah *wasaṭ*, He endowed her with "the most complete legislation, the best Manhaj" — way or method — "and the clearest Madhhab," that is, methodology and manner of proceeding. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, from 3:110, that this community was "raised for mankind" — brought into being to work for the good of others, guiding people towards good deeds and dissuading them from evil. A community appointed to testify on the Day of Resurrection had better be worth believing.

A last note from Ibn Kathir explains the temperature of the objection in ayah 142. **Imam Ahmad** reported from ʿĀʾishah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said of the People of the Scripture: "They do not envy us for a matter more than they envy us for Jumuʿah, to which Allah has guided us and from which they were led astray; for the Qiblah to which Allah has directed us and from which they were led astray; and for our saying 'Āmīn' behind the Imam." The question in ayah 142 was never really a question. It was envy wearing the mask of an objection — and Allah answered it by reminding His servants Who owns the directions.

passages.title: Turn towards the Sacred Mosque; they know it is the truth
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are the moment the Muslim community was given its own direction of prayer: the Prophet ﷺ, who had been looking up at the sky in silent longing, is told his wish is granted and is commanded to turn towards the Sacred Mosque in Makkah. What holds the passage together is a single thread — this change is **the truth from your Lord**, and the very people who objected loudest already knew it was.

## The longing behind ayah 144

Ibn Kathir records, through Ali bin Abu Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, that the first thing abrogated in the Qur'an was the matter of the Qiblah (the direction faced in prayer). When Allah's Messenger ﷺ migrated to Al-Madinah, the majority of its people were Jews, and Allah commanded him to face Bayt Al-Maqdis; the Jews were delighted at this. He ﷺ faced it for "ten and some months" — but, Ibn 'Abbas says, he loved to face the Qiblah of Ibrahim, the Ka'bah. So he would supplicate to Allah and look up at the sky, awaiting the command. Then this ayah came down.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers the explanations scholars have given for that longing, noting they do not really contradict each other. Even before prophethood he ﷺ followed the way of Sayyidnā Ibrahim by the impulse of his own nature, and once revelation began the Qur'an itself declared his Sharī'ah to be in total accord with the Abrahamic way — and the Qiblah of Ibrahim and of Ismā'īl had been the Ka'bah. Then too, the Arab tribes, for all their idolatry, at least claimed to follow the way of Ibrahim and acknowledged the Ka'bah, so making it the Qiblah could open a door to them. And whatever hope there had been that facing Bayt Al-Maqdis might draw the Jews nearer had been dashed over those sixteen or seventeen months; their hostility, fed by vanity, had only grown more intense.

**Notice how he waited.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out something beautiful here. Prophets stand as close to Allah as a human being can, and that exalted station teaches a strict spiritual etiquette: they do not put a request before Allah unless they have been given permission to ask. From this, the commentary reasons that the Prophet ﷺ had already been allowed to make this du'a and hoped it would be granted — which is why he kept turning his face to the sky, anxiously waiting for an angel to bring the injunction he wished for.

**"Indeed, We see you turning your face towards heaven."** Allah does not rebuke that turning; He describes it appreciatively, and promises a Qiblah that will please him. And the promise is fulfilled in the very next breath: *"So turn your face in the direction of the Sacred Mosque."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Qurtubi, Jassās and Mazhari) calls this a manifestation of the subtle workings of divine grace — he ﷺ was first granted the joy of hearing a promise made, and immediately after, the greater joy of seeing it fulfilled.

## Why a direction at all?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān removes a misunderstanding before it can form. Allah is not confined to any direction or dimension — "And the East and the West both belong to Allah." Ibn Kathir notes that when the Jews objected, *"What has turned them from their Qiblah?"* (2:142), Allah answered with *"To Allah belong both the east and the west,"* and with *"wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah"* (2:115). The Qiblah is not because Allah is located over there. It is because a community scattered across the whole earth needs a visible symbol of its unity, and divine wisdom saw fit to assign one. Bayt Al-Maqdis could have served equally well; the Ka'bah was chosen in accordance with the wish of the Prophet ﷺ.

## The word Allah chose: *shaṭr*

Strictly speaking, the Qiblah is the Baytullāh — the Ka'bah itself. So we would expect the command to read "turn your face towards the Ka'bah." Instead it says: *turn your face towards **shaṭr al-Masjid al-Ḥarām***, the direction of the Sacred Mosque. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows that this one choice of wording settles several questions at once.

**First, "al-Masjid al-Ḥarām" rather than "the Ka'bah."** You can face the Ka'bah itself exactly only while you can see it with your own eyes. For anyone at a distance, exact alignment would be too rigorous an obligation — even with instruments it stays difficult and uncertain in far-off towns. But the Sharī'ah always aims at making things easy. So the Qur'an names the Sacred Mosque, which covers a far wider area and is easy to face from anywhere.

**Second, the word *shaṭr* itself.** In Arabic it can mean "the half of a thing," or "the direction in which a thing lies." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that by the consensus of the commentators it carries the second sense here (citing Al-Bahr al-Muhīt). So the word itself contains the ruling: for those far from Makkah it is not even necessary to face the Sacred Mosque exactly; facing *in its direction* is sufficient.

This is how the early authorities read it. Ibn Kathir reports that Al-Hakim related from 'Ali bin Abu Talib that the phrase means **its direction** — and Al-Hakim commented that the chain of this narration is authentic, though Al-Bukhari and Muslim did not include it in their collections. Ibn Kathir adds that this was also the position of Abu Al-'Aliyah, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id bin Jubayr, Qatadah, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas and others.

## "And wherever you are, turn your faces towards it"

Ibn Kathir reads this as a command to face the Ka'bah from wherever one is on the earth. He then lists the exceptions:

- **Voluntary (nafl) prayer while travelling** — one may pray in whatever direction the body is facing, while the heart intends the Ka'bah.
- **When battle is raging** — one prays however one is able.
- **One unsure of the direction** who prays the wrong way believing it to be the Qiblah — because Allah does not burden a soul beyond what it can bear.

## How exact must you be?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a hadith reported by **al-Tirmidhi** from the blessed Companion Abu Hurayrah: *"The Qiblah lies between the East and the West."* That hadith was addressed to the people of Madinah, whose Qiblah lies precisely to the south — and it serves, in effect, as an explanation of the phrase "in the direction of Al-Masjid al-Haram."

For lands east of Makkah, such as Pakistan and India, that direction is the west. Because the sun sets at a different point in summer than in winter, the Fuqahā' (the Muslim jurists) fixed the Qiblah for such lands as lying between those two points — an arc of some 48 degrees, so a deviation of up to 24 degrees either side still leaves the prayer perfectly valid. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is blunt about those who find a mosque off by two or three degrees and pronounce its prayers null and void: they only betray ignorance and a desire to produce confusion among Muslims. The Sharī'ah is meant for all people and all countries until the Day of Judgement, so its injunctions must be practicable for Muslims in far-flung hamlets, mountains, forests and islands, on the basis of their own observation, without instruments or calculations.

**The practical method.** The Successors of the Companions and the generations after them used a simple chain: if a town had a mosque built by the Companions, neighbouring mosques took its orientation, and those in turn became the model for mosques in surrounding villages. So the settled method far from Makkah has always been to conform to an established older mosque nearby. In deserted regions, forests or new settlements with no earlier mosque, one arrives at an approximate direction using the sun, the moon and the Pole-Star — phenomena everyone is familiar with — and any slight deviation one still suspects should simply be ignored. Al-Badā'i', the authoritative work of jurisprudence, holds that such an approximate orientation *stands for* the Ka'bah, and all the rulings of the Qiblah attach to it.

**Ibn Rajab**, the famous Hanbalī scholar of the eighth century after the Hijrah, is quoted to the same effect: astronomy is legitimate, in the view of the scholars generally, insofar as it helps in determining the Qiblah or finding one's way; beyond that it is unnecessary, distracts from weightier things, and indulgence in complex calculation can breed vile doubts about the prayer-niches of the Muslims — even the (totally false) belief that the prayers of the Companions and their Successors had been invalid. Ibn Rajab notes that Imām Ahmad ibn Hanbal forbade taking the Pole-Star as a proof, since what has come is only that the Qiblah lies between the East and the West. 'Allāma Bahr al-'Ulūm sums the matter up in his *Rasā'il al-Arkān*: the only condition is that the one praying be duly convinced his face is turned towards the Ka'bah — the Sharī'ah does not compel us to an orientation obtainable only with instruments — so a deviation invalidates the prayer only when it is as great as the difference between East and West.

## Ayah 145: this was never a negotiation

*"Even if you were to bring every proof to the People of the Book, they would not follow your Qiblah."* Ibn Kathir explains this as a description of their disbelief, stubbornness and defiance of what they know to be true: even if the Prophet ﷺ brought forward every proof, they would never obey him or abandon following their desires. He compares it with *"Truly, those against whom the Word of your Lord has been justified will not believe — even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful torment"* (10:96–97).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a telling detail: the two groups show equal malice even towards each other — the Jews adopted Bayt Al-Maqdis as their Qiblah, the Christians chose the East, and each rejects the other's. This was never a dispute that argument could resolve; it was sheer stubbornness.

**"Nor are you going to follow their Qiblah."** Ibn Kathir reads this as indicating the vigour with which the Messenger ﷺ implements what Allah commands: as tightly as they cling to their own opinions and desires, he adheres to Allah's commands, obeying Him and following what pleases Him, and would never fall in with their desires in any case. This clarifies something in hindsight — praying towards Bayt Al-Maqdis had never been because it was the Qiblah of the Jews, but because Allah had commanded it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the phrase further declares that the Baytullāh will remain the Qiblah until the end of the world, refuting the scoffing allegation of the People of the Book that Islamic injunctions had no stability and that the Muslims might yet revert to Bayt Al-Maqdis (Al-Bahr al-Muhīt).

**The warning at the end of the ayah.** *"If you follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you will surely be among the wrongdoers."* Ibn Kathir notes that Allah is warning those who defy the truth *knowingly*, because the proof against those who know is stronger than against other people. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that a prophet is protected from sin, so such a situation could never actually arise for him ﷺ; the warning is addressed to him outwardly but is in fact intended for his Ummah, so that it grasps the gravity of disobeying the injunction that established the Baytullāh as the Qiblah. And note the logic it lays bare: to keep following an injunction after it has been abrogated, while ignoring the one that replaced it, is not piety — it is disobedience to Allah, dressed up as personal opinion and desire.

## Ayah 146: "as they recognize their sons"

Ibn Kathir explains that the scholars of the People of the Scripture know the truth of what the Messenger ﷺ was sent with just as one of them knows his own child — a parable the Arabs used for something utterly obvious. (He notes the object of "recognize" has been understood as the Prophet ﷺ himself, or as the Ka'bah at Makkah.) In the same connection he relates that the Messenger ﷺ asked a man with a youngster, "Is this your son?" The man said, "Yes, O Messenger of Allah, I testify to this fact."

Ibn Kathir also reports, on the authority of Al-Qurtubi, that 'Umar asked 'Abdullah bin Salam — an Israelite scholar who had become Muslim — "Do you recognize Muhammad as you recognize your own son?" He replied: "Yes, and even more. The Honest One descended from heaven upon the Honest One on the earth with his description and I recognized him, although I do not know anything about his mother's story."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note of interpretive discipline. A simile does not carry every aspect of the two things compared into the comparison — only those relevant to the occasion — so one should not let the imagination roam far afield with this image. The point is simple: a son grows from infancy to manhood under his parents' eyes, so his face or general appearance is enough for a father to recognize him without doubt or hesitation. The Torah and the Evangel had foretold the coming of the final Prophet ﷺ and set down the signs by which he would be known; on the strength of the irrefutable evidence of their own scriptures, the Jews and Christians had that same certainty. To persist in denying him was as dishonest as refusing to recognize one's own son.

And then the sting at the end of the ayah: *"a party of them conceal the truth while they know it."* Ibn Kathir explains that they hide from people what they find in their books about the Prophet ﷺ; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point about the Qiblah — some of them, while denying the truth themselves, tried to keep it concealed from others, knowing full well that this ruling had been established by revelation from Allah Himself.

## Ayah 147: "The truth is from your Lord"

Ibn Kathir reads this as Allah strengthening the resolve of His Prophet ﷺ and of the believers, affirming that what he came with is the truth without doubt: *"so do not be one of those who doubt."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the phrase wider. "The Truth is from your Lord" can also be read in a general sense, as a definition of the nature of truth itself — that alone is truth which comes from Allah. One who has understood that can never allow himself to be in doubt about this particular truth, or about any other truth Allah has revealed to a prophet.

## Living it

**Face the Qiblah — and stop tormenting yourself over degrees.** The word *shaṭr* was chosen to make this easy. Follow the orientation of established mosques around you; where there are none, use the sun, moon and Pole-Star and ignore the slight doubt that remains.

**Let obedience, not agreement, be the reason.** He ﷺ faced Bayt Al-Maqdis because Allah commanded it, and turned from it the moment Allah commanded that. And ayah 144 honours his longing rather than rebuking it: what he wanted, he waited for Allah to give.

**Beware of knowing and still resisting.** The heaviest warning here falls not on the ignorant but on those who recognised the truth as clearly as they recognised their own sons and turned away anyway. The end of ayah 144 leaves it hanging over them: *"And Allah is not unaware of what they do."*

passages.title: The direction settled and the favour completed
passages.tafsir:
