This passage closes the long discussion of the Qiblah — the direction Muslims face in prayer — and then lifts the eye from the direction of the body to the direction of the heart: Allah completed His favour on this community by sending it a Messenger ﷺ, and the fitting response is remembrance and gratitude.

One movement holds these ayat together: **from an outward direction to an inward one.** Ayah 148 notes that every community has an orientation, and tells Muslims to race in good deeds rather than in disputes. Ayat 149 and 150 repeat the command to face Al-Masjid Al-Ḥarām, adding a fresh reason each time. Ayah 151 names the crowning favour — the Prophet ﷺ himself. Ayah 152 draws the conclusion: *remember Me, I will remember you.*

## "Everyone has a direction they turn to" (148)

The word is **wijhah** (وجهة). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that it lexically signifies "the thing one turns one's face to," and that the blessed Companion Ibn ʿAbbās interpreted it as *Qiblah* — religious orientation. The word *Qiblatun* itself appears in the reading of the Companion Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, which, Maʿārif notes, leaves no ambiguity in interpreting the phrase.

Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that this concerns "followers of the various religions" — every nation and tribe has its own Qiblah that it chooses, while Allah's appointed Qiblah is what the believers face. Abul-ʿĀliyah put it sharply: "The Jew has a direction to which he faces. The Christian has a direction to which he faces. Allah has guided you, O Ummah, to a Qiblah which is the true Qiblah." Ibn Kathīr notes that this statement was also related from Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ Ad-Daḥḥāk, Ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, As-Suddī and others.

Maʿārif draws out the argument: if every traditional community observably has a religious orientation of its own — whether appointed by Allah or chosen by itself — why should anyone object that Allah has appointed one peculiar to the Islamic Ummah? Islam is a regular and distinct tradition in its own right, indeed the last of all traditions; that makes a distinct Qiblah all the more necessary.

## "So race to the good things"

Here the passage turns. Having established the Muslims' right to their own Qiblah, Allah does not tell them to win the argument. He tells them to run.

The verb is **fastabiqū** — rendered by Ibn Kathīr's text "so hasten towards all that is good," and by Maʿārif "strive, then, to excel in good deeds." Maʿārif reads it so: once the divine commandment has been promulgated, Muslims need not worry about the objections or the ridicule of others; they should give up fruitless controversies and strive to excel in good deeds, since they must appear before Allah on the Day of Judgment and be rewarded or punished according to their deeds. Unnecessary discussion makes a person neglect his real task — preparing himself for death and for the world to come — and the anxiety to win over others in disputes only betrays attachment to the temporal world, when wisdom lies in caring more for what is everlasting.

**A second sense: do it now.** Maʿārif draws a further implication from "strive to excel" — one should hasten to perform a good deed, whether Ṣalāh, fasting, Ḥajj or Zakāh, as soon as the opportunity comes. The *ability* to do a good deed is itself a favour from Allah, so negligence in performing it amounts to ungratefulness and disrespect towards Allah; it is to be feared that procrastination may be punished with a withdrawal of that divine favour, and that a person may altogether lose the ability to perform good deeds. May Allah protect us from such a fate.

**Where the jurists differed.** Some *fuqahāʾ* (jurists) concluded from this phrase that it is more meritorious to offer each of the five daily prayers as soon as its appointed time begins; this view is shared by **Imām Shāfiʿī**. **Imām Abū Ḥanīfah and Imām Mālik** held that certain prayers are more meritoriously offered a bit late, as the Prophet ﷺ indicated by his speech or action, while the rest should be offered as early as possible within the prescribed time. Maʿārif's evidence: **Al-Bukhārī** reports from the Companion Anas the superior merit of offering ʿIshāʾ rather late in the night, and Maʿārif adds — citing Qurṭubī — that the Companion Abū Hurayrah also reports such a preference on the part of the Prophet ﷺ. Similarly, **Al-Bukhārī and Al-Tirmidhī** report from the Companion Abū Dharr that on a journey Bilāl wanted to call the adhān as soon as Ẓuhr's time began, but the Prophet ﷺ asked him to wait till it was a bit cooler, remarking that the heat of the noonday is a part of the fire of Hell. What all agree on: **by the consensus of the fuqahāʾ, once a prescribed prayer's time has come one should not delay it without a valid excuse** — either a clear-cut specification in the Sharīʿah, or a physical disability such as illness.

The ayah then dissolves the geography of the argument: *"Wherever you may be, Allah will bring you all together."* Directions differ; the destination does not. Ibn Kathīr explains *"Truly, Allah is able to do all things"* as meaning He is able to gather you from the earth even if your bodies and flesh have disintegrated and scattered.

## Why the same command three times (149–150)

Ayat 149 and 150 repeat what ayah 144 already commanded. Ibn Kathīr calls ayah 150 "a third command from Allah to face Al-Masjid Al-Ḥarām from every part of the world," and traces a rising sequence:

- **Ayah 144** answers the Prophet's ﷺ longing — *"Verily, We have seen the turning of your face towards the heaven. Surely, We shall turn you to a Qiblah that shall please you."*
- **Ayah 149** shifts the ground: *"that is indeed the truth from your Lord."* Ibn Kathīr says this upgrades the subject beyond the first ayah, in which Allah agreed to what His Prophet ﷺ had wished for — here Allah states that this is also **the truth from Him**, which He likes and is pleased with.
- **Ayah 150** refutes the Jewish assertion that the Prophet ﷺ faced their Qiblah, since they knew from their Books that he would later be commanded to face the Qiblah of Ibrāhīm, the Kaʿbah. The Arab disbelievers lost their argument too: the Qiblah of Ibrāhīm is more respected and honoured than the Qiblah of the Jews, and the Arabs used to honour the Kaʿbah and liked the fact that the Messenger ﷺ was commanded to face it.

Maʿārif adds **Al-Qurṭubī's** reading, in which the repetition becomes more than mere emphasis — each phrase, in being repeated, acquires a new implication. Commands in the singular address the Prophet ﷺ himself; those in the plural address the blessed Companions and the Muslims in general. Ayah 144 pertains to those in Madinah or in their own home town, making clear the injunction is not particular to the Prophet's ﷺ mosque but applies to every town or village and every quarter of a town. Ayah 149 adds *"from wheresoever you set out"*, showing that the injunction now refers to the state of a journey; and since a journey involves different situations — unbroken travel for days, or a short or long stay along the way — ayah 150 repeats it again to cover them all.

Maʿārif also relates a résumé of explanations borrowed from Maulana Muhammad Idris. Among them: this was **the first occasion in the Islamic Sharīʿah when a new commandment came to abrogate an earlier one**, so repetition was necessary to impress the significance of the occasion; and since the abrogation of any commandment is likely to give rise to doubts and to produce internal or external disorder, emphatic reiteration becomes all the more essential. Maʿārif adds that the reiteration also suggests that this is the **final and definite** decision regarding the Qiblah, and that no further change can be expected.

## "So that people have no argument against you" (150)

Ibn Kathīr explains: the People of the Book knew from the description of the Muslim Ummah that they would be ordered to face the Kaʿbah, and had the Muslims remained on the Qiblah of Bayt Al-Maqdis — which was also the Qiblah of the Jews — this fact could have been used as the basis of argument against them. Maʿārif adds that the Torah and the evangel had indicated that the promised Last Prophet ﷺ would have the Kaʿbah as his Qiblah; the new commandment takes the ground from under the opponents' feet, and at least the just ones among them can no longer raise this kind of objection. The stubborn and malignant ones, Maʿārif notes, would still carp — claiming that it was Bayt Al-Maqdis, not the Kaʿbah, which had been the Qiblah of the earlier prophets.

**"Except those of them who do wrong."** Ibn Kathīr identifies these as the *mushrikīn* (polytheists) of Quraysh, whose reasoning was the unsound statement: this man claims that he follows the religion of Ibrāhīm — so if facing Bayt Al-Maqdis was part of that religion, why did he change it? The answer: Allah chose His Prophet ﷺ to face Bayt Al-Maqdis first for a certain wisdom, and he obeyed; then Allah changed the Qiblah to the Qiblah of Ibrāhīm, and he obeyed in that too. **He obeys Allah in all cases and never engages in the defiance of Allah even for an instant — and his Ummah imitates him in this.**

**"So fear them not, but fear Me."** Ibn Kathīr: do not fear the doubts that unjust, stubborn persons raise — fear Allah alone, for indeed Allah alone deserves to be feared. Maʿārif states it bluntly: the only thing which can be harmful to the Muslims is not the hostility of men but the disobedience to or disregard of divine commandments.

**"And so that I may complete My favour upon you… and that you may be guided."** Ibn Kathīr: I will perfect My bounty on you by legislating for you to face the Kaʿbah, **so that the Sharīʿah is complete in every respect** — and you will be directed and guided to what the nations have been led astray from, "We have guided you to it and preferred you with it." Maʿārif adds that this steadfastness is itself a blessing from Allah, and that the blessing will appear in its perfect glory in the other world.

## The favour completed: the Messenger ﷺ (151)

Ayah 151 begins with *kamā* — "just as" — and that small particle does real work, as Maʿārif shows with an observation that lights up the whole passage.

**These ayat answer the duʿāʾ of Ibrāhīm** (peace be upon him) made earlier in this very surah (2:127–129). He had prayed that Allah accept his founding of the Kaʿbah, and that He send among his progeny a Messenger from among themselves. The discussion of the Qiblah has already shown that **the first prayer was heard and accepted**. Ayah 151 declares that **the second request was granted too** — and the Qiblah then makes obvious sense: since the Prophet ﷺ was sent in answer to the prayer of the founder of the Kaʿbah, it is no wonder the Kaʿbah should be appointed as his Qiblah. The ayah even names him with the very attributes Ibrāhīm specified: he recites to them the verses of the Qur'an; he teaches them the Book and the wisdom; he purifies them; and he teaches them things they did not know of, which could not be found in the earlier divine books nor reached through individual reason.

Ibn Kathīr fills in what this favour did to a people. The Messenger ﷺ recites Allah's clear Ayat, **purifies and cleanses them from the worst types of behaviour, the ills of the souls and the acts of Jāhiliyyah** (the pre-Islamic era), takes them from the darkness of disbelief to the light of faith, and teaches them the Book and the **Ḥikmah** — the wisdom, which Ibn Kathīr identifies as the Prophet's ﷺ Sunnah. In Jāhiliyyah they used to utter foolish statements; later, with the blessing of that Message, they were elevated to the status of the *awliyāʾ* (loyal friends of Allah) and the rank of the scholars, acquiring the deepest knowledge among people, the most pious hearts and the most truthful tongues. On the ayah about those "who have changed the favours of Allah into disbelief" (14:28), **Ibn ʿAbbās commented: "Allah's favour means Muhammad."**

## "Remember Me, I will remember you" (152)

The response asked for is short: *fadhkurūnī adhkurkum wa'shkurū lī wa lā takfurūn.*

Mujāhid read the *kamā* of 151 as leading straight here: **therefore remember Me in gratitude for My favour.** Maʿārif notes that Al-Qurṭubī connects that "as" with the first phrase of 152 — "Remember Me, then" — on which reading **the very ability to remember Allah is as much a blessing as the ordination of the new Qiblah and the coming of the Last Prophet ﷺ**, so that men should render thanks and continue to receive His favours. Al-Ḥasan Al-Baṣrī explained the exchange: "Remember Me regarding what I have commanded you, and I will remember you regarding what I have compelled Myself to do for your benefit" — His rewards and forgiveness. Maʿārif puts the same point plainly: if men remember Allah by obeying His commandments, He will remember them by granting His pardon and His rewards.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathīr cites what he calls an authentic Hadith in which Allah the Exalted says: *"Whoever mentions Me to himself, I will mention him to Myself; and whoever mentions Me in a gathering, I will mention him in a better gathering."* He then gives a fuller narration — reported by **Imām Aḥmad** from **Anas**, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said:

> "O son of Ādam! If you mention Me to yourself, I will mention you to Myself. If you mention Me in a gathering, I will mention you in a gathering of the angels — or he said, in a better gathering. If you draw closer to Me by a hand span, I will draw closer to you by a forearm's length. If you draw closer to Me by a forearm's length, I will draw closer to you by an arm's length. And if you come to Me walking, I will come to you running."

Ibn Kathīr states that its chain is *ṣaḥīḥ* and that it was recorded by **Al-Bukhārī**. The promise is overwhelming: every step the servant takes toward Allah is answered from His side with more than the servant offered.

**Gratitude and its opposite.** The ayah pairs gratitude with its refusal: *"and be grateful to Me… and never be ungrateful to Me."* Ibn Kathīr says that in this ayah Allah commands that He be thanked and appreciated, and promises even more rewards for thanking Him: *"If you give thanks, I will give you more; but if you are thankless, verily My punishment is indeed severe"* (14:7). Ibn Kathīr also relates from Abū Rajāʾ Al-ʿUtāridī that ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn once came to them wearing a fine silken garment they had never seen him wear before or after, and said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that whomever Allah has favoured with a bounty, Allah likes to see the effect of His bounty on His creation — or, as one narrator had it, "on His servant." Gratitude is not only felt; it shows.

## What dhikr actually is

**Dhikr belongs first to the heart.** Maʿārif explains that remembrance essentially pertains to the heart, but since the tongue is the interpreter of the heart, the oral recitation of a divine name or a verse of the Qur'an is also described as dhikr — and oral dhikr can be worth the name only when the remembrance of the heart accompanies it. Maʿārif quotes the great Sufi poet Rūmī: reciting a divine name can have no efficacy if one keeps thinking of cows and donkeys while repeating it mechanically with the tongue. **And yet, do not despair of the mechanical:** Maʿārif relates, citing Qurṭubī, that when a man complained of exactly this state, the great Sufi Abū ʿUthmān remarked that one should be grateful to Allah even for the favour of having drawn at least one organ of the body — the tongue — into His service.

**Obedience is the substance of remembrance.** The commentator Saʿīd ibn Jubayr interpreted dhikr as obedience and submission to Allah: "He who has not obeyed Him has not remembered Him, even though he has kept himself externally busy in offering (voluntary) prayers and reciting His praises." Maʿārif notes that Al-Qurṭubī supports this with a hadith cited on the authority of *Aḥkām al-Qurʾān* by Ibn Khuwayz Mandādh, in which the Prophet ﷺ said that one who has been obeying Allah — following the injunctions regarding the lawful and the unlawful — has truly been remembering Allah, in spite of being deficient in voluntary prayer and fasting, while one who has been disobeying the divine commandments has in fact forgotten Allah, in spite of devoting long hours to voluntary prayer, fasting and recitation of His praises.

Maʿārif gathers a few more voices on the merits of dhikr. Abū ʿUthmān once claimed he knew the time when Allah remembers His servants; asked how, he replied that by the promise made in the Qur'an, **the instant a Muslim turns to Allah and remembers Him, Allah remembers him.** Dhū al-Nūn al-Miṣrī said that the man who remembers Allah in the full sense of the term forgets everything else, and that in reward for such total absorption Allah Himself takes care of all his concerns and grants him something far more valuable for everything he loses. And the Companion Muʿādh remarked that, so far as winning absolution from divine wrath is concerned, no good deed of man's can compare with dhikr.

## Living it

**Stop relitigating the question of direction** — the anxiety to win over others in disputes, Maʿārif warns, betrays attachment to the temporal world. **Turn that energy into a race:** take the chance to do good as soon as it comes, because the ability itself is a favour from Allah that can be withdrawn. **And live in remembrance and gratitude** — with the heart, with the tongue when the heart is slow, and above all with obedience.

The greatest favour you were given was not earned. It was a duʿāʾ made by Ibrāhīm beside a house he was raising, granted generations later in a Messenger ﷺ who recited, purified, taught, and lifted a people from foolish speech to the ranks of the *awliyāʾ*. *Fadhkurūnī adhkurkum.*

passages.title: Patience, the living martyrs, and testing
passages.tafsir:
**These five ayat hand the believer a survival kit.** They name the two tools that carry a person through hardship, correct the way we speak about the greatest loss of all, warn that testing is coming, teach the exact words to say when it arrives, and close with what those words earn from Allah. One question holds the passage together: *how do you stay standing when life presses down?*

## The moment behind the words

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. The surrounding passages have been answering the enemies of Islam who objected to the change in the direction of the qiblah, hoping to plant doubts about the validity of Islam as a religion. Those objections had been answered — but some opponents simply ignored the answers and persisted in their hostility anyway.

That is a particular kind of exhaustion: the truth has been given, refused, and the pressure does not let up. The Muslims were likely to be disheartened. Ayah 153 arrives there, and instead of adding another argument it prescribes a method for overcoming grief and anxiety.

And note how it is worded. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out (citing Mazhari) that Allah does not say "seek help in such-and-such a situation." The command *seek help* is left unqualified — a generalizing expression — so that although the context was specific, the remedy is general: the elixir for all the ills that are a necessary part of human existence, whether wants and needs or anxiety and suffering.

## Ayah 153: sabr is a much bigger word than "patience"

The Arabic *ṣabr* is far wider than its usual English equivalent. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the lexical sense: **restraining oneself, keeping oneself under control.** Not passivity — grip. In the terminology of the Qur'an and the hadith it has three modes:

1. **Restraining yourself from what the Sharīʿah has declared impermissible (ḥarām).**
2. **Forcing yourself to be regular in worship** and steadfast in obeying the commandments of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ.
3. **Enduring every kind of trouble and pain** — understanding clearly and believing that it is Allah's will that you suffer this, and hoping for reward for it.

Then comes a point worth pausing on: people generally identify ṣabr with the third mode alone and ignore the first two, which are in fact more basic and essential. All three are equally obligatory. *Al-Ṣābirūn* — "the patient ones" — is the title of those steadfast in observing all three with equal rigour.

Ibn Kathir divides the same ground slightly differently — one patience for avoiding prohibitions and sins, one for acts of worship and obedience — adding that the second carries more reward than the first, and that a third kind, patience in the face of afflictions and hardships, is mandatory, like repentance. He also transmits from ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam a two-part division: patience for Allah's sake concerning what pleases Him, even when hard on the heart and the body, and patience in avoiding what He dislikes, even when it is desired.

**A mercy inside the definition.** Since ṣabr is self-restraint, does a cry of pain break it? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, on the authority of Saʿīd ibn Jubayr as cited by Ibn Kathir, that if a person cannot help uttering a word of grief or a sigh of pain, this does not go against ṣabr or nullify it. Patience is not the absence of pain. It is what you do with it.

**Its weight on the Last Day.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān mentions a hadith that on the Day of Judgment a call will go out — *"Where are the Ṣābirūn?"* — and those who had been constant in observing the three forms will stand and be allowed to enter Paradise without having to present the account of their deeds. Ibn Kathir notes this is corroborated by the Qur'an itself: *"The Ṣābirūn shall certainly receive their full reward without reckoning"* (39:10).

Ibn Kathir also cites a hadith that frames a believer's whole life: *"Amazing is the believer, for whatever Allah decrees for him, it is better for him! If he is tested with a bounty, he is grateful for it and this is better for him; and if he is afflicted with a hardship, he is patient with it and this is better for him."* Every state has its tool. There is no third condition in which the believer loses.

## Why mention prayer, when prayer is already part of sabr?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the question itself: ṣabr already covers the forms of worship, prayer among them, all of them being its branches. So why single ṣalāh out? **Because ṣalāh is the most perfect model of ṣabr.** In prayer you bind yourself to obedience and worship and restrain yourself not only from everything sinful or reprehensible but even from what is otherwise permissible — eating, drinking, talking. Prayer is a visible demonstration of what ṣabr means.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that prayer possesses a special efficacy in releasing a person from all kinds of trouble and pain and in fulfilling his needs — a quality present in its very nature, as happens with certain medicines too, which we may not be able to explain rationally. But the efficacy shows itself only when prayers are offered properly, according to the physical and spiritual etiquette laid down by the Sharīʿah; if ours seem fruitless, the deficiency is there, and in not turning to Allah in single-minded devotion and total submission. And according to the hadith, whenever the Prophet ﷺ faced a grave problem of any kind he always hastened to offer nafl (voluntary) prayers, and through their barakah — their blessing, the benediction carried in them — Allah came to his aid and resolved the problem.

Ibn Kathir links the ayah to its earlier twin: *"And seek help in patience and As-Salah (the prayer) and truly, it is extremely heavy and hard except for Al-Khāshiʿīn"* (2:45) — heavy for everyone, Ibn Kathir's rendering explains, except the true believers in Allah.

**"Truly, Allah is with the patient."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān locates the secret of the whole prescription here. How does ṣabr rescue a person? Because as a reward for it he receives the honour of the "company" of Allah — and when the might of the Lord of the Worlds Himself has come to a man's aid, what pain or trouble can overcome him, and who can prevent his concerns from prospering?

## Ayah 154: do not call them dead

Why does the passage turn suddenly to those killed in Allah's path? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two reasons. First, the sacrifice of life is a grand sacrifice — whoever steadfastly endures *that* loss will undoubtedly learn to be patient over losses of lesser magnitude. Second, it suited the situation: those objecting over the orientation of the Kaʿbah were what the Muslims were facing.

Ibn Kathir says the ayah indicates that the martyrs are alive and receiving their sustenance. **Muslim** reported in his Ṣaḥīḥ that the souls of the martyrs are inside green birds that move about in Paradise wherever they wish, then take refuge in lamps hanging under the Throne; their Lord looked at them and asked what they wish for. They answered, "What more could we wish for while You have favoured us with what You have not favoured any other of Your creation?" He repeated the question, and when they realised they would keep being asked, they said they wished to be sent back to the earthly life to fight in His cause and be killed in it once more — because of the rewards of martyrdom they now enjoy. The Lord then said that He has written that they will not be returned to it again.

Ibn Kathir then reports from **Imam Ahmad**, from ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Kaʿb bin Mālik from his father, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"The believer's soul is a bird that feeds on the trees of Paradise until Allah sends it back to its body when the person is resurrected."* Ibn Kathir draws a generous conclusion: this hadith includes **all** the believers in its general meaning. So the Qur'an's singling out of the martyrs serves to honour, glorify and favour them — while the other believers share in the rewards they enjoy.

### What kind of "life" is meant

A number of scholars have gathered material to support various views; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān restricts itself to the considered and very balanced view of its author's teacher, Maulana Ashraf ʿAlī (raḥimahullāh) of Thana Bhawan.

The framework is *barzakh* — the intermediary stage that begins with death and stretches till the Day of Resurrection. According to Islamic traditions every dead person is given some kind of new life there, developing in him a sensitivity to punishment and reward; this is given to everybody, believer or disbeliever, virtuous or vicious. But that life has many categories, and the martyr's is qualitatively different: for the fullness and sensitivity of life, his perception is keener and deeper. The illustration is memorable — there is life-sensation in the fingertips and in the heels alike, but the fingertips are sharper than the heels.

That finer life-quality reaches even the martyr's physical body, so that it does not waste away, decay or mingle with dust but retains its freshness and a semblance of being alive — duly endorsed, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, by ahadith and observations. They are therefore reported as living, and we are forbidden to call them dead.

**And yet** — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is equally clear that "it is correct and even allowed to call him 'dead'," and that for all worldly purposes martyrs are treated at par with the dead: their properties are divided and their wives can remarry. What is forbidden is regarding their death like ordinary deaths.

The prophets stand higher still: their life-sensitivity is even finer and keener than the martyrs', and in some ways its manifestation extends to this life as well — their properties are not divided and their wives cannot remarry. The order of strength in retaining this life-quality is therefore prophets, then martyrs, then ordinary human beings. And according to some ahadith, some of the men of Allah and virtuous people share this excellence with the martyrs — apparently including those who die while exercising stringent discipline against their own selves. So while the ayah refers specifically to martyrs, it does not for that reason exclude the virtuous and the truthful.

**An honest difficulty.** What if a martyr's body does decay? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that this is what made the author of Rūḥ al-Maʿānī doubt, and answers that what the hadith denies is the *earth* consuming the body — which does not deny decay caused by other factors such as geo-chemical reaction, body enzymes and bacteria. A further answer: martyrs' bodies remain comparatively unspoiled for a very long time, and immunity from decay for such a long time is in itself an "excess on the customary behaviour" of dead bodies.

**"But you perceive it not."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this closing clause as the Qur'an asserting that the life of barzakh transcends all sensory perception. We are told *that* they live; we are told we cannot detect *how*.

## Ayah 155: the testing is certain — and measured

The ayah opens with emphasis: Allah *will* test you. Ibn Kathir links it to *"And surely, We shall try you till We test those who strive hard and As-Sabirin (the patient), and We shall test your facts"* (47:31) — the trial sorting the truthful from the liar — and notes that Allah tests sometimes with bounty and sometimes with the afflictions of fear and hunger.

But look closely at the wording. Ibn Kathir notes the phrase *bi-shayʾin min* — "with **something** of fear, hunger" — and glosses it: **a little of each.** The trial is real, and it is rationed. He sets it beside another ayah, which he renders *"So Allah made it taste extreme of hunger (famine) and fear"* (16:112) — where the Arabic word used is *libās*, which Ibn Kathir glosses as cover or clothes, because the frightened and the hungry show the effects of the affliction outwardly.

Ibn Kathir then walks the list:

- **Loss of wealth** — some of the wealth will be destroyed.
- **Lives** — losing friends, relatives and loved ones to death.
- **Fruits** — the gardens and farms will not produce the usual or expected amounts.

Fear, hunger, property, people, produce: nearly everything a person can lose. And immediately after that catalogue comes *"but give glad tidings to As-Sabirin (the patient)"* — glad tidings inside the announcement of loss.

**Why forewarn at all?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers plainly: whatever their magnitude, accidents are unnerving, but prior knowledge of such accidents makes them easier to bear and easier to be patient about. Since the entire Ummah is addressed here, it should realise that this world is a place of hardships and labour, a place of ordeal.

## Ayah 156: the words that steady the heart

Ayah 156 defines the patient not by a feeling but by a sentence: *"Truly, to Allah we belong and truly, to Him we shall return."* Saying it is called *istirjāʿ*.

Those who recite it, Ibn Kathir says, comfort themselves in the face of their loss with three certainties: that they belong to Allah; that He does what He wills with His servants; and that nothing — no deed, even of an atom's weight — will be lost with Allah on the Day of Resurrection. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls the same sentence a formula of peace in hardship: it brings excellent reward, relieves the burden of sorrow and suffering, and effectively consoles the grieved heart.

**Umm Salamah's story.** Ibn Kathir reports from **Imam Ahmad** that Umm Salamah narrated: Abu Salamah once came back from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ delighted by something he had heard him say — that no Muslim is struck with an affliction and says istirjāʿ and then says, *"O Allah! Reward me for my loss and give me what is better than it,"* except that Allah does just that for him.

She memorised the words. Then Abu Salamah died — and she said them. And immediately her own heart objected: *who is better than Abu Salamah?* When her ʿiddah (the period of time before a widow may remarry) finished, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked permission to see her, and proposed. She raised three obstacles: it was not that she did not want him, but she was very jealous and feared he might experience some wrong mannerism from her for which Allah would punish her; she was old; and she had children. He answered each: *"As for the jealousy that you mentioned, Allah the Exalted will remove it from you. As for your being old as you mentioned, I have suffered what you have suffered. And for your having children, they are my children too."* She said, "I have surrendered to Allah's Messenger." He married her, and she said later: "Allah compensated me with who is better than Abu Salamah: Allah's Messenger ﷺ." Ibn Kathir notes that **Muslim** reported a shorter version of this hadith.

She could not imagine the answer even as she asked for it — the replacement Allah promises is measured by His knowledge, not by our imagination.

## Ayah 157: what patience earns

Ibn Kathir explains *ṣalawāt from their Lord* and *raḥmah* together as meaning that Allah's praise and mercy will be with them — those blessed and forgiven; Saʿīd bin Jubayr adds that it means safety from the torment.

ʿUmar bin al-Khaṭṭāb's comment is the finest reading of the ayah's structure: *"What righteous things, and what a great heights."* The blessings and the mercy are the two righteous things; *"and it is they who are the guided ones"* is the heights — and the heights, Ibn Kathir explains, mean more rewards: these people will be awarded their rewards, and more.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a proportion: the reward of mercy is common to everyone who *strives* to be patient, but since the quality and degree of patience varies from person to person, everyone will be rewarded individually, commensurate with his own.

## Living it

- **Widen your definition of ṣabr.** If you practise it only in grief, you are practising a third of it — and, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān insists, not the most basic third.
- **Do not read your own tears as failure.** A word of grief or a sigh of pain does not go against ṣabr or nullify it.
- **When the ground shifts, go to prayer** — including nafl, as the Prophet ﷺ did whenever a grave problem came upon him — and learn the words of ayah 156 with the duʿāʾ that follows them: "O Allah! Reward me for my loss and give me what is better than it."

passages.title: Safa and Marwah among Allah's symbols
passages.tafsir:
# Safa and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah (2:158)

**What this passage is about.** Ayah 158 settles an anxiety that troubled the first Muslims: two hills beside the Ka'bah, Safa and Marwah, had been walked between in the days of ignorance, and idols had stood on them. Was the walk between them now tainted? Allah answers by naming the two hills *among the symbols of Allah*, and then removes the doubt directly: *So it is not a sin on him who performs Hajj or 'Umrah of the House to perform Tawaf between them.* The ayah then closes by opening a door wider than the rite itself: *And whoever does good voluntarily, then verily, Allah is All-Recognizer, All-Knower.*

**How it fits what came before.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the thread. The subject of the Ka'bah began back at ayah 124, "And when his Lord put Ibrahim to a test," and continued with the House being made a place of repeated convergence, a sanctuary, and a centre of divine worship as ordained (ayah 125), and then with Ibrahim's prayer that he and his people be taught the correct method of the *manāsik* — the required rites, which include Hajj and ʿUmrah (ayat 126–129). The centrality of the House was expressed when it was declared the qiblah, the direction of every Salah wherever it is offered; and its importance was established again when it was made the objective of Hajj and ʿUmrah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the symmetry: earlier Allah removed the *disbelievers'* objection to instituting the Ka'bah as the qiblah of Muslim prayer; here, by a correlated assertion, He removes the *Muslims'* own doubt about the propriety of Saʿī — the brisk walking between Safa and Marwah — in a Hajj and ʿUmrah of which the Ka'bah is the desired hub. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, that the text is closely bound together by this reason is not difficult to see.

## Why the doubt arose: two groups, two anxieties

This is the heart of the ayah, and the sources give the story in the words of those who lived it.

'Urwah asked 'Ā'ishah about this ayah — the report is from Imam Ahmad — and put to her the reading, "By Allah! It is not a sin if someone did not perform Tawaf around them." 'Ā'ishah rejected that firmly: "Worst is that which you said, O my nephew! If this is the meaning of it, it should have read, 'It is not a sin if one did not perform Tawaf around them.'" In other words, the Arabic says there is no sin in *doing* it, not that there is no sin in *leaving* it.

Then she gave the real occasion. The ayah was revealed regarding the Ansar, who before Islam used to assume *iḥlāl* (iḥrām for Hajj) in the area of Mushallal for their idol Manāt, which they used to worship. Those who assumed iḥlāl for Manāt used to hesitate to perform the going between Safa and Marwah. So, in the Islamic era, they asked Allah's Messenger ﷺ about it, saying, "O Messenger of Allah! During the time of Jāhiliyyah, we used to hesitate to perform Tawaf between As-Safa and Al-Marwah." Allah then revealed this ayah. 'Ā'ishah concluded: Allah's Messenger ﷺ made it the Sunnah to perform Tawaf between them, "and thus, no one should abandon performing Tawaf between them." Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith is reported in the Ṣaḥīḥayn.

There was a second group with the opposite worry. Az-Zuhrī reports that 'Urwah later mentioned 'Ā'ishah's statement to Abu Bakr bin 'Abdur-Rahman bin Al-Harith bin Hisham, who said, "I have not heard of such information. However, I heard learned men saying that all the people, except those whom 'Ā'ishah mentioned, said, 'Our Tawaf between these two hills is a practice of Jāhiliyyah.'" And some others among the Ansar said, "We were commanded to perform Tawaf of the Ka'bah, but not between As-Safa and Al-Marwah." So Allah revealed, *Verily, As-Safa and Al-Marwah are of the symbols of Allah.* Abu Bakr bin 'Abdur-Rahman's conclusion was, "It seems that this verse was revealed concerning the two groups." Ibn Kathir adds that Al-Bukhari collected a similar narration by Anas.

Ash-Sha'bī supplies the physical detail that explains the discomfort: "Isaf (an idol) was on As-Safa while Nā'ilah (an idol) was on Al-Marwah, and they used to touch (or kiss) them. After Islam came, they were hesitant about performing Tawaf between them. Thereafter, the Ayah was revealed."

So picture the two anxieties side by side. One group had assumed iḥlāl for an idol and hesitated to make the walk at all. Another group had seen the practice as a leftover of Jāhiliyyah, or had understood that they were commanded to circle the Ka'bah but not to go between the two hills. The ayah answers both, and Abu Bakr bin 'Abdur-Rahman read it as having come down for both groups: the hills are *Allah's* signs.

## The wording: "no sin" that does not weaken the ruling

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān warns against a possible doubt that may arise while reading the words of the ayah. A reader may think the Qur'an simply says there is "no sin" in the Saʿī — which at most would prove it is one of many merely 'allowed' acts. But *lā junāḥ* ("no sin") is used here in relation to a question. The question concerned the idols sitting on top of Safa and Marwah, and the fact that it was to show devotion to those idols that the people of the Jāhiliyyah used to make the walk between them — in which case the practice should be ḥarām. It is in answer to *that* doubt that it was declared, "there is no sin" in it. This being the real and authentic Abrahamic tradition, there is no reason why it should be considered tainted with sin; the malpractice of a pagan band of people in that intervening period does not end up making a "sin" of what is "good" in the sight of Allah. So, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, the expression "no sin" does not go against the rite's being wājib.

**Three words worth opening up** (from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān):

- **Shaʿā'ir** (شعائر) is the plural of *shaʿīrah*, which means a sign, mark or token. So *shaʿā'ir Allāh* signifies what Allah has determined to be the marks of the Islamic faith. To call the hills His symbols is to say they are markers He appointed.
- **Ḥajj** lexically means to aim, to intend. In the terminology of the Qur'an and Hadith, the act of deciding to go solely on a pilgrimage of the House of Allah and performing the required rites while there is called Hajj.
- **ʿUmrah** lexically means *ziyārah*, a visit or pilgrimage. In the terminology of the Shariʿah, the visit to al-Masjid al-Ḥarām and the doing of ṭawāf and Saʿī there is called ʿUmrah.

## From the Sunnah: how the Prophet ﷺ read this ayah

Muslim recorded a long hadith in his Ṣaḥīḥ from Jābir, in which Allah's Messenger ﷺ finished the ṭawāf around the House, then went back to the Rukn — the Black Stone — and kissed it. He then went out from the door near Safa while reciting *Verily, As-Safa and Al-Marwah are of the symbols of Allah*, and said, "I start with what Allah has commanded me to start with" — that is, he began the Saʿī, the fast walking, from Safa. In another narration, of An-Nasā'ī, he ﷺ said, "Start with what Allah has started with," meaning Safa.

Imam Ahmad reported that Ḥabībah bint Abu Tajrah said: "I saw Allah's Messenger ﷺ performing Tawaf between As-Safa and Al-Marwah, while the people were in front of him and he was behind them walking in Saʿī. I saw his garment twisted around his knees because of the fast walking in Saʿī," and he was reciting, "Perform Saʿī, for Allah has prescribed Saʿī on you."

## The ruling: how the scholars weighed it

Ibn Kathir notes that the hadith of Ḥabībah was used as a proof that Saʿī is a **rukn** (an essential pillar) of Hajj. It was also said that Saʿī is **wājib** and not a rukn — and that if one does not perform it, by mistake or by intention, he could expiate the shortcoming with *damm* (a sacrificial offering).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the schools, noting that details of the method governing Hajj, ʿUmrah and Saʿī are easily available in the books of fiqh:

- **Imam Ahmad** — Saʿī is *mustaḥabb*, a desirable or commendable practice of the Prophet ﷺ.
- **Imam Malik and Imam Ash-Shafiʿi** — it is *farḍ*, an absolute obligation.
- **Imam Abu Hanifah** — it is *wājib*, a necessity, which means one who abandons it would have to slaughter a goat in compensation.

These are genuine differences among the imams and are reported here as such.

## Why we walk: Hajar between the two hills

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah's statement that this walk is among His symbols means it is among the acts that Allah legislated during the Hajj for Prophet Ibrahim. And he recalls the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, mentioned earlier in his tafsir, that the origin of this ṭawāf comes from the ṭawāf of **Hajar** — Prophet Ibrahim's wife — between Safa and Marwah, seeking water for her son Ismaʿil.

Ibrahim had left them in Makkah, where there was no habitation for her. When Hajar feared that her son would die, she stood up and begged Allah for His help and kept going back and forth in that blessed area between Safa and Marwah. She was humble, fearful, frightened and meek before Allah. Allah answered her prayers, relieved her of her loneliness, ended her dilemma, and made the well of Zamzam bring forth its water for her: "a tasty (or nutritional) food and a remedy for the illness."

Ibn Kathir then draws the lesson out plainly: whoever performs Saʿī between Safa and Marwah should remember his meekness, his humbleness, and his need for Allah to guide his heart, to lead his affairs to success, and to forgive his sins. He should also want Allah to eliminate his shortcomings and errors and to guide him to the straight path. He should ask Allah to keep him firm on this path until he meets death, and to change his situation from that of sin and errors to that of perfection and being forgiven — the same providence which was provided to Hajar.

So notice what the ayah does for the questioners. They had hesitated over hills that idols had stood upon. Allah names those hills among His own symbols, and Ibn Kathir points to what the walk actually commemorates: a mother's desperate appeal to Allah, and Allah's answering her.

## "And whoever does good voluntarily"

The ayah does not end with the ruling. It adds *wa man taṭawwaʿa khayran* — "and whoever does good voluntarily." Ibn Kathir records more than one understanding:

- that the ayah describes performing the ṭawāf more than seven times;
- that it refers to a voluntary ʿUmrah or Hajj;
- that it means volunteering to do good works in general, as Ar-Razi has stated — the third opinion being attributed to Al-Hasan Al-Basri.

Ibn Kathir leaves the matter with the scholar's habit: **Allah knows best.**

## The close: *All-Recognizer, All-Knower*

The ayah ends, *then verily, Allah is All-Recognizer, All-Knower.* Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: Allah's reward is immense for the little deed, and He knows about the sufficiency of the reward — hence He will not award insufficient rewards to anyone. He brings as witness Allah's word elsewhere: *"Surely, Allah wrongs not even of the weight of an atom, but if there is any good (done), He doubles it, and gives from Him a great reward"* (4:40).

Hold the two together as Ibn Kathir presents them. He knows what reward suffices, so no one is ever short-changed; and His reward for the small deed is immense, so no small deed is ever wasted.

## Living it

- **Do the rite as a rite of Allah's.** The hills are His signs, and the going between them is among the acts Allah legislated in the Hajj for Ibrahim. As 'Ā'ishah said, Allah's Messenger ﷺ made it the Sunnah — "and thus, no one should abandon performing Tawaf between them."
- **Start with what Allah has started with.** The Prophet ﷺ went out by the door near Safa, reciting this very ayah, and said, "I start with what Allah has commanded me to start with," beginning the Saʿī at Safa.
- **Walk as Hajar walked.** Ibn Kathir's counsel is not decorative: remember your meekness, your humbleness, and your need for Allah — to guide your heart, forgive your sins, keep you firm on the straight path until you meet death, and change your state from sin and error to being forgiven, asking for the same providence given to Hajar.
- **Do not despise the small extra.** *And whoever does good voluntarily* — Allah's reward is immense for the little deed, and He knows exactly what reward suffices.

passages.title: Concealing guidance and the door of repentance
passages.tafsir:
Ayah 159 delivers a verdict of terrifying weight on those who hide revealed truth; ayah 160 immediately swings open a door of escape; ayat 161–162 show that door closing for good at death.

Read together, the passage moves in three beats: **the curse**, **the exception**, and **the curse made final**. That middle beat is the heart of it. Allah does not leave the accusation standing without an exit, and He names Himself, in the very moment of pardon, "the One Who accepts repentance, the Most Merciful."

## The setting: a truth that was recognised and buried

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places this passage in relation to the qiblah discussion of several verses earlier, where the text had pointed out how the People of the Book went about concealing the truth concerning the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ, for whom the Kaʿbah was appointed as the qiblah. It points back to ayah 146 of this same surah, where Allah said of them that they "recognize him (The Holy Prophet) as they recognize their own sons. And, in fact, a group of them does conceal the truth while they know."

That is the background. These were not people who missed the evidence; they knew it the way a father knows his own child. Having named the concealment in ayah 146, Maʿārif explains, the text now concludes the subject by warning those who do not merely conceal but, "going further ahead in obstinacy, persist in their effort."

Ibn Kathir reports from Abu Al-ʿAliyah that these ayat "were revealed about the People of the Scripture who hid the description of Muhammad ﷺ." But Ibn Kathir does not leave the ruling locked in the past. He reads the ayat as a stern warning against anyone who hides "the clear signs that the Messengers were sent with which guide to the correct path and beneficial guidance for the hearts, after Allah has made such aspects clear for His servants through the Books that He revealed to His Messengers."

## What exactly is being hidden

Ayah 159 names **al-bayyināt** — the clear proofs and evidences — and **al-hudā**, the guidance. In Ibn Kathir's description these are the signs the Messengers were sent with: they guide to the correct path, and they are guidance beneficial for the hearts. They are not only a map; they are meant to work on the one who follows them.

Notice also the timing built into the ayah, as Ibn Kathir renders it: this is concealment "**after We have made it clear**." Allah made it clear; they covered it over; and the only way back, in ayah 160, will be to "**openly declare (the truth which they concealed).**" The crime is not ignorance. It is putting out a light that Allah Himself lit.

## "And cursed by the cursers"

The word **laʿnah** deserves precision, because English "curse" suggests foul language. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the definition: laʿnah means "**to remove away from the mercy of Allah Almighty**." To be cursed is to be pushed outside the reach of mercy. That is what makes it the most serious thing that can be said about anyone.

Ayah 159 says they are cursed by Allah "and cursed by **al-lāʿinūn**, those who curse" — and, as Maʿārif observes, the words "have not identified those who do that." The commentators read that silence in two complementary ways:

- **Abu Al-ʿAliyah, Ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas and Qatadah** said it means the angels and the believers will curse them (Ibn Kathir).
- **Mujahid and ʿIkrimah** said that the very absence of specification suggests they are cursed by everything and every living being — even animals and insects join in, "since their misdeeds hurt all created life forms" (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān). Maʿārif adds that this is supported by a hadith from the Companion Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib in which the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that *al-lāʿinūn* refers to all animal life that moves on the earth (Qurtubi quoting Ibn Majah).

Ibn Kathir cites Mujahid on how this works: "When the earth is struck by drought, the animals say, 'This is because of the sinners among the Children of Adam. May Allah curse the sinners among the Children of Adam.'" Sin damages the world, and the world registers the damage.

Then Ibn Kathir sets the mirror image beside it, and this is perhaps the most beautiful thing in the passage. **Everything asks forgiveness for the scholar — even the fish in the sea and the bird in the air.** The one who teaches what Allah revealed has all of creation praying for him; the one who hides it has all of creation praying against him. Same creation, opposite verdict. Ibn Kathir concludes that those who hide knowledge will be cursed in this life and on the Day of Resurrection "by Allah, the angels, all humanity, and those who curse (including the animals) each in its own distinct way. Allah knows best."

## From the Sunnah: the bridle of fire

Ibn Kathir cites a hadith in the **Musnad**, narrated through several chains of narrators, that Abu Hurayrah reported that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said:

> "Whoever was asked about knowledge that one has, but he hid it, then a bridle made of fire will be tied around his mouth on the Day of Resurrection."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes the same teaching, narrated by Abu Hurayrah and ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀs and reported by **Ibn Majah** (citing Qurtubi): anyone asked about something of religion which he knows would, if he conceals it, "be brought forth by Allah on the Doomsday harnessed with a rein of fire."

The image is exact. A bridle goes in the mouth to stop the animal from going where it wants. The mouth that refused to move when truth needed speaking is fixed shut with fire.

Maʿārif then records an important qualification from the jurists (**fuqahāʾ**): this warning applies to a person who is **the only one available** in a given situation. If other knowledgeable people are present, he has the option of suggesting the issue be discussed with an ʿālim who knows (Qurtubi and Jassas).

**Abu Hurayrah** himself lived under this ayah. Ibn Kathir records from Al-Bukhari that Abu Hurayrah said: "If it was not for an Ayah in Allah's Book, I would not have narrated a Hadith for anyone" — and then recited ayah 159. Maʿārif reports the same from the Sahih of Al-Bukhari, and notes that some other Companions have been reported to have used similar words while narrating hadith.

Maʿārif draws out what that reveals about the Companions' understanding: the ayah warns against concealing what has been revealed in the Qur'an, and does not mention hadith as such. Yet the Companions ruled that the hadith of the Prophet ﷺ was covered under this reference, so that concealing a hadith would place them under the same warning. Their practice is itself a statement about the standing of the Sunnah.

## Concealment is not the same as discretion

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to stop this ayah from being misused, and derives three rulings from it:

1. **It is forbidden to conceal knowledge which must be disclosed and disseminated widely.**
2. **One who does not himself possess sound knowledge of religious injunctions and rulings should not try to explain them.** Speaking without knowledge is not the cure for silence.
3. **Answers to religious questions that are intricate, deeply involved and far beyond the comprehension of ordinary people should not be offered before them,** lest they fall prey to misunderstanding. This is *not* concealment of knowledge, because what is not allowed is the concealment of the clear guidance of the Qur'an and Sunnah, which must rather be disclosed and spread widely — and Maʿārif finds a strong suggestion of this in the very expression "**of clear signs and guidance**."

Maʿārif supports this with the words of the Companion ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿūd: "If you recite ahadith which people do not understand fully, you will be throwing them into a nest of discord" (Qurtubi). And, as reported in **Sahih al-Bukhari**, Sayyidnā ʿAli said: "Disclose to the common people only that much of knowledge as they have the capacity to understand. Do you want them to deny Allah and His Messenger ﷺ?" For, Maʿārif explains, anything beyond their comprehension would breed doubts in their minds, and they may refuse to accept it.

From this comes the rule that it is the responsibility of a scholar or guide to speak to people only after assessing their ability to receive what is being communicated. Maʿārif also reports that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not withhold wisdom from those who deserve it, for if you do so, you will be unjust to them; and do not place it before those who do not deserve it, for if you do so, you will be unjust to it." Both are injustices. The teacher stands between two errors and must judge his audience.

In view of this, Maʿārif reports Imam al-Qurtubi's deduction: a disbeliever who engages in polemics against Muslims, or a promoter of misguided innovation who invites people to his ideas, should not be initiated into the Islamic disciplines unless it is certain such teaching would correct his thinking. Likewise, the executive authority of a time should not be given rulings they could misuse to unleash a reign of terror over their citizens; and the concessions (*rukhsah*) in religious injunctions and the legal stratagems (*hiyal*) should not be brought forth in public unnecessarily, lest people get used to being "excuse-seekers" while acting upon the injunctions of the faith (Qurtubi).

## Ayah 160: three verbs and an open door

Then comes the exception — "**Except those who repent and do righteous deeds, and openly declare (the truth which they concealed).**"

Three verbs, and each one undoes a stage of the sin. Ibn Kathir explains this ayah as referring to "those who regret what they have been doing and correct their behavior and, thus, explain to the people what they have been hiding." Regret in the heart; reform in the conduct; and then the public declaration — because a concealment done in public is not repaired in private. What was hidden must be brought out.

And then Allah does not say "I will forgive them" and leave it there. He says: "**These, I will accept their repentance. And I am the One Who accepts repentance (at-Tawwāb), the Most Merciful (ar-Rahīm).**" He answers the deed with His own names — as though to say that receiving the returning sinner is not a concession He makes but who He is.

Ibn Kathir draws the widest possible conclusion from this: the ayah "also indicates that those who used to **call to innovation, or even disbelief**, and repent to Allah, then Allah will forgive them." Not merely those who fell into error, but those who led others into it. Even the caller to disbelief has this door.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the same mercy from the other side: though the ultimate fate of this senseless persistence is all too obvious, "Allah Almighty **still** extends the promise of His mercy and forgiveness" to those who repent and reflect on what they did, retrace their steps, correct their negative attitude towards divine truth, and come forward to state the truth clearly and publicly. And Maʿārif notes what this must mean concretely for the addressees of these ayat: the natural consequence of such a reformed attitude would be that they enter the fold of Islam, believing in Allah and His Prophet ﷺ — "which is the touchstone for any disbeliever's honest change of heart."

## Ayat 161–162: when the door closes

Ayah 161 is the mirror of 159, but harder: "those who disbelieve, **and die while they are disbelievers**." The condition is not the state of the life but the state at the end of it. As long as breath remains, ayah 160 is available. What ayah 161 describes is the case where it was never taken.

Upon these is "the curse of Allah and of the angels and of mankind, **combined**." Ibn Kathir explains that they will suffer this curse until the Day of Resurrection and after that in the fire of Jahannam.

Ayah 162 then removes, one by one, every hope a person might reach for. **Khālidīn fīhā** — they will abide therein. "Their punishment will neither be lightened" — Ibn Kathir: "the torment will not be decreased for them." "Nor will they be reprieved" — no reduction and no pause; "the torment will not be changed or tempered for even an hour. Rather, it is continuous and eternal." Ibn Kathir ends this section as a believer should: "We seek refuge with Allah from this evil end."

## Cursing: where the scholars differed

Because this passage is about laʿnah, both commentaries stop to ask when a believer may pronounce it — and here they genuinely differ, so both views deserve stating.

**Ibn Kathir** reports that there is no disagreement that it is lawful to curse the disbelievers **as a category**; ʿUmar bin Al-Khattab and the Imams after him used to curse the disbelievers in their Qunut supplication during the prayer and otherwise. As for cursing a *specific* disbeliever, he reports two positions: some scholars said it is not allowed, "because we do not know how Allah will make his end"; others said it is allowed, citing the story of the man repeatedly brought to be punished for drinking, when a man said "May Allah curse him!" and the Prophet ﷺ replied, "**Do not curse him, for he loves Allah and His Messenger**" — which they took to indicate that cursing is allowed for those who do not love Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. Ibn Kathir closes with "Allah knows best."

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** takes the stricter position, and derives it from the very words of ayah 161. Because the curse in the ayah is attached to those who "died while they were disbelievers," al-Jassas, al-Qurtubi and some others formulated the view that it is not permissible to curse a disbeliever about whom it is not certain that he will die in that state. Since we have no way of finding out for sure how anyone will die, we are bound by the ruling that it is not permissible to curse a disbeliever by name. That the Prophet ﷺ cursed some by name is explained by the fact that their death in disbelief was divinely revealed to him. As for disbelievers as a whole, including tyrants and the unjust, cursing them without particularising individuals is technically correct.

Maʿārif then presses the point home. If cursing is disallowed even against a disbeliever whose end is unknown, how could it be permitted against a Muslim — or even against an animal? It warns that common people in Muslim societies neglect this aspect of Muslim behaviour, and singles out the very hard language some use about those they dislike among their acquaintances. And it closes the loophole: the ruling attaches to the **meaning**, not the word. Since laʿnah means to remove someone away from the mercy of Allah Almighty, "all damnatory swearing and cursing, whatever the shade, circumstance or language, falls under the purview of laʿnah."

## Living it

The passage puts a small number of very concrete demands on a believer:

- **When you are asked about something of the religion that you know, and you are the one who is there — answer.** Silence is the sin the bridle of fire is tied for. If other knowledgeable people are present, you may direct the questioner to a scholar who knows.
- **Do not speak about the religion from a place of ignorance.** Refusing to hide is not permission to guess.
- **Weigh your listener.** Give the clear guidance freely; be careful with what will only breed doubt. That discretion is not concealment — it is the teacher's duty, and its measure is ʿAli's: only as much as they have the capacity to understand.
- **Guard your tongue from laʿnah.** You are asking that a soul be removed from Allah's mercy, and you do not know how any life will end.
- **If you have hidden or misrepresented the truth, the way back is exactly three steps** — regret it, correct your conduct, and state plainly and publicly what you had buried. Ayah 160 was revealed for people who had done far worse than most of us ever will, and it still calls them home.

passages.title: One alone worthy of worship: His signs, and the rivals disowned
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These five ayat make a single argument. Ayah 163 states the claim: there is only One worthy of worship. Ayah 164 lays out the evidence for it, drawn from the sky, the sea, the rain and the wind. Ayat 165–167 then turn to those who reject the claim anyway — who set up "rivals" to Allah and love them as Allah alone should be loved — and follow them to the Day when those rivals will publicly disown them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives us the key that unlocks the whole unit. When the *mushrikīn* (the "associators" — those of Arabia who worshipped others alongside Allah) heard the words **"And your god is one God,"** it ran against everything they believed. They were puzzled: how could there be a single object of worship for the whole wide world? And if this was a serious claim, there had to be some proof in support. That proof, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is "tersely encased in the present two verses." So ayah 163 is the thesis and ayah 164 is the argument — and ayat 165–167 are what happens to a person who is shown the argument and turns away from it.

---

## "Your God is One God" — the claim (ayah 163)

Ibn Kathir's comment is compact: in this ayah Allah mentions that He is the only deity, and that He has no partners or equals. He is Allah, the One and Only, the Sustainer, and there is no deity worthy of worship except Him.

Ibn Kathir renders the second half of the ayah — *lā ilāha illā Huwa* — as "there is none who has the right to be worshipped but He."

**What "One" actually means.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing al-Jassās, sets out a summary view of *Tawḥīd*, the Oneness of Allah, in four senses of *Wāḥid* (the One):

1. **One in the state of His being** — there exists in the universe of His creation no entity like Him. He is without any duplicate or replica and without any equal or parallel. So unshared and pristine is His station that He alone is deserving of being called *Wāḥid*.
2. **One in claiming the right of being worshipped** — in view of the nature of His Being, the comprehensiveness of His most perfect attributes, and the great charisma of His creation and its nurture, all human obedience, all *ʿibādah*, all worship has to be for Him alone.
3. **One in being free of any conceivable composition** — free of segments and fragments, units and organs, substances and elements, atoms and particles. There is just no way He can be analysed, divided, or resolved.
4. **One in being the anterior and the posterior** — He existed when nothing did, and He will remain existing when nothing will. Who then, if not Him, shall be called *Wāḥid*, the only One?

**And the One is the Merciful.** The ayah does not end at oneness. It ends with *Ar-Raḥmān, Ar-Raḥīm* — the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Ibn Kathir notes that the meanings of these two Names were explained at the beginning of Sūrat al-Fātiḥah.

**A hadith on this ayah.** Ibn Kathir relates that Shahr bin Hawshab reported that Asmāʼ bint Yazīd bin as-Sakan narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that **Allah's Greatest Name is contained in these two ayat** — this ayah, 2:163, and the opening of Sūrah Āl ʿImrān: *"Alif-Lām-Mīm. Allah! There is none who has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One Who sustains and protects all that exists"* (3:1–2). (Ibn Kathir gives this report without naming a collection, so it is presented here exactly as he presents it.)

Ibn Kathir then moves on: Allah next mentions some of the proof that He alone is the deity, that He is the One who created the heavens and the earth and all the various creatures between them, all of which testify to His Oneness.

---

## The evidence: signs anyone can see (ayah 164)

Having stated the claim, Allah answers the demand for proof — and He does it not with abstract philosophy but by pointing out of the window. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses this: stated simply, these signs "can be grasped by the learned and the ignorant alike." Ibn Kathir titles this section simply *The Proofs for Tawhid*.

**The heavens and the earth.** Ibn Kathir has us look up at the sky — its height, its intricate design, its vastness, the heavenly objects in orbit — and then down at the earth, with its density, its lowlands, mountains, seas, deserts and valleys, and the other structures and beneficial things it has. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks: how can one bypass the wonder of the creation of the heavens and the earth? Their origination and their perpetuity is the work of His perfect power alone, and there is absolutely no being other than Him who can take that credit.

**The alternation of night and day.** One comes and then goes, followed by the other, which does not delay for even an instant. Ibn Kathir cites *"It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day. They all float, each in an orbit"* (36:40). And the balance is never static: sometimes the day grows shorter and the night longer, sometimes the reverse, one taking from the length of the other — *"Allah merges the night into the day, and He merges the day into the night"* (57:6), meaning He extends the length of one from the other and vice versa.

**The ships that sail the sea.** Ibn Kathir points to the shaping of the sea in this manner, so that it is able to carry ships from one shore to another — people benefiting from what the other region has, and exporting what they have in return. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān dwells on this beautifully. Consider that water, a substance so liquid and fluid, was given the property of lifting on its back ships that carry tons and tons of weight all the way from the East to the West. Had the substance of water not been given a state in which the molecules move freely among themselves while remaining in one mass — a functional fluidity, in other words — all this maritime activity would not be there. And even that fluidity would not be enough without help from the winds: *"If He wills, He can still the winds, then ships shall remain standing on the back of the seas"* (42:33). These are great signs, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān; they tell us they were created and operated by a supreme being, the One who is All-Knowing, All-Aware, All-Wise. The Qur'an's phrase **"with what benefits people"** points, it notes, to the countless benefits that accrue to human beings when they mutually trade their goods across the seas — benefits that vary from country to country and from age to age.

**The rain that revives dead earth.** Ibn Kathir links it to *"And a sign for them is the dead land. We give it life, and We bring forth from it grains, so that they eat thereof"* (36:33). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a striking meditation. The water comes down *drop by drop*, released in a measure and manner that hurts nothing — if it always came in the form of a flood, nothing would have survived, man or animal or things. And the raining of water is not all: it is the *storage* of water on earth that baffles human ingenuity. Imagine everyone being asked to store six months' worth of water for personal use — and then to keep it potable and hygienic all that time. Instead, water was stored openly in ponds and lakes for humans and animals; the same water was lowered into the earth under the mountains and valleys as an unsensed network of hidden pipelines, accessible to anyone taking the trouble of digging; and a huge sea of ice was stored on top of the mountain ranges, secure against spoilage, melting out slowly and reaching all over the world through nature's own water lines. As the Qur'an says, *"Then, We made water stay in the earth, although We were capable of letting it flow away"* (23:18).

**The scattered creatures.** Ibn Kathir: creatures of every kind, in various shapes, colours, uses and sizes, whether small or large — and Allah knows all that, sustains it, and nothing is concealed from Him: *"And no moving creature is there on earth but its provision is due from Allah. And He knows its dwelling place and its deposit. All is in a Clear Book"* (11:6).

**The veering of the winds.** Sometimes, Ibn Kathir says, the wind brings mercy and sometimes torment. Sometimes it brings the good news of the clouds that follow it; sometimes it leads the clouds, herding them, scattering them, directing them. Sometimes it comes from the north, sometimes from the south, sometimes from the east striking the front of the Kaʿbah, sometimes from the west striking its back. He adds, with characteristic restraint, that there are many books about the wind, rain and stars and the regulations related to them, but here is not the place to elaborate on that — *and Allah knows best*.

**The clouds held between sky and earth.** The clouds run between the sky and the earth to wherever Allah wills of lands and areas.

**"Signs for people of understanding."** Ibn Kathir sums it up: all these things are clear signs that testify to Allah's Oneness. And he pairs the ayah with its sister passage in Āl ʿImrān, which shows what the right response looks like: *"…there are indeed signs for men of understanding. Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and lying down on their sides, and think deeply about the creation of the heavens and the earth, saying: 'Our Lord! You have not created all this without purpose, glory to You! Give us salvation from the torment of the Fire'"* (3:190–191).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes this section by summing up that Allah's Oneness has been proved in these verses by citing some manifestations of His perfect power — and notes that commentators of the Qur'an have taken up the subject in great detail, directing the interested reader to al-Jassās, al-Qurṭubī and others.

---

## The rivals, and the love that belongs to Allah (ayah 165)

After the evidence comes the tragedy. **"And of mankind are some who take others besides Allah as rivals — they love them as they love Allah."**

Ibn Kathir explains that in these ayat Allah mentions the condition of the polytheists in this life and their destination in the Hereafter. They appointed equals and rivals with Allah, worshipping them along with Allah and loving them just as they love Allah — "however, Allah is the only deity worthy of worship, Who has neither rival nor opponent nor partner."

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir reports that it is recorded in the *Ṣaḥīḥayn* that ʿAbdullāh bin Masʿūd said: *I said, "O Messenger of Allah! What is the greatest sin?" He said: "To appoint a rival to Allah while He Alone has created you."* Note the last clause — **while He Alone has created you** — and read it back against ayah 164, where the whole proof was the creating.

**The counter-portrait: "those who believe love Allah more."** Ibn Kathir explains why: because these believers love Allah, know His greatness, revere Him and believe in His Oneness, they do not associate anything or anyone with Him in worship. Rather, they worship Him alone, depend on Him, and seek help from Him for each and every need.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens the contrast into something you can test in your own life. A polytheist may turn away from his self-made god in the event of an impending loss; but a true believer "reposes his total confidence in Allah, in gain and loss alike, retaining His love and pleasure as his lasting possession, never leaving his Creator whatever the odds against him be."

**The warning, and the missed opportunity.** *"If only those who do wrong could see, when they will see the torment, that all power belongs to Allah…"* Ibn Kathir: if these people knew what they will face and the terrible punishment they are to suffer because of their disbelief and *Shirk*, they would shun the deviation they live by. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notices something subtle here — the opportunity to correct their position was there. Through their frustrations with their gods they could have recognised that these were helpless and that real power rested with Allah. But they missed the opportunity and must now learn the hard way. Hence the stern warning.

---

## The disowning (ayat 166–167)

Towards the end of ayah 165 it was said that the punishment of the Hereafter is severe. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that *how* severe it will be is the subject of ayah 166 — and the answer is not primarily about fire. It is about betrayal.

**Those who were followed disown those who followed.** Ibn Kathir shows that this scene recurs across the Qur'an, with every category of false object of devotion turning on its devotees:

- **The angels** — whom they used to claim that they worshipped — will declare their innocence of them in the Hereafter: *"We declare our innocence before You. It was not us they worshipped"* (28:63); *"Glorified be You! You are our Wali instead of them. Nay, but they used to worship the Jinn; most of them were believers in them"* (34:41).
- **The jinn** will also disown those who worshipped them, and will reject that worship: *"…and when mankind are gathered, they will become their enemies and will deny their worshipping"* (46:5–6).
- **The gods taken for honour, power and glory** will do the same: *"Nay, but they will deny their worship of them, and become opponents to them"* (19:81–82).
- **Ibrāhīm** said to his people exactly this: *"You have taken idols instead of Allah. The love between you is only in the life of this world, but on the Day of Resurrection you shall disown each other and curse each other, and your abode will be the Fire, and you shall have no helper"* (29:25).
- **The arrogant leaders and those deemed weak** will cast the blaming word one to another: the weak saying "Had it not been for you, we should certainly have been believers," the arrogant answering "Did we keep you back from guidance after it had come to you?" — and each party concealing its own regrets when they behold the torment (34:31–33).
- **Shayṭān** delivers the final speech when the matter has been decided: *"Verily, Allah promised you a promise of truth. And I too promised you, but I betrayed you. I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me. So blame me not, but blame yourselves"* (14:22).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes it recognisable: it is very much like what happens in our mortal world when people share in the illegal but wriggle out when apprehended — so much so that they would even go to the limit of refusing to recognise their accomplices.

**"All their relations will be cut off."** Ibn Kathir explains that when they see Allah's torment, their power and means of salvation are all cut off: they will have no way of making amends, nor will they find a way of escape from the Fire. And he preserves a precious one-word gloss: ʿAṭāʼ reported that **Ibn ʿAbbās** said this means **"the friendship."** **Mujāhid** is reported to have said something similar in another narration by Ibn Abī Najīḥ. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, whatever bonds of leading and following may have existed between them would be snapped apart.

**"If only we had one more chance."** In ayah 167 the followers cry out for a return to the worldly life, so that they might disown their leaders as they were disowned. Ibn Kathir reads the wish plainly: *if only we had a chance to go back to the life, so that we could disown them — their idols, leaders and the rest — shun their worship, ignore them, and worship Allah alone instead*. And then he says something devastating: **they utter a lie in this regard**, because if they were given the chance to go back, they would only return to what they were prohibited from doing. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the wish with the same eye: seeing their leaders' turnabout, they fret and fume, wishing for a return to the world where they could at least square up with them — "maybe this time they come back to us seeking our allegiance, which would be a perfect time to say no to them and to distance ourselves from them and to do to them what they did to us." "But what price are these dreams now? They are not going anywhere."

**Deeds shown to them as regrets.** *"Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets for them."* Ibn Kathir explains: their works will vanish and disappear. He offers three images the Qur'an itself uses — deeds made *"as scattered floating particles of dust"* (25:23); works *"as ashes, on which the wind blows furiously on a stormy day"* (14:18); deeds *"like a mirage in a desert. The thirsty one thinks it to be water"* (24:39). Hence the last words of ayah 167: **"And they will never get out of the Fire."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the reason directly — the punishment for *shirk*, the grave sin of associating partners with Allah, is to remain in the Fire for ever.

---

## Living it

*What follows is reflection on the passage, drawn from the commentary above rather than added to it.*

**Let ayah 164 do its work.** The passage's own answer to doubt is not abstraction but attention. Rain, wind, the alternation of night and day, a ship on water, an animal whose provision is due from Allah and whose dwelling place He knows — these were offered as proof, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān insists they can be grasped by learned and unlearned alike. The Āl ʿImrān parallel Ibn Kathir cites shows what to do with them: remember Allah standing, sitting and lying down, think deeply about the creation, and let the reflection end in *"Our Lord! You have not created all this without purpose."*
