**Audit your loves.** Ayah 165 does not describe people who deny Allah's existence; it describes people whose love went to the wrong place. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's test is a fair one to apply to ourselves: is my confidence in Allah the kind that holds "in gain and loss alike" — or is it the sort that turns away the moment a loss looms?

**Be careful whom you follow, and whom you lead.** Ayat 166–167 are, at bottom, about bonds of leading and following being snapped apart. Every allegiance not built on truth will be gone at the moment it is most needed. And no one will be able to plead that they were forced: as Shayṭān says in 14:22, *"I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me."*

**Do not save repentance for later.** The wish in ayah 167 is for a second chance that will not be granted — and which, Ibn Kathir tells us, would be squandered if it were. The only life any of us will get to disown falsehood in is the one we are living right now.

passages.title: Lawful food and blind imitation of ancestors
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are about who gets to decide what is permitted. Allah opens His earth to all people and tells them to eat freely from its lawful and wholesome provision (168) — then exposes the two forces that take that freedom away: a whispering enemy who forbids what Allah permitted (168–169), and the dead weight of inherited custom that refuses to hear anything new (170–171).

**What holds the passage together.** It looks like two subjects — food, then the blind imitation of ancestors. It is really one. Ibn Kathir explains the "footsteps of Shayṭān" in ayah 168 as precisely the livestock taboos of pre-Islamic Arabia: animals people declared off-limits in the name of idols. Ayah 170 gives the excuse by which such customs survive — *"Rather, we shall follow what we found our fathers following"* — and then, in its own second half, answers that excuse with a question: *did those fathers understand anything? were they guided?* Ayah 171 follows with a parable for people in that state: a flock that hears the call and takes in only noise.

## "Eat of what is lawful and good on the earth"

Ibn Kathir places ayah 168 in the flow of what came before. Allah had established that there is no deity worthy of worship except Him and that He alone created the creation; now He states that He is also the Sustainer of all His creation, and mentions a favour He granted them — He has permitted them to eat any of the pure, lawful things of the earth that do not harm the body or the mind. Notice the logic: the One who made you is the One who feeds you, and therefore the only One with the right to say what you may put in your mouth. And notice whom He addresses — *"O humanity"*, or in Ibn Kathir's rendering, *"O mankind."*

**Ḥalāl — an untied knot.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word for us: the root sense of *ḥalla* is *to open a knot*. When something is called *ḥalāl*, the picture is of a knot loosened and a restriction removed. Permission here is not a grudging exemption; it is a rope taken off. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes the Companion Sahl ibn ʿAbdullah: "Salvation depends on three things — eating ḥalāl, fulfilling (Divine) obligations and following the Sunnah of the Holy Prophet ﷺ."

**Ṭayyib — why one word was not enough.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *ṭayyib* as "good," inclusive of the clean and the pure, covering two aspects at once: that a thing is lawful and permissible, and that it is naturally desirable. Ḥalāl answers the legal question; ṭayyib answers the human one — matching Ibn Kathir's gloss that what is permitted is what does not harm the body or the mind.

## The footsteps of Shayṭān

**The word.** *Khuṭuwāt* is the plural of *khuṭwah*, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines as the distance between the two feet when a person strides; here it means Satanic deeds. The image is exact: you are warned not against a leap into disbelief but against stepping into a footprint — one ordinary pace at a time, each placed where somebody else's foot already went.

**What those footprints were.** Ibn Kathir explains the footsteps as Shayṭān's ways and methods, by which he misguides his followers, and gives examples the first audience knew at once — animals withdrawn from human use in the name of idols:

- the **Baḥīrah** — a she-camel whose milk was spared for the idols, and nobody was allowed to milk her;
- the **Sāʼibah** — a she-camel let loose for free pasture for the idols, on whom nothing was allowed to be carried;
- the **Waṣīlah** — a she-camel set free for the idols because she gave birth to a she-camel at her first delivery and again at her second.

These, Ibn Kathir says, along with everything else Shayṭān made attractive to them during the time of Jāhiliyyah, are the footsteps meant. Note the direction of the tampering. Every example he gives is a *prohibition* — a thing Allah left lawful that people placed off-limits in the name of idols.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites a report recorded by Muslim from ʿIyāḍ ibn Ḥimār, that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said that Allah the Exalted says: *"Every type of wealth I have endowed My servants is allowed for them…"* — and in it — *"I have created My servants ḥunafāʼ (pure or upright), but the devils came to them and led them astray from their (true) religion and prohibited them from what I allowed for them."* Read beside ayah 168, the passage lights up: the original human state is upright, provision is originally lawful, and the corruption came later, from outside — and it worked by *prohibiting*.

**Wider than food.** Qatādah and As-Suddī, as Ibn Kathir reports, took the phrase at its broadest: every act of disobedience to Allah is among the footsteps of Satan. And ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said any vow or oath a person makes while angry is among the footsteps of Shayṭān, and its expiation is that of the vow — so the man who in a rage swears to cut someone off has stepped into a footprint, and the law tells him how to step back out.

**"He is to you an open enemy."** Ibn Kathir reads this as a warning against Satan, and reinforces it from elsewhere in the Qurʼan: *"Surely, Shayṭān is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy. He only invites his followers that they may become the dwellers of the blazing Fire"* (35:6), and *"Will you then take him and his offspring as protectors and helpers rather than Me while they are enemies to you?"* (18:50). The enmity is declared, out in the open. The only way a declared enemy harms you is if you forget that he is one.

## Ayah 169: how the enemy actually works

**Sūʼ and faḥshāʼ.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *sūʼ* as something that bothers any good and reasonable person, and *faḥshāʼ* as what is immodest; it adds that some commentators read *sūʼ* as sin as such and *faḥshāʼ* as the major sins. Ibn Kathir reads the sequence as escalation: your enemy commands you to commit evil acts, then what is worse than that — such as adultery and the like — and then worse still.

**"He only incites."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the restrictive *innamā yaʼmurukum*, "he only orders you," and explains this "ordering" as the instigating of a suggestion in the heart. He cannot compel; he can propose. It illustrates this with a hadith reported from the Companion ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿūd, that the Prophet ﷺ said the son of Ādam is influenced by a suggestion from the Satan and a suggestion from the angel: the Satanic suggestion works by bringing forward the expedient gains in evil deeds, opening the avenues of negating the truth, while the angelic suggestion promises reward and success for good deeds and leaves the heart at peace in its attestation of the truth. Both voices reach the heart; neither takes it by force.

**The worst of the three.** Ibn Kathir marks *"and that you should say about Allah what you know not"* as the gravest item — worse, in his reading, than the sins of appetite listed before it — and adds that it includes every innovator and disbeliever. The ordering is worth sitting with: a sentence spoken about Allah without knowledge is placed above the sins people usually think of as the serious ones.

## Ayah 170: the excuse, and its answer

Ibn Kathir states the case plainly: when the disbelievers and polytheists are called to follow what Allah revealed to His Messenger ﷺ and to abandon the practices of misguidance and ignorance they were engaged in, they answer *"Rather, we shall follow what we found our fathers following"* — meaning, worshipping the idols and the false deities.

Ibn Isḥāq reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said this ayah was revealed about a group of Jews whom Allah's Messenger ﷺ called to Islam. They refused, saying, "Rather, we shall follow what we found our forefathers following" — and Allah revealed 2:170. The words land in one specific encounter; yet Ibn Kathir explains the same ayah under the heading of the polytheist imitating other polytheists. Inherited practice held above revelation is not one community's failing.

**What they were really claiming.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a detail that makes the answer less stubborn and more understandable: they clung to their inherited practice *because they assumed their models were divinely appointed to follow the way they adopted*. They were not knowingly choosing custom over Allah; they believed the custom came from Allah. That is how inherited error survives.

**Allah's one-line refutation.** The second half of the same ayah puts the question: *"even though their fathers did not understand anything nor were they guided?"* Ibn Kathir glosses "their fathers" as those whom they follow and whose practices they imitate, and the two negations as meaning they had no sound understanding or guidance. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the challenge: how could they go on following the ways of their fathers, under all conditions and to the exclusion of every other way, even if those fathers did not understand much about the true faith and were not blessed with guidance given by their Lord? The Qurʼan does not say "your fathers were wrong because they were fathers." It asks a question — *did they understand? were they guided?* — and lets the answer do the work.

## Ayah 171: the parable of the herdsman's call

Ibn Kathir explains: in their injustice, misguidance and ignorance the disbelievers are just like wandering animals that do not understand what they are told — if the shepherd heralds them, or calls them to what benefits them, they do not grasp what is actually being said, for they only hear unintelligible sounds. He reports this from Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, ʿAṭāʼ, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, ʿAṭāʼ al-Khurāsānī and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas.

Feel the sharpness of it. The problem is not that they cannot hear — it is that meaning does not arrive. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it precisely: they do hear, but not what is intended to correct them.

The faculties are then stripped one by one. Ibn Kathir: **deaf**, as they do not hear the truth; **mute**, as they do not utter it; **blind**, as they do not see or recognise its path and way — *"so they do not understand"*, that is, they do not comprehend or understand anything. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds: tight-lipped when it comes to accepting the truth, and blind in that they do not see their benefit or loss — their vital senses so dulled that they seem to understand nothing.

## Does ayah 170 condemn following scholars?

This ayah is often quoted against *taqlīd* — a non-specialist following the rulings of a qualified scholar. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes that up directly; the argument is given here as it stands, with its attribution.

It grants at once that the ayah does censure the blind following of forefathers. But the censure arrives with attending conditions — *lā yaʿqilūn* (they understood nothing) and *lā yahtadūn* (nor had they been on the right path). The forefathers are rejected as models *because* they lacked reason and guidance. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines the terms: "guidance," the right path, signifies the injunctions Allah revealed openly and clearly, while *ʿaql* (reason) stands for guidance deduced by *ijtihād* — disciplined legal reasoning — from the recognised sources of the Sharīʿah. Those identified in the text had neither: no revealed set of laws from Allah, and no ability to deduce injunctions from the Word of Allah.

From this, it argues, it follows that where a scholar genuinely has both — perfect knowledge of the Qurʼan and Sunnah, and, in the absence of a clear and direct instruction from those two sacred sources, a mujtahid's expertise to arrive at rulings from their texts by analogical deduction — it is permissible to follow him. And it is careful about what "follow" means: not that one obeys *his* injunctions or follows *his person*, but that one obeys the injunctions of Allah alone; it is only because direct and trustworthy knowledge of those injunctions in all their ramifications is not readily available to us that we follow a qualified scholar in order to act in accordance with them.

The same position is reported there from al-Qurṭubī: the prohibition concerns following forefathers *in false beliefs and deeds*; following them in correct beliefs and good deeds is not included, as the words of Sayyidnā Yūsuf (peace be upon him) show — *"I have chosen to follow the community of my fathers, Ibrāhīm and Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb"* (12:37–38). Al-Qurṭubī's own words, as quoted: some people have cited this verse to support their criticism of taqlīd; as far as following the false is concerned, this is correct, but it has nothing to do with following what is true, which is in fact a basic religious principle and a great means of protecting the religion of Muslims, inasmuch as one who does not have the ability to do ijtihād must rely on "following" in matters of religion.

**What the ayah tests for,** on this reading, is not whether you follow someone, but whether the one you follow has understanding and guidance.

## Two rulings drawn from ayah 168

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out two practical points.

1. **Ayah 168 does not make idol-dedicated animals lawful.** Some have wrongly read it that way. Polytheistic practices — releasing animals in the name of idols, or dedicating them, whether big or small, to a saint or to anyone other than Allah — are declared unlawful in ayah 173, which follows shortly. Ayah 168's objective is the opposite of a loophole: animals Allah has made lawful must not be made unlawful by dedicating them to idols. Let them be what they are and use them for personal benefit. Why go about making things unlawful on your own, which is a grave sin — and when a thing is dedicated to someone other than Allah it becomes impure, and what is impure is unlawful.

2. **There is a way back.** If someone dedicated an animal to other than Allah out of ignorance or carelessness and wishes to make amends, he should resolve to retreat from his misdeed and repent of what he did — and the meat of that animal then becomes lawful for him.

## Living it

**Eat with an open hand and a clear conscience.** The default this passage sets is permission: the earth's provision has been untied for you, and the two questions to ask of your food are the ayah's own — is it lawful, and is it wholesome.

**Watch the direction of the tampering.** Ayah 168 warns about a misguidance that does not feel like sin at all. Every example Ibn Kathir gives is a restriction nobody revealed, imposed in the name of something other than Allah; and the report he cites has the devils prohibiting people from what Allah allowed them. The Baḥīrah and the Sāʼibah are its ancient form; the instinct is not ancient.

**Guard your tongue about Allah.** Of everything in ayah 169, what Ibn Kathir singles out as worst is speaking about Allah without knowledge. "Allah says," "this is ḥarām" — these are heavy sentences. "I do not know; let me ask someone who does" is not weakness; on this passage's own logic it is the safe ground.

**Ask why you believe what you believe.** Ayah 170's excuse is answered with a question about understanding and guidance — worth turning on our own inherited practice. Not to throw off what our families gave us: on the reading Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from al-Qurṭubī, following forefathers in what is true is permissible, indeed desirable. It is to know which habits rest on revelation and which rest only on always having been done that way.

**Keep the ears of your heart open.** The frightening detail in ayah 171 is that the sound arrived and the meaning did not. A person can sit through the Qurʼan and take in only noise. The remedy is the verb the passage keeps returning to — *yaʿqilūn*: to actually understand what you have just heard.

passages.title: Eat the good things; what is forbidden
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat take the argument of the preceding passage — where the idolaters of Makkah were rebuked for inventing prohibitions — and turn it toward the believers. Ayah 172 tells them what to eat and how to receive it (with gratitude); ayah 173 tells them what Allah has actually forbidden, and it is a short list. Together they set the whole question of food on a single foundation: what is lawful is defined by Allah alone, not by custom, not by ancestors, and not by our own scruples.

## The setting: a correction that becomes an invitation

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the connection precisely. Earlier, the aim was to correct the error of the mushrikīn — the polytheists — who "made unlawful what was good and permissible." Now, in ayah 172, the believers are warned against falling into that same error, and as a corollary they are reminded of Allah's blessings and taught to be grateful to Him. Then in ayah 173, the other half of the correction: what is prohibited must remain prohibited and should never be treated as lawful, "something the mushrikin used to do when they ate carrion or animals slaughtered in a name other than that of Allah." Implied along with it is a warning that it is an error to declare any animal, other than those specified, unlawful.

So the passage cuts in both directions at once. Do not forbid what Allah permitted. Do not permit what Allah forbade. Both are the same disease — a human being setting himself up as the one who decides.

## "Eat of the good things" — and the man whose duʿāʾ is not answered

Ibn Kathir summarises ayah 172 simply: "Allah commands His believing servants to eat from the pure things that He has created for them and to thank Him for it, if they are truly His servants." Notice the closing clause of the ayah — *and be grateful to Allah, if it is indeed He Whom you worship*. Gratitude is not an optional garnish on the meal; it is the proof that the worship is real.

Then Ibn Kathir adds something that lifts this out of the kitchen entirely: "Eating from pure sources is a cause for the acceptance of supplications and acts of worship, just as eating from impure sources prevents the acceptance of supplications and acts of worship." He cites a hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad, that Abu Hurayrah said that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said:

> "O people! Allah is Tayyib (Pure and Good) and only accepts that which is Tayyib. Allah has indeed commanded the believers with what He has commanded the Messengers, for He said: *O (you) Messengers! Eat of the Tayyibāt and do righteous deeds. Verily, I am well-acquainted with what you do* (23:51), and: *O you who believe! Eat of the lawful things that We have provided you with* (2:172)."

He ﷺ then mentioned a man "who is engaged in a long journey, whose hair is untidy and who is covered in dust, he raises his hands to the sky, and says, 'O Lord! O Lord!' Yet, his food is from the unlawful, his drink is from the unlawful, his clothes are from the unlawful, and he was nourished by the unlawful, so how can it be accepted?" Ibn Kathir notes it was also recorded by Muslim and At-Tirmidhi.

Sit with the picture. Every condition for an answered prayer is present — travel, dishevelment, dust, raised hands, the repeated call *yā Rabb*. And the sources of his life are rotten. The word Allah uses of Himself in this hadith is *Tayyib*, the same word family as *tayyibāt* in our ayah: pure, wholesome, good. Like accepts like. And note the claim the hadith makes before it recites the two ayat: Allah "has indeed commanded the believers with what He has commanded the Messengers" — 23:51 addressed to the Messengers, 2:172 addressed to the believers. The believer's plate is held to prophetic standards. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same observation from 23:51: Allah has told all His prophets to eat from what is good and do what is righteous, which "shows that eating and using what is halal plays a vital role in doing what is good and virtuous."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also spells out the inner mechanics: eating harām "promotes evil instincts, kills the taste of ʿibādah and makes the prayers ineffective," while eating halāl "generates inner light, creates a distaste for evil deeds, leads towards high morals, and creates a state in which the heart welcomes ʿibādah and finds the very thought of sin sickening."

## *Innamā* — the grammar of a short list

Ayah 173 opens with *innamā ḥarrama ʿalaykum* — "He has forbidden you only…". Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that *innamā* is a **restrictive particle** — a small word whose job is to fence a statement in and shut out everything outside it. The sense becomes: Allah has forbidden *only* the things mentioned, and nothing else. The same thing is stated even more clearly in 6:145, where the Prophet ﷺ is told to proclaim that in what has been revealed to him there is nothing harām except the few things named.

This raises a real problem, and the commentary faces it honestly: the unlawfulness of many other things is established by other ayat and by ahadith. So what does the restriction mean? The answer given is that halāl and harām are not being discussed here in the absolute sense. They are discussed "with reference to those particular animals only which the polytheists of Makkah took as halal or haram on the basis of their pagan beliefs." The restriction is relative — set squarely in opposition to their polytheistic beliefs. Read against that background, the ayah says: your long list of forbidden animals has no basis; Allah's list is this short, and you manage to ignore even that.

Ibn Kathir relays a hadith that carries the same spirit — Ibn Majah reported that Salman said that Allah's Messenger ﷺ was asked about butter, cheese and fur, and said: "The allowed is what Allah has allowed in His Book and the prohibited is what Allah has prohibited in His Book. What He has not mentioned is a part of what He has pardoned." Silence in the revelation is not a gap to be filled with anxiety. It is a pardon.

## The four things

**1. Al-Maytah — the dead animal.** Ibn Kathir defines these as animals "that die before being slaughtered; whether they die by strangling, a violent blow, a headlong fall, the goring of horns or by being partly eaten by a wild animal." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the technical definition: in Islamic terminology it means an animal not slaughtered in accordance with the requirements of the Sharīʿah.

Sea creatures are excluded, on the basis of *Lawful to you is the pursuit of watergame and its use for food* (5:96), the hadith about the whale recorded in the Sahih, and the words of the Prophet ﷺ about the sea recorded in the Musnad, Al-Muwaṭṭaʾ and the Sunan: "Its water is pure and its dead are permissible." Ash-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, Ibn Majah and Ad-Daraqutni reported that Ibn ʿUmar said that the Prophet ﷺ said: "We have been allowed two dead things and two bloody things: fish and locusts; and liver and spleen."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds practical detail. Fish that has decomposed and starts floating on the surface is harām (Jassas). An animal not within range for the hunter to slaughter can still become lawful if, after saying *Bismillāh*, he inflicts a wound on it with a sharp-edged weapon such as an arrow — merely being wounded is not enough; the wound must come from a sharp-edged weapon. Two rulings follow from this. First, if an animal wounded by a gunshot dies before it can be slaughtered, it is treated as an animal that dies from a fatal strike with a baton or rock — what the Qur'an calls *mawqūdhah* in 5:3, where it is classed as harām; if it is slaughtered before it dies, it becomes lawful. Second, some ʿulamāʾ held that the common bullet with a conical nose-top falls under the category of an arrow, but the view of the majority is that it does not: it bores and tears the flesh by the force of the explosive charge, the weapon itself having no sharp edge — so an animal hunted with such a bullet is not permissible without slaughtering it.

The prohibition of maytah is absolute — eating it, buying it, selling it — and the same applies to impurities in general, so much so that one may not deliberately feed carrion even to an animal, though there is no harm if a dog or cat takes it on its own (Jassas, Qurtubi). But 6:145 clarifies that it is the *eatable* parts that are meant, so bones and hair are clean and usable, and 16:86 permits the use of such wool and hair without any condition of slaughter; hide, which carries impurities such as blood, becomes permissible once tanned (Jassas). The fat of a dead animal, and anything made with it, is forbidden — though on soap the commentary counsels precaution while noting that some leeway exists, partly because Companions such as Ibn ʿUmar, Abu Saʿid al-Khudri and Abu Musa al-Ashʿari ruled the fat forbidden as food while permitting its external use (Jassas).

On milk and eggs found inside dead unslaughtered animals there is genuine disagreement: according to Ash-Shafiʿi and other scholars they are not pure, because they are part of the dead animal, while in one narration Malik said they are pure in themselves but become impure because of their location. On cheese made from such milk, the popular view of the scholars is impurity, though they noted that the Companions ate from cheeses made by the Magians; Al-Qurtubi commented that since only a small part of the dead animal is mixed in, it is permissible, "because a minute amount of impurity does not matter if it is mixed with a large amount of liquid." On rennet taken from an animal slaughtered un-Islamically, Imams Abu Hanifah and Malik considered it clean; Imams Abu Yusuf, Muhammad and Thawri and others considered it unclean and impure (Jassas, Qurtubi) — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counsels avoiding cheese where such rennet is likely, while noting that leeway exists under the position of Abu Hanifah and Malik. Cheeses containing pork fat are absolutely harām and impure.

**2. Ad-Dam — blood.** Mentioned here in the absolute sense, but qualified in 6:145 as *masfūḥan*, that which **flows**. On that basis, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, the fuqahāʾ agree that congealed blood such as the kidney or the spleen is clean and permissible. And since it is flowing blood that is forbidden, the blood remaining on the flesh after slaughter is clean — a point on which the Muslim jurists, the blessed Companions, their successors and the Ummah in general agree; by the same reasoning the blood of mosquitoes, flies and bedbugs is not unclean, though if it is significant it must be washed off (Jassas). Because blood is forbidden in the absolute sense, its external use, and buying and selling it, and income derived from it, are likewise forbidden.

**3. Laḥm al-khinzīr — the flesh of swine.** Ibn Kathir notes the prohibition covers the meat of swine "whether slaughtered or not," and includes its fat. Why then does the ayah say *flesh*? Al-Qurtubi's answer, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays it, is elegant: the aim is not to restrict the ruling to flesh — all parts of the swine, the bones, the skin, the hair, the ligaments, are forbidden by the consensus of the Muslim community — but to point out that the swine is not like other prohibited animals, which can be purified by slaughtering even while eating them stays prohibited. The flesh of the swine "does not get purified even if the swine is slaughtered, as it is absolutely impure and unlawful." (The use of its bristles to sew leather, the commentary notes, has been permitted in hadith — Jassas, Qurtubi.)

**4. Wa mā uhilla bihi li-ghayrillāh — what is offered to other than Allah.** Here the passage stops being about biology altogether. The first three are matters of substance; the fourth is a matter of the heart. Ibn Kathir explains it as what was slaughtered in a name other than Allah's, "be it for monuments, idols, divination, or the other practices of the time of Jāhiliyyah."

Al-Qurtubi supplies the key. It was the customary practice of the Arabs, when they were about to slaughter, to call aloud the name of the entity the slaughter was intended for; the practice was so much in vogue among them that in this ayah their intention — "their seeking of the pleasure of one other than Allah, which is the real cause of forbiddance" — was identified by the word *ihlāl*, the call. What ruins the animal, in other words, is not a syllable; it is the turning of the heart to someone besides Allah.

From this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distinguishes three forms. First, slaughtering to seek the pleasure of someone other than Allah while calling that one's name — unanimously forbidden by consensus of the Muslim community; the animal is maytah, and no benefit may be taken from any of its parts. Second — and this is the case that touches many Muslims — slaughtering to seek the pleasure of an elder or a leader *while pronouncing Allah's name* over it. The fuqahāʾ agree such an animal is a carcass, though they differ on the reasoning. The Ḥawāshī of al-Bayḍāwī states that every animal over which a name other than Allah's was called is harām even if slaughtered in the name of Allah, and adds that the ʿulamāʾ agree that a Muslim who slaughters intending to seek the pleasure of anyone other than Allah becomes an apostate, his slaughter counting as an apostate's. Al-Durr al-Mukhtār rules that slaughtering to celebrate the visit of a dignitary is harām, "because that comes under ma uhilla bihi lighayrillah even though the name of Allah has been mentioned at the time of slaughter," and Al-Shami concurs.

Others hesitate to stretch the phrase that far linguistically, and instead attach this case by *commonality of cause* — the intention of seeking the pleasure of someone other than Allah — supported by the ayah *wa mā dhubiḥa ʿalā al-nuṣub* (5:3), where *nuṣub* means everything worshipped falsely, so the phrase signifies animals slaughtered for false gods. The author of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this view the most sound, cautious and safe, and records on this point a special note from his teacher, Ḥakīm al-Ummah Maulānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānawī: since *wa mā uhilla bihi li-ghayrillāh* has already been mentioned and clearly covers the animal over which another name was recited, the separate mention of *dhubiḥa ʿalā al-nuṣub* — where no recitation of another name is mentioned — covers the act of slaughtering with the intention of pleasing idols, including animals in fact slaughtered for other than Allah though His name was recited over them.

Al-Qurtubi grounded his own position in the rulings of Sayyidunā ʿAlī and Sayyidah ʿĀ'ishah. In the days of ʿAlī, Ghālib the father of the poet Farazdaq slaughtered a camel, with no report to confirm that any name other than Allah's was mentioned over it; ʿAlī still judged it to fall under *mā uhilla bihi li-ghayrillāh* and to be harām, and the Companions accepted the verdict. And Al-Qurtubi reports a lengthy hadith from Sayyidah ʿĀ'ishah, on the authority of Yahya ibn Yahya, the teacher of Imam Muslim, in which a woman asked her about gifts of meat sent by non-Arab foster relatives from their festivals. She said: "Do not eat what has been slaughtered for that day, but you can eat (fruits) from their trees." Ibn Kathir cites the same answer from Al-Qurtubi: do not eat from what was slaughtered for the feast, but eat from their vegetables.

By the same logic of shared cause, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān extends the ruling to *nadhr li-ghayrillāh* — food or sweets offered against vows in the name of someone other than Allah, as Hindus do in their temples and ignorant Muslims at shrines: eating it, feeding it, buying and selling it all become harām. But there is an important limit. An animal released after having its ear lobe cut or being branded, in reverence for something other than Allah, is a third case: such animals are *baḥīrah* or *sā'ibah*, and it is the practice of releasing them that the Qur'an forbids. The false belief does not make the animal itself unlawful — "if such animals are held to be forbidden, it will amount to supporting their false beliefs." The animal remains lawful like any other, and by the principles of Muslim law it never leaves its owner's ownership, whatever he imagines; so if it is sold or gifted, it is perfectly lawful for the one who receives it to buy, slaughter, eat or sell it.

## The exception: when a life is at stake

*But if one is forced by necessity without willful disobedience nor transgressing due limits, then there is no sin on him.* Ibn Kathir explains that Allah permitted eating these things "when needed for survival or when there are no permissible types of food available."

The early authorities read the two conditions closely. Mujahid, and likewise Saʿid bin Jubayr, said the licence applies to one who would otherwise have to resort to highway robbery, rising against the rulers, or some other disobedience to Allah; but one who eats "transgressing the limits, or continually, or out of disobedience to Allah" has no licence "even if he is in dire need." Saʿid and Muqatil bin Hayyan explained *ghayra bāgh* as "without believing that it is permissible." Ibn ʿAbbas said it means eating the dead animal "and not continuing to do so." Qatadah said it means not eating from dead animals when the lawful is available.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens the definition: in the terminology of the Sharīʿah, *muḍṭarr* means a person whose **life is in danger** — "ordinary pain or need cannot qualify a person to be known as muḍṭarr." Two conditions attach: the aim must be to save life and not to enjoy eating; and he must eat only as much as would serve to save his life — eating to fill the stomach, or much more than one needs, remains prohibited even then.

And it is not merely a permission. Masrūq said, "Whoever is in dire need, but does not eat or drink until he dies, he will enter the Fire." Ibn Kathir concludes that for one who needs it for survival, eating is "not only permissible but required."

There is a further limit worth noting. When someone in dire straits can obtain other people's food without risking the loss of his hands or causing harm, he may not eat the dead animal. Ibn Kathir supports this with the report of ʿAbbād bin Shuraḥbīl Al-Ghubarī, recorded by Ibn Majah: in a year of famine he entered a garden in Al-Madinah, cleaned and ate some grain and put some in his garment; the owner roughed him up and took his garment. The Prophet ﷺ said to the owner, "You have not fed him when he was hungry — or he said starving — nor have you taught him if he was ignorant," then commanded that the garment be returned and a wasq, or half a wasq, of food be given to him. Ibn Kathir notes the chain is sufficiently strong and supported by many witnessing narrations, such as the hadith that ʿAmr bin Shuʿayb narrated from his father from his grandfather, that the Messenger ﷺ was asked about hanging clusters of dates and said, "There is no harm for whoever takes some of it in his mouth for a necessity without putting it in his garment." The hungry may take enough for the mouth — not enough for the pocket.

## "There is no sin on him" — a deliberate choice of words

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān highlights something easy to miss. The Qur'an does not say that these things *become lawful* under compulsion; it says *lā ithma ʿalayh* — there is no sin on him. If the objective had been to make them lawful under compulsive need, a simple exception from the ruling of unlawfulness would have been enough. Instead the wording makes a point: "what is harām remains harām as it is, and using it is nothing but sin, however, the muḍṭarr has been forgiven this sin." The permission never becomes comfortable. It never becomes a taste one acquires.

That is exactly why the ayah closes with two names of Allah rather than a legal formula: *Truly, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful*. Muqatil bin Hayyan applied it to "what is eaten out of necessity." Saʿid bin Jubayr drew out both names: Allah is pardoning for what has been eaten of the unlawful, and Merciful in that He allowed the prohibited during times of necessity.

## Living it

Ibn Kathir's opening line is the practical heart of the passage: what you eat reaches your prayer. The man in the hadith did everything right at the moment of asking and had already lost the case long before, at the point of earning and buying. Ayah 172 asks a believer to care about the *source* of what he consumes, and then to be grateful — because gratitude, the ayah says, is what worship looks like at the table.

Ayah 173 asks for two disciplines pulling in opposite directions. Do not add to Allah's prohibitions out of scruple or hearsay: what the Book has not mentioned is pardoned. And do not subtract from them out of convenience, custom or reverence for a shrine, a grave or a great man — because the fourth prohibition shows that a slaughter can be ruined by nothing more than an intention.

For medicine, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān applies the same framework, since the licence in this ayah is what proves it. The default is set by the words of the Prophet ﷺ as reported in al-Bukhari, that Allah has placed no cure for the Muslims in what is harām. Some jurists argued for permission from the episode of the ʿUraynah tribe, whom the Prophet ﷺ permitted camel milk and urine and who were cured by it, but the commentary judges that episode to carry several possibilities and holds to the original position: unless the conditions of extreme necessity exist, harām medicine is not permissible. Five conditions are given for the necessity case — that one's life be in danger; that another lawful medicine does not work or is not available; that it be normally certain the disease will be cured by it; that enjoying its use not be the aim; and that no more be used than is needed. Al-Durr al-Mukhtār records that the apparent position of the madhhab forbids medication through the unlawful, while al-Ḥāwī al-Qudsī is quoted there as reporting that some ʿulamāʾ permitted it where the cure is known and no other medicine is known — likened to the permission granted to the critically thirsty. The same reasoning governs blood transfusion, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes is "doubtlessly permissible" under compulsive conditions — where the patient faces a life-or-death situation, no life-saving drug is effective or available, and there is a strong likelihood the transfusion will save the life — resting that verdict expressly on "this Qur'anic text which clearly permits the saving of one's life by eating the flesh of a dead animal, if compelled by necessity." Where there is no compulsion and other treatments could work, the jurists differ, some permitting and some not.

A short list of prohibitions, a wide field of good things, and a door held open for the one whose life is at stake. That is the balance these two ayat strike — and the closing words tell you Whose character it reflects.

passages.title: Selling Allah's revelation for a small price
passages.tafsir:
# Selling Allah's revelation for a small price (2:174–176)

These three ayat are about people who possessed Allah's revelation, recognised the truth in it, and then hid it — because telling the truth would have cost them income and standing. The passage holds together as a single sentence of judgement: ayah 174 names the crime and its punishment, ayah 175 sums up the transaction they made, and ayah 176 explains *why* such a punishment is deserved. Running through all three is one image: a sale. These people bought and sold, and every item they traded away was worth infinitely more than what they got for it.

## Where this passage sits

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the movement of the sūrah here. The verses just before this dealt with **unlawful things which are tangible**. Now the Qurʼān turns to **the intangible deeds that have been made unlawful** — evil deeds, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, inner and outer. That is a deliberate shift: from what a person handles to what a person is.

And yet the vocabulary does not change. The verse does not say these people *earn* fire — it says they **eat** it, into their bellies. A wrong done with knowledge and with a fee is described in exactly the language of a meal.

## The story behind the verse

Ibn Kathir is direct about who is being addressed. He says these are **the Jews who concealed their Book's descriptions of Muhammad ﷺ**, all of which testify to his truth as a Messenger and a Prophet.

Why hide it? Ibn Kathir gives the motive plainly, and it is not theological. They concealed it so they would not lose the authority and the position they held with the Arabs, who would bring them gifts and honour them. They feared that if they announced what they knew about the Prophet ﷺ, the people would abandon them and follow him. **So they hid the truth so that they might retain the little that they were getting** — and, in Ibn Kathir's words, they sold their souls for this little profit. They preferred the little that they gained over guidance, over following the truth, over believing in the Messenger ﷺ and having faith in what Allah sent him with.

Then Ibn Kathir adds the detail that turns this from a warning into a tragedy. **It did not even work.** As for this world, Allah made the truth about His Messenger ﷺ known anyway, by the clear signs and the unequivocal proofs. The very people the concealers feared would follow the Prophet ﷺ believed in him and followed him anyway — and became his supporters against them. So they earned anger on top of the wrath they had already earned before. Ibn Kathir's verdict on the whole affair: **they have profited failure and loss in this life and the Hereafter.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān widens the same picture with a second example: religious scholars among them were addicted to giving out false verdicts in favour of people who bribed them, and would go to the limit of **distorting the verses of the Torah to suit the desire of their client.** Not merely staying silent about the truth — reshaping the text so the paying customer heard what he wanted.

## The language of the marketplace

Notice how relentlessly the passage speaks in the vocabulary of buying and selling. In ayah 174 they "purchase a small gain therewith" (*yashtarūna bihi thamanan qalīlan*). Ibn Kathir explains that "small gain" as **the joys and delights of this earthly life** — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it *insignificant worldly gains*. Not necessarily a trivial amount in human terms, but trivial when set against what was handed over for it.

Then in ayah 175 the same verb returns twice, and the price tag is stated in full:

- *ishtarawu al-ḍalālata bi'l-hudā* — "they have purchased error **at the price of** guidance."
- *wa'l-ʿadhāba bi'l-maghfirah* — "and torment **at the price of** forgiveness."

The rendering itself tells you which way the goods moved. Guidance and forgiveness are what went out; error and torment are what came in. Ibn Kathir spells out what "guidance" meant concretely in their case: announcing the Prophet's description that they found in their own Books, the news of his prophecy, the good news of his coming which the previous Prophets proclaimed, and then following and believing in him. That is what they opposed. Instead they preferred misguidance — denying him, rejecting him, concealing what their Books said of him. And on the other side of the ledger, Ibn Kathir notes, **they preferred torment over forgiveness** for the sins they had committed. Forgiveness was genuinely available; they let it go.

## "They eat nothing but fire"

Of every phrase in this passage, this is the one that lodges in the memory: *mā yaʼkulūna fī buṭūnihim illā al-nār* — "they eat into their bellies nothing but fire."

Ibn Kathir's explanation is that **whatever they eat in return for hiding the truth will turn into a raging fire in their stomachs on the Day of Resurrection.** He cites the parallel from Sūrah al-Nisāʼ, where Allah says of those who unjustly eat up the property of orphans that "they eat up only fire into their bellies, and they will be burnt in the blazing Fire" (4:10) — the same image, the same mechanism, applied to a different theft.

Ibn Kathir also brings a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ, which he reports as authentic: **"Those who eat or drink in golden or silver plates are filling their stomachs with the fire of Jahannam (Hell)."** (Ibn Kathir does not name the collection here, so neither will we.) What the comparison establishes is that what a person swallows in this life is not neutral matter; it carries a consequence into the Hereafter.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws this out at ayah 175. A person who changes an injunction of the Sharīʿah in his greed for worldly gains **should know that these worldly gains he consumes are like embers of fire he is storing in his stomach, because that is the ultimate end of his deeds.** And it reports that some perceptive ʿUlamāʼ have said that unlawful wealth **is, in reality, the very fire of Hell** — even though we do not sense it as such during our lifetime in this mortal world; but once one dies, his or her deeds will appear in the form of fire.

Whether one takes the fire as the ultimate end of the deed or as its hidden present reality, the practical upshot is the same, and it is worth sitting with: the bribe felt like dinner.

## The sentence in ayah 174

Ayah 174 does not stop at the fire. It lists what will happen on the Day of Resurrection with terrible economy:

**"Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection"** — Ibn Kathir explains that this is because Allah is furious with them for concealing the truth; they thus deserve Allah's anger, so He will not look at them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it: He will not speak to them affectionately.

**"Nor purify them"** — Ibn Kathir glosses this as: He will not praise them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as: nor will He purify them by forgiving their sins. Both senses converge on the same loss — no cleansing, no commendation, nothing.

**"And theirs will be a painful torment"** — He will instead cause them to taste a severe torment.

There is a symmetry here worth pausing over. They withheld what Allah sent down from the people who needed it; on that Day, Allah has no word for them.

## "How bold they are for the Fire" (175)

The closing phrase of ayah 175 — *fa-mā aṣbarahum ʿalā al-nār* — is among the most arresting in the sūrah, and the two commentaries render it differently.

**Ibn Kathir** takes it as a statement about the Hereafter: Allah states that they will suffer such severe, painful torment that **those who see them will be amazed at how they could bear** the tremendous punishment, torture and pain they will suffer. He follows the comment with a supplication, and it is worth borrowing: *we seek refuge with Allah from this evil end.*

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** renders the sense as an astonished remark about the people themselves: "They must be very courageous in that they are all set to go into Hell" — the tone of someone watching a person walk calmly toward a fire and wondering what kind of nerve that takes.

Read together, the two renderings look at the same short phrase from either side of death: composure now, endurance then, and in both cases something that should not be possible.

## Why it is deserved (176)

Ayah 176 supplies the justification, and it begins with "That is **because**." Everything in the two preceding ayat rests on what follows.

**"Allah has sent down the Book in truth."** Ibn Kathir explains: they deserve this painful torment because Allah revealed Books to His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ and to the Prophets before him, and these revelations **bring about truth and expose falsehood** — yet they took Allah's signs for mockery. Their Books ordered them to announce the truth and to spread the knowledge; instead they defied the knowledge and rejected it. The Final Messenger ﷺ called them to Allah, commanded them to work righteousness and forbade them from committing evil — and they rejected him, denied him, defied him, and hid the truth that they knew about him.

That is the aggravating circumstance. This was not ignorance. It was informed refusal, by people whose own scripture had made disclosure a duty. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the same point from the other end: all these punishments come to them because they elected to stray away from the Book of Allah, **something so clear and true.**

**"And verily, those who disputed about the Book are far away in opposition"** — *la-fī shiqāqin baʿīd*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the sense: they must be victims of serious intransigence and are far out in schism, as a result of which they can expect to deserve a matching punishment. The punishment matches the distance.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān refuses to let this stay a passage about somebody else. In this criticism, it says, there is **a veiled warning given to the ʿulamāʼ, the religious scholars of the community of the Last of the Prophets**: that they should keep away from such practices and never fall short in disclosing the true injunctions of Allah for any material reason or vested interest of their own.

That is the passage's own application, and it is worth stating without softening:

- **Knowledge you possess is a trust, not an asset.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes concealing the contents of the Book of Allah as a *breach of trust*. The one who knows an answer owes it.
- **The price is always small.** Not because the sums were trivial — Ibn Kathir says they held real authority and position among the Arabs, who brought them gifts and honoured them — but because of what sat on the other side of the scale. His judgement on the whole affair is that they profited failure and loss, in this life and the Hereafter.
- **Fear of losing an audience is exactly the motive the verse indicts.** Ibn Kathir names it: they feared that if they announced what they knew, the people would abandon them and follow the Prophet ﷺ. Anyone who softens or withholds a ruling to keep a following should recognise the shape of that fear.
- **And it did not save them anyway.** Allah made the truth known by the clear signs and the unequivocal proofs. The concession bought nothing.

The passage ends where it began — with a Book sent down in truth. Truth does not need our protection; it needs our honesty. What we risk by hiding it is not the truth. It is ourselves.

passages.title: What righteousness truly is
passages.tafsir:
This single, unusually comprehensive ayah answers a question that the long dispute over the qiblah had made urgent: what actually makes a person righteous? The answer moves the eye away from a compass direction and onto a whole life — what a person believes, what he does with his money, how he stands before Allah, how he keeps his word, and how he holds up when everything is against him. Ibn Kathir says of it that it "contains many great wisdoms, encompassing rulings and correct beliefs," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats it as the doorway into the second half of Sūrah al-Baqarah.

## The moment this was revealed into

Ibn Kathir sets the scene. Allah had first commanded the believers to face Bayt al-Maqdis, and then to face the Kaʿbah in prayer. That change was hard on some of the People of the Book, and even on some Muslims. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that when the House of Allah at Makkah replaced Bayt al-Maqdis as the qiblah, the Jews, the Christians and the mushrikīn — who were eager to find fault with Islam — were stirred up and produced objection after objection against Islam and against the Prophet ﷺ. Earlier ayat of the sūrah answered those objections in detail. This ayah closes the file, and it does so in a strikingly different way: not by arguing about directions at all, but by putting directions in their place.

Abu al-ʿĀliyah explains why east and west specifically are named: "The Jews used to face the west for their qiblah, while the Christians used to face the east." So the opening words touch each party where they stood. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the address may well be to Jews, Christians and Muslims all at once, with this sense: real *birr* and real merit lie in obedience to Allah. The direction He tells you to face becomes meritorious *because* He told you to face it. In itself, east or west or any other orientation carries no weight — these are directions in an absolute sense, and cannot be turned into the object of faith to the exclusion of everything else Allah has legislated.

That is the hinge of the whole ayah. Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: facing east or west does not by itself produce righteousness or obedience unless Allah has legislated it. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, so long as the command was to face Bayt al-Maqdis, obeying *that* was the act deserving of merit; now that the command is to face the House of Allah at Makkah, obeying *this* is what earns merit. The value was never in the geography. It was in the obeying.

Ibn Kathir draws the parallel with the sacrifices: **"It is neither their meat nor their blood that reaches Allah, but it is the piety from you that reaches Him"** (22:37). The animal is real, the ritual is commanded — but what ascends is the taqwa inside it.

## *Birr* — the word the ayah is built on

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes *birr* as an umbrella word in Arabic for what is good in the absolute sense: it gathers into itself every act of righteousness and obedience, inward and outward alike. Its essence, the commentary says, is *obedience*. This is why the ayah does not answer "righteousness is not facing east or west" with a competing direction; it answers with an entire human being.

There is a fine point in how the answer is phrased. The Arabic does not say "but righteousness is *to believe*"; it says "but righteousness is *the one who* believes." Ath-Thawrī recited it as **"but birr is the one who believes in Allah"** and said that what follows are the *types* of birr — and Ibn Kathir comments, "He has said the truth." Whoever acquires the qualities listed here, Ibn Kathir adds, has embraced all aspects of Islam and put into practice every kind of righteousness. Abu al-ʿĀliyah's summary of the ayah is worth holding onto: "this is faith, and its essence requires implementation." The same was reported from al-Hasan and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas.

## The architecture of the ayah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān maps the ayah as a complete syllabus of religion in four departments, in order:

- **Belief** — "that one believes in Allah…" and what follows.
- **Worship of Allah** — running through to "and pays the Zakah."
- **Dealings with people** — "and those who fulfil their promise."
- **Morals, the inner deeds** — "the patient."

And then the verdict: those who live all of this are the true ones, and they are the God-fearing. The commentary observes that articles of belief, deeds flowing from them, and morals are the essence of every religious injunction — all details fall under these three — so this one ayah houses them all. That is why Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that everything that follows to the end of Sūrah al-Baqarah is effectively an explanation and elaboration of this verse: retaliation, wills, fasting, jihād, hajj, spending, divorce, marriage, ʿiddah, dower, trade, witnessing — the chapters of *birr*, unfolded one by one.

## What the ayah asks you to believe

The ayah names them: belief in Allah, in the Last Day, in the Angels, in the Book, and in the Prophets.

Ibn Kathir explains several of these. Believing in Allah means believing that He alone is worthy of worship. Believing in the angels means believing in them as the emissaries between Allah and His Messengers. The Books are the revelations sent down by Allah to the Prophets, finalised by the most honourable Book, the Qurʼān — which supersedes and abrogates all previous Books, mentions every type of righteousness and the way to happiness in this life and the Hereafter, and testifies to all of Allah's Prophets, from the first Prophet to the Final Prophet, Muhammad ﷺ.

## Wealth given "in spite of love for it"

Notice where the ayah goes next. Belief is stated, and immediately the subject is money — before even the prayer is mentioned.

The phrase is *ʿalā ḥubbihi*, "upon love of it." Ibn Kathir says it refers to those who give money away *while still desiring and loving it*. He supports this with the hadith recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥayn (the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections) from Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: **"The best charity is when you give it away while still healthy and thrifty, hoping to get rich and fearing poverty."** The charity that costs you nothing to part with is not the charity being praised. He also cites **"By no means shall you attain birr unless you spend of that which you love"** (3:92), and the description of those who feed the poor, the orphan and the captive saying, **"We feed you seeking Allah's Face only. We wish for no reward, nor thanks from you"** (76:8-9). Higher still, Ibn Kathir notes, is **"and give them preference over themselves even though they were in need of that"** (59:9) — those people give away what they *need*, while the people described here give away what they *covet* though may not need.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the phrase from the grammar. The pronoun in *ḥubbihi* ("its/His love") can refer to three things, giving three meanings:

1. **To Allah** — spend out of love for Allah, not from material motives or to be seen; His exalted majesty demands utterly unmixed sincerity (real *ikhlāṣ*, not the word used as a casual pleasantry).
2. **To the wealth** — only what you actually love qualifies. Giving away your throw-aways is not charity (though passing on something usable to someone who can use it beats binning it).
3. **To the act of giving itself** — be content in your heart with what you give; it should not be that the hand gives while the heart aches.

Imām al-Jaṣṣāṣ held that all three meanings may well be intended together.

**Who receives it.** Ibn Kathir works through the list. *Relatives* have more right to your charity than anyone else, as the hadith he cites states: charity given to the poor is charity, while charity given to a relative is two things — charity and *ṣilah*, the nurturing of kinship; they are the most deserving of you and your kindness and charity. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah has commanded kindness to relatives in many places in the Qurʼān. *Orphans* are children with no one to look after them, who lost their fathers while still young and weak, unable to find their own sustenance since they have not reached the age of work. The *miskīn* is one who lacks enough food or clothing, or has no dwelling, and should be granted enough provision to meet his needs. Here Ibn Kathir cites the Ṣaḥīḥayn, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"The miskīn is not the person who roams around, and whose need is met by one or two dates or one or two bites. Rather, the miskīn is he who does not have what is sufficient, and to whom the people do not pay attention and, thus, do not give him from the charity."** That is a quietly devastating line: the neediest person in your city is probably not the one you can see. *Ibn as-sabīl*, the wayfarer, is the needy traveller who has run out of money and should be given whatever helps him get back to his land — and likewise anyone on a permissible journey, who is given what he needs there and back; guests are included in this category. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said the wayfarer is the guest hosted by Muslims, and Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Abu Jaʿfar al-Bāqir, al-Hasan, Qatādah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, az-Zuhrī, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān said the same. *Those who ask* are those who beg from people and are given from zakāh and general charity. And *in freeing necks* refers to servants seeking to free themselves who cannot find enough money to buy their freedom.

**A grammatical detail with a practical point.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to a change of construction: every earlier category is named directly, but the last is introduced with *fī*, "in" — "and (spends) *in* (freeing) slaves." The preposition signals that the money is not handed over to the enslaved person as a personal amount to spend at will; it is spent *on the transaction* — buying them from their masters and setting them free.

**Zakāh is a floor, not a ceiling.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that two forms of spending other than zakāh are mentioned *before* zakāh, and suggests the reason: people habitually neglect these rights on the assumption that paying zakāh settles everything. It does not. Citing al-Jaṣṣāṣ and al-Qurṭubī, the commentary gives cases where spending becomes obligatory beyond zakāh: supporting relatives who have a valid excuse for being unable to earn their own living; saving the life of someone dying in poverty in front of you, even after your zakāh is paid; and building mosques and schools of religious education. The difference is that zakāh has a special law of its own which must be observed in full under all conditions, while these other obligations track need — where the need is real, spending becomes obligatory; where it is not, it does not.

## Prayer and zakāh

"And establishes the prayer" — Ibn Kathir explains this as praying *on time* and giving the prayer its due right: the bowing, the prostration, and the attentiveness and humbleness Allah requires. "And gives the zakāh" means the required charity due on one's money, as Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān stated.

## Keeping your word

Here the ayah shifts style, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the shift audible. Up to this point the qualities came as verbs — *believed*, *gave*, *established*. Now, for dealings with people, the Qurʼān switches to a noun form: *al-mūfūna bi-ʿahdihim*, "the ones who fulfil their covenant." The noun denotes a settled, continuing habit. A chance fulfilment of a compact is not enough to put you on this list; even a disbeliever or a sinner would accomplish that once in a while.

Why should promise-keeping stand for the whole domain of human dealings? Because, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out, standing by a contract entered into is the essence of all dealings — buying and selling, leasing, renting, partnership. Break your word and there is nothing left of any of them.

Ibn Kathir links the phrase to **"Those who fulfil the covenant of Allah and break not the bond"** (13:20), and notes that the opposite of this quality is hypocrisy — as found in a hadith: the signs of a hypocrite are three, that if he speaks he lies, if he promises he breaks his promise, and if he is entrusted he breaches the trust; and in another version, if he speaks he lies, if he vows he breaks his vow, and if he disputes he is lewd.

## The patient — and why they get their own salute

Three arenas of patience are named: *al-baʼsāʼ* (extreme poverty), *aḍ-ḍarrāʼ* (ailment and affliction) — Ibn Kathir glosses these as the time of meekness and ailment — and *ḥīna al-baʼs*, at the time of fighting, which Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Abu al-ʿĀliyah, Murrah al-Hamdānī, Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Qatādah, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, as-Suddī, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, Abu Mālik, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and others explained as being on the battlefield while facing the enemy. Ibn Kathir observes that calling them "the patient" here is itself a form of praise, because of the importance of patience in these circumstances and the suffering and difficulties that accompany them.

The Arabic makes that praise structural. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the word appears as *aṣ-ṣābirīn* (accusative) rather than *aṣ-ṣābirūn*, which is what the parallel with *al-mūfūn* just before would have led you to expect. Commentators call this *naṣb ʿalā al-madḥ* — the accusative of praise, where an unspoken word of praising governs it. The grammar itself steps out of line to point at them. And rightly so, the commentary says: among the righteous, the patient are worthy of special praise, since *ṣabr* gives a person special power to perform righteous deeds. Of all the inner virtues, only patience is named here, because *ṣabr* means to control the human self and guard it against evil — it is the essence of all inner deeds, the means by which high morals are achieved and low ones eliminated.

## "Those are the ones who have been true"

Ibn Kathir explains the closing verdict: whoever acquires these qualities is truthful in his faith, because he has achieved faith in the heart and realised it in deed and upon the tongue — so these are the truthful ones. And they are *al-muttaqūn*, the pious, because they avoided the prohibitions and performed the acts of obedience.

## Living it

The ayah is a mirror, and it is meant to be uncomfortable in a particular way. It does not ask whether you are pointed in the right direction; it asks what is happening across every department of your life. Is your belief whole — in Allah, in the Last Day, in the angels, in the Book, in the Prophets — or do you quietly hold some of it more firmly than the rest? Does money leave your hand while you still want it — and does it reach relatives, orphans, the overlooked poor, the stranded traveller? Is your prayer on time and given its due right, or merely performed? Does your word hold as a settled habit, not an occasion? And can you hold steady in poverty, in illness, and at the moment of real danger?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's closing note is the right one to end on: this verse holds in its fold the important principles of all departments of faith, and its eloquent hints tell us the degree of importance of each one of them.

passages.title: The law of retaliation and its wisdom
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These two ayat lay down the Qur'an's law for murder: the killer is the one answerable with his life, while the family of the victim holds a door of mercy they may open by pardoning in return for blood-money. Ayah 178 gives the ruling and its conditions; ayah 179 gives the reason behind it: *there is life for you in retaliation*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the point plainly — the law of even retaliation does not take life, it gives life, because such a deterrent law makes people fear the punishment for killing, and so lives are saved.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notes the placement: the ayat just before this gave a brief introduction to the nature of righteousness, and from here the text enters into the description of the related subsidiary injunctions. This law of retaliation is the first of them.

## The word Qiṣāṣ

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the word *qiṣāṣ* literally means **likeness**. In usage it denotes "even retaliation" — to return like for like. In Islamic juristic terminology it means the equal retaliation of an aggression committed against the body of a person, allowed **only** on condition that the principle of "like for like" is strictly observed.

That principle is not an isolated idea. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points the reader forward to ayah 194 of this same surah — "So aggress against him in the like manner as he did against you" — and to the concluding ayat of Sūrat al-Naḥl: "And if you retaliate, then retaliate just as you have been oppressed against" (16:126). So as a term of the Sharīʿah, *qiṣāṣ* is a punishment for killing or wounding in which the principle of equality or likeness is taken into full consideration. The word itself carries a limit. Anything beyond likeness is no longer *qiṣāṣ*.

Notice also how the ayah opens — *kutiba ʿalaykum*, which Ibn Kathir renders as "has been ordained on you." This is something laid down as law, and as we will see below, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds that its execution belongs to lawful authority rather than to private hands.

## The occasion: a demand the ayah came to break

Two accounts stand behind this ruling in the sources.

Ibn Kathir gives the first as the reason behind Allah's command that the set limits not be transgressed as others before had transgressed them. The Jewish tribe of Banū al-Naḍīr had invaded Qurayẓah, another Jewish tribe, during the time of Jāhiliyyah, and defeated them. On that basis they made it a law that when a man of al-Naḍīr killed a man of Qurayẓah, he was not killed in retaliation but only paid a hundred *wasq* of dates (*wasq* being the unit such goods were measured in); but when a man of Qurayẓah killed a man of al-Naḍīr, he would be killed for him. And if al-Naḍīr wanted a ransom instead, the man of Qurayẓah had to pay **two hundred** *wasq* — double the blood-money al-Naḍīr paid. So, Ibn Kathir says, Allah commanded that justice be observed regarding the penal code, and that the path of the misguided and mischievous be avoided: those who, in disbelief and transgression, defy and alter what Allah has commanded them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a second occasion, which Ibn Kathir reports on the authority of Ibn Abī Ḥātim: just before the advent of Islam, war broke out between two tribes and many were killed on both sides — men and women, free people and slaves. Their case was still undecided when the Islamic period set in and both tribes entered the fold of Islam. Now, as Muslims, they began talking about retaliation for their dead — and the more powerful of the two tribes insisted that they would agree to nothing less than **a free man killed for their slave, and a man killed for their woman**.

It was to refute this demand, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, that the ayah was revealed.

## What "the free for the free, the slave for the slave, the female for the female" means

Read against that background, the phrase is doing something very precise. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that by saying *free man for a free man, slave for a slave, female for a female*, the ayah negates their absurd demand that a free man be killed for a slave, or a man for a woman, **even though he may not be the killer at all**. The just law Islam enforced is that the killer is the one who has to be killed in *qiṣāṣ*. If a woman is the killer, why should an innocent man be killed in retaliation? If the killer is a slave, there is no sense in retaliating against an innocent free man. That, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is an injustice which can never be tolerated in Islam.

And it clarifies the misreading immediately: the ayah does **not** mean that *qiṣāṣ* is not taken from a man who kills a woman, or from a free man who kills a slave. The clear proof is in the ayah's own opening words — *al-qiṣāṣ fi'l-qatlā*, "the *qiṣāṣ* has been enjoined upon you in the case of those murdered" — which is universal in application. Other ayat state the point even more explicitly, for instance *al-nafs bi'l-nafs*, "the person for the person." So the ruling Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records is that in intentional homicide of this nature the killer is killed — free man for a free man, slave for a slave, female for a female, **and likewise a man for a woman**.

Ibn Kathir records the same conclusion in the language of abrogation: the clause "the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female" was abrogated by the statement *life for life* (5:45).

## Where the scholars genuinely differed

Ibn Kathir records two live disagreements, and it is worth giving both sides as he does.

**A Muslim killing a non-Muslim.** The majority of scholars agree that a Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever whom he kills. Al-Bukhari reported that ʿAlī narrated that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said: *"The Muslim is not killed for the disbeliever."* Ibn Kathir states that no opinion opposing this ruling could stand correct, nor is there an authentic hadith to contradict it. He then notes that **Abū Ḥanīfah** thought the Muslim could be killed for a disbeliever, following the general meaning of the ayah in Sūrat al-Māʾidah (5:45).

**A group killing one person.** The Four Imams — Abū Ḥanīfah, Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad — and the majority of scholars stated that a group is killed for the one person they murder. ʿUmar said, about a boy who was killed by seven men, "If all the residents of Ṣanʿāʾ collaborated on killing him, I would kill them all." Ibn Kathir observes that no opposing opinion was known among the Companions at that time, which constitutes a near consensus. There is, however, an opinion attributed to Imam Aḥmad that a group is not killed for one person, and that only one person is killed for one person; Ibn al-Mundhir also attributed this opinion to Muʿādh, Ibn al-Zubayr, ʿAbd al-Malik bin Marwān, al-Zuhrī, Ibn Sīrīn and Ḥabīb bin Abī Thābit.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a defining condition for the whole subject: the principle of even retaliation is applied **exclusively** in cases of culpable homicide, where someone has been killed intentionally with a lethal weapon causing injury and blood-loss.

## The door of pardon — and what "forgiven" means here

*"But if the killer is forgiven by the brother of the killed…"* Ibn Kathir explains that this refers to accepting blood money — the relatives of the victim taking it in return for pardoning the killer — in cases of intentional murder, an opinion he attributes to Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Abū al-Shaʿthāʾ, Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and Muqātil bin Ḥayyān. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said that Ibn ʿAbbās said the meaning is that the killer is pardoned by his brother — that is, the relative of the victim — and the *diyah* is accepted after capital punishment has already become due against him. **That**, Ibn ʿAbbās said, is the ʿafw the ayah speaks of.

Note the word the ayah itself uses for the party who pardons: the killer's *brother*. Ibn Kathir, transmitting from Ibn ʿAbbās, glosses it as the relative of the victim — the very family with the grievance.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān works out the details:

- If, in a case of intentional killing, the murderer is given **full** pardon — for instance, both surviving sons of the deceased pardon and forgo their right of retaliation — the killer is free of any claim against him.
- If the pardon is **not that full** — one of the two sons pardons and the other does not — the killer stands released right there from the retaliatory punishment, but the son who did not pardon is entitled to **half** of the blood-money. In the Sharīʿah this *diyah* amounts to one hundred camels, or one thousand dinars, or ten thousand dirhams, or approximately nineteen pounds of silver according to current weights and measures.
- Just as an incomplete pardon makes payment of blood-money necessary, a mutual settlement between the parties on a certain amount likewise makes retaliation inapplicable and payment of the agreed amount necessary — governed by conditions that appear in the books of *fiqh* (Islamic jurisprudence).
- The inheritors of the person killed, whatever their number, own the right of retaliation and blood-money **in accordance with their share in the inheritance**. But because *qiṣāṣ* is indivisible, a pardon given by any one of the inheritors holds good and becomes inclusive of the right of retaliation held by the others — though they still receive the blood-money according to their share.

## "Sought in a good manner… paid respectfully"

Having opened the door, the ayah sets the manners on both sides of it. Ibn Kathir explains: *fa-ttibāʿun bi'l-maʿrūf* means that when the relative agrees to take the blood money, he should collect his rightful dues **with kindness**; and *wa-adāʾun ilayhi bi-iḥsān* means the killer should accept the terms of settlement **without causing further harm or resisting the payment**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same from the other direction: the *diyah* must be paid as fixed, in a fair manner, and promptly — and the claimant too should pursue the matter in a recognised manner, causing no harassment to the defendant. Both halves of the instruction guard against the settlement becoming a fresh source of harm.

## "An alleviation and a mercy from your Lord"

Ibn Kathir explains this phrase as meaning that the legislation which allows you to accept blood money for intentional murder is itself an alleviation and a mercy from your Lord — it lightens what was required from those who were before you, who had either to apply capital punishment or to forgive.

Saʿīd bin Manṣūr reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said the Children of Israel were required to apply the Law of equality in murder cases and were not allowed to offer pardons in return for blood money — and that Allah then addressed this Ummah with these words; hence "pardoning" or "forgiving" here means accepting blood money in intentional murder cases. Ibn Kathir notes that Ibn Ḥibbān also recorded this in his Ṣaḥīḥ. Qatādah put it as a comparison of three communities: the People of the Torah were allowed either to apply the penal code or to pardon the killer, but were not allowed to take blood money; the People of the Injīl were required to pardon, with no *diyah* legislated; and this Ummah is allowed to apply the penal code, or to pardon and accept the blood money. Ibn Kathir says similar was reported from Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Muqātil bin Ḥayyān and al-Rabīʿ bin Anas.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this law of blood-money and pardon a relief granted by Allah Almighty in His grace; otherwise there would have been no choice but to face the punishment of death.

## "Whoever transgresses after that"

Ibn Kathir explains that those who kill in retaliation **after** taking or accepting the *diyah* will suffer a painful and severe torment from Allah — the same being reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ bin Anas, al-Suddī and Muqātil bin Ḥayyān. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān widens it to crossing the limit Allah has set anywhere in this area — for instance, filing a false or doubtful case of murder, or re-opening a murder case after a pardon has been given. Whoever does so, it says, will be severely punished.

## Not private vengeance

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is emphatic on a point that is easy to miss. The right of even retaliation is indeed vested in the legal heirs of the person killed — but in accordance with the consensus of the Muslim community, they do not have the right to settle the score by themselves; they cannot kill the killer on their own, and must instead seek the help of a Muslim ruler or his deputy to realise their right. The reason given is practical and humane: *qiṣāṣ* is an intricate issue whose details are simply out of reach for an average person, and heirs who do not know the particular circumstances in which retaliation does or does not become necessary may commit some sort of excess under the heat of their anger. So by unanimous agreement of the scholars, the right of retaliation must be secured and made effective through the agency of an Islamic government (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurṭubī).

## Ayah 179: "And there is life for you in retaliation"

Then comes the reason. Ibn Kathir explains that legislating this law — that the murderer be killed — carries great benefits for you: the sanctity of life will be preserved, because the killer will refrain from killing, being certain that if he kills he would be killed. Hence life will be preserved.
