He then makes a comparison. In previous Books there is a statement that *killing stops further killing* — and he says this meaning came in much clearer and more eloquent terms in the Qur'an: *"And there is a saving of life for you in al-qiṣāṣ."*

Abū al-ʿĀliyah said: "Allah made the Law of equality a 'life'. Hence, how many a man who thought about killing, but this Law prevented him from killing for fear that he will be killed in turn." Ibn Kathir reports similar statements from Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Abū Mālik, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ bin Anas and Muqātil bin Ḥayyān.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums it up: wise people should have no difficulty in seeing that the law of even retaliation does not take life — instead it gives life, for such a deterrent law will make people fear the punishment for killing somebody, and thus lives will be saved.

**"O people of understanding."** The address is chosen. The ayah calls on *ulū al-albāb* — "O you who have sound minds, comprehension and understanding," as Ibn Kathir renders it. And what such a mind is being asked to weigh is exactly what Abū al-ʿĀliyah described: not only the punishment carried out, but the killings that never happened because of the fear of it.

**"That you may attain taqwā."** Ibn Kathir gives the meaning as: perhaps by this you will be compelled to refrain from transgressing the prohibitions of Allah and what He considers sinful. And he defines *taqwā* itself — a word that means **doing all acts of obedience and refraining from all prohibitions**. So the aim of the law reaches past the courtroom: it is not only that murder be deterred, but that a person live in obedience to Allah across the whole of his life.

## Living it

- **The one who killed is the one answerable.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān repeats it: the one who has killed will be the one to be killed in *qiṣāṣ*; it is not permissible to kill an innocent man in place of the actual killer. Punishing a substitute of the "right" status is precisely what these ayat came to abolish.
- **Status does not change the ruling.** The whole force of the occasion of revelation is that a more powerful tribe wanted a heavier price for its own dead. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the injunction as: the killer will be killed, irrespective of the status of the parties involved.
- **Pardon is a real option, and it is called an alleviation and a mercy from your Lord.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān speaks of the aggrieved party relenting *on its own* — the right belongs to the heirs of the victim.
- **Settle cleanly.** Collect with kindness, pay as fixed, fairly and promptly, cause no harassment — and never re-open a murder case after a pardon has been given.
- **Leave enforcement to lawful authority.** The scholars agreed unanimously, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, that this right is realised through a Muslim ruler or his deputy — not least because heirs acting alone may, in the heat of their anger, commit an excess.

passages.title: Bequests and the correction of an unjust will
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat deal with one subject from three angles: the wasiyyah — the will a person leaves behind when death draws near. Ayah 180 lays down the duty of making it, ayah 181 warns whoever changes it after the testator's voice has fallen silent, and ayah 182 carves out the one exception: the person who steps in not to distort a will but to straighten a crooked one. Together they form a small, complete law of the deathbed: make your bequest justly, let it be honoured faithfully, and correct it only to restore justice.

The passage as Ibn Kathir gives it reads: "It is prescribed for you, when death approaches any of you, if he leaves wealth, that he makes a bequest to parents and next of kin, according to reasonable manners. (This is) a duty upon Al-Muttaqin (the pious) (180) Then whoever changes it after hearing it, the sin shall be on those who make the change. Truly, Allah is All-Hearer, All-Knower (181) But he who fears from a testator some unjust act or wrongdoing, and thereupon he makes peace between the parties concerned, there shall be no sin on him. Certainly, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful (182)."

## The words themselves

**Al-wasiyyah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the word literally means an order to do something — an instruction that may take effect either during the life of the one who gives it or after his death. In common usage, however, it settled on the second sense: what must be done after death. Hence "will" or "bequest."

**Khayr — "if he leaves khayran."** Ibn Kathir's rendering of the ayah is "if he leaves wealth." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the basis for that: out of the many meanings the word khayr carries in Arabic, "wealth" happens to be one of them — as in the verse "Surely he is passionate in his love for good things," where, by the unanimous agreement of the commentators, khayr means wealth. So the ayah is speaking of the person who leaves property behind.

**"A duty upon Al-Muttaqin."** Ayah 180 closes with the phrase Ibn Kathir renders "(This is) a duty upon Al-Muttaqin (the pious)" — those who are conscious of Allah.

## The historical arc: what this ayah asked for, and what changed

To understand these ayat you have to see where they sat in the unfolding of the law. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene: in early Islam, the shares of inheritance had not yet been fixed by the Shariʿah. The rule at that stage was that a dying person could make a will within one third of the inheritance, leaving it in the name of his parents and relatives in whatever proportion he chose. That much was their right; the rest went to his children. That is the situation ayah 180 addresses.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān breaks the ruling of the ayah into three parts:

1. No shares were fixed for any inheritors except the children; everything else was to be determined through the will the dying man made.
2. Making such a will for those relatives was **obligatory** on him.
3. Bequeathing more than one third of the inheritance was not permitted.

**The first ruling was abrogated by the verse of inheritance.** Ibn Kathir states that this ayah contains the command to include parents and relatives in the will, which was obligatory — according to the most correct view — before the ayah about inheritance was revealed. When that ayah came, this one was abrogated, and Allah Himself legislated fixed shares for those who deserve them. Deserving inheritors now take their fixed inheritance without needing to be included in the will, and without being reminded of the favour of the person they inherit from.

Ibn Kathir marshals the reports. Imam Ahmad recorded that Muhammad bin Sirin said: Ibn ʿAbbas was reciting Surat al-Baqarah, and when he reached "...if he leaves wealth, that he makes a bequest to parents and next of kin," he said, "This ayah was abrogated." The same was recorded by Saʿid bin Mansur and by Al-Hakim in his Mustadrak, where Al-Hakim said it is Sahih according to the criteria of Al-Bukhari and Muslim. Ibn Abu Hatim reports Ibn ʿAbbas naming the abrogating verse: "There is a share for men and a share for women from what is left by parents and those nearest related, whether the property be small or large — a legal share" (4:7).

This was not one man's opinion. Ibn Abu Hatim lists a long roll of authorities who held that 2:180 was abrogated by the inheritance verse: Ibn ʿUmar, Abu Musa, Saʿid bin Musayyib, Al-Hasan, Mujahid, ʿAtaʾ, Saʿid bin Jubayr, Muhammad bin Sirin, ʿIkrimah, Zayd bin Aslam, Ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas, Qatadah, As-Suddi, Muqatil bin Hayyan, Tawus, Ibrahim An-Nakhaʿi, Shurayh, Ad-Dahhak and Az-Zuhri. When that many of the Companions and the generation after them converge, you are looking at the settled understanding of the early community.

Alongside it Ibn Kathir cites what the Prophet ﷺ said in a speech, narrated by ʿAmr bin Kharijah and found in the Hadith narrated in the Sunan and other books:

> **"Allah has given each heir his fixed share. So there is no will for a deserving heir."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the same hadith from Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan sahih, and locates it precisely: it was part of the sermon delivered before some one hundred and fifty thousand Companions on the occasion of the Prophet's ﷺ last Hajj. A narration from Ibn ʿAbbas carries an extra clause — that there is no will for an inheritor *unless all the inheritors permit it*. The essence of the hadith, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws it out, is that Allah Almighty has Himself fixed the shares of the inheritors; a person therefore does not even have permission to make a will in favour of an heir — but should the other inheritors allow such a will to be carried out, it becomes permissible.

**The second ruling — the obligation to make such a will — also stands abrogated**, by the consensus of the Muslim Ummah, on the strength of that same hadith from the last Hajj.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a nuance worth noticing: in another narration from Ibn ʿAbbas it is said that the verse of inheritance abrogated the making of a will in the name of those who have a fixed share, while the injunction to make a will in favour of relatives who have *no* share in the inheritance still holds good (Jassas, Qurtubi). But it should be borne in mind, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān continues, that by the consensus of the Ummah it is not obligatory to make a will in their favour either; so that obligation too is abrogated, and such a bequest is now only a desired (mustahabb) act — and that, too, subject to their need (Jassas, Qurtubi).

## Can a hadith abrogate a verse? — the discussion Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on

This is where the commentary becomes genuinely interesting, because it raises a question a thoughtful reader will already be asking: how can a report from the Prophet ﷺ set aside a ruling stated in the Qur'an?

Imam Al-Jassas answers that this hadith was reported from a group of the blessed Companions and was accepted unanimously by the jurists of the Muslim community, so it is an uninterruptedly ensured (mutawatir) hadith — one whose veracity, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the term, stands ensured through an uninterrupted chain of transmitters from many sides who are unlikely to agree on a lie — and a report of that calibre makes the abrogation of a verse of the Qur'an permissible.

Imam Al-Qurtubi puts the principle more broadly: the scholars of the Muslim community unanimously agree that an injunction which comes to us from the Prophet ﷺ and is known with full certitude — as with mutawatir and mashhur (widely known) reports — stands on a par with an injunction of the Holy Qur'an and must be taken as the command of Allah Almighty. So the abrogation of a verse by a hadith of that kind is no cause for doubt.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then addresses the objection head-on. Yes, the hadith invalidating a will in favour of an heir is a solitary report (al-khabar al-wahid). But consider the circumstances: it comes from the sermon of the Prophet's ﷺ last Hajj, openly proclaimed before the largest ever gathering of the blessed Companions, and it was then received by their consensus and the consensus of the Muslim community after them. Had there been the slightest doubt about it, they would never have abandoned a verse of the Qur'an and agreed to this abrogating command through the hadith. Their unanimous acceptance is itself the proof.

## What still stands

**The one-third ceiling remains, by consensus.** The third of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's three rulings still holds good with the unanimous approval of the Ummah: it is not permissible to bequeath more than one third of what one leaves behind — though should the inheritors themselves allow more, even the whole of it, that becomes permissible.

The anchor for this is the exchange recorded in the Sahihayn, where Saʿd bin Abu Waqqas said: "O Allah's Messenger! I have some money and only a daughter inherits from me, should I will all my remaining property (to others)?" He ﷺ said, "No." "Then may I will half of it?" "No." "One-third?" **"Yes, one-third, yet even one-third is too much. It is better for you to leave your inheritors wealthy than to leave them poor, begging from others."**

Read that last sentence slowly. The Prophet ﷺ himself names the reason: the family left behind should not be reduced to begging from others. Ibn ʿAbbas took the counsel further still — Al-Bukhari mentions in his Sahih that he said, "I recommend that people reduce the proportion of what they bequeath by will to a fourth (of the whole legacy) rather than a third," precisely because the Prophet ﷺ had said, "One-third, yet even one-third is too much."

**Bequests to non-inheriting relatives remain recommended.** Ibn Kathir holds that it is recommended for the remaining relatives who have no designated fixed share of the inheritance to be willed up to a third, due to the general meaning of the ayah about the will. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the qualification already noted, citing Jassas and Qurtubi: by consensus this is not obligatory — it is mustahabb, a desired act, and that too subject to their need. Ibn Kathir adds that there are many other ayat and ahadith ordering kindness and generosity to one's relatives.

**Having a will ready remains a standing sunnah.** Ibn ʿUmar reported, in the Sahihayn, that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said: **"It is not permissible for any Muslim who has something to will to stay for two nights without having his last will and testament written and kept ready with him."** Ibn ʿUmar commented, "Ever since I heard this statement from Allah's Messenger ﷺ, no night has passed, but my will is kept ready with me." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses the same practical point: even though the *particular* will commanded in ayah 180 stands abrogated, making a will is still necessary — especially for a person who owes debts to others or holds something in trust — and he should make sure these are taken care of in his will. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also relays, without naming a collection, that the Prophet ﷺ said that a person who has some rights of other people due against him should not let three nights pass without having his written will with him. And a person retains the right, during his lifetime, to make some change in his will or cancel it altogether.

## Ayah 181: the sin travels to the one who changes it

"Then whoever changes it after hearing it, the sin shall be on those who make the change."

Ibn Kathir explains that this means whoever changed the will and testament or altered it by addition or deletion — including hiding the will, as is obvious — then "the sin shall be on those who make the change."

Ibn ʿAbbas and others said: **"The dead person's reward will be preserved for him by Allah, while the sin is acquired by those who change the will."** This is one of the most consoling lines in the passage. The testator who did his duty is not robbed of his reward by someone else's greed. The reward is preserved; the sin is acquired by the one who tampers.

Then: "Truly, Allah is All-Hearer, All-Knower." Ibn Kathir's gloss is that this means Allah knows what the dead person has bequeathed and what the beneficiaries (or others) have changed in the will. Both halves of the matter — the bequest and the alteration — lie open to Him. My own reflection, and not something the commentators say here: the tamperer may act when no witness is left alive to contradict him, but he is not acting unobserved.

## Ayah 182: correcting a crooked will is not tampering

Having sealed the door in ayah 181, ayah 182 opens a narrow and necessary window: "But he who fears from a testator some unjust act or wrongdoing, and thereupon he makes peace between the parties concerned, there shall be no sin on him."

The key word is **janaf**. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Al-ʿAliyah, Mujahid, Ad-Dahhak, Ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas and As-Suddi glossed it as **"error."** The ayah pairs it with *ithm*, sin. Ibn Kathir's examples show the range covered:

- An heir indirectly acquires more than his fair share — for instance, by being allocated that a certain item mentioned in the legacy be sold to him.
- The testator includes his daughter's son in the legacy so as to increase his daughter's share in the inheritance.

And Ibn Kathir is careful about motive: such errors "might occur out of the kindness of the heart without thinking about the consequences of these actions, or by sinful intention." A man who loves one child dearly and quietly tilts the will towards her may believe he is doing good. The category still covers him.

In such cases, Ibn Kathir says, the executive of the will and testament is allowed to correct the errors and to replace the unjust items in the will with a better solution, **so that both the Islamic law and what the dead person had wished for are respected and observed**. That balance is the heart of the ayah: the aim is not to override the deceased but to honour his wish and the law together. Such a correction would not constitute an alteration in the will — and Ibn Kathir notes that this is precisely why Allah mentioned it specifically, so that it is excluded from the prohibition against altering the will mentioned in the preceding ayah. He closes, as the scholars do, with "And Allah knows best."

And the ayah itself ends not with a threat but with two of Allah's names: "Certainly, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."

## Living it

Ibn Kathir sums up the standard the will must meet: it should be fair, in that one designates a part of the inheritance to his relatives **without committing injustice against his qualified inheritors and without extravagance or stinginess**. Two ditches on either side of a narrow road.

He closes his commentary with a report from ʿAbdur-Razzaq, from Abu Hurayrah, that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said:

> **"A man might perform the works of righteous people for seventy years, but when he dictates his will, he commits injustice and thus his works end with the worst of his deeds and he enters the Fire. A man might perform the works of evil people for seventy years, but then dictates a just will and thus ends with the best of his deeds and then enters Paradise."**

Abu Hurayrah then said: "Read if you wish — 'These are the limits ordained by Allah, so do not transgress them'" (2:229).

Seventy years, hanging on a dictated sentence. It is a startling thing to place at the end of a passage about paperwork, and it tells you how heavily this act is weighed. A will is a person's final deed, performed when he can no longer undo it, and it lands on people who will live with it for the rest of their lives.

So the passage asks four concrete things of a believer. Keep a will written and ready — Ibn ʿUmar did not let a single night pass without one. Make sure any debts you owe and any trusts you hold are named in it, since Maʿārif ul Qurʼān singles these out as the reason a will is still necessary today. Do not use the will to redistribute what Allah has already apportioned to your heirs, and stay inside the one third — remembering that even a third was called "too much," and that Ibn ʿAbbas preferred a fourth. And if you are the one holding someone else's will in your hands, understand exactly where you stand: you may not alter it by addition or deletion, but where it leans into error you are permitted — and this is the mercy of ayah 182 — to correct it and make peace between the parties.

passages.title: The prescription of the fast of Ramadan
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat prescribe the fast of Ramadan: the obligation and its purpose (183), its measure and its concessions (184), then the month named, its link to the revelation of the Qur'an, and the law in final form (185). They move from *why* to *how much* to *when* — and underneath runs a persistent gentleness, summed up in ayah 185: "Allah intends for you ease, and He does not want to make things difficult for you."

## What "fasting" means

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān begins with the word. **Ṣawm** literally means *to abstain*. In the terminology of Islamic law it means abstaining from eating, drinking and sexual intimacy, on two conditions: that the abstention runs continuously from dawn to sunset, and that there is an *intention* to fast. Both do real work — eat or drink even a minute before sunset and the fast is not valid; abstain from all these things all day with no intention to fast, and there is no fast either. Ibn Kathir joins the same two elements: abstaining from food, drink and sexual activity "with the intention of doing so sincerely for Allah the Exalted alone." Fasting is an act of worship — regarded as a pillar and a sign of Islam — not a diet with a religious label.

## "As it was prescribed for those before you"

Ayah 183 does not simply command; it places the command in a long line. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah ordained fasting for this Ummah just as He ordained it for those before them, "they being an example for them in that, so they should vigorously perform this obligation more obediently than the previous nations" — and links it to "To each among you, We have prescribed a law and a clear way… so compete in good deeds" (5:48).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the psychology. Mentioning the earlier communities shows on the one hand how weighty fasting is, and on the other it *encourages*: there may be some inconvenience in fasting, but the same inconvenience was faced by the communities before you, and "if an inconvenience is faced by a large number of people, it becomes easier to bear" (Rūḥ al-Maʿānī).

Who are "those before you"? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds that the phrase is used in a **general** sense, taking in all religious communities from Sayyidnā Ādam (peace be upon him) to the last of the Prophets ﷺ — which tells us that, like ṣalāh, fasting was enjoined upon the community of every prophet without exception. As for commentators who read "before you" as referring to the Christians, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes — citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī — that they intend that merely as an *example*, not to exclude other communities.

One caution follows. The ayah says fasts were enjoined on Muslims *as* they were enjoined on past communities; it does not follow that their fasts were identical in every respect with ours. There may have been differences in the number and the timings, and in fact there were (Rūḥ al-Maʿānī).

## Why: "that you may attain taqwā"

The ayah names its own purpose: *laʿallakum tattaqūn*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this points to an inherent quality of fasting, one that contributes significantly to a person's ability to abstain from sins and to fear Allah: fasting grows in a person a power that helps him control his desires, and that self-mastery "is really the foundation of Taqwā" — the very special Qur'anic term, tentatively translated as fear of Allah, abstinence, and the warding off of evil. Fasting does not merely test the appetite; it trains the will everything else depends on.

Ibn Kathir adds that fasting **purifies the souls** and cleanses them of the evil that might mix with them and of ill behaviour, and that "the fast cleanses the body and narrows the paths of Shayṭān." He cites the ḥadīth recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥayn (the two Ṣaḥīḥs):

> "O young people! Whoever amongst you can afford marriage, let him marry. Whoever cannot afford it, let him fast, for it will be a shield for him."

That is the purpose in miniature: the fast is protection.

## "A fixed number of days"

Ayah 184 opens with *ayyāman maʿdūdāt*, days few in number. Ibn Kathir's comment is quietly beautiful: the fast occurs during a fixed number of days **so that it does not become hard on the hearts**, thereby weakening their resolve and endurance.

## The concession for the sick and the traveller

**Who counts as sick?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: the word refers to one who cannot fast without an unbearable hardship, or who has strong apprehension that his illness will be aggravated. The evidence is internal to the passage — ayah 185's "and He does not want hardship for you" gives a clear indication to this effect — and the position is also accepted by the consensus of the Muslim jurists. Ibn Kathir agrees: the ayah indicates that ill persons who are unable to fast, or who fear harm by fasting, along with the traveller, are allowed to break the fast, and are then obliged to fast other days instead.

**Why "on a journey" and not "a traveller"?** Here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a fine linguistic observation. In granting the concession, the Qur'an chooses the phrase *ʿalā safarin* rather than the word *musāfir*, "traveller." This points out that simply leaving home and going out is not enough to claim the exemption: *ʿalā safarin* means one should have **embarked** on a journey, which does not mean going five or ten miles from home. The precise duration is not fixed in the words of the Qur'an; guided by the statement of the Prophet ﷺ and the subsequent practice of his blessed Companions, the great Imām Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him) and many jurists fixed the distance at what can be covered in three days by walking in three daily stages — put by the later-day jurists at 48 miles.

The same phrase yields a second ruling: the exemption lasts only so long as the travel continues. Stopping in between to rest or take care of something does not cut off the onward journey, unless the stay is for a considerable period of time — set at **fifteen days**, following a statement of the Prophet ﷺ. Whoever intends to stay at a given place for fifteen days no longer comes under the umbrella of *ʿalā safarin*. But someone who intends to stay out fifteen days **not at one place, but at different places and towns**, continues to hold the status of a traveller and keeps the concession, because he is still in the state of *ʿalā safarin*.

**Making up the days.** *Fa-ʿiddatun min ayyāmin ukhar* — literally "then, a number from other days." Fasts abandoned because of the compulsion of sickness or journey must be replaced by qaḍāʾ. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that rather than saying simply "their replacement is on them," the Qur'an chose this wording, which suggests the qaḍāʾ falls due once the sick person becomes healthy and the traveller returns home and lives on long enough to replace the fasts he missed — so one who dies before that happens is not held to it, nor required to make a will for the payment of ransom. The wording also leaves qaḍāʾ free of any fixed order: they may be kept in sequence or at random. One who missed the first ten days of Ramadan may begin with the tenth or the ninth and replace the earlier ones later, or fast with gaps at his convenience. Ibn Kathir agrees: making up missed days is not required to be consecutive; fasting consecutive days is required exclusively during Ramadan itself.

## The stages: how the law reached its final form

The sources let us watch the obligation settle. Ibn Kathir cites al-Bukhārī and Muslim from ʿĀʾishah: "ʿĀshūrāʾ was a day of fasting. When the obligation to fast Ramadan was revealed, those who wished fasted, and those who wished did not." Al-Bukhārī recorded the same from Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Masʿūd.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out the sequence from a long ḥadīth of the Companion Muʿādh ibn Jabal (may Allah be pleased with him) reported in the Musnad of Aḥmad, which describes three changes in the injunctions of fasting during the early period of Islam:

- When the Prophet ﷺ came to Madīnah, he used to fast three days in a month and on the tenth of Muḥarram. Then the command to observe the fasts of Ramadan was revealed — and under *kutiba ʿalaykum al-ṣiyām* there was an **option** either to fast or to pay ransom, with a preference given to fasting.
- Then Allah revealed "those of you who witness the month must fast therein" (185), which took away that option from those who had the strength and made fasting the only alternative — while the earlier command remained valid for the very old, who could pay ransom for the fasts they missed.
- The third change concerned the nights rather than the days: at first, eating, drinking and marital intimacy after ifṭār were permitted only if one had not slept, sleeping being taken as the beginning of the next fast. Then Allah revealed "It is made lawful for you, in the nights of fast, to have sex with your women," which made eating, drinking and intimacy permissible through the night until the break of dawn, and *suḥūr* was declared to be the sunnah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also reports that all the Imams of ḥadīth — al-Bukhārī, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasāʾī, al-Tirmidhī, al-Ṭabarānī and others — narrated from the Companion Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ that when *wa ʿalā alladhīna yuṭīqūnahu* was revealed they were given the choice of fasting or paying fidyah for each fast, and that when *faman shahida minkum al-shahra fal-yaṣumhu* was revealed the choice was withdrawn and fasting alone became necessary for those who had the strength.

Ibn Kathir gathers the same reports around *wa ʿalā alladhīna yuṭīqūnahu fidyatun ṭaʿāmu miskīn*. Muʿādh said: "In the beginning, those who wished fasted and those who wished did not fast and fed a poor person for each day." Al-Bukhārī recorded Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ saying that those who did not wish to fast used to pay the fidyah until ayah 185 was revealed, abrogating the earlier ayah; and it was reported from Nāfiʿ that Ibn ʿUmar said, "It was abrogated." *Yuṭīqūnahu* was glossed as "those who find it difficult to fast," as Ibn Masʿūd stated.

**Where the ruling did not lapse.** Ibn Kathir preserves the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, reported by al-Bukhārī from ʿAṭāʾ: "(This ayah) was not abrogated; it is for the old man and the old woman who are able to fast with difficulty, but choose instead to feed a poor person for every day." So the abrogation applies to the healthy person who is not travelling. The old man or woman who cannot fast is allowed to abstain and does not have to fast another day instead — he is not likely to improve and be able to fast other days — but pays a fidyah for every day missed. This was the opinion of Ibn ʿAbbās and several others among the Salaf, and of al-Bukhārī, who pointed to Anas: for one or two years after he became old, he fed some bread and meat to a poor person for each day he did not fast. Al-Bukhārī attributed this to Anas without a chain of narrators, but Abū Yaʿlā al-Mawṣilī collected it with a continuous chain in his Musnad, from Ayyūb ibn Abū Tamīmah: "Anas could no longer fast. So he made a plate of tharīd and invited thirty poor persons and fed them." The same ruling, Ibn Kathir says, applies to pregnant and breast-feeding women if they fear for themselves or their children: they pay the fidyah and do not have to fast other days in place of those they missed.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the same point from the other side: the option of paying ransom was valid in the early days of Islam, when the purpose was to familiarise people with fasting, and was then abrogated for normal people — but according to the consensus of the Ummah it remained applicable to people of very old age and to those who suffer from a permanent illness with no hope of recovery (Jaṣṣāṣ and Maẓharī). It puts the ransom for one missed fast at half a ṣāʿ of wheat or its cost — approximately 1.632 kilograms — given to a poor person.

Ayah 184 closes by praising those who exceed the minimum: *faman taṭawwaʿa khayran* — Ibn Kathir reads this as feeding **an extra** poor person; "it is better for him." Then the Qur'an's verdict over the whole concession: "and that you fast is better for you, if only you knew."

## Ayah 185: the month, and why it was chosen

Ayah 185 names the month by what happened in it. Ibn Kathir: Allah praised the month of Ramadan above the other months by choosing it to send down the Glorious Qur'an, just as He did for all of the Divine Books He revealed to the Prophets. Imām Aḥmad reported from Wāthilah ibn al-Asqaʿ that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said the Pages of Ibrāhīm were revealed during the first night of Ramadan, the Torah during the sixth, the Injīl during the thirteenth, and the Qur'an on the twenty-fourth night of Ramadan. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the same narration, and adds another from the Companion Sayyidnā Jābir (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Zabūr (the Psalms) was revealed on the twelfth of Ramadan and the Evangel on the eighteenth.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then draws a distinction worth pausing on. All the previous Books mentioned in that ḥadīth were revealed on those dates *in their entirety*. It is a peculiarity of the Qur'an that it was sent **whole** from the Preserved Tablet down to the Firmament of the Earth in one night of Ramadan — while being revealed to the Prophet ﷺ gradually over a period of twenty-three years. That night was the Night of Power, as the Qur'an itself says: "We have revealed it in the Laylat al-Qadr." The ḥadīth above places the revelation on the twenty-fourth, and according to Sayyidnā Ḥasan the Night of Power falls on the twenty-fourth, which aligns the ḥadīth with the statement of the Qur'an. Should that alignment be unacceptable, the fact remains that the statement of the Qur'an is above everything else — whatever night is the Night of Power is what the Qur'an intends.

On "guidance for mankind, and clear proofs for the guidance and the criterion," Ibn Kathir says Allah revealed the Qur'an as guidance for the hearts of those who believe in it and adhere to its commands; and *bayyināt* means clear and unambiguous signs and unequivocal proof for those who understand them — proofs that testify to the truth of the Qur'an and its guidance, and mark the distinction between truth and falsehood, the permissible and the prohibited.

## "Whoever of you witnesses the month must fast it"

*Shahida* is derived from *shuhūd*, which means presence; *al-shahr* means the month, and here denotes Ramadan. Ibn Kathir: this ayah requires the healthy persons who witness the beginning of the month, while residing in their land, to fast the month, and it abrogates the ayah that allowed a choice between fasting and paying the fidyah. Having ordered the fast, Allah then **again mentions** the permission for the ill person and the traveller — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why: now that the choice of paying ransom had been cancelled, a doubt could creep in that the concession granted to the sick and the travelling had been abrogated along with it, so the provision was positively repeated.

"Witnessing" the month, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, simply means that a person finds the blessed month *with the ability to fast* — that he or she is Muslim, sane, of age, resident, and purified from all impurities including those of menstruation and childbed. So those who lacked the initial ability are not addressed by the obligation: should a disbeliever embrace Islam in the middle of Ramadan, or a minor reach maturity, they fast from that point onward and do not make qaḍāʾ for the earlier days. But the insane person, being a Muslim adult, does have the underlying ability; so if he regains his sanity during part of Ramadan, qaḍāʾ for the previous days becomes obligatory on him — and likewise for a woman who becomes purified in the middle of the month, a sick person who becomes healthy, or a traveller who becomes a resident. They had the capacity and were only temporarily excused.

## Fasting on a journey: the Sunnah's balance

Ibn Kathir assembles the reports carefully, and they do not all pull the same way. The authentic Sunnah states that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ travelled during Ramadan for the battle for Makkah, and that he marched until he reached the area of Kadīd, then broke his fast and ordered those with him to do likewise — recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs. Yet this was not binding, since the Companions used to go out with him during Ramadan, some fasting and some not, and neither group criticised the other; had the command required breaking the fast, the Prophet ﷺ would have criticised those who fasted. He ﷺ himself sometimes fasted while travelling. It is reported in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs that Abū al-Dardāʾ said of one intensely hot Ramadan journey, "Only Allah's Messenger ﷺ and ʿAbdullāh ibn Rawāḥah were fasting at that time."

Ibn Kathir's judgement is that observing the permission to break the fast while travelling is better, citing the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "Those who did not fast have done good, and there is no harm for those who fasted," and, in another ḥadīth, "Hold to Allah's permission that He has granted you." Some scholars say the two actions are the same, citing what ʿĀʾishah narrated: Ḥamzah ibn ʿAmr al-Aslamī said, "O Messenger of Allah! I fast a lot, should I fast while travelling?" and the Prophet ﷺ said, "Fast if you wish, or do not fast if you wish" — a ḥadīth in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs. And where fasting becomes difficult while travelling, breaking it is better: Jābir reported that the Prophet ﷺ saw a man being shaded by others, asked about him, was told he was fasting, and said, "It is not a part of birr (piety) to fast while travelling" — recorded by al-Bukhārī and Muslim. A corollary follows: those who ignore the Sunnah and believe in their hearts that breaking the fast while travelling is disliked are *required* to break it and are not allowed to fast.

## "Allah intends for you ease"

Ibn Kathir reads this as the reason behind every concession: Allah allowed such persons, **out of His mercy and to make matters easy for them**, to break the fast when ill or travelling, while the fast remains obligatory on the healthy person who is not travelling; and "you must complete the same number" means He commanded the make-up days so that you complete the days of one month. He gathers the Sunnah on the same theme — Imām Aḥmad's report from Anas ibn Mālik, also collected in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, "Treat the people with ease and don't be hard on them; give them glad tidings and don't fill them with aversion"; the words in the Ṣaḥīḥayn to Muʿādh and Abū Mūsā when he sent them to Yemen, adding "and love each other, and don't differ"; and, from the compilers of the Sunan and the Musnad, "I was sent with the easy Ḥanīfiyyah."

## Ending in takbīr and gratitude

The passage closes not with a rule but with a response: *wa li-tukabbirū Allāha ʿalā mā hadākum wa laʿallakum tashkurūn*. Ibn Kathir explains this as remembering Allah upon finishing the act of worship, as in "So when you have accomplished your rites, remember Allah…" (2:200), and "Then when the Jumuʿah prayer is ended… remember Allah much" (62:10) — which is why the Sunnah encouraged tasbīḥ, taḥmīd and takbīr after the compulsory prayers. Ibn ʿAbbās said, "We used to know that Allah's Messenger ﷺ had finished the prayer by the takbīr." Several scholars have stated that reciting the takbīr during ʿĪd al-Fiṭr is specified by this very ayah.

Note where the gratitude points. Not "magnify Allah because you managed to fast," but **"for having guided you"** — the guidance itself is the gift. Ibn Kathir's last word on *laʿallakum tashkurūn*: if you adhere to what Allah commanded you, obeying Him by performing the obligations, abandoning the prohibitions and abiding by the limits He set, then perhaps you will be among the grateful.

## Living it

**Intend it** — abstention becomes worship only when the heart chooses it for Allah alone. **Take the concession when it is yours**, without guilt: the ill, the traveller, the very old, the nursing mother who fears for her child are not falling short of the law; they are addressed by it. **And do not let the ease lower the aim** — "and that you fast is better for you, if only you knew." The measure is taqwā: the strength to refuse what is lawful, so that refusing what is unlawful becomes possible.

passages.title: Allah is near; the nights of the fast
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat sit in the middle of the Qur'an's legislation of fasting and finish it in two very different registers. Ayah 186 answers a question about Allah Himself — how near is He to the one who calls Him — and ayah 187 lifts a real hardship off the community by opening up the nights of Ramadan. One quality binds them: nearness expressed as mercy. Allah is close enough to hear a whisper, and close enough to notice His servants struggling and lighten the load.

## Why a verse about du'a lands here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the placement. The ayat before this gave the injunctions and merits of fasting, and the long ayah after it returns to fasting and i'tikaf. In between, this brief ayah is inserted "to persuade servants of Allah to obey the commands of Allah by recognizing how He, in His special grace, hears and answers their prayers." Fasting is demanding even with its concessions; it is to make the trial bearable that Allah says **innī qarīb** — I am near My servants; when they pray, I answer their prayers and take care of what they need. Under such conditions, says Maʿārif, it is only fitting that servants of Allah should bear the hardships that come with carrying out what He has commanded.

Ibn Kathir, as Maʿārif reports him, sees a second wisdom: the ayah hints that du'a made at the completion of a fast is accepted, so one should be very particular about praying then. The sources cite the Prophet ﷺ as saying that the prayer made by one who is fasting, at the time of his iftar, is accepted — Maʿārif quotes this without naming a collection, so we pass on the teaching without attaching it to one. This is why the Companion 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar would gather his family members around him at the time of iftar and pray.

## "And when My servants ask you about Me"

Ibn Kathir gives ayah 186 in full: *And when My servants ask you (O Muhammad ﷺ) concerning Me, then answer them — I am indeed near. I respond to the invocations of the supplicant when he calls on Me. So let them obey Me and believe in Me, so that they may be led aright.*

The answer comes in the first person throughout: *I* am near, *I* respond, obey *Me*, believe in *Me*. Ibn Kathir glosses "when he calls on Me" as **without any mediator or intercessor**, and explains "I am indeed near" as near to them **by His knowledge**.

**The occasion of revelation.** Maʿārif, citing Ibn Kathir, reports that a visitor from a village asked the Prophet ﷺ: "Tell me if our Lord is near us, then we shall pray in a lowered voice; and if He is far, we shall call Him with raised voices." Thereupon this ayah was revealed. Maʿārif's ruling follows directly: du'a should be made slowly and quietly; to raise the voice while praying is not desirable.

Ibn Kathir records from Imam Ahmad, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, that on a journey during a battle the Companions raised their voices with *Allahu akbar* at every hill and valley, until the Prophet ﷺ came by them and said:

> "O people! Be merciful to yourselves, for you are not calling a deaf or an absent one, but One Who is All-Hearer, All-Seer. The One Whom you call is closer to one of you than the neck of his animal."

He then addressed Abu Musa by his name 'Abdullah bin Qais and taught him "a statement that is a treasure of Paradise: *La hawla wa la quwwata illa billah* — there is no power or strength except from Allah." Ibn Kathir notes this hadith was also recorded in the Two Sahihs, and that Abu Dawud, An-Nasa'i, At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah recorded similar wordings. He also records from Imam Ahmad, from Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah the Exalted said, 'I am as My servant thinks of Me, and I am with him whenever he invokes Me.'"

## What "I respond" actually means

Ibn Kathir gathers the hadiths that keep this promise from being read as a guarantee that every request is granted in the form and moment we want. From Imam Ahmad, from Abu Sa'id: no Muslim supplicates to Allah with a du'a free of sin and of cutting the relations of the womb but Allah grants him one of three things — He hastens the response to his supplication, saves it for him until the Hereafter, or turns an equivalent amount of evil away from him. They said, "What if we were to recite more?" He said, "There is more with Allah." A related report — from 'Ubadah bin As-Samit, recorded by 'Abdullah the son of Imam Ahmad and by At-Tirmidhi — says the same in shorter form: there is no Muslim man on earth who supplicates to Allah but Allah either grants it to him or averts from him a harm of equal proportions, so long as his supplication does not involve sin or cutting the relations of the womb.

Impatience is what spoils it. Imam Malik recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said, "One's supplication will be accepted as long as he does not become hasty and say, 'I have supplicated but it has not been accepted from me'" — recorded in the Two Sahihs from Malik, and this is the wording of Al-Bukhari. Muslim's version adds the picture of the man who "supplicated and supplicated," sees no answer, then loses interest and abandons supplicating altogether.

Some are never turned back. From the Musnad of Imam Ahmad and the Sunans of At-Tirmidhi, An-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah, from Abu Hurayrah: three persons will not have their supplication rejected — **the just ruler, the fasting person until breaking the fast**, and the oppressed person, whose supplication Allah raises above the clouds on the Day of Resurrection, and the doors of heaven are opened for it, and Allah says, "By My grace! I will certainly grant it for you, even if after a while." The fasting person stands in the middle of that list. And the ayah ends with a demand, not only an offer: *let them obey Me and believe in Me.*

## Ayah 187: the hardship that was lifted

To feel this ayah you must know what the rule had been. Ibn Kathir explains that in the early years of Islam, Muslims were allowed to eat, drink and have relations with their wives only until the 'Isha' prayer — unless one slept before 'Isha'. Whoever slept before 'Isha', or offered it, was not allowed any of the three until the next night. The Muslims found that difficult.

Al-Bara' bin 'Azib told the story of **Qays bin Sirmah al-Ansari**. He was fasting one day and working in his land. When the time to break the fast came he went to his wife and asked whether she had food. She said, "No. But I could try to get you some." While she was gone, sleep overcame his eyes; she returned and found him asleep, and said, "Woe unto you! Did you sleep?" — for his sleep had shut the door on eating until the following night. In the middle of the next day he lost consciousness. This was mentioned to the Prophet ﷺ, and this ayah was revealed. "Consequently," says Al-Bara', "they were very delighted."

Al-Bukhari recorded from Al-Bara' another side of it: when fasting Ramadan was ordained, Muslims used to refrain from sleeping with their wives the entire month, but some men "used to deceive themselves" — and Allah revealed *Allah knows that you used to deceive yourselves, so He turned to you and forgave you.* Ibn 'Abbas, as narrated by Ali bin Abu Talhah, said that some Muslims — including 'Umar bin Al-Khattab — did go to their wives and eat after 'Isha'; they took the matter to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and Allah sent down *…so He turned to you and forgave you. So now have sexual relations with them.*

Maʿārif adds a principle. The abrogated rule — the unlawfulness of eating and drinking after a post-iftar nap — appears nowhere in the text of the Qur'an; the Companions acted on it as the Prophet ﷺ had set it. Yet this ayah first gives that rule the standing of a divine command and then abrogates it — from which we learn that some rules established by the Sunnah can be abrogated through the Qur'an, and that in Islamic law the decision of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ carries the same authority as the injunction of the Qur'an.

## Two words worth slowing down for

**Rafath.** Maʿārif notes the literal sense is general and broad — covering everything a husband suggests, says or does in seeking his wife's consent — but there is total agreement of the Muslim Ummah that here it means sexual intercourse; Ibn Kathir reports the same from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Mujahid, and a long list of others including Sa'id bin Jubayr, Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Az-Zuhri.

**Libas.** *They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them.* Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id bin Jubayr, Al-Hasan, Qatadah and others explained it as: your wives are a resort for you, and you for them; Ar-Rabi' bin Anas said, "They are your cover and you are their cover." In short, Ibn Kathir concludes, husband and wife are that intimately joined — and this is why they were permitted marital relations during the nights of Ramadan, so that matters would be made easier for them.

## The white thread and the black thread

The ayah fixes the start of the fast with an image: eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct from the black thread — *of dawn*. Maʿārif explains the likeness: the darkness of the night is the black thread, the light of dawn the white. Ibn Kathir cites Sahl bin Sa'd: before the words *of dawn* were revealed, some people who intended to fast tied black and white threads to their legs and went on eating until they could tell them apart — then Allah revealed *of dawn*, and it became clear that night's darkness and day's light were meant.

Al-Bukhari recorded from Ash-Sha'bi that 'Adi said he took two strings, one black and one white, kept them under his pillow and looked at them throughout the night without being able to distinguish them. He told the Messenger of Allah ﷺ the whole story the next morning, and he ﷺ said, "Your pillow is very wide if the white and black threads are under it!" In Al-Bukhari's fuller narration 'Adi bin Hatim asks whether they are actual threads, and he ﷺ answers, "Rather, they are the blackness of the night and the whiteness of the daylight" — which is why Ibn Kathir rejects as weak the claim that the remark meant 'Adi was not smart.

**The qualifier that governs everything: *until it becomes distinct*.** Maʿārif builds a careful balance on this word. It was added, he says, to eliminate the chances of extremism in either direction: one should not act like the chronically skeptical and treat eating and drinking as unlawful before dawn breaks, nor become so heedless as to go on eating after having become certain of the light of dawn. The certainty of daybreak is the line of demarcation — before it, eating is not haram; after it, any indulgence is haram and may lead to the spoiling of the fast, even if it exceeds the limit by a minute.

Ibn Kathir cites from the Two Sahihs, from Al-Qasim, that 'A'ishah narrated the Prophet ﷺ said: "The Adhan pronounced by Bilal should not stop you from taking Suhur, for he pronounces the Adhan at night. Hence, eat and drink until you hear the Adhan by Ibn Umm Maktum, for he does not call the Adhan until dawn." Maʿārif warns against a misreading of this: because the hadith was reported only in part, some contemporaries concluded that a person who wakes late may hurry to eat a little after the Fajr adhan. The hadith says the opposite — one must stop with Ibn Umm Maktum's adhan, which was called precisely at daybreak, and the Qur'an itself has set the deadline at certainty of dawn. The narrations of latitude in suhur reported from Companions and early elders are explained by Maʿārif — and, he notes, by Ibn Kathir — as aiming to avoid excessive precautionary self-restriction *before* one becomes certain, not as licence after it. Ibn Kathir also transmits reports guarding the other side of the line: from Imam Ahmad, from Qays bin Talq from his father, that dawn is not the ascending glow of white light on the horizon but the spreading redness; and from Ibn Jarir, from Samurah bin Jundub, "Do not be stopped by Bilal's Adhan or the ascending whiteness, until it spreads."

**When you genuinely cannot tell.** Maʿārif reports Imam al-Jassas in *Ahkam al-Qur'an* that where the horizon is not in open view, or one cannot identify daybreak, and doubt remains, it is desirable not to go ahead and eat; one who does eat in a state of doubt is not a sinner, but if dawn had in fact set in, that fast must be made up (*qada'*). But one who wakes late while the usual calls of adhan are being made — which makes daybreak certain — and eats knowingly, is both sinful and bound to make the fast up.

## Suhur, and the two ends of the day

Because Allah permitted eating and drinking until dawn, Ibn Kathir argues, this is proof that suhur is encouraged: it is a *rukhsah*, a concession, and Allah likes that the concession be accepted and implemented. It is reported in the Two Sahihs that Anas narrated the Prophet ﷺ said, "Eat the Suhur, for there is a blessing in Suhur." Muslim reported from 'Amr bin Al-'As: "The distinction between our fast and the fast of the People of the Book is the meal of Suhur." And Imam Ahmad reported from Abu Sa'id: "Suhur is a blessed meal. Hence, do not abandon it, even if one just takes a sip of water. Indeed, Allah and His angels send Salah (blessings) upon those who eat Suhur."

It is preferred that suhur be delayed until close to dawn. Imam Ahmad recorded from Abu Dharr, "My Ummah will always retain goodness as long as they hasten in breaking the fast and delay the Suhur," and in the Two Sahihs Zayd bin Thabit, asked how much time there was between the adhan and their suhur with the Prophet ﷺ, answered: "The time that fifty Ayat take to recite."

**A ruling that follows.** Since intimacy is lawful until dawn, one may begin the fast in a state of *janabah* (major ritual impurity) and bathe any time in the morning after waking. Ibn Kathir states this is the opinion of the Four Imams and the majority of the scholars; Al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded from 'A'ishah and Umm Salamah that the Prophet ﷺ used to wake in that state, take a bath and fast — and Umm Salamah added that he would not break his fast or make up for that day. Muslim records a man asking about this and the Prophet ﷺ answering, "And I. The prayer time starts while I am Junub and I fast."

**The other end: *then complete your fast till the nightfall*.** This ayah orders breaking the fast at sunset. It is recorded in the Two Sahihs that 'Umar bin Al-Khattab reported the Prophet ﷺ said: "If the night comes from this direction, and the day departs from that direction, then the fasting person breaks his fast." Sahl bin Sa'd As-Sa'idi narrated, "The people will retain goodness as long as they hasten in breaking the fast," and Imam Ahmad recorded from Abu Hurayrah: "Allah the Exalted said, 'The dearest among My servants to Me are those who hasten in breaking the fast the most'" — At-Tirmidhi recorded this and graded it Hasan Gharib. Hence too the prohibition of *wisal*, continuing the fast through the night to the next without eating — a practice, Ibn Kathir notes, that was one of the special qualities of the Prophet ﷺ, who was given help in it and said, "I am not like you, I am given food and drink during my sleep by my Lord." What is allowed to us, by a hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, is at most to hold off from sunset until suhur.

## I'tikaf: the exception inside the concession

Then the ayah pulls one thing back: *and do not have sexual relations with them while you are in I'tikaf in the Masjids.* Maʿārif explains that i'tikaf literally means to stay at some place in seclusion, and in Qur'anic and Sunnah usage is the act of staying in a mosque under particular conditions. The universality of the phrase "in the mosques" proves it may be performed in any masjid; the juristic condition that it be a masjid where congregational prayer is regularly held is a derivation from the very purpose of a masjid, since individual prayer can be offered in a house, a shop, anywhere.

Maʿārif frames the ruling precisely: in the state of i'tikaf the permission to eat and drink at night remains exactly as it is for everyone else — what differs is intimacy with one's wife, which is not permissible even at night. Ibn 'Abbas said Allah prohibited the man in i'tikaf from approaching women, night or day, until he finishes. Ad-Dahhak reported that formerly a man in i'tikaf would leave the mosque and, if he wished, go to his wife, until this ayah came — meaning, do not touch your wives as long as you are in i'tikaf, whether inside the mosque or outside it. Mujahid, Qatadah and several others held the same, and Ibn Abu Hatim reports the like from Ibn Mas'ud, Muhammad bin Ka'b, 'Ata', Al-Hasan, Ad-Dahhak, As-Suddi, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas and Muqatil. Ibn Kathir calls this the agreed-upon practice among the scholars: one who steps out for a need such as relieving himself or eating may not kiss or embrace his wife or busy himself with anything besides his i'tikaf, and may not even visit the sick, only ask after them while passing by. What is forbidden is intercourse and anything like kissing or embracing that might lead to it; ordinary help from a wife is allowed — the Two Sahihs record 'A'ishah saying he ﷺ would bring his head near her so she could comb his hair.

Ibn Kathir also relates the incident of Safiyyah bint Huyai visiting the Prophet ﷺ in the mosque during i'tikaf, and his walking her home at night; when two Ansari men hurried past out of shyness he called them back and said, "Do not run away! She is Safiyyah bint Huyai," explaining, "Shaytan reaches everywhere in the human body that the blood reaches. I was afraid lest Shaytan might suggest an evil thought in your minds." Imam Ash-Shafi'i commented that he ﷺ was teaching his Ummah to eliminate an evil thought at once, so they never fall into the prohibited — those two men had far more fear of Allah than to think ill of him ﷺ.

Placing i'tikaf right after fasting, Ibn Kathir notes, draws attention to practising it in the month of the fast, especially its last part: the Prophet ﷺ used to perform i'tikaf during the last ten nights of Ramadan until he died, and his wives performed it after him, as the Two Sahihs record from 'A'ishah.

## "These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them"

Ibn Kathir reads this as: all that has been explained, ordained, specified, allowed and prohibited concerning the fast — these are the limits Allah has legislated and made clear, so do not come near them or transgress them. 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam took the limits to be the four mentioned from *It is made lawful for you…* through *then complete your fast till the nightfall.*

Maʿārif draws out the practical force of *do not go near*: a boundary you do not approach is a margin of safety, because if you go near, you may cross. So while fasting it is *makruh* (reprehensible) to overdo gargling, since water may slip down the throat; likewise using medicine inside the mouth; likewise kissing and embracing one's wife. It is better, as a precaution, to stop eating a couple of minutes before the time allowed for suhur ends, and to delay iftar by a couple of minutes. Becoming heedless and ease-prone in these matters runs against this command from Allah.

The passage then closes as the fasting section opened: *that they may attain taqwa*. Ibn Kathir explains "Thus does Allah make clear His Ayat to mankind" to mean that just as He explains the fast and its rulings, He explains His other rulings by the words of His servant and Messenger, Muhammad ﷺ — so that people may know how to acquire true guidance and how to worship.

## Holding the two ayat together

A servant asks how near Allah is, and Allah answers that He is closer than the neck of the mount you ride, that He hears the lowered voice, and that He answers — now, or stored up for the Hereafter, or by turning away a harm you never saw. Then He proves that nearness concretely: He knows that Qays bin Sirmah collapsed in his field, and He opens the nights. Mercy and law arrive in one sentence — *He turned to you and forgave you… so now have relations with them* — and the limits drawn after it are not a withdrawal of that mercy but its protection.

passages.title: Do not devour one another's wealth unjustly
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

Ayah 188 is a single, tightly built prohibition against taking what belongs to other people. It has two halves that belong together: first, the broad ban — *do not consume one another's wealth unjustly* — and then a specific and especially ugly way of doing it: dragging the matter before judges and rulers so that a court's ruling launders the theft, *while you know* you have no right to it. The verse begins with the crime and ends with the excuse people hide behind. That is what holds it together.

## Why it comes right after the verses on fasting

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the placement. The verses just before this dealt with fasting, where lawful things are forbidden for a fixed period and at fixed times. Now, immediately after, comes the prohibition of acquiring and using unlawful wealth.

The connection is not accidental. The real purpose of fasting, as an act of worship, is to train a person to abstain from what is otherwise lawful for him. If he can do that, there is every likelihood that abstaining from what is *totally* unlawful will become far easier. Fasting is the training ground; ayah 188 is the field.

There is a second link, sharper still. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that a person must make the effort to break his fast with what is halal. Someone who goes through the rigours of fasting all day and then breaks his fast in the evening with what is haram will find his fast unacceptable in the sight of Allah.

## "Do not eat up **your** wealth"

The wording repays close attention. The Qur'an says *amwālakum* — "**your** property" — not "the property of others." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws two subtle points from this.

**First**, it holds a mirror up to the encroacher. Whoever reaches for someone else's property must think that the other person has the same sort of love and concern for his property as the encroacher has for his own. Had the positions been reversed, he would certainly have been hurt.

**Second**, by calling it all "your property," the verse suggests something about the community as a whole. If encroaching on others' property became common practice, the natural consequence is that others would encroach on yours, giving you what you gave them. Looked at from this angle, taking unlawfully is really an invitation to others to come and take from you in the same way. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān illustrates this with an everyday picture: imagine a society where adulterating articles of daily use becomes common practice. A dealer earns a little extra by adulterating butter with cheaper oil or fat; he then goes to the milk shop and is handed milk adulterated with water; he buys spices, and they are adulterated; he buys medicines, and it is the same. One person earns more by adulteration while the next takes that extra earning back out of his pocket, and the cycle goes on and on. The adulterer feels good about the extra he puts in his coffers, but he never looks at the hole underneath — in reality he keeps none of it.

**And "eating" does not only mean eating.** The words of the Qur'an forbid "eating" quite clearly, but Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the drive of the meaning is not restricted to eating as such: it means *using* in the absolute sense — by eating, drinking, wearing, or any other mode of use. Metaphorically all such uses are covered by the expression "to eat," as when we say "A ate up the property of B," which is only a manner of speaking, since not all of that is something one can literally eat.

## How wide is "unjustly"?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses that the words of this divine injunction are **general**, and lists what falls under them:

- usurping someone's property, theft, and robbery — where what belongs to someone is taken away by force;
- interest (ribā), gambling, bribery;
- all defective sales and transactions that Islamic law rules impermissible — **even where the parties genuinely consented**;
- any money or property acquired through lying or a false oath;
- any earning that Islamic law has prohibited, **even if the person personally sweated to earn it**.

That last category is worth pausing on. Effort does not sanctify income. Neither does mutual agreement. On interest and gambling in particular, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the reason: they are harmful to public interest. As a result of their presence in a society, some individuals grow as parasites while the whole community is thrown into poverty. So even a transaction of this kind carried out by mutual consent is not permissible, because it is nothing but a formalised crime against the whole community.

## Why the criterion has to come from Allah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a broader argument here that is worth following. The whole world agrees that money and materials are needed and that life depends on them, and equally agrees that some ways of acquiring them are favoured and others forbidden — virtually the whole world looks down on theft, robbery, and fraud. What people generally lack is a *sound criterion* for determining which means are permissible, and it may be that this is simply not possible for them, since it relates to the well-being of the peoples of the entire world and affects humanity as such.

If human beings were left to forge their own criterion, those who give it a legal framework would naturally think more about their own nation, country, or community, and would think differently about others. Even an international body representing the whole world, as experience shows, cannot satisfy everyone. The result is legal injustice, ending in nothing but wars and chaos. A universal criterion — sound and reasonable — can therefore come only from the Lord-Creator of all the worlds, through the medium of revelation.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then sketches what that revealed law looks like in practice. Everything of common utility is left as such, especially things to which all human beings claim equal rights — air, water, vegetation, heat, un-owned forests, and the produce of uninhabited mountain growth. These are the commonly shared property of all human beings; **it is not permissible for anyone to take them over as an owner**. Things which, if shared, would disturb human society or generate conflict and violence are placed under the law of private ownership. The law governing initial ownership of land or its produce differs from the law of the transfer of ownership. The law is so formulated that no human being is left deprived of the necessities of life, on condition that he puts in his effort to acquire them, with special attention given to the consideration that no one usurps others' rights or brings loss to them and thereby concentrates capital in the hands of a few. And in every transfer of ownership — whether in accordance with the divine injunctions on inheritance after death, or through buying and selling as agreed by the parties — it is binding that there be absolutely no fraud or deception, and no ambiguity or insufficiency that might lead to bickering and dispute later. Consent, too, must be *genuine*, not extracted under pressure. In Islamic law, every transaction known as void, invalid, or sinful has some such defect inherent in the deal.

**The present verse, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, covers all such impermissible situations and aspects.**

## The second half: using the courts as a weapon

The verse continues: *nor give bribery to the rulers that you may knowingly eat up a part of the property of others sinfully*. Ibn Kathir explains this as bribery given to the rulers — the judges, before presenting your cases.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the sense of the second half this way: do not take property cases to the authorities so that through them you eat up some portion of people's property sinfully, while you know full well that you have no right in it and are simply putting up a false case.

**Ibn 'Abbas on what the verse targets.** Ibn Kathir reports, through 'Ali bin Abu Talhah, that Ibn 'Abbas said this ayah is about the indebted person when there is no evidence of the loan. He denies having taken the loan and the case goes to the authorities — even though he knows that it is not his money and that he is a sinner, consuming what is not allowed for him. Ibn Kathir notes that the same opinion was reported from Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, al-Hasan, Qatādah, as-Suddī, Muqātil bin Hayyān, and ʿAbdur-Rahmān bin Zayd bin Aslam. They all stated it in one sentence: **"Do not dispute when you know that you are being unjust."**

## The occasion of revelation

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing *Rūh al-Maʿānī*, records that the verse was revealed against the background of a particular event: a land dispute between two of the noble Companions, which came up for hearing in the court of the Prophet ﷺ.

The plaintiff had no witnesses. In accordance with Islamic legal norm, the Prophet ﷺ asked the defendant to take an oath. The man was all set to take it. Then, as a matter of good counsel, the Prophet ﷺ recited to him:

> *Surely, those who take a small price out of the covenant of Allah and out of their oaths, for them there is no share in the Hereafter.* (3:77)

When the Companion heard this verse — which warns those who try to take over someone's property through a false oath — he abandoned his intention to take the oath and surrendered the land to the plaintiff.

Notice what happened. The procedure was about to hand him a legal victory. One verse about the Hereafter was enough to make him let it go.

## A court's ruling does not change reality

This is the heart of the passage, and both commentaries dwell on it. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith reported **in the Two Sahihs** from Umm Salamah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "I am only human! You people present your cases to me, and as some of you may be more eloquent and persuasive in presenting his argument, I might issue a judgment in his benefit. So, if I give a Muslim's right to another, I am really giving him a piece of fire; so he should not take it."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the same hadith from Bukhari and Muslim, from Umm Salamah, in nearly the same wording: he should not take it, "because, in that case, I shall be allotting him a plot from Hell."

Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion plainly: **the judgment of the authorities in any case does not change the reality of the truth.** The ruling does not allow what is in fact prohibited, nor prohibit what is in fact allowed. If the ruling agrees with the truth, there is no harm. Otherwise, the judge will acquire his reward, while the cheater will acquire the evil burden.

Qatādah's words, quoted by Ibn Kathir, are worth reading slowly: "O son of Adam! Know that the judge's ruling does not allow you what is prohibited or prohibit you from what is allowed. The judge only rules according to his best judgment and according to the testimony of the witnesses. The judge is only human and is bound to make mistakes. Know that if the judge erroneously rules in some one's favor, then that person will still encounter the dispute when the disputing parties meet Allah on the Day of Resurrection." There, the unjust person will be judged swiftly and precisely, with that which will surpass whatever he acquired by the erroneous judgment he received in the life of this world.

**A point of jurisprudence.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that according to Imam Abu Hanifah, in transactions involving a contract or an annulment where the qādī has authority under Islamic law, a judgment the qādī gives — even if it be on the basis of a false oath or false witness — will render that contract or annulment valid under Islamic law, and the rules of lawful and unlawful will stand imposed on it; although, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds in the same breath, the curse of lying and of engineering false witnesses will hang round his neck. The source itself keeps the two things apart: what the judicial act does in law, and what remains on the conscience of the man who obtained it.

## "While you know" — the mercy in the last words

The ayah ends *wa antum taʿlamūn*, "while you know." Ibn Kathir gives the meaning: while you know the falsehood of what you claim.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the relief hidden in this clause. A person who claims something on the basis of a **misunderstanding** and files a suit in court to acquire it is not covered by this warning. The verse is not aimed at people who go to court in good faith and turn out to be wrong. It is aimed at the man who knows.

And the Umm Salamah hadith completes the picture from the other side. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that a Muslim judge may give a judgment under some misunderstanding in which one party's legal right is unlawfully given to the other — and such a judgment does not make the thing lawful for him. The converse is also true: it does not become unlawful for the one to whom it is lawful. In short, the judgment of a court does not make the lawful unlawful, or the unlawful lawful. Anyone who succeeds in grabbing something belonging to someone else through a court by means of fraud, false witness, or false oath carries the weight of that on his shoulders, and should — thinking of the ultimate accountability in the Hereafter and his appearance before Allah, the All-Knowing, the All-Aware — leave it off.

## Halal earning brings blessing; haram earning poisons everything

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers a body of teaching showing that human deeds and morals are enormously affected by eating what is lawful. If a person does not eat and drink halal things, it is almost impossible to expect good morals and righteous deeds from him. Allah says:

> *O messengers, eat of the good things and be righteous in deeds. I am aware of what you do.* (23:51)

The command to eat what is pure is combined here with the command to do what is righteous. The hint, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is that righteous deeds can issue forth only when a person eats and drinks what is lawful. In a hadith the Prophet ﷺ made clear that although this verse addresses the prophets, the command is not restricted to them — all Muslims are charged with it. Towards the end of that hadith he also said that **the prayer of a person who eats what is unlawful is not answered**: there are many who take great pains in their acts of worship and then raise their hands before Allah saying "O Lord, O Lord," while what they eat is haram, what they drink is haram, what they wear is haram — so how is such a prayer to be answered?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that a great portion of the Prophet's ﷺ teaching was devoted to saving his ummah from the unlawful and calling it to what is lawful. Among the teachings it gathers under this ayah:

- **Reported by Tirmidhi, who calls it sahih:** "One who ate halal, followed the sunnah and people were not hurt by him, he will go to Paradise." When the Companions said that these things were common in his community and that most Muslims observed them strictly, he said: "Yes! In future too, in every age, there will be people who shall abide by these rules."
- To ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar, the Prophet ﷺ said there are four traits which, if they are in a person and he has nothing else in the world, will suffice him: guarding a trust, telling the truth, good morals, and being particular in eating what is halal.
- Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqās asked the Prophet ﷺ to pray that he become one whose prayers are accepted. He said: "O Saʿd, make what you eat permissible and pure, and you shall become one whose prayers are responded to." He added an oath — by Him in whose hands rests the life of Muhammad ﷺ — that when a servant of Allah slips a morsel of what is haram into his stomach, no deed of his is accepted for the next forty days; and that for a person whose flesh is made of unlawful acquisitions, the fire of Hell is the only recipient of that flesh.
- ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿūd reports that the Prophet ﷺ swore that no servant of Allah becomes a Muslim unless his heart and tongue become Muslim and until his neighbours become secure from his distressing deeds; and that when a servant acquires the unlawful and gives it in charity, it is not accepted; if he spends out of it, it stays deprived of blessings; and if he leaves it behind for his heirs, it becomes his wherewithal for the trip to Hell. Allah does not help an evil wash off another evil — but He does help the washing away of an evil deed with a good deed.

*(Of these four, only the first is named to a collection in the source; the other three are conveyed as the source reports the Prophet's ﷺ teaching, without a collection being named.)*

## Standing before Allah with the question

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes with two narrations that put the whole ayah into its final frame.

Muʿādh ibn Jabal reports that the Prophet ﷺ said no servant of Allah shall move a step on the Day of Resurrection until he is made to answer four questions: about his life — in what did he spend it; about his youth — in what did he consume it; **about his wealth — where did he earn it from and in what did he spend it**; and about his knowledge — how far did he act in line with it. (*Al-Bayhaqi, Targhīb*)

Two of those four questions concern time, one concerns knowledge — and one concerns exactly what ayah 188 legislates. Not merely *how much* wealth, but *where from*.

And ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar reports a sermon in which the Prophet ﷺ sought Allah's refuge against five traits taking root in a people: immodesty, for when it prevails a people are hit by plagues, epidemics, and ever-new diseases not even heard of by their elders; **cheating in weights and measures, for when this grips a people they are hit by famine, price-hikes, rigorous labour and overwork, and oppressive rulers**; non-payment of zakah, for when people do not pay it the rains are stopped; the breaking of a community's covenant with Allah and His Messenger, after which Allah makes alien enemies sit over them who snatch away what belongs to them without any justification; and the apathy of ruling authority, for when rulers fail to decide matters in accordance with the Book of Allah because His injunctions do not suit their fancies, Allah causes mutual hatred and disputation to descend upon them. (*Reported by Ibn Majah, al-Bayhaqi and others; al-Hakim has called it sahih according to the standard set by Muslim.*)

## Living it

Read together, ayah 188 asks a believer for something more demanding than simply avoiding theft.

**Check the source, not just the amount.** One of the questions a servant will be made to answer is where his wealth came from, not only how much of it there was.

**Do not let legality do the work of honesty.** A contract you drafted, a technicality you exploited, a case you won — none of these change the reality of the truth. If a ruling hands you what is not yours, the Prophet ﷺ called it a piece of fire.

**Do not litigate what you know is not yours.** The authorities Ibn Kathir lists all reduce it to one sentence: do not dispute when you know that you are being unjust.

**And if you already hold something like this, leave it off.** The Companion in the background of revelation was one oath away from keeping the land — and surrendered it.

*May Allah Almighty give us and all Muslims the most perfect ability to stay safe against such unfortunate happenings.*

passages.title: The crescent moons and entering houses by their doors
passages.tafsir:
# The Crescent Moons, and Entering Houses by Their Doors (2:189)

A single ayah, but it moves in two steps: first a question the Companions put to the Prophet ﷺ about the crescent moon and the answer Allah gave them, and then a correction of a custom from the days of ignorance about how one enters a house. What binds them is the theme of **al-birr** — righteousness — that has been running since ayah 177, and the season of Hajj: the moon is what fixes the time of Hajj, and the house-entering custom was something people practised precisely when they were in ihram for Hajj.
