Allah answers the question about the moon by telling them what the moon is *for*, and then, in the same breath, tells them that righteousness is not where they imagined it to be.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places the ayah in its sequence: the theme of righteousness begun at ayah 177 is still unfolding, and the injunctions given so far have covered equitable retaliation, bequest, fasting, iʿtikāf and abstaining from the unlawful. Now the subject turns to Hajj and to fighting — and before those rulings come, it is settled that the lunar months and days are what govern Hajj and the other religious obligations.

## The question — and the manners of asking it

Al-ʿAwfī related that Ibn ʿAbbās said: "The people asked Allah's Messenger ﷺ about the crescent moons," and then this ayah was revealed.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān preserves a striking observation from Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās about the men who asked it. The Companions had a mannerliness all their own: out of the great respect they held for the Prophet ﷺ, they asked him very few questions — unlike the communities of earlier prophets, who asked many questions and thereby failed to keep the etiquette owed to a prophet. Ibn ʿAbbās counted the questions the Companions asked that the Qur'an itself records: fourteen in all. One of them has only just appeared, in ayah 186 — *"And when My servants ask you…"* — and the second is this one. Six more occur within Sūrah al-Baqarah itself, and the remaining six come up in various other sūrahs. Fourteen questions in the whole of the Qur'an: that is the measure of their restraint.

**What exactly were they asking?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the new moon in the early part of the month appears in a shape unlike the sun's: it begins as a thin crescent, slowly grows to a full circle, then reduces in the same manner. So the question was either about the *cause* of this waxing and waning, or about the *wisdom* underlying it. Both possibilities exist.

Notice, then, what the answer does. It states the wisdom and the benefit. If that is what they asked, the answer synchronizes with the question exactly. But if the question was aimed at the underlying cause — a direction Maʿārif ul Qurʼān considers far from the Companions' well-mannered habit — then the answer, by electing to give the wisdom and benefit rather than the reality, quietly hints at something: finding out the reality of the heavenly bodies is not an area under man's control anyway, and the knowledge of that reality is not necessary for any practical purpose, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter. So the question of "reality" is beside the point. What *can* be asked, and what *can* be explained, is the benefit that reaches us through the rising and setting, the waxing and waning of the moon: that people may easily determine the time factor in their transactions and contracts, and know the days of Hajj.

The lesson sits in what the answer chooses to give — not a mechanism that lies beyond us and serves no practical need, but a benefit we can live by.

## "Signs to mark fixed periods of time"

The answer calls the crescents **mawāqīt**: appointed markers of time, rendered by Ibn Kathir as *"signs to mark fixed periods of time for mankind and for the pilgrimage,"* and by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as *"indicative of time for the people and of the Hajj."*

Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report of al-ʿAwfī, unpacks *"for mankind"* concretely: so that people may mark **their acts of worship**, **the ʿiddah of their women** (the period of time a divorced woman or a widow is required to wait before remarrying), and **the time of their Hajj**. Notice the range — worship, family law, pilgrimage. The crescent is not decoration in the sky; it is the calendar on which a believing community's obligations hang.

**From the Sunnah.** ʿAbdur-Razzāq reported that Ibn ʿUmar narrated that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said:

> "Allah has made the crescents signs to mark fixed periods of time for mankind. Hence, fast on seeing it (the crescent for Ramadan) and break the fast on seeing it (the crescent for Shawwāl). If it was obscure to you, then count thirty days."

Ibn Kathir adds that this hadith was also collected by Al-Ḥākim in his *Mustadrak*, and that al-Ḥākim said: "The chain is Ṣaḥīḥ, and they (al-Bukhārī and Muslim) did not record it."

The hadith is the ayah turned into practice. *Mawāqīt* is not an abstraction — it means you look at the horizon, and you fast; you look again, and you break the fast. And if cloud hides it, you do not fall into paralysis: you count thirty days and move on.

## Why the lunar calendar

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out at length why Islam settled on the moon.

The ayah itself tells us no more than that the moon will help identify the count of months and days on which rest transactions and acts of worship such as Hajj. Sūrah Yūnus deals with the same subject — *"And determined it (the moon) by stations, that you might know the number of the years and the reckoning"* (10:5) — so that the benefit of the moon's passage through its different stages is that people may find out through it the count of years, months and days. Yet a verse of Sūrah Banī Isrā'īl connects this count to the sun as well: *"Then We erased the sign of the night and brought out the sign of the day to see, so that you seek the blessing from your Lord and get to know the number of years and the reckoning"* (17:12).

So years and months *can* be counted with the help of a solar calendar. But the words used of the moon here — *"They are indicative of time for the people and of the Hajj"* — indicate very clearly, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading, that the lunar calendar is a fixed choice in the Sharīʿah of Islam, especially in prescribed acts of worship that relate to a particular month and its dates: the months of Ramadan and Hajj, the days of Hajj, Muḥarram and Laylat al-Qadr — all of them tied to the sighting of the new moon. It is established by this ayah that the lunar calendar is the one to be trusted upon in the sight of Allah.

**Why the moon and not the sun?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it plainly: the Sharīʿah opted for the lunar calendar because it rests on something every sighted person can see on the horizon and be informed by. Knowing it is equally easy for the scholar and the unlettered, the villager, the islander and the mountain-dweller. This stands in contrast with the solar calendar, which depends on meteorological equipment and mathematical computations that cannot so easily become the common personal experience of everybody. A calendar anyone can read for himself keeps the appointed times of worship within everyone's reach.

**Is using the solar calendar wrong?** No — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here. The solar calendar has not been prohibited juristically; the lunar has been fixed as an obligation in the sphere of ʿibādāt, and has been *favoured* in social and business transactions too, both because it serves as a basis for the acts of Islamic worship and because it is a symbol of Islamic identity. The only condition is that the use of the solar calendar should not become so widespread that people forget all about the lunar calendar — because that would necessarily affect obligatory ʿibādāt like fasting and Hajj adversely. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that a sampling of this is already visible in our time: in offices and businesses, government and private, the solar calendar is used with such frequency that many people do not seem to even remember all the Islamic months by name. The practical remedy suggested is modest: use the solar calendar where you must deal with non-Muslims, but for other office correspondence, private dealings and daily requirements, use the lunar — and in doing so earn the *thawāb* of performing a *farḍ ʿalā al-kifāyah*, an obligation which, if performed by some, suffices for others.

## The turn: "It is not righteousness that you enter the houses from the back"

Then the ayah pivots. Ibn Kathir gives the occasion of revelation.

**Al-Bukhārī recorded that al-Barā' said:** "During the time of Jāhiliyyah, they used to enter the house from the back upon assuming the Iḥrām." Thereafter, Allah revealed: *"It is not al-Birr that you enter the houses from the back, but al-Birr is from Taqwā. So enter houses through their proper doors."*

Abū Dāwūd aṭ-Ṭayālisī recorded the same hadith from al-Barā' but with the wording: "The Anṣār used to enter their houses from the back when returning from a journey," and then this ayah was revealed.

And al-Ḥasan said that when some people during the time of Jāhiliyyah would leave home to travel and then decide not to travel, they would not enter the house from its door — rather, they would climb over the back wall. Of that, Allah said: *"It is not righteousness that you enter the houses from the back."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes how far this went: a person in iḥrām who needed to get into his house would go in from the back, even if it had to be through a hole bored in the wall for the purpose — because they thought it was **prohibited** to enter houses from the front door while in iḥrām. And they did not merely tolerate this; **they even rated it as righteousness.** That is why the correction comes immediately after the mention of Hajj: right where the moon fixes the times of pilgrimage, Allah tells them that entering houses from the backs is no righteousness at all.

**Real righteousness lies elsewhere.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it directly: real righteousness lies in abstaining from what has been made unlawful by Allah. Since coming into houses through their doors is not forbidden, the question of abstaining from it does not arise. So whoever wishes to go into his house should enter through its door. And the centre-piece of all the principles here is the closing command: people must keep fearing Allah, so that they can hope to have the best of both the worlds.

## The ruling this ayah establishes

This is where the ayah reaches far past a discarded desert custom. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān derives a governing rule from *"And it is not righteousness that you come into your houses from their backs"*:

> Something the Sharīʿah of Islam has not classed as **wājib** (necessary), and has not given the status of an act of **ʿibādah** (worship), should not be taken as necessary or as worship on one's own. That is not permissible. And likewise, **taking something to be a sin while it is permissible under Islamic law is a sin in itself.**

That is exactly what those people had done. Entering houses through doors was permissible under religious law, yet they made it out to be a sin; coming into the house from its back by breaking through the wall was not necessary under religious law, yet they made it out to be necessary. This was why they were admonished.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then names the wider consequence: this is the very reason **bidʿah** — innovation in religious matters — is not permissible. Innovation is what happens when unnecessary things are taken to be necessary, like the *farḍ* or the *wājib*, or when permissible things are taken to be forbidden. This ayah makes it very clear that doing so is prohibited — and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, that single principle gives us the guiding rule in thousands of acts in vogue.

There is a quiet mercy in this. Religion is not made heavier by our zeal; what Allah did not make necessary, we are not to make necessary on our own.

## Taqwā, and what success means

The ayah closes: *"and have Taqwā of Allah that you may be successful."*

Ibn Kathir defines both halves without ornament. **Taqwā of Allah** means to *do what He has commanded you and refrain from what He has forbidden for you.* Not more, and not less — which is the exact point the house-doors made. And **"that you may be successful"** means: tomorrow, when you stand before Him and He thus rewards you perfectly.

So the ayah begins in the sky and ends at the door of a house, and both are about the same thing: submitting to the shape Allah actually gave to worship. He set the crescent in the heavens so that people may know *when* to obey. He sent this ayah to make clear that obedience is defined by Him, not added to by us. And He ties the whole to taqwā — doing what He commanded and refraining from what He forbade — because that is what will stand up on the day we meet Him.

passages.title: Fighting those who fight you, and its limits
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat are where the Qur'an first tells the Muslims to fight — and in the same breath tells them how far they may not go. That pairing holds the passage together: every permission arrives wrapped in a limit. Fight, but only those who fight you. Kill them wherever you find them, but not at the Sacred Mosque. Fight until there is no more *fitnah* — disbelief, shirk, and the barring of people from worship — but the moment they cease, you cease. Retaliate, but only with the like of what was done to you. And it closes not with a sword but with a purse: spend in the way of Allah, and do good.

## The moment behind the words

Ma'arif ul Qur'an explains that through the whole Makkan period fighting was not permitted: the revelations of those years told the believers to be patient against the pain inflicted on them, and to overlook and forgive where they could. The Companions had absorbed this so deeply that, as Ma'arif ul Qur'an puts it, before this verse came down they were under the impression that killing the disbelievers was bad and prohibited.

After the emigration to Madinah that changed. Abu al-'Aliya — quoted by Ibn Kathir through al-Rabi' ibn Anas — said plainly: **"This was the first Ayah about fighting that was revealed in Al-Madinah."** (Ma'arif ul Qur'an notes a narration from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, naming a different verse as the first on the subject; the majority of the Companions and their successors held it is this one.)

Ma'arif ul Qur'an then anchors ayah 191 to a precise moment. In the sixth year after the Hijrah the Prophet ﷺ set out for 'Umrah and the idolaters turned him back from the Sacred House; Ibn Kathir, citing Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Qatadah, Miqsam, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and 'Ata, notes the month was Dhul-Qa'dah. The treaty struck at Hudaybiyyah let the Muslims come the following year instead, so in 7 AH the Prophet ﷺ prepared to travel for the make-up 'Umrah (*'umrat al-qada'*) — and the Companions were worried, for two reasons:

1. **The disbelievers could not be trusted with a treaty.** If they attacked again, the fighting would fall inside the sacred precincts of Makkah, where fighting is not permitted.
2. **The month was Dhul-Qa'dah** — one of the four sacred months, in which fighting anyone, anywhere, was forbidden.

They were walking into a place and a time where they were not sure they could even defend themselves. Ayat 191 and 194 answer those two exact fears — not abstract legislation, but reassurance handed to anxious pilgrims on the eve of a journey.

## Ayah 190: fight *those who fight you*

**"And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but transgress not the limits. Truly, Allah likes not the transgressors."**

Two conditions sit inside the sentence. The first is *fi sabil Allah*, in the way of Allah — a matter of intention, not spectacle. Ibn Kathir cites the report in the Two Sahihs from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari: asked whether the man fighting from bravery or the one fighting to show off is in Allah's cause, the Prophet ﷺ answered, **"He who fights so that Allah's Word is superior, then he fights in Allah's cause."**

The second condition is the clause *alladhina yuqatilunakum*, "those who fight you." Ibn Kathir insists this phrase is doing real work: it "applies only to fighting the enemies who are engaged in fighting Islam and its people." Here the scholars differed — 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam held the restriction was later abrogated by 9:5, "then kill them wherever you find them," while Ibn Kathir rejects that as "not plausible," since "those who fight you" already names who is meant, and Allah says elsewhere, "fight against the Mushrikin collectively as they fight against you collectively" (9:36).

## "Do not transgress" — the limits, spelled out

The Qur'an does not leave *la ta'tadu* vague. Ibn Kathir reports al-Hasan al-Basri defining the transgression meant as: **mutilating the dead, theft from the captured goods, killing women, children and old people who do not participate in warfare, killing priests and residents of houses of worship, burning down trees, and killing animals without real benefit** — and adds that Ibn 'Abbas, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and Muqatil ibn Hayyan held the same. Note what is on that list: not only the killing of non-combatants, but theft from the spoils and the needless burning of a tree. A man could win a battle and still be among those "Allah likes not."

**From the Sunnah.** Muslim recorded in his Sahih that Buraydah narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Fight for the sake of Allah and fight those who disbelieve in Allah. Fight, but do not steal (from the captured goods), commit treachery, mutilate (the dead), or kill a child, or those who reside in houses of worship."* It is reported in the Two Sahihs that Ibn 'Umar said a woman was found dead during one of the Prophet's battles, and the Prophet ﷺ then forbade killing women and children. Ma'arif ul Qur'an adds a hadith from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) in Abu Dawud — *"Do not kill anyone old and weak, any young child or any woman"* — and the same instructions from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq to Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan, adding the prohibition of killing the religiously devoted, monks and priests, and labourers employed by the disbelievers who do not take part in the fighting.

Ma'arif ul Qur'an also states the limit of that protection: the jurists ruled that if a woman, an old man or a religious person takes part in the actual fighting, or helps the enemy in any way against the Muslims, they fall under "those who fight you." The protection tracks conduct, not label.

## Ayah 191: the sanctuary clause

**"And kill them wherever you find them, and turn them out from where they have turned you out."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is exact: *"Your energy should be spent on fighting them, just as their energy is spent on fighting you, and on expelling them from the areas from which they have expelled you, as a law of equality in punishment."* The believers had been driven from their homes; the verse authorises the same in return, no more.

Then the qualification the Companions needed. Ma'arif ul Qur'an observes that "kill them wherever you find them" is worded generally, and that generality might suggest killing was allowed even within the Haram — so the next sentence particularises it: **"And do not fight them near al-Masjid al-Haram unless they fight you there,"** covering the mosque and all its environs in Makkah. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith in the Two Sahihs in which the Prophet ﷺ declared that Allah made this city a sanctuary the day He created the heavens and the earth, and it remains so by Allah's decree until the Day of Resurrection — its trees not to be cut, its grass not uprooted — fighting in it having been made lawful for him ﷺ for one hour of one day, and for no one else.

Ma'arif ul Qur'an records two rulings. In the Haram it is not permissible to kill even a bird or an animal, let alone a human being — yet if someone begins killing within the sacred precincts, the other may fight back in defence, and the jurists are agreed on this. And the prohibition on *initiating* fighting is specific to al-Masjid al-Haram and its precincts; elsewhere, initiating it is valid too.

## "And al-Fitnah is worse than killing"

Ma'arif ul Qur'an explains why this clause is here: the Companions had spent years being taught that bloodshed was forbidden, and this sentence removes the misconception. Killing is indeed a terribly evil act — *and what the disbelievers of Makkah were doing was worse*: insisting on their kufr and shirk, and stopping Muslims from fulfilling their religious obligations, from Hajj and 'Umrah. Ma'arif ul Qur'an leaves *fitnah* untranslated "for want of a perfect equivalent in English," noting that here it inescapably means kufr, shirk, and preventing Muslims from their worship. Ibn Kathir reports the same from Abu al-'Aliya, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' ibn Anas: **"Shirk is worse than killing."**

## Ayat 192–193: the war has an off-switch

Twice the same phrase turns the whole thing off: *fa-in intahaw*, "but if they cease."

In ayah 192 the response is not merely a truce but forgiveness: **"then Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."** Ibn Kathir explains that if they cease fighting in the Sacred Area, come to Islam and repent, Allah forgives their sins — *even if they had before killed Muslims in Allah's Sacred Area* — for His forgiveness encompasses every sin, whatever its enormity, when the sinner repents of it. Men who had shed believers' blood in the most sacred place on earth are told there is a road back.

Ayah 193 names the goal — **"until there is no more fitnah and the religion is for Allah"** — which Ibn Kathir, following Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliya, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Rabi', Muqatil ibn Hayyan, al-Suddi and Zayd ibn Aslam, glosses as: until there is no more shirk, and so that the religion of Allah becomes dominant above all other religions. He cites the report in the Two Sahihs: *"I have been ordered (by Allah) to fight the people until they proclaim, 'None has the right to be worshipped but Allah'. Whoever said it, then he will save his life and property from me, except for cases of the law, and their account will be with Allah."*

Then the brake: **"But if they cease, let there be no transgression except against the wrongdoers."** Ibn Kathir gives two readings: if they stop their shirk and their fighting against the believers, warfare must cease and *whoever fights them afterwards is himself committing an injustice* — which he says is the sense of Mujahid's statement that only combatants should be fought; or, if they abandon their injustice, do not begin aggression afterwards. He ties the wording to ayah 194 and to 16:126, "punish them with the like of that with which you were afflicted." The response is capped at the size of the injury.

## Ibn 'Umar and the misuse of ayah 193

Al-Bukhari recorded from Nafi' that during the conflict of Ibn al-Zubayr two men came to Ibn 'Umar and said the people had fallen into shortcomings — was he not the son of 'Umar, and the Prophet's ﷺ Companion? So what kept him from going out? He answered, "What prevents me is that Allah has forbidden shedding the blood of my (Muslim) brother." They quoted this very ayah at him. His reply cuts to the bone:

> "We did fight until there was no more Fitnah and the religion became for Allah Alone. **You want to fight until there is Fitnah and the religion becomes for other than Allah!**"

That is where Nafi's report ends. Ibn Kathir then gives a separate addition from 'Uthman ibn Salih, reporting a different occasion: a man came to Ibn 'Umar and asked why he performed Hajj one year and 'Umrah another and left aside jihad, though Allah has so encouraged it. Ibn 'Umar answered by naming the five pillars on which Islam is built. When this ayah and 49:9 were then put to him, he said, "That we did during the time of Allah's Messenger ﷺ when Islam was still weak and (the Muslim) man used to face trials in his religion, such as killing or torture. When Islam became stronger (and apparent), there was no more Fitnah."

Two separate exchanges, then, and in both a Companion who had lived under the Prophet ﷺ refuses to let the verse become a licence for shedding Muslim blood.

## Ayah 194: the sacred month

**"The sacred month is for the sacred month, and for the prohibited things there is the Law of equality (qisas)."** This answers the second fear. Ma'arif ul Qur'an lists the four sacred months — Dhul-Qa'dah, Dhul-Hijjah and Muharram, consecutive, and Rajab. Fighting in them was considered unlawful even before Islam, the disbelievers of Makkah observing their sanctity too, and the law was still in force through 7 AH — exactly why the Companions were perplexed. The verse tells them that just as a state of defence grants an exception to the sanctity of the Haram, it allows the same exception for the sacred months. Ma'arif ul Qur'an adds that by the consensus of the Ummah this unlawfulness was later abrogated and permission to fight was given, yet it remains preferable not to *initiate* fighting in these months without need to defend: their sanctity was not abrogated totally, but holds like the sanctity of the Haram.

Ibn Kathir gives the Prophet's ﷺ own practice, from a report of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah recorded by Imam Ahmad with what he calls an authentic chain: *"Allah's Messenger ﷺ would not engage in warfare during the Sacred Month unless he was first attacked, then he would march forth. He would otherwise remain idle until the end of the Sacred Months."* And when word reached him at Hudaybiyyah that 'Uthman, sent as his emissary to the polytheists, had been killed, he ﷺ took the pledge from the fourteen hundred under the tree to fight; on learning 'Uthman was not killed, **he abandoned the fight and reverted to peace.**

Ibn Kathir notes that "whoever transgresses against you, you transgress likewise against him" *ordains justice even with the polytheists.* The ayah closes: "And fear Allah, and know that Allah is with al-Muttaqin" — a command, says Ibn Kathir, that Allah be obeyed and feared out of taqwa, and news that He is with the people of taqwa **by His aid and support in this life and the Hereafter.**

## Ayah 195: the destruction you choose

The passage ends somewhere unexpected: **"And spend in the cause of Allah and do not throw yourselves into destruction, and do good. Truly, Allah loves al-Muhsinin."** Ma'arif ul Qur'an notes this is the tenth injunction in the sequence on righteousness begun at ayah 177, and that from it the jurists deduced financial obligations beyond Zakah — not permanent, not bound by a threshold or quantity, but binding whenever there is need, and lapsing when there is none.

Then the phrase argued over for centuries: *do not throw yourselves into destruction (al-tahlukah)*. The most striking explanation comes from a Companion who lived it. Aslam Abu 'Imran related that at Constantinople a man from the Ansar broke through the enemy lines, and people said he was throwing himself to destruction. Abu Ayyub al-Ansari answered:

> "We know this Ayah better, for it was revealed about us… When Islam became strong, we, the Ansar, met and said to each other … 'Warfare has ceased, so let us go back to our families and children and attend to them.' So this Ayah was revealed about us."

The destruction, he said, was staying with families and estates and abandoning the struggle. Ibn Kathir names Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abu Hatim, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim among those who recorded it, and notes al-Tirmidhi graded it *Hasan Sahih Gharib*. Ma'arif ul Qur'an adds that Abu Ayyub spent his entire life in that struggle away from Madinah, meeting the end of his life at Constantinople and being buried there.

Al-Bukhari recorded that Hudhayfah said of this ayah simply, "It was revealed about spending." Ibn Abu Hatim reported him saying the same, and — this is a separate line of reporting, not al-Bukhari's — added that the like is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Suddi and Muqatil ibn Hayyan. Ibn 'Abbas put it flatly: "This is not about fighting. But about refraining from spending for the sake of Allah, in which case, one will be throwing his self into destruction." Ma'arif ul Qur'an gathers further readings — losing hope in the mercy and forgiveness of Allah (from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib); spending so lavishly in the way of Allah that the family's rights are compromised; throwing oneself into an offensive fight where it is already obvious one can do nothing against the enemy but die — and rather than declaring a winner reports al-Jassas's synthesis: **all of these rulings can be inferred from this verse.**

Ibn Kathir reads the command broadly: to spend in Allah's cause in every area and way that involves obedience and drawing closer to Him, and especially in fighting the enemies and in what strengthens the Muslims against them — for those who make a habit of withholding here face certain ruin.

**And the last word is beauty.** Ibn Kathir says "and do good" commands *ihsan*, excellence in the religion, "the highest part of the acts of obedience." Ma'arif ul Qur'an explains it in two directions, both from the Prophet ﷺ. In worship, ihsan is what he ﷺ defined in the well-known hadith of Jibra'il (peace be upon him): that you worship Allah as if you are seeing Him, and if you cannot reach that degree, then at the least know that Allah is seeing you. In social dealings, he ﷺ explained it — in a report from Mu'adh (may Allah be pleased with him) in the Musnad of Ahmad — as liking for others what you like for yourself, and disliking for them what you dislike for yourself.

## Living it

- **A permission never outgrows its limit.** The boundary is as much revelation as the licence.
- **When the other side stops, you stop** — continuing makes you the wrongdoer.
- **Retaliation is capped at the size of the injury,** and justice is owed even to an enemy.
- **Remember Ibn 'Umar:** a verse revealed about ending fitnah must never become a pretext for spilling a brother's blood.
- **Give**, and **do it beautifully** — as though you see Him, wanting for others what you want for yourself.

passages.title: Completing Hajj and 'Umrah and its concessions
passages.tafsir:
# Al-Baqarah 196–199: Completing Hajj and 'Umrah, and its concessions

These four ayat take the pilgrimage from the moment a person enters ihram to the moment he leaves 'Arafat and Muzdalifah — and at every step they pair a command with a concession. What holds them together is a single rhythm: *finish what you began for Allah's sake; and where you truly cannot, here is Allah's mercy in the form of a substitute.*

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān places this in a longer sequence: since ayah 177 Sūrat al-Baqarah has been laying out the injunctions of righteousness, and Hajj is the eleventh of them. It notes that the obligation of Hajj itself was already established elsewhere — by the majority view, in the third year of Hijrah through the ayah of Sūrah Āl 'Imrān. So ayah 196 is not announcing that Hajj is obligatory. It is legislating *how* the rites are held to, and what happens when a pilgrim is stopped.

## "And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah"

Ibn Kathir explains that after Allah mentioned the rulings of fasting and jihad, He turned to the rites, commanding the Muslims to *complete* Hajj and 'Umrah — meaning to finish them once one has started. The proof is the very next clause, "but if you are prevented," which only makes sense for someone already underway. On this, Ibn Kathir says, the scholars agree: beginning the acts of Hajj and 'Umrah obliges you to finish them.

The early authorities read the word "complete" (*atimmū*) in several complementary ways, and Ibn Kathir preserves them all:

- **Makhūl:** complete them means begin them from the *mīqāt* — the stations the Prophet ﷺ designated for entering ihram.
- **'Umar** (via az-Zuhri): perform each of them separately, and perform 'Umrah outside the months of Hajj — citing "The Hajj is in well-known months."
- **As-Suddi:** maintain the performance of Hajj and 'Umrah.
- **Ibn 'Abbās:** "Hajj is 'Arafat, while 'Umrah is Tawāf" — each rite named by its defining pillar.
- **'Alqamah**, reporting Ibn Mas'ūd's recitation, and **Ibrāhīm**: "complete Hajj and 'Umrah *to the House*."

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān draws out an important limit here. Sūrah Āl 'Imrān declares Hajj obligatory but says nothing of 'Umrah; this ayah mentions 'Umrah but never says whether it is obligatory in the first place. All it establishes is that once you enter ihram, completing it becomes *wājib* — necessary — exactly as voluntary prayer or fasting becomes binding once begun. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān notes that Ibn Kathir cites, with reference to at-Tirmidhi, Ahmad and al-Bayhaqi, that Jābir asked the Prophet ﷺ whether 'Umrah is wājib, and he answered that it is not wājib, but doing it is better and merit-worthy (at-Tirmidhi grading it *hasan sahih*). On this basis Imam Abū Hanīfah, Imam Mālik and others held 'Umrah to be sunnah rather than wājib.

## Hudaybiyyah: the moment behind the ayah

The concession clause has a face and a date. Ibn Kathir says "But if you are prevented, sacrifice a hady such as you can afford" was revealed in the sixth year of Hijrah, the year of the treaty of al-Hudaybiyyah, when the idolaters blocked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from reaching the House. (Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān, agreeing that the ayah concerns Hudaybiyyah, places the event in 7 AH.) Fourteen hundred Companions were camped there, with seventy camels brought for sacrifice — one camel shared among every seven men.

What happened next is one of the most human scenes recorded of them. When the Prophet ﷺ ordered them to shave their heads and leave ihram, they did not move. Ibn Kathir gives the reason plainly: they were awaiting that order to be abrogated. Only when they saw him ﷺ come out having shaved his own head did they follow. Some shaved; some only shortened. He ﷺ said, "May Allah award His mercy to those who shaved." They asked about those who shortened. Only on the third time did he add, "And to those who shortened."

That is the moment the ayah addresses. They had set out for the House, they were stopped short of it, and the command came to release themselves from ihram before ever reaching it. The ayah meets that with a ruling rather than a rebuke: offer whatever sacrifice you can afford, and be released.

## Who counts as "prevented"?

Ibn Kathir is careful that *hasr* — being prevented — reaches beyond the obvious cases; he says it includes more than being sick, fearing an enemy, or getting lost on the way to Makkah. Imam Ahmad reported from al-Hajjāj ibn 'Amr al-Ansāri that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say, "Whoever suffered a broken bone or a limb, will have ended his ihram and has to perform Hajj again." Al-Hajjāj mentioned this to Ibn 'Abbās and Abū Hurayrah and both said he had spoken the truth. Ibn Kathir notes it is also in the Four Collections, and that in the version of Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah the wording includes "or became ill." Ibn Abī Hātim records that Ibn Mas'ūd, Ibn az-Zubayr, 'Alqamah, Sa'īd ibn al-Musayyib, 'Urwah, Mujāhid, an-Nakha'i, 'Atā' and Muqātil ibn Hayyān all held that hasr covers an enemy, an illness or a fracture. Ath-Thawri went broadest: "everything that harms the person." Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān reports the same position from Imam Abū Hanīfah and other jurists — the words "if you are prevented" are general enough to include sickness.

There is also a prudent step you can take *before* setting out. Ibn Kathir cites the Two Sahihs, from 'Ā'ishah, that the Prophet ﷺ visited Dubā'ah bint az-Zubayr ibn 'Abdul-Muttalib, who said, "O Messenger of Allah, I intend to perform Hajj but I am ill." He said, "Perform Hajj and make the condition: *My place is where You prevent me.*" Muslim records similarly from Ibn 'Abbās. From this, Ibn Kathir says, the permissibility of making such a condition is derived.

**What must be offered.** "Whatever hady you can afford" is deliberately elastic. Ibn 'Abbās said the hady includes eight kinds of animals — camels, cows, goats and sheep — and, in al-'Awfi's report, "if one can afford it, then camels, otherwise cows, or sheep." 'Urwah put it simply: *depending on the price*. Imam Mālik reported that 'Ali ibn Abī Tālib allowed a sheep. Ibn Kathir supports this from the Two Sahihs, where 'Ā'ishah said the Prophet ﷺ once offered sheep as hady. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān adds Imam Abū Hanīfah's ruling on the phrase "until the hady reaches its place": it must be taken into the sacred precincts of the Haram and slaughtered there, and if one cannot do it personally, he may authorise someone else.

**And afterwards?** Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān points out that the Prophet's ﷺ own practice settles it: releasing from ihram by sacrifice is permitted, but the Hajj or 'Umrah remains owed as *qadā'* when circumstances allow. That is precisely why he ﷺ and his Companions returned the following year to perform the 'Umrah they had missed at Hudaybiyyah.

**A point of disagreement worth noting.** Ibn Kathir holds that "do not shave your heads until the hady reaches the place of sacrifice" attaches to "complete the Hajj and 'Umrah," not to the clause about being prevented — and says Ibn Jarīr erred in tying it to the latter. His evidence is that at Hudaybiyyah they shaved and slaughtered *outside* the Haram, whereas in normal conditions one may not shave until the hady reaches its place. He cites the Two Sahihs, where Hafsah asked why others had left ihram for 'Umrah but he ﷺ had not, and he replied, "I matted my hair and I have garlanded my hady, so I will not leave ihram until I offer the sacrifice."

## Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah and the lice

"And whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head" has a named face too. Al-Bukhāri reports — from 'Abdur-Rahmān ibn Asbahāni, who heard 'Abdullah ibn Ma'qil — that Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, sitting with him in the mosque of Kufah, was asked about the fidyah of fasting and said: **"This was revealed concerning my case especially, but it is also for you in general."** Ka'b was carried to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with lice falling in great numbers onto his face. He ﷺ said, "I never thought that your ailment had reached such an extent as I see. Can you afford a sheep?" Ka'b said no. So he ﷺ said, "Fast for three days or feed six poor persons, each with half a *sā'* of food, and shave your head." Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān — citing a hadith of Sahih al-Bukhari for the same episode — reckons that half a sā' at roughly 1.632 kilograms of wheat, or its cash value.

Ibn Kathir's summary of this is a small masterclass in how law is derived: *"So this is a general judgement derived from a specific case."*

He also notices something beautiful. In Imam Ahmad's version, the Prophet ﷺ listed the options as sacrifice, feeding, then fasting — while the Qur'an's own wording begins with fasting and moves to sacrifice. Ibn Kathir explains: the Qur'an begins with the *easiest* and ascends to the more demanding; the Prophet ﷺ advised Ka'b beginning with the *most rewarding*. "Each text is suitable in its place and context."

## Tamattu' and the ten fasts

"Then when you are secure" means, Ibn Kathir says, when you are able to complete the rites. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān explains the two ways of combining 'Umrah and Hajj within the Hajj months: entering ihram for both together from the mīqāt — *Qirān* — where one stays in ihram until Hajj ends; or entering ihram for 'Umrah alone, completing it, leaving ihram, and re-entering ihram for Hajj within the Haram before going to Minā on the eighth of Dhul-Hijjah — *Tamattu'*. Literally, it notes, *tamattu'* ("to benefit") covers both, and the Qur'an's *fa-man tamatta'a* is used in that general sense.

There is real history in this permission. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān records that in Jāhiliyyah the Arabs would not combine Hajj and 'Umrah in the Hajj months and thought it a sin. Ibn Kathir cites the Two Sahihs, where 'Imrān ibn Husayn said, "We performed Hajj at-Tamattu' in the lifetime of Allah's Messenger ﷺ and then the Qur'an was revealed. Nothing was revealed to forbid it, nor did he forbid it until he died. And somebody said what he wished according to his own opinion." Al-Bukhāri said 'Imrān meant 'Umar. Ibn Kathir is scrupulous here: 'Umar did discourage Tamattu', but **he never declared it unlawful** — he discouraged it so that people would make more separate journeys to the House, for Hajj in its months and 'Umrah through the year, as 'Umar himself stated.

The sacrifice for Tamattu' is, Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān says, an expression of gratitude for being permitted to combine two acts of worship. If one cannot afford it: three fasts during Hajj and seven on returning. Ibn Kathir records Ibn 'Abbās (via al-'Awfi) placing the three before the day of 'Arafah, and Ibn 'Umar specifying the day before Tarwiyah, Tarwiyah itself (the eighth), then the day of 'Arafah (the ninth) — the same reported from 'Ali. If one missed them, 'Ā'ishah and Ibn 'Umar said, as al-Bukhāri reports, that fasting the days of Tashrīq was permitted only for one who found no hady; 'Ali held the same. Ibn Kathir reconciles this with what Muslim reports from Qutaybah al-Hudhali, that the Prophet ﷺ said "The days of Tashrīq are days of eating and drinking and remembering Allah" — that narration is general, while 'Ā'ishah's and Ibn 'Umar's is specific.

The whole procedure appears in al-Bukhāri's report from Ibn 'Umar of the Farewell Hajj: whoever brought a hady stays in ihram until his Hajj is complete; whoever did not should make tawāf of the Ka'bah and between Safā and Marwah, cut his hair, leave ihram, then enter ihram for Hajj — and if he cannot afford a hady, fast three days during the Hajj and seven when he returns home.

**"That is ten complete."** Why say it, when three and seven are plain? Ibn Kathir says it is Arabic emphasis — as one says "I saw with my eyes, heard with my ears, wrote with my hand" — comparing "nor a bird that flies with its two wings" (6:38) and Mūsā's thirty nights plus ten, "and he completed the term of his Lord: forty nights" (7:142). A second view he mentions: it stresses that the ten are a floor, not to be reduced.

**Who is exempt.** "That is for one whose family is not present at al-Masjid al-Harām." Tāwus said Tamattu' is for those whose families do not reside in the Haram, not the residents of Makkah, and 'Abdur-Razzāq reports Ibn 'Abbās saying similarly. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān frames the reasoning: for those living within the mīqāt it is no hardship to return for 'Umrah after the Hajj months, whereas someone travelling from far away cannot easily make a separate journey.

Ayah 196 closes with taqwā and a warning: "know that Allah is severe in punishment." Ibn Kathir applies it to whoever defies His command. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān applies it with unusual directness to pilgrims today — that many do not trouble to learn the rules of Hajj and 'Umrah before going, and many who know them do not keep them strictly. That is the practical edge of this passage: *the rites are not yours to improvise.*

## Ayah 197: the months, and the three abstentions

"The Hajj is in well-known months." Ibn Kathir uses this to establish that ihram for Hajj is only assumed in those months — from Ibn 'Abbās, Jābir, 'Atā', Tāwus and Mujāhid — reasoning that Hajj has a fixed time exactly as prayer does. Ibn Khuzaymah records Ibn 'Abbās saying it is part of the Sunnah of Hajj to assume ihram in the Hajj months, and Ibn Kathir notes that a Companion saying "this is from the Sunnah" carries the weight of a hadith with the majority, especially from Ibn 'Abbās, the *tarjumān* (interpreter) of the Qur'an. He is honest about the weaker material too: a report raised to the Prophet ﷺ through Ibn Marduwyah has a "reasonable" chain, but he says the narration from Jābir himself, recorded by ash-Shāfi'i and al-Bayhaqi, is *more reliable* than the one raised to the Prophet ﷺ.

The months, per al-Bukhāri from Ibn 'Umar: Shawwāl, Dhul-Qa'dah, and the first ten days of Dhul-Hijjah — a view Ibn Kathir traces through a long roll of authorities. Ibn Jarīr defended calling this "months": Arabs say "I visited him this year" for a part of a year, and the Qur'an itself says "whoever hastens to leave in two days" for what is really a day and a half. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān adds that these were the Hajj months even in Jāhiliyyah, and that while some Imams hold Hajj invalid with a pre-Shawwāl ihram, Imam Abū Hanīfah rules it valid but *makrūh*.

Then the three prohibitions:

**Rafath.** Ibn Kathir: sexual intercourse, and by extension embracing, kissing, and talk of such matters — Ibn 'Umar included "mentioning this subject with the tongue," and Tāwus included saying "when I leave ihram I will do such-and-such with you." Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān adds that an *indirect* allusion is not prohibited. It also explains why intercourse was singled out from the general category of sin: other ihram violations can be repaired by *kaffārah*, but intercourse before the standing at 'Arafat invalidates the Hajj itself, obliges a cow or camel, and requires the whole Hajj to be repeated.

**Fusūq.** Ibn 'Abbās and a long list of early scholars: disobedience in general. Ibn 'Umar narrowed it to what Allah forbade in the sacred area. Others said cursing, on the strength of the authentic hadith "Cursing the Muslim is fusūq, while fighting him is kufr." 'Abdur-Rahmān ibn Zayd said slaughtering for idols; ad-Dahhāk said insulting nicknames. Ibn Kathir judges those who took it as all disobedience to be correct — noting that Allah specifically forbids wrongdoing in the sacred months (9:36) and in the sacred precinct (22:25) though it is forbidden always. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān leans the other way, preferring Ibn 'Umar's reading as more fitting to the context, since sins are forbidden in every state anyway; it then lists the six things forbidden by ihram alone: intercourse and its preliminaries; hunting land game or guiding a hunter; cutting hair or nails; perfume — these four for men and women alike — and for men, stitched clothing and covering the head and face (with Abū Hanīfah and Mālik also holding that a woman may not cover her face in ihram).

**Jidāl.** Ibn Mas'ūd, as Ibn Jarīr relates, defined it as arguing with your companion until you make him angry — a reading also related from Ibn 'Abbās and a great many of the Successors. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān offers a historical layer: in Jāhiliyyah people quarrelled over whether the standing was at 'Arafat or Muzdalifah, and over whether Hajj fell in Dhul-Hijjah or Dhul-Qa'dah, each side accusing the other of misguidance. "No quarrelling" ended it: the standing is at 'Arafat, then Muzdalifah, and Hajj is in Dhul-Hijjah alone.

**Why the Qur'an says "no," not "do not."** Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān draws attention to the grammar: *lā rafatha wa lā fusūqa wa lā jidāl* are words of *negation* — "there is no obscenity, no sin, no quarrel" — where a straightforward prohibition ("do not…") was available. The switch is deliberate. It hints that such things have no place in Hajj at all; they cannot even be conceived within it. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān also reads the three prohibitions against the conditions of Hajj: long separation from family, immense crowds of men and women at the tawāf area, the sa'y, 'Arafat, Muzdalifah and Minā, where desire is hard to govern; crowds where sins such as theft creep in; and cramped conditions where tempers flare. Each prohibition meets a real pressure.

And the promise attached: "Whatever good you do, Allah knows it." Ibn Kathir says that after forbidding evil in deed and tongue, Allah encouraged righteous deeds, affirming that He knows them and will reward them best on the Day of Resurrection. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān presses further — avoiding violations is not enough; treat this as a once-in-a-lifetime occasion and fill it with worship, dhikr and good.

Ibn Kathir also cites the Two Sahihs, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"Whoever performed Hajj to this House and did not commit rafath or fusūq, will return sinless, just as the day his mother gave birth to him."**

## "Take provision — and the best provision is taqwā"

Al-Bukhāri and Abū Dāwūd report from Ibn 'Abbās that the people of Yemen used to set out for Hajj without adequate supplies, saying, "We are the people of *tawakkul*" — and this ayah was revealed. Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Marduwyah report from Ibn 'Umar that people would throw away their provisions on entering ihram; Allah forbade this and required them to carry flour and *sawīq*.

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān's comment is the heart of it: going unprepared is not trust in Allah, because it ends with you begging on the road, suffering, and burdening others. Real *tawakkul* is to gather the means Allah has provided to the best of your ability and *then* place your trust in Him — and this, it says, is the explanation of tawakkul reported from the Prophet ﷺ. Abandoning the means and calling it trust is sheer ignorance.

Then the turn: having told you to pack for the journey of this world, Allah names the provision for the next. Ibn Kathir pairs it with "and the raiment of taqwā — that is better" (7:26): the material covering mentioned first, then the spiritual one — which includes humbleness, obedience and taqwā — and the latter declared better and more beneficial. "So fear Me, O people of understanding" — addressed, Ibn Kathir says, to people of reason.

## Ayah 198: earning is not a sin

Al-Bukhāri reports Ibn 'Abbās saying that 'Ukāz, Mijannah and Dhul-Majāz were trading posts in Jāhiliyyah, and people disliked trading during the Hajj season — until this ayah came. Abū Dāwūd's report adds their reasoning: "these are the days of dhikr."

Ahmad records that Abū Umāmah at-Taymi asked Ibn 'Umar, "We buy and sell during Hajj — is our Hajj valid?" Ibn 'Umar answered with a question: "Do you not perform tawāf around the House, stand at 'Arafat, throw the pebbles and shave your heads?" Then he told him that a man had put the same question to the Prophet ﷺ, who gave no answer until Jibrīl came down with this ayah — whereupon he ﷺ summoned the man and told him, "You are pilgrims." Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān gives the questioner's trade: he hired out camels to pilgrims and travelled with them.

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān then reads the wording closely. Allah did not say "earn"; He said **"there is no blame upon you"** — which carries the hint that avoiding it, where possible, is still better for the perfect sincerity Hajj deserves. And He called it *"bounty from your Lord"* — reforming what the Arabs had turned into a trade fair. So the question turns on intention: if trade is the real purpose and Hajj an adjunct, or the two are equal, that cuts against sincerity and diminishes the reward. But if a person sets out intending Hajj and runs short, earning to cover the shortfall is not against sincerity at all — though it is far better to leave the five special days of Hajj free for worship and dhikr, which is why some scholars ruled trading forbidden in those days specifically.

## 'Arafat and Muzdalifah

Ibn Kathir calls 'Arafat the place of standing and a pillar of Hajj. Imam Ahmad and the Sunan compilers record from 'Abdur-Rahmān ibn Ya'mar ad-Dīli that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said three times, **"Hajj is 'Arafat"** — "so whoever reached 'Arafah before dawn has performed it. The days of Minā are three, and there is no sin on one who hastens in two days, nor on one who stays."

The reassurance in that is felt in the story of 'Urwah ibn Mudarris, recorded by Ahmad and the Sunan compilers and graded *sahih* by at-Tirmidhi. He reached the Prophet ﷺ at Muzdalifah at prayer time, exhausted: "I came from the two mountains of Tayy'; my animal is tired and I am tired. I have not left a mountain but I stood on it. Do I have a valid Hajj?" He ﷺ answered: "Whoever performed this prayer with us, stood with us until we moved forth, and had stood at 'Arafat before that, by day or night, has completed his Hajj and fulfilled its rites."

The window, Ibn Kathir says, runs from noon on the day of 'Arafah to dawn of the day of Sacrifice. In the Farewell Hajj the Prophet ﷺ stood after Zuhr until sunset, and said, "Learn your rituals from me." Ibn Abī Hātim records from Ibn 'Abbās that in Jāhiliyyah people would leave 'Arafat while the sun still sat on the mountaintops "as a turban sits on a man's head"; the Messenger of Allah ﷺ deliberately delayed until sunset.

Muslim's long narration from Jābir gives the departure itself: he ﷺ stood until the sun's disc had gone, seated Usāmah behind him, and reined in al-Qaswā' so tightly her head touched the saddle, gesturing with his right hand and calling, **"Proceed calmly, people, calmly!"** — loosening her rein a little at each rise of sand. At Muzdalifah he prayed Maghrib and 'Ishā' with one adhān and two iqāmahs, with no voluntary prayer between them, then lay down until dawn, prayed Fajr with adhān and iqāmah, rode to al-Mash'ar al-Harām, faced the qiblah, supplicated, glorified Allah, declared *lā ilāha illallāh*, and remained standing until the daylight was very clear. Asked in the Two Sahihs about his pace, Usāmah ibn Zayd said: slow — unless he found space, then a little faster.

**Where is al-Mash'ar al-Harām?** Ibn 'Umar said all of Muzdalifah is al-Mash'ar al-Harām — "the Mount and the surrounding area"; Ibn 'Abbās and others said it is what lies between the two mounts. Imam Ahmad records from Jubayr ibn Mut'im that the Prophet ﷺ said: "All of 'Arafat is a place of standing, and keep away from 'Uranah. All of Muzdalifah is a place of standing, and keep away from the bottom of Muhassir. All the areas of Makkah are a place of sacrifice, and all the days of Tashrīq are days of sacrifice." Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān identifies al-Mash'ar al-Harām as a mountain in Muzdalifah — *mash'ar* meaning "sign" or "symbol," *harām* meaning sacred — and rules that spending the night on that plain is wājib, as is combining Maghrib and 'Ishā' there.

**Why the name 'Arafat?** 'Abdur-Razzāq reports from 'Ali ibn Abī Tālib that Jibrīl was sent to Ibrāhīm to teach him the rites, and when Ibrāhīm reached the place he said, *"'Araftu"* — "I know this place," having come there before. Ibn al-Mubārak relates from 'Atā' similarly: Jibrīl taught, and Ibrāhīm kept saying "I have known it, I have known it." Similar is attributed to Ibn 'Abbās, Ibn 'Umar and Abū Mijlaz. Ibn Kathir adds that the mount in the middle of 'Arafat is called Jabal ar-Rahmah, the Mount of Mercy. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān offers a further sense of the name: 'Arafat is the plain where a person comes to *know* his Lord and, through worship and dhikr, learns how to draw near Him — and where Muslims from East and West come to know one another by direct contact.

**"And remember Him as He has guided you."** Ibn Kathir reads this as a reminder of Allah's favour in teaching the rites — the guidance of Ibrāhīm al-Khalīl — against what came before: "and indeed, before that, you were of those astray." Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān extracts a principle of worship from the same phrase: *as He has guided you*, not as you please. A person is not free to invent his own forms of dhikr and worship. Human reasoning would have said to pray Maghrib at its time and 'Ishā' at its own — yet on that night Allah favours combining them. Allah accepts neither subtraction nor addition, nor a change of time or place, even when the change looks like *more* worship. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān applies this pointedly to people who add features of their own to voluntary prayers and charity, then treat the addition as necessary, and finally judge as astray those who omit it.

## Ayah 199: "Then depart from where the people depart"

This last ayah is a demolition of pride, and it names its target.

Al-Bukhāri reports from 'Ā'ishah that Quraysh and their allies, called *al-Hums*, used to stay at Muzdalifah while the rest of the Arabs stood at 'Arafat; when Islam came, Allah commanded His Prophet ﷺ to stand at 'Arafat and depart from there. Ibn Kathir notes that before Islam they justified remaining in the sanctuary by saying they were the people of Allah's Town and the servants of His House. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān gives the same excuse and its real motive: as custodians of the Ka'bah and caretakers of the Haram, they claimed it was improper for them to step outside the sacred limits — and Muzdalifah lies inside them while 'Arafat lies outside. The truth, it says plainly, was that they loved to display their pride and to keep common people at a distance.

Ibn Kathir records from Imam Ahmad — and notes it is in the Sahihayn — that Jubayr ibn Mut'im lost his camel, went out searching on the day of 'Arafah, and saw the Prophet ﷺ standing at 'Arafat. He said to himself: "By Allah, he is from the Hums. What has brought him here?"

Ibn Jarīr chose the view that "the people" means the general body of pilgrims at 'Arafat, and said there is *ijmā'* on it. Ibn Kathir also relays al-Bukhāri's report from Ibn 'Abbās that the departing here refers to proceeding from Muzdalifah to Minā to stone the pillars, and closes, as he often does, with *Allah knows best.*

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān turns this into the passage's moral summit. Standing apart and behaving as special is a standing act of arrogance in any circumstance — but in the garment of ihram, in a place and purpose that teach that rich and poor, learned and ignorant, big and small are all equal, it is worse. It draws the social principle out: people of higher status must not cut themselves off from those below them, but live among them as members of one large family in how they eat, stay and travel. That is what builds brotherhood, concern and love, and dissolves the walls between rich and poor, employer and employee. It recalls that in his last sermon at Hajj the Prophet ﷺ declared for all time that no Arab is superior to a non-Arab and no white person to a black person; superiority rests on taqwā and obedience to Allah.

Hence the ending. Those who had contrived a separate station for themselves at Muzdalifah are told that this was a sin, and that they must seek forgiveness for it so that Allah may forgive them and bless them with His mercy: **"and seek Allah's forgiveness; indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful."**

Ibn Kathir observes that Allah frequently orders remembrance after acts of worship are finished — the way, as Muslim reports, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would seek Allah's forgiveness three times after finishing the prayer, and as the Two Sahihs record his encouraging *Subhān Allah*, *al-hamdu lillāh* and *Allāhu akbar* thirty-three times each after prayer.

And he offers the words themselves. Ibn Marduwyah collected the hadith that al-Bukhāri reported from Shaddād ibn Aws, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said the master of seeking forgiveness is for the servant to say: *"O Allah, You are my Lord, there is no deity worthy of worship except You. You have created me and I am Your servant. I am on Your covenant, as much as I can be, and awaiting Your promise. I seek refuge with You from the evil that I have committed. I admit Your favour upon me and admit my faults. So forgive me, for none except You forgives the sins."* Whoever says these words at night and dies that same night enters Paradise; whoever says it during the day and dies enters Paradise. And in the Two Sahihs, 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr relates that Abū Bakr asked the Prophet ﷺ to teach him an invocation for his prayer, and he taught him: *"O Allah, I have done great injustice to myself, and none except You forgives sins, so forgive me with forgiveness from Yourself and be merciful to me; indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful."*

## Living it

Notice how the passage ends its two halves. Ayah 196 closes on "Allah is severe in punishment"; ayah 199 closes on "Allah is Forgiving, Merciful." The rites are held with both hands — seriousness about what Allah has fixed, and hope in what He forgives.

What these ayat ask of a believer is concrete. **Finish what you begin for Allah** — do not treat a devotion as disposable once started. **Learn the rules before you go**; Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān names ignorance of them as the standing failure of pilgrims. **Prepare properly and then trust** — packing is not the opposite of tawakkul, it is its very essence. **Keep the tongue and the temper**, because the enormous gathering Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān describes is exactly where rafath, fusūq and jidāl find their opening. **Worship as you were taught**, not as you improvise. And **stand where everyone stands** — for a person who cannot bear to be indistinguishable from the rest of Allah's servants for a few days has not yet understood what the ihram is for.

passages.title: Remembrance after the rites and the better prayer
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These four ayat close the Qur'an's block of instruction on Hajj by telling the pilgrim what to do when the rites are over — and what to ask for. One word holds them together: *dhikr*, the remembrance of Allah. Ayah 200 commands remembrance the moment the rites end; ayat 200–202 hold up two kinds of supplication, one that reaches no further than this world and one that asks for both; ayah 203 returns to remembrance during the days at Mina and closes the Hajj section with taqwa and the gathering to come.

## The scene these ayat walked into

The command in ayah 200 is not abstract. It corrects a specific custom.

Sa'id bin Jubayr reported that Ibn 'Abbas said: "During the time of Jahiliyyah, people used to stand during the (Hajj) season, and one of them would say, 'My father used to feed (the poor), help others (end their disputes, with his money), pay the Diyah (i.e., blood money),' and so forth. The only Dhikr that they had was that they would remember the deeds of their fathers." Then Allah revealed the command to remember Him "as you remember your forefathers, or with far more remembrance" (Ibn Kathir).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the picture. Once the pre-Islamic Arabs had finished at ʿArafat and Muzdalifah, performed their tawaf and sacrifice, and settled into their stay at Mina, they would hold gatherings to recite poetry and eulogise the achievements of their forefathers — gatherings "obviously devoid of the remembrance of Allah." These were the most blessed days available to them, and they filled them with family boasting.

So the ayah empties the old content out — stop reciting your lineage — and fills the same slot with Allah's name. Maʿārif adds urgency: Hajj comes only after a long and generally exacting journey, separation from family and business, and great expense, so completing it at all is a mercy calling for gratitude, "which further demands that one should keep busy in remembering Allah, avoid wasteful gatherings, engagements or conversations." It then names the modern version: nobody recites tribal poetry at Mina today, but thousands still spend these days in "wasteful gatherings, entertainments, amusements, shoppings" — and "this verse is enough to warn them."

## "Or with far more remembrance"

The Arabic is *aw ashadda dhikran* — "or more intense in remembrance." Ibn Kathir pauses on that "or" (*aw*), because it could be misread as uncertainty, as though Allah were unsure which of the two is greater. He says plainly that Allah "meant to encourage the people to remember Him more than they remember their forefathers, not that the word entails a doubt (as to which is larger or bigger)." He lines up four places where the Qur'an uses *aw* in this same rising sense: hearts "as stones or even worse in hardness" (2:74); those who "fear men as they fear Allah or even more" (4:77); "a hundred thousand (people) or even more" (37:147); and "two bows' length or (even) nearer" (53:9). In each the second option is the true one, and the "or" is there to push the listener upward. Maʿārif adds an angle from some commentators, citing *Rūh al-Bayān*: a small child depends on his father for everything and so remembers him constantly — and a grown, rational man is far more dependent on Allah than that child ever was. And as for boasting about the honour of one's fathers, this ayah eliminates that too: real honour comes through the dhikr of Allah.

## Two kinds of asking (200–201)

Ibn Kathir notes the sequence built into the passage: Allah "encourages calling Him in supplication after remembering Him, because this will make it more likely that the supplication will be accepted." Praise first, then ask. So the ayah turns to what people actually ask for. Both are asking; only one is really praying.

Again from Sa'id bin Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas (Ibn Kathir): "Some bedouins used to come to the standing area ('Arafat) and supplicate saying, 'O Allah! Make it a rainy year, a fertile year and a year of good child bearing.' They would not mention any of the affairs of the Hereafter." About them the words of ayah 200 were revealed — "Our Lord! Give us (Your bounties) in this world!" — and for such there is no portion in the Hereafter. Ibn Kathir adds that the criticism is placed here "to discourage other people from imitating those mentioned."

Maʿārif catches a detail easy to walk past. The first prayer is *rabbanā ātinā fi'd-dunyā* — "Our Lord, give to us in this world" — with no *hasanah*, no "good," attached. He does not even ask that what he gets be *good*. "They are so drunk with their craze for material things that nothing short of a constant fulfillment of their desires would satisfy them. They just do not bother to check if it is good or bad, procured rightly or wrongly." The one in ayah 201 asks for *hasanah* in this world, *hasanah* in the next, and protection from the Fire. The difference between the two prayers is one word — and it is the whole difference. Maʿārif turns this on the reader: it warns those whose profusion of *waẓāʼif* (litanies) and *nawāfil* (voluntary acts of worship) convinces them they are specially devoted and pious, while "hidden behind this facade is the same love of the mundane life." Everyone, it says, must assess his own deeds, and especially the intention behind them.

## What *hasanah* covers

Ibn Kathir: this du'a "includes all good aspects of this life and seeks refuge from all types of evil." The good of this life covers well-being, spacious dwelling, pleasing mates, sufficient provision, beneficial knowledge, good profession or deeds, comfortable transportation and good praise — and even all of that is only "a part of the good that is sought in this life." The good of the Hereafter is chiefly Paradise, which also means safety from the greatest horror at the gathering place, along with a light reckoning. Safety from the Fire is not only for later: it "includes being directed to what leads to this good end in this world, such as avoiding the prohibitions, sins of all kinds and doubtful matters."

Maʿārif adds *barakah* in lawful livelihood, good character, honour and prestige, strength of faith, guidance into the straight path and perfect sincerity in worship; and for the Hereafter, everything from Paradise with its countless and endless blessings, to the pleasure of Allah Almighty and "the privilege of seeing Him." This du'a, Maʿārif concludes, "is a compendium of all prayers."

## This du'a in the Sunnah

**Al-Bukhari** reported that Anas bin Malik narrated that the Prophet ﷺ used to say: *"O Allah, our Lord! Give us that which is good in this life, that which is good in the Hereafter and save us from the torment of the Fire."*

**Imam Ahmad** reported that Anas said: Allah's Messenger ﷺ visited a Muslim man who had become as weak as a sick small bird. He ﷺ said to him, "Were you asking or supplicating to Allah about something?" He said, "Yes. I used to say: O Allah! Whatever punishment you saved for me in the Hereafter, give it to me in this life." Allah's Messenger ﷺ said: *"All praise is due to Allah! You cannot bear it — or stand it. You should have said: Our Lord! Give us in this world that which is good and in the Hereafter that which is good, and save us from the torment of the Fire!"* The man began reciting this du'a and he was cured. **Muslim** also recorded it.

Notice what that corrects: a prayer that was not greedy but pious, even heroic in intention — and still wrong, because it asked for a burden no human frame can carry. Maʿārif adds that it is *masnūn* — established by the Prophet's ﷺ practice — to make this du'a particularly while performing tawaf.

Maʿārif swings the correction the other way too, at those who imagine real worship means praying only for the next world: a person depends on his worldly needs met not merely for life and sustenance but in order to perform acts of worship and obedience at all, and "the blessed practice of the prophets of Allah has been that they prayed to Allah for the good of both the worlds." What is required is not that one stop asking for this world, but that one refuse to treat material needs as the purpose of life, and show far more concern for what comes after.

## Ayah 202: a share of what they earned

Al-Hakim reported that Sa'id bin Jubayr said: a man came to Ibn 'Abbas and said, "I worked for some people and settled for a part of my compensation in return for their taking me to perform Hajj with them. Is this acceptable?" Ibn 'Abbas answered with this very ayah: "You are among those whom Allah described: *For them there will be allotted a share for what they have earned.*" Al-Hakim commented that this hadith is authentic according to the criteria of the Two Shaykhs (Al-Bukhari and Muslim), although they did not record it. And on "Allah is swift at reckoning," Maʿārif observes that His all-pervading knowledge and most perfect power suffice to assess the lifelong deeds of every person who ever breathed, with none of the computing mechanisms human beings depend on.

## Ayah 203: the appointed days

"And remember Allah during the Appointed Days" — *ayyām maʿdūdāt*, "numbered days."

Ibn 'Abbas said the Appointed Days are the Days of Tashriq (11th, 12th, 13th of Dhul-Hijjah), while the "Known Days" mentioned elsewhere are the first ten days of Dhul-Hijjah. A second report, from Miqsam from Ibn 'Abbas, makes them four: the Day of Sacrifice (10th) and the three days after it — and Ibn Kathir lists a long roll of authorities who held this, among them Ibn 'Umar, Ibn Az-Zubayr, Abu Musa, 'Ata', Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id bin Jubayr, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Az-Zuhri and Malik bin Anas. He notes that the apparent sense of the next clause — "whoever hastens to leave in two days... and whoever stays on" — supports it.

What does the remembrance consist of? 'Ikrimah said it means reciting the *takbir* — *Allāhu akbar, Allāhu akbar* — during the days of Tashriq after the compulsory prayers, and Maʿārif states that in these days the takbir (*Allāhu akbar, Allāhu akbar, lā ilāha illa'llāh, wa'llāhu akbar, Allāhu akbar, wa li'llāhi'l-hamd*) is *wajib*, necessary. Ibn Kathir widens it: the command covers remembering Allah when slaughtering, after the prayers, in supplication generally, and while throwing the pebbles each day of Tashriq. He cites a hadith collected by **Abu Dawud** and several others: *"Tawaf around the House, Sa'i between As-Safa and Al-Marwah and throwing the pebbles were legislated so that Allah is remembered in Dhikr."* That reframes every physical rite of Hajj — the walking, the running, the stones are all scaffolding around dhikr.

**A festival, not an austerity.** **Imam Ahmad** reported that 'Uqbah bin 'Amr said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"The day of 'Arafah, the day of the Sacrifice and the days of the Tashriq are our 'Id (festival) for we people of Islam. These are days of eating and drinking."* **Imam Ahmad** also reported that Nubayshah Al-Hudhali said he ﷺ said: *"The days of Tashriq are days of eating, drinking and Dhikr (remembering) of Allah"* — **Muslim** also recorded this. And **Ibn Jarir** reported from Abu Hurayrah that he ﷺ sent 'Abdullah bin Hudhafah to Mina proclaiming: *"Do not fast these days, for they are days of eating, drinking and remembering Allah the Exalted and Most Honored."* The dhikr commanded here is not the dhikr of hunger and withdrawal; it sits inside food, drink and celebration.

## "No sin on him" — closing an old quarrel

Maʿārif explains why the ayah says it twice. The stay at Mina and the deadline for throwing pebbles at the three Pillars had been a live dispute among the people of Jahiliyyah: one group held that staying through the 13th and stoning the three Pillars was necessary, and anyone returning on the 12th was a sinner; another held the reverse. The ayah corrects both — "no sin" on the one who hurries, "no sin" on the one who stays — "thereby proving that both parties calling each other sinners are involved in excess and error." Ibn Kathir cites the narration of 'Abdur-Rahman bin Ya'mar Ad-Diyli: *"The days of Mina (Tashriq) are three. Those who hasten in two days then there is no sin in it, and those who delay then there is no sin in it."*

The correct position, Maʿārif says, is that the pilgrim has the option of acting on either permission, though it is better and preferable to stay through the third day, the 13th. The jurists add a rule: whoever leaves Mina before sunset on the 12th need not perform the *ramy* (throwing of pebbles) for the third day; but if the sun sets while he is still in Mina, he may not leave until he has done it — with the concession that the third day's ramy may also be done between the post-morning and pre-noon hours.

Even in granting the easier option, the ayah attaches taqwa. Maʿārif reads the whole concession as arranged for the convenience of one who fears Allah and obeys His commands, "for he really deserves the Hajj," citing the Qur'an's own principle, stated elsewhere, that Allah accepts acts of prayer and worship only from those who fear Him and obey Him. A man involved in sins long before Hajj, negligent during it and unchanged after, has validly fulfilled the formal obligation — but his Hajj, Maʿārif says frankly, "is certainly not going to be of any good to him."

## The last line: fear Allah, and know you are being gathered

The eight-verse Hajj unit ends: "And fear Allah, and know that you will surely be gathered unto Him." Ibn Kathir places this at exactly the moment the crowds disperse and everyone starts to return to their areas, and pairs it with "And it is He Who has created you on the earth, and to Him you shall be gathered back" (23:79). The gathering at Mina dissolves; a greater gathering does not.

Maʿārif calls this line "the essence of all Hajj injunctions given in these verses," and reads its taqwa as covering three stretches of time: before the Hajj, during it — guarding against any shortcoming in the prescribed acts — and after it, guarding against "any pride of performance." Once so great an act of worship is behind us, Shaytan generally injects the thought of self-righteousness, "which simply ruins all his deeds." Maʿārif conveys a teaching that one who returns having accomplished his Hajj is so cleansed of his sins as if he was born that day — which is why the warning is needed, since a person newly purified has the most to lose. And whoever returns with his heart free from the love of the world and turned toward the Hereafter, the 'ulama' have said, has his Hajj accepted, his sins forgiven and his prayers answered. Maʿārif presses the point: all over the Hajj, before Allah's House, people pledge their obedience to Him — how can such pledges be thoughtlessly broken afterwards?

Two stories close Maʿārif's comment, from opposite sides. A pious elder said: "When I returned from Hajj, it was by chance that a suggestion of sin crept into my heart, whereupon I heard a voice from the Unseen: *Didn't you perform the Hajj?* This voice became a wall between me and that sin. Allah Almighty protected me." Against that, a disciple of the famous Maulana Jami lost his unusual spiritual state after returning from Hajj. His teacher's diagnosis: before Hajj he had the gift of humbleness and wept before Allah counting himself a sinner; afterwards he grew proud — "therefore, this very Hajj of yours became the cause of your pride."

Which is where the passage lands. It begins by telling the pilgrim to stop celebrating his fathers and start remembering his Lord; it ends by warning him not to start celebrating himself. In between it teaches the prayer that holds both worlds at once — *"Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter and save us from the punishment of Fire."*

*O Allah, give us the ability to do what You love and are pleased with — in word, deed and intention.*

passages.title: The impressive speaker and the self-selling soul
passages.tafsir:
# Two Men, One Phrase: Sūrah al-Baqarah 204–207

**What this passage is about.** Allah holds up two portraits of human beings side by side: a man whose speech dazzles you but whose heart and hands work ruin, and a man who sells his own self seeking the pleasure of Allah. What binds the four ayat into a single unit is a repeated opening — *wa mina'n-nās man*, "and of mankind there is he who…" — used first of the hypocrite in ayah 204 and then of the sincere believer in ayah 207. The same doorway, two completely different rooms.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that this pairing continues the theme just before it. In the preceding verses two kinds of people were described by how they pray: one asks for everything right here in this world, the other asks for the good of both the passing world and the eternal one. Here, says Maʿārif, those same two kinds are named again — the hypocritical and the sincere.

## Who was being described?

The commentators preserve more than one report about the occasion of these ayat, and Ibn Kathir lays them out without forcing them into one.

**As-Suddi** said they were revealed about **Al-Akhnas bin Shariq Ath-Thaqafi**, a man who came to Allah's Messenger ﷺ and announced his Islam while his heart concealed the opposite. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the detail that makes the portrait bite: Akhnas ibn Shurayq was *known for his eloquence*. He would come to the Prophet ﷺ and try to impress him with sworn allegiance to Islam — and no sooner had he walked out of that company than he was busy again with mischief-making against the Muslims.

**Ibn ʿAbbās** narrated that these ayat came down about some of the hypocrites who criticised **Khubayb and his companions**, who were killed during the Rajīʿ incident. Allah then sent down His condemnation of those hypocrites and, in ayah 207, His praise of Khubayb and his companions.

**Qatādah, Mujāhid, ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas** and several others held that the ayat refer to hypocrites and believers in general, not one named individual — and Ibn Kathir says this view *is correct*. A specific occasion does not shrink a verse; it illustrates it.

## "Their tongues are sweeter than honey"

Ibn Jarīr related from al-Qurazī that **Nawf al-Bikālī**, who used to read the previously revealed Books, said he found in them a description of some members of this Ummah: people who use the religion to gain material benefit, whose *tongues are sweeter than honey but whose hearts are more bitter than ṣabir* (a bitter plant, aloe); they show people the appearance of sheep while their hearts hide the viciousness of wolves. The passage he cites continues with Allah's words that such people dare to challenge Him while they are deceived by Him, and His oath by Himself to send upon them a trial that would leave the wise man bewildered. Nawf said he then reflected on these statements and found them in the Qur'an describing the hypocrites — in ayah 204. Ibn Kathir states that this statement by al-Qurazī is *Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ*.

That is the register of this passage: not crude villainy, but *charm*. The danger described here is a man you would be glad to listen to.

## Ayah 204: the words in detail

**"whose speech may please you… in this worldly life."** The pleasing quality of his talk is tethered explicitly to *al-ḥayāt ad-dunyā*, the life of this world. It is speech built for an audience that will not be alive to see the verdict.
