That ayah 217 establishes the prohibition in the four sacred months — Rajab, Dhul-Qaʿdah, Dhul-Hijjah and Muharram — is agreed. It is reinforced by Qur'an 9:36, "four of them are sacred; that is the right religion," and by the Prophet's ﷺ words in his address at the Farewell Hajj naming four sacred months, three consecutive and "Rajab of Mudar."

- **ʿAta ibn Abi Rabah**, a leading early exegete, **declared on oath** that this ruling stands forever, and several of the Tabiʿin (Successors) held it to be un-abrogated.
- **The majority of jurists**, as reported by **al-Jassas**, held that the ruling was abrogated. They differed over what abrogated it: some pointed to Qur'an 9:36 ("fight the disbelievers, all of them"), many to Qur'an 9:5 ("slay the disbelievers wherever you find them"), reading *ḥaythu* as "whenever"; others pointed to the Prophet's ﷺ own conduct, citing the siege of Ta'if and the expedition of Awtas. **Ruh al-Maʿani** and **al-Baydawi** report a consensus of the community on the abrogation.
- **Al-Tafsir al-Mazhari** answers these arguments: the sanctity of the sacred months is stated within Qur'an 9:36 itself — among the last of the fighting verses to be revealed — and the Farewell Hajj address, delivered only about eighty days before the Prophet ﷺ passed away, affirms it. So those verses cannot abrogate it. And the siege of Ta'if fell in Shawwal, not a sacred month.

**The conclusion Maʿārif ul Qurʼān settles on:** what was lifted is the *absolute* prohibition — Muslims may defend themselves or counter-attack if fighting is begun against them in these months, as clarified by "the sacred month for the sacred month" (Qur'an 2:194). **Initiating** a fight in these months remains forbidden forever. Al-Jassas reports from the Companion Jabir ibn ʿAbdullah that the Prophet ﷺ did not fight in any sacred month unless the disbelievers began the fighting.

---

## The warning about turning back

Ayah 217 ends by naming the true catastrophe — not being killed, but abandoning faith: whoever turns back from his religion and dies a disbeliever, his deeds are lost in this life and the Hereafter.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains "lost in this life" through concrete consequences in classical law: the marriage bond dissolves, inheritance from a Muslim relative is forfeited, prayers and fasts performed in the state of Islam are reduced to nothing, and the funeral prayer and burial among Muslims are withheld. "Lost in the Hereafter" means no reward for acts of worship, and Hell without end.

Where the scholars differed, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names them: if such a person returns to Islam, is he obliged to repeat a Hajj already performed, and does the reward for his earlier prayers and fasts return to him? **Imam Abu Hanifah** held that the Hajj must be repeated and did not hold that the earlier prayers and fasts are rewarded; **Imam ash-Shafiʿi** differed on both points. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also cites the difference with one who was never a Muslim: his good deeds are held in abeyance, and if he accepts Islam he receives their reward — the meaning, it says, of the report that one enters Islam "with all the good deeds performed earlier." (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān further records the classical juristic penalties for apostasy — execution for an unrepentant man, life imprisonment for a woman — on the reasoning that such conduct is an assault on the religion's standing.)

Set beside the Nakhlah story, the placement is pointed: the men of Nakhlah made a serious mistake and were corrected, and this ayah shows what a mistake is *not*. Erring within faith and walking out of it are not the same thing.

---

## Ayah 218: the door of hope

The men of ʿAbdullah bin Jahsh, once the revelation lifted their dread, came with a further hope. Ibn Ishaq records their words to the Prophet ﷺ: *"O Messenger of Allah! We wish that this incident be considered a battle for us, so that we gain the rewards of the Mujahidin."* And Allah revealed ayah 218 — those who believed, who emigrated, and who strove in the way of Allah "hope for Allah's mercy; and Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful." Ibn Kathir: "Allah has greatly elevated their hopes of gaining what they had wished for."

Read the ayah's own wording closely. It does not say they have *earned* mercy; it says **they hope for it** — even these men, believers, emigrants, strivers, with a marked expedition behind them. Effort at its highest still ends standing at the door of mercy, not walking past it. And the two names Allah closes on — *Ghafūr* (Oft-Forgiving) and *Raḥīm* (Most Merciful) — are exactly the two the situation called for: forgiveness for what went wrong at Nakhlah, and mercy for the men who bore it.

---

## Living it

- **When Allah's command cuts against your instinct, suspect your instinct before you suspect the command.** That is the plain instruction of ayah 216, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān grounds it not in piety alone but in evidence: your own life is full of goods you avoided and harms you pursued.
- **Aversion is not disobedience.** The ayah says outright that the believers disliked this. Allah legislated anyway — and did not rebuke them for the feeling. Serve the command; you are not required to enjoy it first.
- **Zeal without instruction is a liability.** The men at Nakhlah were sincere, obedient and brave, and they still overstepped what they had been sent to do. Their initial hesitation was the sounder instinct.
- **The one who stays behind still has a duty.** Az-Zuhri's words, quoted by Ibn Kathir, leave nobody outside the circle: support, aid, readiness — and, at minimum, that the matter genuinely lives in your heart.
- **Be alert to sanctity invoked selectively.** Ayah 217 concedes the objection's substance and then sets it against the objectors' own record. Truth is served by weighing the whole scale, not one pan of it.
- **A serious mistake is not the end.** Ayah 218 came down for the very men who had caused the crisis. The end of the road for them was hope in Allah's mercy — and Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

passages.title: Wine, gambling, spending, and orphans' property
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These two ayat belong to a run of questions the Companions put to the Prophet ﷺ, each introduced by *"They ask you…"* and each answered by revelation. Three questions come together here: what to make of wine and gambling, how much of one's wealth to give away, and how to handle the property of orphans in one's care. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this verse "forms part of the series of questions asked by the noble Companions."

What holds them together is that all three are about **wealth and the self** — what a believer takes in, what he gives out, and what he holds in trust for someone weaker than himself. And all three are answered the same way: not with a bare rule, but with a weighing. Weigh the harm against the benefit. Weigh your own need against your generosity. Weigh the orphan's welfare against your convenience. Then, at the hinge between the two ayat, comes the instruction that governs all of it — *"so that you may reflect, upon this world and the Hereafter."*

---

## The question that started it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān tells the story behind ayah 219. When Islam came, drinking was ordinary practice, part of the general state of Jāhilī custom, and when the Prophet ﷺ emigrated to Madinah he found its people accustomed to wine and gambling too. People were attached to them because the benefits were obvious and the harms were not.

But some Companions began to feel uneasy. Sayyidunā ʿUmar al-Fārūq and Muʿādh ibn Jabal, along with some of the Anṣār, came to the Prophet ﷺ and told him plainly how wine and gambling not only spoil a man's reason but drain his wealth, and they asked his guidance. **Ayah 219 was revealed in answer to their question.**

Note what kind of answer they received. Ibn Kathir observes that this ayah "was the beginning of the process of prohibiting Khamr, not explicitly, but it only implied this meaning." Ibn ʿUmar, Ash-Shaʿbī, Mujāhid, Qatādah, Ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Aslam all stated that this was **the first ayah revealed about wine**.

## The great sin and the small benefits

*"In them is a great sin, and some benefits for men, but the sin of them is greater than their benefit."*

Ibn Kathir explains the balance precisely. The harm of wine and gambling strikes at the **religion**; their benefit is merely **material** — bodily effects, the pleasant sensation, the money made from selling wine, and in gambling, winnings a man might spend on his family. These are real. The Qur'an does not pretend otherwise. But, says Ibn Kathir, "these benefits are outweighed by the clear harm that they cause which affects the mind and the religion."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the key word. **Ithm** — sin — here "includes everything that may become a preliminary to sin." Wine dulls the senses and weakens reason, and reason is what acts as a brake on human indulgence. "Once reason is blocked out, the door is opened for all sorts of evil deeds." The sin is not only in the cup; it is in everything the cup makes possible.

**Two legal principles** are drawn from this weighing in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān:

1. **The presence of some benefit does not stop a thing from being ḥarām.** Nothing in this world is utterly without benefit — poison, the snake, the scorpion all have uses. Theft, fraud and adultery are not chosen by anyone unless some gain is perceived in them. A thing is judged by whether its harm outweighs its good.
2. **Removing harm takes precedence over gaining benefit.** Where a benefit comes with harm attached, the benefit is let go in order to be safe from the harm.

## Why the prohibition came in stages

This is one of the most instructive things in the passage, and both commentaries dwell on it.

**Stage one** is our ayah: wine is named as sin-prone and corrupting, and left there. Not forbidden — but, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, "a manner of saying that the habit of drinking is worth leaving." Some Companions took the counsel immediately and stopped then and there. Others reasoned that wine had not actually been declared unlawful, only identified as a cause of sin — so if they could keep clear of the sin, why stop?

Then ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf invited some Companions to dinner. Wine was served as usual. Maghrib came, they stood for prayer, and the man leading them — drunk — recited Sūrah al-Kāfirūn wrong.

**Stage two** followed: *"O you who believe, do not go near the prayer while you are intoxicated"* (4:43). Ibn Kathir adds that after this, when the prayer was called, a man would announce on behalf of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "No drunk person should attend the prayer." Some Companions had already concluded that whatever stops a man from ṣalāh can hold no good at all. Others kept to drinking outside prayer hours.

Then ʿItbān ibn Mālik hosted a gathering that included Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ. After dinner and wine, the party turned to poetry and boasting. Saʿd recited a qaṣīdah satirising the Anṣār and praising his own tribe. An Anṣārī youth, enraged, struck him with a camel's jaw-bone and badly injured his head. Saʿd came to the Prophet ﷺ to complain, and the Prophet ﷺ raised his hands and prayed: *"O Allah, give us a clear and conclusive guidance in the matter of wine."*

**Stage three and four** came in Sūrah al-Māʾidah, declaring wine and gambling an abomination of Shayṭān's handiwork to be shunned utterly (5:90–91).

Ibn Kathir preserves this same history from ʿUmar's side, in a narration Imam Ahmad recorded from Abū Maysarah, also collected by Abū Dāwūd, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʾī, and which ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī and at-Tirmidhī said has a sound and authentic chain. After each stage, ʿUmar kept praying, "O Allah! Give us a clear ruling regarding al-Khamr" — until the ayah of al-Māʾidah was recited to him and he reached *"So will you not then abstain?"* Then he said: **"We did abstain, we did abstain."**

**Why so gradual?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers with a principle from the Qur'an itself: *"Allah does not obligate anyone beyond his or her capacity"* (2:286). Scholars have said it is harder to break a man of an ingrained habit than to wean an infant from the breast. So Islam first stressed the evil, then closed off the hours of prayer, and only then forbade it outright.

But the same wisdom that required patience before the ruling required force after it. Ibn Kathir records ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb's definition of khamr: **"It includes all what intoxicates the mind."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that the Prophet ﷺ warned that wine is the source of evils and indecencies, and that one who indulges in it may go on to the worst of sins. In a hadith he said, *"Wine and faith cannot be combined"* — these narrations appear in **al-Nasāʾī**. And in the **Jāmiʿ of at-Tirmidhī** there is a narration from Anas that the Prophet ﷺ cursed ten people in relation to wine: the one who presses it, the one who distils it, the one who drinks it, the one who serves it, the one who carries it, the one it is carried to, the seller, the buyer, the one who gives it as a gift, and the one who consumes its income.

## The obedience that followed

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lingers on what happened when the crier went through the streets of Madinah. ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar reported that whoever had a vessel of wine in his hand threw it away where he stood; whoever had cups or flasks at home brought them out and smashed them. Anas was serving wine to a gathering that included Abū Ṭalḥah, Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Suhayl; when the announcement reached their ears they said, "Now pour all this out and break the cups." Some narrations say a man with the cup at his lips flung it down. Wine ran through the streets of Madinah like rainwater — and long afterwards, rain would still draw its smell and colour up out of the ground.

The Prophet ﷺ went himself to where the commercial stock had been deposited and slit many of the leather wine-bags with his own blessed hands. And one Companion, a merchant, had taken his entire capital to Syria and returned with a cargo of wine, only to learn at the city limits that it had been forbidden. He stacked it on a hillside, came and asked what he should do, was told to tear the bags open — and poured his whole fortune into the sand without hesitating.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets this against the failed attempt at prohibition in the United States, backed by experts, media, law and a constitutional amendment. The difference, it says, is that **Islam never relied on law alone.** The Makkan years were spent forming people through worship, restraint, and a living concern for the life to come; the law came after the men were made. "No doubt, the Americans too did their best… but they had everything with them except the concern for the life to come."

## Maysir — and why it is wider than you think

**Maysir** is a verbal noun meaning, lexically, *to distribute*; one who distributes is a *yāsir*. The name came from a Jāhilī game: a camel was slaughtered and shares of the meat gambled over, some men taking more than one share and some none, with the man left out paying for the whole animal. The meat itself went to the poor — so the game passed for generosity, and a man who refused to join was called a miser.

Some scholars derive the word instead from *yusr*, **ease** — because through gambling one takes another's property easily, without labour.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that all the Companions and the Successors held unanimously that maysir covers **every form of qimār**, and all of it is ḥarām. Ibn Kathir and al-Jaṣṣāṣ in *Aḥkām al-Qurʼān* report from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, Qatādah, Muʿāwiyah ibn Ṣāliḥ, ʿAṭāʾ and Ṭāwūs that qimār of every kind is maysir — "even the games of children with dice and walnuts." Ibn ʿAbbās said *mukhāṭarah* — putting something at stake — falls under qimār. Ibn Sirīn said, "That which involves stakes is included in maysir."

The technical definition given (from *Shāmī*) is a deal in which ownership of something of value hangs on a contingency whose two sides are equal — an equal chance of taking everything or losing everything. That, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, sweeps in modern lotteries, prize crossword competitions where entrants pay a fee, and money staked on cards, chess or backgammon.

**The crucial exception:** if a prize is offered by one side only, to whoever performs a certain feat, and no fee is taken from the competitor, this is not qimār. The reason is exact — the deal does not hang between gain and loss, but between gain and no gain.

In **Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim** there is a report from Buraydah that the Prophet ﷺ said one who plays backgammon is like one who dyes his hands in the flesh and blood of swine. ʿAlī said chess is included in maysir; ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar said chess is worse than backgammon (Tafsīr Ibn Kathir).

**Why gambling is worse than it looks:** in gambling, one man's gain is precisely another's loss. Nothing is produced; wealth is not increased, only siphoned. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it starkly — a man who ought to be a source of good for others "starts seeing his life in the death of his brother, and finding delight in his distress." Contrast trade, where both buyer and seller profit and wealth circulates. And the addicted gambler loses even the habit of earning, because he is always dreaming of taking what belongs to another with no work at all. On the modern scale, small losses spread invisibly across a whole population while a few conspicuous winners hide the fact that a nation's wealth is draining into very few hands. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the Islamic economic principle bluntly: any deal that siphons the wealth of a whole community into the coffers of a few capitalists is ḥarām — and it grounds this in the Qur'an's own principle for the distribution of wealth, explaining that the Qur'anic rule for sharing out the spoils of war among the different segments of society exists precisely so that wealth does not shrink and concentrate in the hands of a few.

One further note from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: gambling was permissible in the early period, and when the Qur'an foretold the Byzantines' return to victory (Sūrah al-Rūm), Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq staked a wager with the deniers of Makkah. When the prophecy came true he collected and brought it to the Prophet ﷺ, who was pleased — but told him to give the money away in charity. Allah kept His Messenger ﷺ clear of what was lawful then but would be unlawful later, and some Companions were likewise protected. A narration in *Rūḥ al-Bayān* mentions Jaʿfar aṭ-Ṭayyār, whom Jibrīl said Allah loved for four traits; Jaʿfar explained: he never went near wine, because he saw it ruins reason; never worshipped idols, seeing they neither harm nor help; never committed adultery, out of protectiveness over his own women; and never lied even in Jāhiliyyah, seeing lying to be sheer disgrace.

---

## "What should we spend?" — *al-ʿafw*

The second question in ayah 219 is answered with a single word: **al-ʿafw**, the surplus, what is spare beyond your need.

Ibn Kathir reports through al-Ḥakam from Miqsam from **Ibn ʿAbbās** that it means "whatever you can spare above the needs of your family" — the same view held by Ibn ʿUmar, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Qāsim, Sālim, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the practical sense: give in a way that neither wrecks your own worldly situation nor tramples someone else's rightful claim on you — because that claim will be asked about in the life to come.

**Ibn Jarīr** relates from Abū Hurayrah that a man said, "O Messenger of Allah, I have a dinar." He ﷺ said, *"Spend it on yourself."* — "I have another." — *"Spend it on your wife."* — "I have another." — *"Spend it on your child."* — "I have another." — *"You know best."* Ibn Kathir notes that **Muslim** also recorded this in his *Ṣaḥīḥ*.

**Muslim** records from Jābir that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to a man: *"Start with yourself and give it charity. If anything remains, then your family. If anything remains, then your relatives. If anything remains, then like this and like that."*

Ibn Kathir also cites a hadith — without naming its collection — that whoever gives away his surplus, it is better for him; whoever withholds it, it is worse for him; and a man is not blamed for keeping what is barely sufficient.

The order is worth absorbing. Charity in Islam does not begin with the stranger and work inward. It begins in your own house and moves outward as the surplus allows. The generous man is not the one who impoverishes his dependants to be seen giving.

## The hinge: "so that you may reflect — upon this world and the Hereafter"

This clause closes ayah 219 and spills into ayah 220. Ibn Kathir explains it as Allah's way of saying that just as He has made these commands plain, so He makes plain the rest of His signs, His promises and His warnings — so that you might think about this life and the next together. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reports that **Ibn ʿAbbās** commented that the reflection intended is "about the imminent demise and the brevity of this life, and the imminent commencement of the Hereafter and its continuity."

That is the lens the whole passage asks for. Wine's pleasure is short; gambling's windfall is short; the wealth you hoard is short. Measure them against something that does not end.

## The orphans — mercy in place of hardship

The third question, in ayah 220, has one of the most touching backgrounds in the Qur'an.

Ibn Jarīr reports from **Ibn ʿAbbās** that when *"Come not near the orphan's property except in the way that is best"* (6:152) and *"Those who unjustly consume the property of orphans consume only fire into their bellies"* (4:10) were revealed, the guardians took fright. They separated the orphan's food and drink entirely from their own. Whatever the child left over they set aside untouched until he ate it or it spoiled. The arrangement was miserable for them — and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out, a loss to the orphans too, since food was simply going to waste and the guardians had no right to give it away either. They brought the difficulty to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and this ayah came. So they joined their food and drink with the orphans' again. Ibn Kathir notes this was also collected by **Abū Dāwūd**, **an-Nasāʾī**, and **al-Ḥākim** in his *Mustadrak*, and that Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, ash-Shaʿbī, Ibn Abī Laylā, Qatādah and others among the Salaf reported the occasion similarly. Ibn Jarīr also reports ʿĀʾishah saying, "I dislike that an orphan's money be under my care, unless I mix my food with his food and my drink with his drink."

The answer has three moves:

**"Setting their affairs right is best."** Ibn Kathir reads *iṣlāḥ* as the standing obligation — improving the orphan's condition and property is required in any case. That is the baseline, not the concession.

**"And if you mix your affairs with theirs, then they are your brothers."** There is no harm in joining households, says Ibn Kathir, "since they are your brothers in the religion." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the plain logic: the orphans' welfare is *better* served by a joint arrangement, and brothers share. The word chosen is not "wards" or "dependants" — it is *ikhwān*, brothers.

**"And Allah knows the one who corrupts from the one who sets right."** The permission is not a loophole, because it turns entirely on intention, and intention is precisely what Allah sees. Ibn Kathir: "He knows those whose intent is to cause mischief or righteousness." A guardian who mixes accounts to feed a child is doing one thing; a guardian who mixes accounts to quietly absorb an inheritance is doing another. The two look identical from outside. They are not identical to Allah.

**"Had Allah willed, He could have put you in difficulty. Indeed Allah is Almighty, All-Wise."** Ibn Kathir: if Allah had willed, He would have made this matter hard for you — "but He made it easy for you." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pairs the two names deliberately: He *could* have imposed a harder code, because He is All-Powerful; He gave an easier one, because He is All-Wise and does not burden people with what they cannot bear. The two divine names are not decoration at the end of the ayah — they are the explanation of it.

Ibn Kathir closes with the ruling this permits: the executor of an orphan's estate may spend from it in reasonable proportions, on condition that he intends to repay the orphan later when he is able.

---

## Living it

- **On wine and gambling:** the ruling settled long ago, but the *reasoning* here is still the tool a believer uses on new cases. Ask of any modern form — is the transaction hanging between total gain and total loss with nothing produced? Then it is maysir under a new name, whether it is called a lottery, a prize competition with an entry fee, or something more sophisticated. Ask of any pleasure — does its harm to mind and dīn outweigh what it gives? Then the benefit is let go.
- **On giving:** start with yourself, then your spouse, then your children, then your relatives, then outward — and give from the surplus, not from what your household needs.
- **On the vulnerable in your care:** aim at *what is genuinely best for them*, not at what makes you feel safest from blame. The Companions' over-caution was sincere and still wrong, because it harmed the very children it meant to protect. Allah's answer was to relax the rule and put the weight on the heart instead: mix freely, treat them as brothers — and remember that He distinguishes the one who repairs from the one who ruins, however the books are kept.

passages.title: Marriage with those who associate partners
passages.tafsir:
Ayah 221 sets a boundary around the most intimate bond a person enters in this life: marriage. It forbids the believers from marrying those who associate partners with Allah — in both directions, men and women — and then explains the reason in a single stroke: one road leads to the Fire, the other to Paradise and forgiveness. What holds the ayah together is that it is not merely a rule about who may marry whom; it is a re-education of the heart about what makes a person worth marrying.

## Two prohibitions, not one

Read the ayah slowly and you will notice it says the same thing twice, but from two different sides.

The first half: "And do not marry Al-Mushrikat (idolatresses) till they believe." Ibn Kathir states the ruling plainly: Allah prohibited the believers from marrying Mushrik women who worship idols.

The second half, in the rendering our sources use: "And give not (your daughters) in marriage to Al-Mushrikin till they believe." Ibn Kathir explains its meaning simply: "do not marry Mushrik men to believing women."

He links this second prohibition to Allah's words: "They are not lawful (wives) for them, nor are they lawful (husbands) for them" (60:10) — a two-way severance, stated with complete clarity.

Between the two prohibitions, and again after the second, comes the same refrain in mirrored form: a believing slave woman is better than a free idolatress "even though she pleases you," and a believing servant is better than a free idolater "even though he pleases you." The repetition is deliberate. Whatever the reader was about to plead in exception — but she is beautiful, but he is wealthy — the ayah has already answered before the objection is spoken.

## Who exactly is a mushrikah?

Taken at face value, Ibn Kathir notes, the word Mushrikat is general: it would cover every Mushrik woman, whether from among the idol worshippers or the People of the Scripture. But Allah excluded the People of the Scripture from this ruling, in Surat al-Ma'idah:

> "(Lawful to you in marriage) are chaste women from those who were given the Scripture (Jews and Christians) before your time when you have given their due dowry, desiring chastity … not committing illegal sexual intercourse." (5:5)

Ali bin Abu Talhah said that **Ibn 'Abbas** said of this ayah: "Allah has excluded the women of the People of the Scripture." Ibn Kathir lists a roll-call of early authorities who explained it the same way — **Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id bin Jubayr, Makhul, Al-Hasan, Ad-Dahhak, Zayd bin Aslam, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas** and others.

A second group of scholars took a different route to the same destination: the ayah, they said, is exclusively about idol worshippers and not the People of the Scripture at all — so no exception is needed. Ibn Kathir observes that this meaning is similar to the first, and closes with the scholar's formula: "Allah knows best."

Ma'arif ul Qur'an lays out the same two readings and draws the practical conclusion: if mushrik here means non-Muslims as a whole, then the women of the People of the Book must be exempted because of 5:5; if it means specifically those non-Muslims who are not of the People of the Book — those who believe in no prophet and no scripture — the verse needs no exception at all, since such people were never included.

**Why the difference?** Ma'arif ul Qur'an answers plainly. Islamic belief is tri-polar: Tawhid (the Oneness of Allah), Akhirah (the Hereafter) and Risalah (prophethood). In their original faith, Jews and Christians agree with Muslims about the Hereafter, and in their original faith it is likewise kufr (infidelity) to attribute partners to Allah — that Christians, in their love and over-enthusiasm in honouring Sayyidna 'Isa (peace be upon him), entered the borders of shirk is another matter. The basic difference that remains is that they do not believe in Muhammad ﷺ as Allah's Messenger — and in Islam that belief is cardinal; without it no one can become a true Muslim. Still, their difference is lesser and lighter than that of other non-Muslim groups, and so, says Ma'arif ul Qur'an, the danger of corruptibility is not that great.

## Permitted is not the same as recommended

Here the sources are unusually candid, and the point is easy to miss.

Ibn Kathir reports from Abu Ja'far bin Jarir (At-Tabari) that there is Ijma' — scholarly consensus — that marrying women from the People of the Scripture is allowed. And yet At-Tabari immediately adds that **'Umar** disliked this practice, "so that the Muslims do not refrain from marrying Muslim women, or for similar reasons."

The story that follows makes it vivid. An authentic chain of narrators, says Ibn Kathir, states that Shaqiq said: Hudhayfah married a Jewish woman, and 'Umar wrote to him: **"Divorce her."** Hudhayfah wrote back: "Do you claim that she is not allowed for me so that I divorce her?" 'Umar replied: **"No. But, I fear that you might marry the whores from among them."** Notice what 'Umar did not say. He did not claim the marriage was unlawful. His concern was the practical drift that follows when a permission becomes a habit.

Ibn Jarir also related that Zayd bin Wahb said that 'Umar bin Khattab said: **"The Muslim man marries the Christian woman, but the Christian man does not marry the Muslim woman."** Ibn Kathir notes this report has a stronger, authentic chain of narrators than the previous one. In one sentence 'Umar states the asymmetry the ayah builds in.

Ibn Abu Hatim said that **Ibn 'Umar** disliked marrying the women from the People of the Scripture, relying on his own explanation of this very ayah. Al-Bukhari also reported that Ibn 'Umar said: **"I do not know of a bigger Shirk than her saying that Jesus is her Lord!"**

Ma'arif ul Qur'an draws the same line from a different angle. The permission for a Muslim man to marry a Jewish or Christian woman under a formal nikah (marriage contract) means simply that such a marriage, if made, will be valid and the children born of it legitimate. It does not mean it is viewed with favour. The Prophet ﷺ taught that a Muslim should seek to marry a woman who fully observes Islamic faith and conduct — so that she becomes for him a source of strength in their joint pursuit of their faith, and their children may have the opportunity to grow up under their care as practising Muslims. (Ma'arif ul Qur'an conveys this teaching without naming a collection, so it is passed on here as it stands.) And when marriage with a non-practising Muslim woman was not looked at with favour, Ma'arif ul Qur'an asks, how would it become favourable in the case of a non-Muslim woman? This is why Sayyidna 'Umar al-Faruq, on learning that such marriages were finding alarming currency in Iraq and Syria, stopped them with an executive order which pointed out that such marital relations cause corruption in Muslim families both religiously and politically (Kitab al-Athar li'l-Imam Muhammad).

## The reasoning behind the ruling

Ma'arif ul Qur'an explains why the Qur'an closes this door. Marital relations demand mutual love and harmony; without these the real purpose behind the relationship remains unrealised. But when such close relations of love and affection are established with those committed to shirk, the inevitable effect is one of two things: Muslims may emotionally tilt towards kufr (disbelief) and shirk, or — in a lesser degree, and more insidiously — the very abhorrence of kufr and shirk may simply not remain there in their hearts. That erosion is what the ayah is guarding against, and it ends, says Ma'arif ul Qur'an, in Hell.

**Why then may a Muslim man marry a woman of the People of the Book while a Muslim woman may not marry a man of the People of the Book?** Ma'arif ul Qur'an answers that the two situations are not parallel: the husband has been given a controlling and care-taking role, so the likelihood of a wife being impressed by his beliefs and views is not that remote. A Muslim woman married to a non-Muslim Kitabi therefore stands in real danger of her belief being spoiled; a Kitabi woman married to a Muslim man is unlikely, in principle, to impress her ideas on her husband — and if a man takes the converse position in total disregard of the normal principles and falls prey to his wife's instigation, it will be because of his own fault.

**And what about the hope that the non-Muslim spouse might embrace Islam?** Ma'arif ul Qur'an takes the objection seriously: marital influence runs both ways, so why not let the possibility of guidance offset the risk of ruin? The answer is a principle worth carrying: where the danger of a harm and the hope of a benefit are equally applicable, the reasonable attitude is to pay more attention to preventing harm than to seeking benefit. A well-known Persian saying is quoted — a wise man does not eat the antidote with certainty and the poison with doubt. So the hope of the non-Muslim spouse embracing Islam is set aside, and the apprehension of the Muslim spouse being impressed by an anti-Islamic faith or behaviour is the thing actually taken care of.

## "Better than … even though she pleases you"

This is the moral centre of the ayah. Allah does not merely forbid; He re-ranks the world.

A believing slave woman — at the very bottom of the social ladder as the first listeners knew it — is declared **better** than a free idolatress, however much she pleases you. And Ibn Kathir spells out the mirror image: this ayah indicates that a believing man, even an Abyssinian servant, is better than a Mushrik man, even if he was a rich master.

Set that against everything a marriage negotiation usually weighs — lineage, freedom, wealth, standing, beauty — and the ayah overturns the table. Faith is not one item on the checklist. It is the scale the checklist sits on.

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir brings this home with a hadith recorded in the Two Sahihs, narrated by Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "A woman is chosen for marriage for four reasons: her wealth, social status, beauty, and religion. So, marry the religious woman, may your hands be filled with sand."

The closing phrase is an idiom of urging, not a curse — Ibn Kathir glosses it as "a statement of encouragement." The hadith does not pretend the other three factors do not exist or do not matter; it names them honestly and then tells you which one to close your hand around. Ibn Kathir adds that Muslim reported this hadith from Jabir as well.

Muslim also reported that Ibn 'Amr said that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said:

> "The life of this world is but a delight, and the best of the delights of this earthly life is the righteous wife."

Notice what is named as the best of this world's delights. Not property, not position — a righteous spouse.

## "Those invite you to the Fire"

Then comes the reason, stated as a contrast so stark it needs no argument.

Ibn Kathir explains "Those (Al-Mushrikun) invite you to the Fire": associating and mingling with the disbelievers makes one love this life and prefer it over the Hereafter, leading to the severest repercussions. Note the mechanism — nobody issues a formal invitation to Hell. The invitation works through closeness, through daily company, through slowly coming to want what they want.

Against this: "but Allah invites (you) to Paradise and forgiveness by His leave." Ibn Kathir explains "by His leave" as meaning by His Law, commandments and prohibitions. The very rule that feels restrictive in ayah 221 is itself the invitation. And notice the order of the two gifts — Paradise and forgiveness. The One calling you is also the One who covers over what you have already done wrong.

The ayah ends: "and makes His Ayat clear to mankind that they may remember." The clarity is Allah's doing; the remembering is ours.

## Living it

**Judge a proposal by faith first.** The ayah does not ask you to pretend that wealth, status and beauty are invisible — the hadith of the four reasons names them out loud. It asks you to let religion decide.

**Guardians carry a share of this.** Ma'arif ul Qur'an, in the notes it carries from Maulana Ashraf Thanavi's Bayan al-Qur'an, makes it obligatory on a girl's guardians to first investigate the beliefs of a proposer before they accept the proposal — because a man may be Muslim in outward status while his beliefs are identical with those of a non-Muslim. Thanavi further states that should such corruption of belief occur after the marriage, the nikah breaks of itself.

**Labels are not beliefs.** Both Ma'arif ul Qur'an and Thanavi press the point that many counted as Jews or Christians in census records may, on scrutiny, believe neither in Sayyidna 'Isa (peace be upon him) nor the Bible, neither in Sayyidna Musa (peace be upon him) nor the Torah — not even in Allah or a Day of Judgment. Such people, they conclude, do not come under the purview of the Qur'anic permission of 5:5 at all, and marriage with their women is unlawful like that with other non-Muslims. Those who marry women from the West without first finding out what is involved, Thanavi says bluntly, make a gross mistake.

**Watch what closeness does to you.** The danger Ma'arif ul Qur'an identifies is not only outright involvement in kufr; it is the quieter loss — waking one day to find that the abhorrence of shirk simply no longer remains in the heart. That warning outlives the specific ruling and bears on every intimacy a believer forms.

passages.title: Menstruation and conjugal relations
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat answer a question the Companions actually brought to the Prophet ﷺ: how should a husband treat his wife during her monthly period, and what is lawful between spouses afterwards? What holds them together is a single method — Allah removes a harmful custom, sets one precise boundary, and then leaves the rest of the marriage open, closing with a reminder that even this most private part of life is lived under His gaze.

## The question behind the revelation

Imam Ahmad recorded that Anas said the Jews used to avoid their menstruating women: they would not eat with them, or even mingle with them in the house. The Companions of the Prophet ﷺ asked about this matter, and Allah revealed ayah 222.

The answer is remarkable for where it puts its emphasis. Allah's reply names the condition, not the woman: **"Say: 'That is an Adhā'"** — the tafsir before us leaves this Arabic word as it stands rather than translating it — **"therefore, keep away from women during menses and go not in unto them till they are purified."** And the Prophet ﷺ made the scope of "keep away" unmistakable:

> "Do everything you wish, except having sexual intercourse."

When the Jews were told about the Prophet's statement, they said, "What is the matter with this man? He would not hear of any of our practices, but would defy it." Then Usayd bin Ḥuḍayr and ʿAbbād bin Bishr came and said, "O Messenger of Allah! The Jews said this and that — should we have sex with our women (meaning, during the menstruation period)?" The face of Allah's Messenger ﷺ changed colour, until the Companions thought that he was angry with them, and they left. Soon after, some milk was brought to him as a gift, and he sent some of it for them to drink. They knew then that Allah's Messenger ﷺ was not angry with them. Muslim also reported this hadith.

The narration reports the sequence and nothing more, and the sequence is instructive on its own: a revealed boundary is not something to be renegotiated in reaction to what others say about it — the change in his blessed face says that much. And the cup of milk sent after them shows how a teacher can register displeasure without leaving a wound.

## What "keep away" actually means

Ibn Kathīr explains **"fa'tazilū al-nisā' fī al-maḥīḍ"** ("keep away from women during menses") as meaning: avoid the sexual organ. That is the whole of it, and he cites the Prophet's ﷺ words again — "Do anything you wish except having sexual intercourse." This is why, he says, most of the scholars said that it is allowed to fondle the wife, except for having sexual intercourse while she is having her menses.

The sources fill this out with a picture of an ordinary, warm household:

- Abū Dāwūd reported, through ʿIkrimah, from one of the Prophet's wives, that whenever the Prophet ﷺ wanted to fondle one of his wives during her menses, he would cover her sexual organ with something.
- Abū Jaʿfar bin Jarīr related that Masrūq went to ʿĀ'ishah and greeted her, and she greeted him in return. Masrūq said, "I wish to ask you about a matter, but I am shy." She replied, "I am your mother and you are my son." He asked what a man may enjoy of his wife when she is having her menses. She said, "Everything except her sexual organ." This is also the opinion of Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and ʿIkrimah.
- ʿĀ'ishah said, "Allah's Messenger ﷺ used to ask me to wash his hair while I was having the menses. He would lay on my lap and read the Qur'an while I was having the period." And it is reported in the Ṣaḥīḥ that she said, "While having the menses, I used to eat from a piece of meat and give it to the Prophet ﷺ, who would eat from the same place I ate from. I used to have sips of a drink and would then give the cup to the Prophet ﷺ, who would place his mouth where I placed my mouth."
- It is reported in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs that Maymūnah bint al-Ḥārith al-Hilāliyyah said that whenever the Prophet ﷺ wanted to fondle any of his wives during the menses, he used to ask her to wear an *izār* (a sheet covering the lower half of the body); these are al-Bukhārī's wordings, and similar is reported from ʿĀ'ishah.
- Imam Ahmad, Abū Dāwūd, at-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah reported that ʿAbdullāh bin Saʿd al-Anṣārī asked Allah's Messenger ﷺ, "What am I allowed of my wife while she is having her menses?" He said, "What is above the *izār*."

Read together, the picture is the opposite of exile. Ibn Kathīr states it plainly: one is allowed to sleep next to his wife and to eat with her during her menses. The Prophet ﷺ laying his head on her lap and reciting the Qur'an while she menstruated; drinking from her cup at the very spot her lips had touched — this is a man refusing to let a bodily state put distance between two hearts. Only one act is withheld, and even that is withheld under the single word the ayah gives it: *Adhā*.

## Two purities: "until they are pure" and "when they have purified themselves"

Ayah 222 uses two different expressions, and the difference carries a ruling.

**"Wa lā taqrabūhunna ḥattā yaṭhurna"** — "and go not in unto them till they are purified." Ibn Kathīr says this clause explains the earlier command to keep away from women during menses.

Then: **"Fa idhā taṭahharna fa'tūhunna"** — "and when they have purified themselves, then go in unto them." Ibn ʿAbbās distinguished the two precisely: *ḥattā yaṭhurna* means until they are pure **from blood**, and *fa idhā taṭahharna* means **with water**. This is also the tafsir of Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan, Muqātil bin Ḥayyān and al-Layth bin Saʿd, among others.

So the bleeding stopping is not by itself the end of the matter. Ibn Kathīr states that the scholars agree the woman is obliged to take a bath — or to perform *tayammum* with sand if she is unable to use water — before intercourse with her husband becomes lawful again after the monthly period ends.

And note the direction of the sentence: the prohibition is temporary and clearly fenced. Ibn Kathīr draws the plain inference — Allah prohibited intercourse with the wife during menstruation, indicating that intercourse is allowed otherwise.

## "As Allah has ordained for you"

The phrase **"min ḥaythu amarakum Allāh"** ("as Allah has ordained for you") was read in two ways by the early authorities, and Ibn Kathīr reports both:

- Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and other scholars stated that it refers to **the place** — *al-farj*, the vagina — and from this Ibn Kathīr concludes that anal sex is prohibited, a point he says he will emphasise further.
- Abū Razīn, ʿIkrimah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and others said it refers to **the time** — that is, when they are pure, and not during the menses.

Both readings serve the passage: the first anchors the ruling that ayah 223 will develop, the second reinforces the boundary just laid down.

## Allah loves those who turn back, and those who keep themselves pure

Ayah 222 closes on love, not on threat: **"Truly, Allah loves those who turn unto Him in repentance and loves those who purify themselves."**

Ibn Kathīr comments that "those who turn unto Him in repentance" means from the sin **even if it was repeated** — a mercy worth pausing over for anyone who has fallen into the same failing more than once. And "those who purify themselves" he explains as those who purify themselves from the impurity and the filth that include having intercourse with the wife during the menses, and anal sex.

Maʿārif ul Qur'ān reads the ending the same way, as a practical provision: the basic purpose of these verses is to declare the prohibition of intercourse with a woman in a state of menstruation, and if someone committed it in such a state either unknowingly or carelessly, he has to make *tawbah* — repentance. It is in exactly this context, it says, that the verse states that Allah loves those who are most repenting.

## Ayah 223: "Your wives are a tilth for you"

Ayah 223 answers a second question, and it too has a story behind it.

Al-Bukhārī recorded that Ibn al-Munkadir said he heard Jābir say that the Jews used to claim that if one has sex with his wife from behind (in the vagina), the offspring would become cross-eyed. Then this ayah was revealed. Muslim and Abū Dāwūd also reported this hadith. Ibn Abū Ḥātim reports it likewise from Muḥammad bin al-Munkadir from Jābir bin ʿAbdullāh; and Ibn Jurayj, one of the reporters of the hadith, said that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said: "From the front or from behind, as long as that occurs in the *farj* (vagina)."

Imam Ahmad recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that the ayah was revealed about some people from the Anṣār who came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him about this, and he said to them: "Have sex with her as you like, as long as that occurs in the vagina."

Imam Ahmad also records a fuller version through ʿAbdullāh bin Sābit, who went to Ḥafṣah bint ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Abū Bakr and said, "I wish to ask you about something, but I am shy." She said, "Do not be shy, O my nephew." She then related from Umm Salamah: the Anṣār used to refrain from this, while the Jews claimed that those who did it would have offspring with crossed eyes. When the Muhājirūn came to Madinah they married Anṣārī women, and one of these women would not obey her husband, saying, "You will not do that until I go to Allah's Messenger ﷺ." She went to Umm Salamah and told her the story, and Umm Salamah said, "Wait until Allah's Messenger ﷺ comes." When he came, the Anṣārī woman was too shy to ask him and left. Umm Salamah told him the story, and he said, "Summon the Anṣārī woman." She was summoned, and he recited this ayah to her and added: "Only in one valve (the vagina)." At-Tirmidhī also collected this and said, "Ḥasan."

An-Nasā'ī reported that Kaʿb bin ʿAlqamah said that Abū an-Naḍr asked Nāfiʿ about a statement people were repeating in his name from Ibn ʿUmar — that Ibn ʿUmar had permitted anal sex. Nāfiʿ said, "They have said a lie about me," and then told what really happened: Ibn ʿUmar, reaching this ayah while reciting, asked Nāfiʿ whether he knew the story behind it, and explained that the people of Quraysh used to approach their wives from the back (in the vagina); when they migrated to Madinah and married Anṣārī women and wanted to do the same, those women disliked it and made a big issue out of it, having followed the practice of the Jews — and that it was then that this ayah was revealed. This report has an authentic chain of narrators.

Two things are worth noticing in these accounts. First, the shyness: Masrūq shy before ʿĀ'ishah, ʿAbdullāh shy before Ḥafṣah, the Anṣārī woman too shy to speak — and in every case the answer is given plainly and without embarrassment. Modesty in this religion does not mean ignorance. Second, the woman's objection is what brings the matter to the Prophet ﷺ at all; she is not overruled, she is summoned and answered by him directly.

## The image of the tilth

**"Nisā'ukum ḥarthun lakum"** — "your wives are a tilth for you." Ibn ʿAbbās commented: meaning the place of pregnancy.

Maʿārif ul Qur'ān draws out the metaphor: the woman has been compared with a soil, and the husband with a cultivator. The point is not to reduce her to a field, but to say what the act is *for* — intercourse "has not been allowed for satisfying the sexual lust only, but also to make it a valid source for having children." Reading the image this way, Maʿārif ul Qur'ān says the Holy Qur'an has given "a subtle indication to the prohibition of carnal intercourse, even with one's wife, because it can never be a productive act, and there is no question of 'cultivation' therein." It states its two conditions for lawful intimacy in exactly those terms: "the purity of the woman from her menses, and avoiding the carnal intercourse."

**"Fa'tū ḥarthakum annā shi'tum"** — "so go to your tilth, when or how you will." Ibn Kathīr: wherever you wish, from the front or from behind, as long as sex takes place in one valve — the female sexual organ — as the authentic hadiths have indicated; and the Prophet's ﷺ own added words, "only in one valve," are the commentary on the ayah. Maʿārif ul Qur'ān spells the freedom out concretely, subject to those two conditions: lying over the woman, or beside her, or beneath her, "acceding to the vagina from any side, front or back, sitting or kneeling" — all these and similar positions are allowed, so long as "the ultimate place (of penetration) is a 'soil'."

So the ayah is generous where people expected restriction, and firm on the one point where people had grown lax.

## The prohibition of anal intercourse

Ibn Kathīr gathers the evidence at length:

- Imam Ahmad reported that Khuzaymah bin Thābit al-Khaṭmī narrated that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said: "Allah does not shy from the truth" — he said it thrice — "do not have anal sex with women." This hadith was collected by an-Nasā'ī and Ibn Mājah.
- Abū ʿĪsā at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasā'ī reported that Ibn ʿAbbās narrated that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said: "Allah does not look at a man who had anal sex with another man or a woman." At-Tirmidhī said, "Ḥasan Gharīb"; this is also the narration Ibn Ḥibbān collected in his Ṣaḥīḥ, and Ibn Ḥazm stated that it is authentic.
- Imam Ahmad reported that ʿAlī bin Ṭalaq said, "Allah's Messenger ﷺ forbade anal sex with women, for Allah does not shy away from truth." Abū ʿĪsā at-Tirmidhī also reported it and said, "Ḥasan."
- Abū Muḥammad ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ad-Dārimī reported in his Musnad that Saʿīd bin Yasār Abū Hubāb asked Ibn ʿUmar about it. Ibn ʿUmar said, "What does it mean?" When it was explained, he said: "Does a Muslim do that?" This has an authentic chain of narrators and is, Ibn Kathīr notes, an explicit rejection of the practice from Ibn ʿUmar.
- Abū Bakr bin Ziyād an-Naysābūrī reported that Ismāʿīl bin Rūḥ asked Mālik bin Anas about it. Mālik replied, "You are not an Arab? Does sex occur but in the place of pregnancy? Do it only in the *farj* (vagina)." When told that people claimed he permitted it, he said, "They utter a lie about me, they lie about me."

Ibn Kathīr adds that this was also the view of Saʿīd bin al-Musayyib, Abū Salamah, ʿIkrimah, Ṭāwūs, ʿAṭā', Saʿīd bin Jubayr, ʿUrwah bin az-Zubayr, Mujāhid bin Jabr, al-Ḥasan and other scholars of the Salaf — the Companions and the two generations after them — and that they, along with the majority of the scholars, harshly rebuked the practice, many of them calling it *kufr*.

Twice in this material a false attribution has to be corrected — Nāfiʿ denying it of Ibn ʿUmar, Mālik denying it of himself. It is a reminder of how easily a permissive claim travels under a great name.

## "And send ahead for yourselves"

Ayah 223 does not end with the bedroom. **"Wa qaddimū li-anfusikum"** — "and send for your own selves beforehand." Ibn Kathīr explains: by performing the acts of worship while refraining from whatever Allah has prohibited for you. You are laying something down now that you will collect later.

Ibn Jarīr reported that ʿAṭā' said — or related it to Ibn ʿAbbās — a second and beautifully concrete reading of the same phrase: that it means to mention Allah's Name, saying *Bismillāh*, before intimacy. And al-Bukhārī reported that Ibn ʿAbbās narrated that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said: "If anyone of you, on having sexual relations with his wife, said: 'In the Name of Allah. O Allah! Protect us from Satan and also protect what You bestow upon us from Satan,' and if it is destined that they should have a child, then Satan will never be able to harm him."

Then the closing weight: **"And fear Allah, and know that you are to meet Him."** Ibn Kathīr: meaning He will hold you accountable for all of your deeds. And finally, **"and give good tidings to the believers"** — which Ibn Kathīr defines by conduct: those who obey what Allah has commanded and refrain from what He has prohibited.

## Living it

The passage asks for a few very concrete things.

**Do not exile her.** The custom Anas described kept a menstruating woman from the family's food and even from the shared rooms of the house; the Prophet ﷺ ate from the very place she had eaten, and laid his head on her lap to recite. Whatever instinct treats a woman's cycle as something shameful finds no support here.

**Keep the one boundary, and keep it without inventing others.** "Do everything you wish, except having sexual intercourse" is both a permission and a limit — and the change in the Prophet's ﷺ face when he was asked to move that limit shows that it is not open to renegotiation.

**Wait for the bath, not just for the bleeding to stop.** That is the plain sense of the two different verbs, as Ibn ʿAbbās read them, and Ibn Kathīr reports the scholars' agreement on it.

**If you have already fallen into what these ayat forbid — repent.** Maʿārif ul Qur'ān places the ending of ayah 222 exactly there, and Ibn Kathīr notes Allah's love for the one who turns back even when the sin was repeated.

**Begin with His Name.** The most private act in a marriage opens with *Bismillāh* and a du'ā for the child not yet conceived, and closes — in the ayah itself — with the reminder that you are going to meet Him. Nothing in a believer's life is outside that frame.

passages.title: Oaths, and the vow to abstain from one's wife
passages.tafsir:
# Oaths, and the Vow to Abstain from One's Wife (2:224–227)

These four ayat are about the tongue and what it binds. A person swears by the name of Allah — and then finds that his own oath has become a wall between him and something good. Ayat 224 and 225 deal with oaths in general: which ones bind, which ones do not, and what to do when an oath stands in the way of righteousness. Ayat 226 and 227 take the single most painful case of that — a husband who swears off intimacy with his wife — and give it a hard time limit so that no woman is left suspended indefinitely by a man's angry words.

What holds the passage together is one principle: **an oath is not more sacred than the good it obstructs.** Allah's name is invoked to bind us to what is right, never to lock us out of it.

---

## Ayah 224: when the name of Allah becomes a barrier

The ayah forbids making Allah "an excuse" in your oaths — Ibn Kathir renders it as making His Name a shield against "doing good and acting piously, and making peace among mankind."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens the picture. The warning is aimed at people who swear in the name of Allah that they will *not* do some virtuous deed, or that they will *not* bring about a reconciliation between two estranged parties. By doing this, Maʿārif says, they are "using the name of Allah as a barrier against the good deeds, which is a severe violation of the sanctity of the name of Allah, and they must avoid it in any case."

Feel the reversal in that. The name of Allah is the most honoured thing a human tongue can carry. To take that name and lay it across the road to reconciliation, kindness to relatives, or charity — using the holiest thing you know as the excuse for the meanest thing you do — is the offence being named here. It is a common move: a man who has said "By Allah, I will never speak to him again" now has a reason that sounds religious for a grudge that is merely stubborn.

Ibn Kathir reads the command as: do not *implement* vows made in Allah's name to refrain from pious acts or to sever ties with relatives. He brings a parallel from another surah, where Allah tells those blessed with wealth not to swear off giving to their kinsmen, the poor, and those who left their homes for His cause, and adds: "Let them pardon and forgive. Do you not love that Allah should forgive you?" (24:22). The oath there was made in bitterness; the ayah dissolves it by reminding the swearer that he too wants to be forgiven.

**The principle Ibn Kathir draws out:** "Continuity in a sinful vow is more sinful than breaking it by expiation."

## From the Sunnah: break it, expiate, do the good

Four reports carry this section.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that it is more sinful before Allah for a man to persist in his oath regarding his family — severing relations with his relatives — than to break that promise and pay the *kaffārah* (the expiation Allah has prescribed for a broken oath). Ibn Kathir notes that this is how **Muslim** reported the hadith, and **Imam Ahmad** as well.

Reported in the **Two Sahihs**, Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "By Allah! Allah willing, I will not vow to do a thing and then see a better act, but I would do what is better and break my vow." The Prophet ﷺ is describing his own practice — the oath yields to the better deed, not the other way round.

**Muslim** reported from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever makes a vow and then finds what is better than his vow should break his vow, pay the *kaffārah*, and perform the better deed."

And **Abū Dāwūd**, under the chapter "Vowing while Angry," relates a scene that shows how the Companions applied this. Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib reported that two brothers from the Anṣār both received an inheritance, and one asked that it be divided. The other snapped: "If you ask me about dividing the inheritance again, then all of what I have will be spent on the Kaʿbah's door." ʿUmar's reply is a masterpiece of pastoral good sense: "The Kaʿbah does not need your money. So break your vow, pay the *kaffārah*, and come to terms with your brother." He then cited what he had heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Do not make a vow against yourself, nor to disobey the Lord, cut the relations of the womb, or dispose of what you do not own."

Note the last clause — a vow over something you do not own does not bind you either. And notice that ʿUmar did not treat the man's rash sentence as untouchable piety just because a holy place was named in it.

## The interpretation of Ibn ʿAbbās, and the weight behind it

ʿAlī ibn Abū Ṭalḥah reported that Ibn ʿAbbās explained "make not Allah's Name an excuse in your oaths" as: "Do not vow to refrain from doing good works. If you make such a vow, then break it, pay the *kaffārah*, and do the good work."

Ibn Kathir then lists who else held this — Masrūq, ash-Shaʿbī, Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī, Mujāhid, Ṭāwūs, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ, ʿIkrimah, Makḥūl, az-Zuhrī, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī and as-Suddī — and calls it the majority view. That roll-call is itself the argument: this is not one man's opinion but the settled reading of the earliest generations.

---

## Ayah 225: the oath that binds and the oath that does not

Having told us to break the harmful oath, Allah now relieves us of a different anxiety: not every "by Allah" that leaves your mouth is a contract with Heaven.

**"Allah will not call you to account for that which is unintentional (*laghw*) in your oaths, but He will call you to account for that which your hearts have earned."**

Ibn Kathir explains *laghw* oaths as the unintentional ones — "just like the habitual statements that the tongue repeats, without really intending them." **Abū Dāwūd** reported, under the chapter "The Laghw Vows," that ʿAṭāʾ said that ʿĀʾishah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the *laghw* in oaths "includes what the man says in his house, such as, 'No, by Allah,' and, 'Yes, by Allah'." This is the conversational filler of ordinary domestic speech, not a solemn undertaking.

Ibn Abū Ḥātim reported that Ibn ʿAbbās included in *laghw* an oath sworn while angry; and also an oath forbidding oneself something Allah has permitted — this second type, he said, carries no *kaffārah*. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said the same.

**A related teaching on the tongue's habits.** Reported in the Two Sahihs, Abū Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever swore and unintentionally mentioned al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā in his vow should then say, 'There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah'." Ibn Kathir explains that this was said to some new Muslims whose tongues, before Islam, were used to swearing by their idol al-Lāt. The remedy is exact and beautiful: since the words of *shirk* were said by mistake, the Prophet ﷺ ordered them to recite deliberately the word of *ikhlās* — pure, undiluted monotheism — so that it may eradicate what the tongue let fall.

## Maʿārif ul Qurʼān on the categories of oath

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing *Bayān al-Qurʼān*) lays out the technical scheme, and it is worth having clearly:

**1. *Laghw* — the ineffectual oath.** In its first sense it covers three cases: a false oath sworn without volition about something past; an oath sworn with volition about the past which the swearer *believed* to be true (guided by his information and supposition, he declares that a certain person has arrived, when in fact that person had not); and an oath about the future that came out of his lips by mistake while he had actually wanted to say something else. None of these three is an act of sin — which is precisely why they are called *laghw*, "ineffectual" — and this will not be reprehensible in the Hereafter.

**2. *Ghamūs* — perjury.** By contrast, the oath uttered intentionally, knowing it to be false, is *ghamūs*. This is an act of sin. Yet, according to the Ḥanafiyyah, it does not require *kaffārah*. In a second sense, Maʿārif notes, *laghw* is used simply for that which carries no *kaffārah*, and on that usage *ghamūs* is included under it — sinful, but not entailing the liability of expiation in this world.

**3. *Munʿaqidah* — the binding oath.** This is the oath that *does* require *kaffārah*: someone intentionally declares on oath that he will or will not perform a certain act. Acting contrary to it requires expiation.

Maʿārif observes that the ayah under discussion exclusively takes up the two categories that carry no *kaffārah*.

## "That which your hearts have earned"

Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and several others explained this phrase as swearing about a matter while knowing that one is lying. Mujāhid and others said it is similar to Allah's words elsewhere: "but He will punish you for your deliberate oaths" (5:89).

The dividing line, then, is the heart — not the volume of the words, not who overheard them. **What the tongue does absent-mindedly is passed over; what the heart intends is written down.**

And the ayah closes: **"And Allah is Oft-Forgiving (*Ghafūr*), Most Forbearing (*Ḥalīm*)."** Ibn Kathir explains this to mean that He is Oft-Forgiving to His servants and Most Forbearing with them.

---

## Ayat 226–227: the vow of Īlāʾ

Now the general law meets its hardest case. **Īlāʾ**, Ibn Kathir explains, is a type of vow in which a man swears not to sleep with his wife for a certain period, whether less or more than four months. A marriage is not merely a contract; it has a body and a warmth, and a husband can weaponise his own oath to punish a wife without ever divorcing her — leaving her neither married in any real sense nor free.

**If the vow is for less than four months**, Ibn Kathir says, the man has to wait for the vow's period to end and may then resume relations; the wife must be patient and cannot ask him to end his vow before its term. Here he cites the Prophet ﷺ himself: reported in the Two Sahihs, ʿĀʾishah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ swore he would stay away from his wives for a month, and then came down after twenty-nine days, saying: "The lunar month is twenty-nine days." Similar was narrated by ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, also reported in the Two Sahihs.

**If the vow is for four months or more**, the four-month clock in ayah 226 runs from the time of the vow. At its end the wife may ask her husband to end the Īlāʾ and return to her. Otherwise, Ibn Kathir says, he should divorce her — "by being forced to do so by the authorities if necessary, so that the wife is not harmed." That sentence is the heart of the ruling: the law will not let a man use a pious-sounding oath to hold a woman in limbo, and the authorities may compel him on her behalf.

Ibn Kathir also notes that the wording "their wives" indicates that Īlāʾ involves the wife and not a slave-woman, as the majority of the scholars have agreed.

**"Then if they return"** — Ibn Kathir explains this as returning to a normal marital relationship, resuming intimacy. This is the tafsir of Ibn ʿAbbās, Masrūq, ash-Shaʿbī, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Ibn Jarīr.

And then: **"verily, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."** Ibn Kathir's comment is tender — the forgiveness here is "with any shortcomings that occurred in the rights of the wife because of the vow of Īlāʾ." The months of coldness were a real wrong done to her rights; the man who returns finds Allah forgiving of that.

## Where the scholars differ: what happens when four months pass

Ayah 227 says, **"And if they decide upon divorce, then Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing."** Both commentaries build on this ayah, and they reach different conclusions. This is a genuine difference and should be stated as such.

**Ibn Kathir's position:** the words "if they decide upon divorce" indicate that divorce does *not* occur by merely passing the four-month mark. He supports this with Mālik's report from Nāfiʿ that ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar said: "If the man swears to Īlāʾ from his wife, then divorce does not occur automatically even after the four months have passed. When he stops at the four-month mark, he should either divorce or return." **Al-Bukhari** also reported this. Ibn Jarīr reported from Suhayl ibn Abū Ṣāliḥ, from his father: "I asked twelve Companions about the man who does Īlāʾ with his wife. They all stated that he does not have to do anything until the four months have passed and then has to either retain or divorce her." **Ad-Dāraquṭnī** also reported this from Suhayl. Ibn Kathir adds that it is also reported from ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Abū ad-Dardāʾ, ʿĀʾishah, Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbās, and was the opinion of Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, Mujāhid, Ṭāwūs, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb and al-Qāsim. On this view the man must *act* — return or pronounce divorce.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's position (citing *Bayān al-Qurʼān*):** it sorts the vow into four situations — (A) no time limit fixed, (B) a limit of exactly four months, (C) a limit of more than four months, (D) a limit of less than four months. Situations A, B and C are termed Īlāʾ in the Sharīʿah. In these, if the oath-taker breaks his oath within the four months and resumes relations, he owes *kaffārah* for the oath and his *nikāḥ* (marriage) remains intact. But if the four months expire and he has not broken the oath, an *irrevocable* divorce takes effect — meaning taking her back without remarriage is no longer correct. Maʿārif is careful to add that if the two enter into marriage by mutual consent, that is valid, and *ḥalālah* (an intervening marriage of the woman with a third person) is **not** required. In situation D — a limit of less than four months — breaking the oath requires *kaffārah*, and if the oath is completed the marriage even then remains valid.

So: both agree the four months are a real deadline and that the wife's suspension has an end. They differ on whether the deadline's expiry compels the husband to speak, or itself speaks for him.

## The names that close each ayah

Read the endings in sequence and the passage's logic shows in them:

- **224 — "All-Hearing, All-Knowing."** He heard the oath when you swore it, and He knows the intention underneath it.
- **225 — "Oft-Forgiving, Most Forbearing."** For the slips of the tongue.
- **226 — "Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."** For the husband who returns, over what his wife suffered in the meantime.
- **227 — "All-Hearing, All-Knowing."** And if he chooses divorce instead, the same two names return. Whatever is said in that room, and whatever motive lies behind it, is heard and known.

## Living it

**Your oath does not outrank the good.** If you have sworn yourself out of a kindness, a reconciliation, or a duty to a relative — the Sunnah here is not to admire your own consistency. Break it, pay the *kaffārah*, and do the better thing. ʿUmar's words are the model: the Kaʿbah does not need your money; go and come to terms with your brother.

**Do not let anger legislate for you.** Ibn ʿAbbās counted the oath sworn while angry among the *laghw* vows, and Abū Dāwūd has a chapter under the very title "Vowing while Angry." The words that fly out mid-argument were never meant to become the architecture of your life.

**Watch what the heart earns.** The relief in ayah 225 is for the careless tongue, not for the calculating one. A person who swears knowing he lies is not covered by it.

**And do not use religion as a way to hurt a spouse.** Ayat 226 and 227 exist because it can be done. The Qur'an's response is a clock, a required decision, and — as Ibn Kathir notes — authorities willing to enforce it, "so that the wife is not harmed."

passages.title: The waiting period and the limits of divorce
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat lay down the procedure for ending a marriage: how long a divorced woman waits, how many times a divorce can be taken back, and what happens when the last chance is spent. What holds them together is a phrase repeated throughout — *hudud Allah*, "the limits set by Allah." Divorce is not left to a man's temper; it is fenced in on every side, and the fences are drawn so that the way back to reconciliation stays open as long as possible.

## The waiting period

Ayah 228 commands that a divorced woman "wait three *qurū'*." Ibn Kathir explains that this applies to a woman whose marriage was consummated and who still has menstrual periods; after the three periods she may remarry if she wishes.

What is a *qurū'*? The word is ambiguous in Arabic, and Ibn Kathir devotes real space to settling it. He relates through Ibn Jarir that 'Alqamah said: they were sitting with 'Umar ibn al-Khattab when a woman came and said, "My husband divorced me one or two periods ago. He then came back to me while I had prepared my water [for taking a bath], took off my clothes and closed my door." 'Umar asked 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, "What do you think?" He said, "I think that she is still his wife, as long as she is not allowed to resume praying" — that is, until the third period ends before he takes her back. 'Umar said, "This is my opinion too."

Ibn Kathir piles up the authority for reading *qurū'* as the menstrual periods: Abu Bakr as-Siddiq, 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, Abu ad-Darda', 'Ubadah ibn as-Samit, Anas ibn Malik, Ibn Mas'ud, Mu'adh, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Ibn 'Abbas, then a long roll of the next generation including Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Mujahid, 'Ata', Tawus, al-Hasan, Qatadah and ad-Dahhak. He also cites a hadith reported by **Abu Dawud** and **an-Nasa'i** from Fatimah bint Abu Hubaysh, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to her, *"Do not pray during your Aqra'"* — *aqrā'* being the plural of *qurū'*. As Ibn Kathir puts it, if this hadith were authentic it would have been a clear proof that *qurū'* is the menstruation period. But he is scrupulous: one of its narrators, al-Mundhir, is an unknown person in hadith terminology, as Abu Hatim stated, although Ibn Hibban mentioned him in his book *ath-Thiqat* (the trustworthy). Ibn Kathir had every reason to want this report; he tells you its weakness anyway.

**"It is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs."** This means pregnancy or menstruation, and Ibn Kathir attributes that reading to Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Mujahid, ash-Sha'bi, al-Hakam ibn 'Utaybah, ar-Rabi' ibn Anas, ad-Dahhak and others. He then draws out the logic: the ayah warns women against hiding the truth, indicating that they are the authority in such matters, since they alone know these facts about themselves. Because verifying them is difficult, Allah left the decision with them — and in the same breath attached it to faith: *if they believe in Allah and the Last Day.* She might be tempted to end the 'iddah sooner, or later, according to her own desires. The Qur'an appoints no inspector. It appoints her conscience before her Lord, and commands her to say the truth, no more and no less.

## Rights that run both ways

The middle of ayah 228 turns from procedure to the heart of the matter: *"And they have rights similar to those over them, in what is reasonable."*

Ibn Kathir states the principle plainly: the wife has certain rights over her husband, just as he has certain rights over her, and each is obliged to give the other spouse his due rights. He cites what **Muslim** reported from Jabir, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Fear Allah regarding your women, for you have taken them by Allah's covenant… They have the right to be spent on and to be bought clothes in what is reasonable."*

Ibn Kathir also relates — without naming a collection — that Mu'awiyah ibn Haydah al-Qushayri's grandfather asked, "O Messenger of Allah! What is the right the wife of one of us has?" The Prophet ﷺ answered: *"To feed her when you eat, buy her clothes when you buy for yourself and to refrain from striking her on the face, cursing her or staying away from her except in the house."*

And there is Ibn 'Abbas, reported by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abu Hatim, who read this ayah and drew a conclusion many would not have thought to draw: *"I like to take care of my appearance for my wife just as I like for her to take care of her appearance for me. This is because Allah says, 'And they have rights similar to those over them, to what is reasonable.'"*

**The word carrying the weight is *bi'l-ma'rūf*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks it as what is just, upright, kindly, courteous — what is approved by the Shari'ah, or simply "as recognised." It includes what is neither prohibited under the Shari'ah nor a source of hardship or excess under common custom (*'urf*). The point, Maʿārif says, is that observing the routine of legal provisions is not enough; what will be examined is whether, by customarily approved practice, the other party suffers pain or loss. Coldness, indifference, behaviour that causes pain — these "can hardly be covered under an article of law but the word *bi'l-ma'rūf* does encompass them." A husband who is technically compliant and quietly cruel has not fulfilled this ayah.

Maʿārif also observes that the women's rights are named *first*. One reason, it says, is that a man, given his physical power and God-given precedence, "manages to wrest his rights from women anyway"; the concern should be for the rights of women, since they cannot habitually wrest their rights by force. There is a further hint here, Maʿārif adds, that men should take the first step in giving women their rights. And the word *mithl* ("similar") never meant that the kind of work men do must also be done by women, since the distribution of duties is naturally different; it means that the rights belonging to both must be observed equally and mutually, and that the penalty for negligence is equal too.

## "Men have a degree over them"

Here the two sources must be reported as they actually stand.

Ibn Kathir titles this section "The Virtue Men have over Women" and explains the ayah to mean that men are in a more advantageous position than women physically, as well as in their mannerism, status, obedience (of women to them), spending, taking care of the affairs, and in general, in this life and in the Hereafter. He then links it to Surah an-Nisa': *"Men are the protectors and maintainers of women, because Allah has made one of them to excel the other, and because they spend from their means"* (4:34).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing the same ayah of an-Nisa', frames the degree as one of care-taking and regulation — men "stand care-takers of women" — and heads its own discussion "Man's higher position over woman is for discipline only." It then states the limit of that precedence explicitly: this does not entail that all men are superior to all women, because being superior in the sight of Allah depends wholly on belief and good conduct. In matters of the Hereafter it is not necessary that men alone keep that degree; and as Maʿārif says is elaborated in Qur'anic verses and hadith narrations, this is what will come to pass — that some women, through their obedience to and worship of Allah, will become superior to many men, their degree rising higher than many men's. Maʿārif's summary is that a certain measure of precedence and authority in regulating worldly affairs is for the good of women and is what wisdom dictates; other than that, there is no difference in reward and retribution for deeds, or in the degree of merit attained in the Hereafter.
