It points to *"And whosoever, male or female, does a righteous deed, while he (or she) is a believer, We shall assuredly get him (or her) to live a goodly life"* (16:97).

Most striking is what Maʿārif reports from Ibn 'Abbas (via al-Qurtubi) about what the "degree" obliges: precisely *because* Allah has given men a degree of precedence over women, **they should act with much more forbearance.** Even if women fall short in giving them their rights, the degree of their precedence is such that men should bear it patiently and do nothing to hold back the rights they owe. The advantage is not a licence; it is a heavier load.

Maʿārif adds an insight that could dissolve most marital conflict: each party should watch the fulfilment of its own duties rather than go after demanding rights, since the duties of men are the rights of women and the duties of women are the rights of men. If they succeed in that, "the very issue of demanding rights will cease to exist." The root of today's troubles, it says, lies in people who are alert to their rights but negligent of their duties.

The ayah ends: **"And Allah is All-Mighty, All-Wise"** — Mighty, says Ibn Kathir, in His punishment of those who disobey and defy His commands; Wise in what He commands, destines and legislates.

## Divorce is twice — and what was abrogated

To feel the force of *"The divorce is twice"* in ayah 229, you need the situation it ended. Ibn Kathir explains that in the beginning of Islam a man had the right to take back his divorced wife even if he had divorced her a hundred times, as long as she was still in her 'iddah. This was harmful for the wife, and so Allah made the divorce thrice: revocable after the first and second, irrevocable after the third. Ibn Kathir cites **Abu Dawud**, in a chapter titled "Taking the Wife back after the third (Divorce) is an abrogated practice," reporting Ibn 'Abbas's comment that the man used to have the right to take back his wife even if he had divorced her thrice, and that Allah abrogated this with *"The divorce is twice."* **An-Nasa'i** also collected it.

Ibn Abu Hatim, and Ibn Jarir in his Tafsir, preserve what that abuse looked like. 'Urwah reported that a man said to his wife, "I will neither divorce you nor take you back." She said, "How?" He said, "I will divorce you and when your term of 'iddah nears its end, I will take you back." She went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and told him what happened, and Allah revealed *"The divorce is twice."* That is the cruelty this ayah was aimed at: a woman held in a revolving door, never a wife and never free.

**"Either retain her on reasonable terms, or release her with kindness."** Ibn Kathir: if you divorce her once or twice you have the choice to take her back while she is still in her 'iddah, intending to be kind to her and to mend differences; otherwise await the end of her 'iddah, when the divorce becomes final, and let her go her own way in peace, without committing any harm or injustice against her. 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah reported that Ibn 'Abbas said: "When the man divorces his wife twice, let him fear Allah regarding the third time. He should either keep her with him and treat her with kindness, or let her go her own way with kindness, without infringing upon any of her rights."

Maʿārif adds precision. Revocation during the 'iddah requires no fresh contract — retaining her by revoking the talaq is enough, and the marriage stands reinstated on the basis of the previous *nikah*; but the husband was instructed to revoke only if he intends to correct the situation and looks forward to living in peace, not to harass the woman. *Tasrīh* — to untie, to free, to release — teaches that no further pronouncement, indeed no other action, is needed to sever relations; the 'iddah expiring without revocation is itself sufficient. And releasing "with kindness" (*bi-ihsān*) means the parting must be done with charity, kindness and grace rather than anger and altercation — even letting her depart with some presents, as the Qur'an says: *"the rich man according to his means and the poor one according to his means"* (2:236). Maʿārif records that Abu Dawud reports, on the authority of Abu Razin al-Asadi, that after this verse came down a man asked the Prophet ﷺ, "Allah Almighty has said: *The divorce is twice*. Why was the third talaq not mentioned here?" He said that *"to release in fairness"* is the third.

**Three stages are a ceiling, not a path.** Maʿārif notes that it appears in hadith — without naming a collection — that divorce is the most detested of lawful things with Allah. The best method, *al-talāq al-ahsan*, is to pronounce one talaq during a state of purity (*tuhr*) in which intercourse has not taken place, and then let it stand: when the 'iddah finishes the marriage ends of itself. Maʿārif cites Ibn Abi Shaybah reporting from Ibrahim an-Nakha'i that the noble Companions favoured exactly this. Notice too the grammar it points to. The Qur'an did not say "the divorces are three." It said *"the divorce is twice,"* and then, for the third, *"and if he divorces her" — if.* On this basis Imam Malik and several other jurists ruled the third talaq absolutely impermissible and called it *talāq al-bid'ah*, an innovated divorce without the authority of the Qur'an and Sunnah; other jurists ruled three permissible only if pronounced separately in three states of purity and termed that *talāq al-sunnah* — but, Maʿārif stresses, none of them meant by this that giving three divorces in that manner is desirable. The label meant only that this form does not amount to *bid'ah*. That the third is undesirable, it says, has not been questioned by anyone.

As for three at one sitting, both sources cite Mahmud ibn Labid's report recorded by **an-Nasa'i**: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was told about a man who pronounced three divorces on his wife at one time, and he stood up while angry and said, *"The Book of Allah is being made the subject of jest while I am still amongst you?"* — whereupon a man stood and said, "Should I kill that man, O Messenger of Allah?"

**Where the scholars differed.** Whether such a rushed triple pronouncement counts as three is a genuine disagreement. Maʿārif reports the hadith in **Sahih Muslim** from Ibn 'Abbas that during the time of the Prophet ﷺ, the caliphate of Abu Bakr, and the first two years of 'Umar's caliphate, three talaqs were taken as one; then 'Umar said, "People are becoming haste-prone in a matter in which there was a room for deferment for them. Therefore, it would be appropriate if we enforce it on them" — and he enforced it on them. Imam ash-Shafi'i, Imam Malik, Imam Abu Hanifah, Imam Ahmad and a large number of earlier and later scholars held that three take effect; Tawus and some adherents of the Zahiri school held that only one does. Maʿārif prefers Imam an-Nawawi's reconciliation, reported in his *Sharh Muslim* and called there the most authentic: 'Umar's order concerned the particular case of a man repeating the word of divorce without clearly saying "three," where the words could mean three or could be mere emphasis. In an age of truth and honesty the man's sworn statement of intent settled it — and 'Umar closed that door when honesty declined and men began misusing the concession.

## The dower, and a wife's way out

The ayah forbids a husband to take back anything he gave his wife. Ibn Kathir reads this as a ban on bothering or pressuring her into ending the situation by giving back her *mahr* and any gifts, citing *"and you should not treat them with harshness, that you may take away part of what you have given them"* (4:19) — while noting that if she remits any part of it of her own good pleasure, that is lawful (4:4). Maʿārif names the tactic: cruel husbands who neither wish to retain their wives nor care about their rights nor divorce them, exploiting her helplessness to demand money, property, or the forgiveness or return of the dower in exchange for release. The Qur'an declares this unlawful.

The exception is *khul'* — a wife-initiated release. Ibn Kathir explains that when the differences are irreconcilable and the wife dislikes her husband and becomes unable to live with him any longer, she is allowed to free herself by giving back what he had given her, with no sin on her in doing so nor on him in accepting.

Imam Malik reports in his ***Muwatta'*** that Habibah bint Sahl al-Ansariyah was married to Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, and that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ once went out for the Fajr prayer and found Habibah by his door in the dark. He said, "Who is this?" She said, "I am Habibah bint Sahl, O Messenger of Allah!" He said, "What is the matter?" She said, "I and Thabit ibn Qays" — meaning she could no longer be with her husband. When Thabit came, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him, *"This is Habibah bint Sahl, she said what Allah has permitted her to say."* Habibah also said, "O Messenger of Allah! I still have everything he gave me," and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"Take it from her."* So he took it from her, and she remained in her family's house. Ibn Kathir notes this was reported by Ahmad, Abu Dawud and an-Nasa'i.

**Al-Bukhari** records the same household from another angle: Ibn 'Abbas said that the wife of Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, "O Messenger of Allah! I do not criticize his religion or mannerism. But I hate committing *Kufr* in Islam" — Ibn Kathir glosses that as ignoring his rights over her. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"Will you give him back his garden?"* She said, "Yes." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"Take back the garden and divorce her once."* **An-Nasa'i** also recorded it.

Note what those reports establish: her inability to continue is a real ground, and the release is a single pronouncement — not a bitter three. **At-Tirmidhi** reports that Rubayyi' bint Mu'awwidh ibn 'Afra' obtained khul' during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the Prophet ﷺ ordered her to wait one menstruation period for her 'iddah. The balance is kept from the other side too: for the woman who has no valid reason and still asks for her marriage to be ended, Ibn Jarir reports that Thawban said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"Any woman who asks her husband for divorce without justification, then the scent of Paradise will be forbidden for her."* **At-Tirmidhi** recorded this hadith and stated that it is *hasan*.

**"These are the limits ordained by Allah, so do not transgress them."** This means, says Ibn Kathir, that the laws Allah has legislated are His set limits. He then cites a hadith he describes as authentic, without naming a collection: *"Allah has set some limits, so do not transgress them; and commanded some commands, so do not ignore them; and made some things unlawful, so do not commit them. He has also left some matters (without rulings) as a mercy with you, not because He has forgotten them, so do not ask about them."*

## The third divorce, and the door that closes

Ayah 230: *"And if he has divorced her, then she is not lawful for him thereafter until she has married another husband."* Maʿārif reads this as a consequence with the flavour of a penalty: having transgressed the limits of the Shari'ah by unnecessarily pronouncing the third talaq, and having done away with all his options and the graces the Shari'ah allowed him, the man has "reached a dead end." The contract of marriage stands totally annulled, and the couple cannot simply agree to begin again.

Ibn Kathir insists the second marriage must be a real, legal marriage and genuinely consummated; if she marries a man without consummating the marriage, she will not be eligible for her first husband. **Muslim** reported from 'A'ishah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about a woman whose husband divorced her thrice, who then married another man who divorced her before he had sexual relations with her — would she be allowed for her first husband? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"No, until he enjoys her 'Usaylah (sexual relation)."* **Al-Bukhari** also reported this hadith. And Ibn Kathir explains the word: *'Usaylah* means sexual intercourse — Imam Ahmad and **an-Nasa'i** reported from 'A'ishah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"'Usaylah is sexual intercourse."* Imam Ahmad records the same ruling given to the wife of Rifa'ah al-Qurazi, who hoped to return to her first husband; the Messenger of Allah ﷺ told her she could not unless she and her present husband experienced each other's *'usaylah*. Ibn Kathir notes that al-Bukhari, Muslim and an-Nasa'i also recorded it.

That requirement closes the obvious loophole — the arranged interim marriage, *tahlīl* or *halālah*. Ibn Kathir is blunt: the reason for the second marriage must be that the man desires her and intends an extended married life with her, these being the legal goals of marriage. If the reason was to make her eligible for her ex-husband again, this is the *tahlīl* that the hadiths have cursed and criticised — and if that reason is announced in the contract, it makes the contract invalid according to the majority of the scholars. Imam Ahmad reported that 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ cursed the one who does *tahlīl*, the one in whose favour it is done, those who eat *riba* (usury) and those who feed it." **At-Tirmidhi** and **an-Nasa'i** reported this hadith, and at-Tirmidhi said it is *hasan*. Al-Hakim records in his ***Mustadrak***, from Nafi', that a man asked Ibn 'Umar about a woman divorced three times whose brother-in-law married her to make *tahlīl* without the second husband knowing — was she allowed for the first? He said: "No, unless it is a marriage that involves desire. We used to consider this an act of adultery during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." Al-Hakim said the hadith has a *sahih* chain although al-Bukhari and Muslim did not record it.

If the second marriage ends, the door reopens — but on a condition. *"It is no sin on both of them that they reunite, provided they feel that they can keep the limits ordained by Allah."* Ibn Kathir explains this as living together honourably, and cites Mujahid: "If they are convinced that the aim behind their marriage is honourable." The passage that began by fencing in divorce ends by fencing in reunion — and its closing phrase, *"These are the limits of Allah, which He makes plain for the people who have knowledge,"* points, as Ibn Kathir says, to Allah's commandments and legislation, made plain for those who know.

## Living it

Read whole, these ayat are less about how to leave a marriage than about how hard Allah has made it to leave badly. For readers not divorcing anyone, the centre of the passage is that single line in ayah 228 — *"they have rights similar to those over them, in what is reasonable"* — with Ibn 'Abbas's two commentaries on it: that a husband should take care of his appearance for his wife as he likes her to for him, and that the "degree" Allah gave him is a reason to act with much more forbearance, not less.

passages.title: Releasing wives fairly and nursing the child
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat take a marriage that is ending — or has ended — and refuse to let it end badly. Ayah 231 governs the husband as the waiting period runs out; ayah 232 governs the people around the woman once the marriage is finally over — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that its address covers both the husband who divorced her and her guardians; ayah 233 governs both parents when a nursing child is caught in between. One phrase binds them: **bi'l-maʿrūf**, "in fairness," in the manner well-recognised and approved. Every party in the wreckage of a marriage is handed a limit, and behind every limit stands the reminder that Allah knows and Allah sees.

## Ayah 231: two doors, and both must be walked through decently

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene: after the law of divorce in the previous ayat come the rules for the closing days of the ʿiddah, the waiting period after a revocable divorce. Ibn Kathir puts the command plainly. When a man has divorced his wife with a reversible divorce and her term nears its end, he has exactly two doors. He may **take her back** — kindly, and, Ibn Kathir notes, with witnesses that he has taken her back — and live with her with kindness. Or he may **release her**, letting the ʿiddah finish and then kindly asking her to depart from his house, without disputing, fighting with her, or using foul words.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that "in fairness" appears separately at *both* doors. Keeping her has conditions; letting her go has conditions. Neither may be decided "under the heat of spot anger or sentiments." If a man's heart softens, the Sharīʿah tells him what that return must mean: to wash out past anger and displeasure and resolve to live anew in good family relationship, with the intention to give her her due rights — not to hold the woman in captivity or to harass and torture her. It adds the procedure from Sūrah al-Ṭalāq: *"And let two trustworthy persons from amongst you be witnesses"* (65:2). Witnesses protect her — they can be used if she later files a legal claim about the revocation, and they stop a man from coming up with a claim, even after the ʿiddah has expired, that he had already revoked the divorce beforehand.

If the anger has not gone away, then the second door: **"Or release them in fairness."** Hostile emotions, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān warns, do not stay between two people; starting from two persons they can envelope two families and become "a danger for both this world and the Hereafter." So it lists what releasing fairly costs: she stays in the family house during the ʿiddah and he pays for her total sustenance; the dower (*mahr*) is paid in full if still unpaid and intercourse has occurred, or, if the divorce came before intercourse, half of it — "paid in good cheer." Beyond those obligatory rights, it is not only desirable but excellent that she leaves on her parting day with "some cash or at the least, with a set of clothing" — the *matāʿ* of ayah 241. Marriage was a transaction and mutual contract, and divorce is the termination of a transaction; there is no reason why that termination should be a hotbed of enmity and hostility.

## The trick this ayah outlawed

Then the prohibition. Ibn Kathir renders it: **"But do not take them back to hurt them,"** and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same words *"do not retain them with intent to harm them unjustly."* Ibn Kathir records that Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Masrūq, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Rabīʿ and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān all explained it identically. A man used to divorce his wife; when her ʿiddah came near its end he took her back — to harm her and to stop her from marrying someone else. Then he divorced her again, and she would begin her ʿiddah once more; and again. Her waiting could be prolonged without end: married in name, abandoned in fact, unable to leave. After that, Allah prohibited this practice.

**"And whoever does that, then he has wronged himself."** Ibn Kathir: meaning, by defying Allah's commandments. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the logic — he thinks he is punishing her, but the Hereafter is where every injustice and cruelty will be avenged, and "the oppressor is not going to move one step forward unless the oppressed is avenged." Fairly often the consequences overtake him here too, as in the Persian couplet of Shaykh Saʿdī (may Allah have mercy on him) that it quotes: the oppressor presumed he had hit his victim, but the weapon sailed past him and boomeranged back into his own neck.

## "And treat not the verses of Allah in a jest"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two explanations. One: making a mockery of the verses of Allah means acting against the divine ordinances in matters of marriage and divorce at all. The second, reported from Sayyidnā Abū al-Dardāʼ (may Allah be pleased with him), is specific — in pre-Islamic Arabia some men would give a divorce or free a slave, then go back on their word and say that it was all in fun, that no divorce or freeing was intended. Ibn Kathir records the same explanation from al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, ʿAṭāʼ al-Khurāsānī, al-Rabīʿ and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān: the man who divorces his wife and says "I was joking," or frees a servant or gets married and says "I was only joking." The ayah was revealed, and such men "were made to bear the consequences of their actions."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a teaching of the Prophet ﷺ that there are three things in which acting seriously and acting in jest are equal — divorce, freeing a slave, and marriage — reported, it says, by Ibn Marduwayh from Ibn ʿAbbās and by Ibn al-Mundhir from ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, and in a wording from Sayyidnā Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) listing marriage, divorce and revocation. Go through the offer and acceptance before witnesses and the marriage stands solemnised anyway; give a divorce in clear words and it takes effect. "I had no intention" is not accepted as a valid excuse.

Ibn Kathir cites here a report Ibn Jarīr gives from Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ once became angry at the Ashʿarī tribe, and when Abū Mūsā asked him about it, he ﷺ said that one of them says "I divorced her," then says "I took her back!" — and that this is not the appropriate way Muslims conduct divorce; rather, divorce the woman when she has fulfilled the term of the prescribed period. From the universal and unqualified words *"when you have divorced women,"* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a related rule: the basic and true method is one revocable divorce in clear and unambiguous words, so the choice of taking her back remains open — not words that cause sudden severance of the marriage (*al-ṭalāq al-bāʼin*), and not driving on to three, after which even a fresh marriage between the couple becomes unlawful.

The ayah then lifts its eyes. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it: *"And remember the grace of Allah on you and what He has revealed to you of the Book and the wisdom giving you good counsel thereby."* Ibn Kathir explains the favour as His sending His Messenger ﷺ with the right guidance and clear signs; the Book is the Qur'an, and *al-Ḥikmah* he explains as the Sunnah — and the instruction means He commands you, forbids you, and warns you against transgressing His prohibitions. *"And fear Allah, and know that Allah is All-Aware of everything"* — none of your secret or public affairs ever escapes His knowledge. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān applies it where it stings: He knows the secrets hidden in your hearts and your intentions, so release her intending to avoid disputes and injustice, not to release anger on her or to disgrace or hurt her.

## Ayah 232: the brother who swore an oath

The marriage is now genuinely over and the ʿiddah has expired, and the ayah turns to the people around her: *"do not prevent them from marrying their husbands when they mutually agree with fairness."* Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that this concerns the man who divorces his wife once or twice, her ʿiddah finishes, then he thinks about taking her back in marriage and the woman also wishes that — yet her family prevents her. Masrūq, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, al-Zuhrī and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said the same.

**Al-Bukhārī reported in his Ṣaḥīḥ** the incident behind it. The husband of the sister of Maʿqil ibn Yasār al-Muzanī divorced her; he waited until her ʿiddah finished, then asked to remarry her — and Maʿqil refused. In al-Tirmidhī's narration, which Ibn Kathir notes al-Tirmidhī rendered authentic, she had wanted it too, and Maʿqil's words to the man were: "O ungrateful one! I honoured you and married her to you but you divorced her. By Allah! She will never be returned to you." Then comes the line that turns the whole story: *"But Allah knew his need for his wife and her need for her husband"* — and He revealed the ayah. When Maʿqil heard it he said, "I hear and obey my Lord," summoned the man, and told him he would honour him and let him remarry his sister; Ibn Marduwayh adds that he said he would pay the expiation for breaking his vow. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports a similar incident concerning a cousin of Sayyidnā Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh (may Allah be pleased with him), who likewise carried out the instruction.

Notice what the ayah overturned: not a vice, but an angry sense of honour. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that Maʿqil spoke as he did "in anger against the man's act of divorce," and that the noble Companions were true lovers of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ — such was the beneficence of the ayah that his anger cooled down the moment he heard it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the motives the ayah addresses — a former husband who considers her remarriage a violation of his honour, guardians who stall out of greed, relatives who turn hostile to the man after the divorce — and calls stopping a woman from marrying at her choice, without a valid reason admitted by Islamic law, "a grave injustice."

**But the condition cuts both ways.** The licence is for when "they mutually agree *with fairness*" — that is, when the two agree to marry in accordance with the rules set by the Sharīʿah. Where the arrangement is itself unlawful — agreeing to live together without marrying, entering a new marriage illegitimately after three divorces, intending to marry during the ʿiddah — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says every Muslim, especially close relatives, has a right to stop it, and it is obligatory to do so within the limits of one's ability. Yet from the very words "when they mutually agree" it derives that a sane, adult girl **cannot be given in marriage without her consent or permission**. Ibn Kathir notes a further inference drawn from this ayah — that a woman is not permitted to give herself in marriage but requires a *walī*, a guardian such as her father, brother or adult son, to give her away — as Ibn Jarīr and al-Tirmidhī stated when they mentioned this ayah.

The ayah then closes. Ibn Kathir renders it *"That is more virtuous and purer for you"* and explains the meaning: obeying Allah's Law by returning the women to their ex-husbands, and abandoning your displeasure, is purer and cleaner for your hearts. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the same sentence as a modality of purity and cleanliness, and warns of what the opposite produces — cruelty to these women, their rights denied, their chastity endangered, and forced marriages that end in perpetual discord or in divorce and *khulʿ*. And then: *"Allah knows and you know not"* — He knows the benefits in what He commands and forbids; you go ahead with imperfect thoughts, chasing an assumed honour that will be rolling in the dust, or money that may drag you into conflict.

## Ayah 233: the child in the middle

Then, mid-stream, the subject changes to nursing. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the placement is deliberate: the ayat before and after take up the injunctions of divorce, and it generally happens that issues concerning the feeding and upbringing of children are disputed following a divorce — and since these disputes lead to violence, this ayah offers moderate injunctions that both man and woman can carry out easily.

**One word carries the whole tone.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a beautiful observation. The ayah calls the mothers *al-wālidāt*, plainly "mothers." But it does not call him *al-wālid*, "the father," though the Qur'an uses that word elsewhere: *"no father shall be of avail to his child"* (31:33). It says instead **al-mawlūd lahu** — "the one to whom the child is born." Why the longer phrase? Because the father is the one obligated to pay the child's expenses, and it was possible he would find that burdensome. Both father and mother share in the birth of the child, but the child is ascribed to the father and the lineage comes from him — so the very title used to name him reminds him the child is his, and the expense should not sit heavy on him. The Qur'an does not describe law the way the governments of the world do; it presents it in a sympathetic and affectionate manner, so that people can accept it and act on it.

**Two full years.** Ibn Kathir: a direction from Allah to the mothers to suckle their infants through the complete term of suckling, which is two years — "for those who desire to complete the term of suckling." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that suckling is naturally the mother's own obligation: if she refuses without a valid reason, out of hostility or displeasure, she is a sinner, and she cannot accept payment for it from her husband while she is married to him, because it is her own duty. Unless there is some special reason, completing the two years is the right of the child.

The limit also settles a legal question. Ibn Kathir explains that *taḥrīm* through milk — the bond that makes marriage permanently unlawful between milk-relatives — is established only by suckling that occurs before the two years end. He cites **al-Tirmidhī**, narrating from Umm Salamah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said suckling establishes taḥrīm if it is on the breast and before weaning; al-Tirmidhī said this hadith is *ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ*, and that the majority of the people of knowledge among the Companions of Allah's Messenger ﷺ and others acted upon it. **Al-Dāraquṭnī** related from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said suckling establishes taḥrīm only within the first two years. Ibn Kathir records the dissent honestly: it is reported in the Ṣaḥīḥ that ʿĀʼishah held that milk given to someone beyond the age of two also establishes taḥrīm — as did ʿAṭāʼ ibn Abī Rabāḥ and Layth ibn Saʿd — relying on the case of Sālim, the freed slave of Abū Ḥudhayfah; but the rest of the Prophet's wives ﷺ did not agree and held that this was only a special case, and this is also the opinion of the majority of the scholars. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that Imam Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him) ruled that the legal effects of suckling still apply up to thirty months, and that feeding beyond two and a half years is unanimously forbidden.

**The father pays.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it: *"And on him, to whom the child is born, falls the provision of food and clothing for them (the mothers) with fairness. Nobody is obligated beyond his capacity."* Ibn Kathir: the father is obliged to provide the mother's expenses and clothing in reasonable amounts usually used by similar women in that area, without extravagance or stinginess, spending within his means — as Allah says, *"Let the rich man spend according to his means"* (65:7). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān separates two obligations: the mother's maintenance is the father's responsibility for as long as the marriage or the ʿiddah lasts, but once the ʿiddah has matured, the father remains obligated to pay for the suckling of the child. And if the father is not alive, *"And on the (father's) heir is incumbent the like of that"* — which, Ibn Kathir says, the majority of scholars read as requiring the father's inheritor to spend on the mother of the child just as the father was spending, preserving her rights and refraining from harming her.

**And then: no one may use the child as a weapon.** *"No mother shall be treated unfairly on account of her child, nor father on account of his child."* Ibn Kathir gives it teeth in both directions. The mother should not decline to rear her child in order to harm its father — she may not refrain from suckling him the milk necessary for his survival, though later she is allowed to give up custody so long as she does not intend harm by it. And the father is not allowed to take the child from its mother in order to harm her. This is the tafsir of Mujāhid, Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Zuhrī, al-Suddī, al-Thawrī and Ibn Zayd, and others. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pictures it in ordinary life: a mother genuinely unable to nurse, pressed by the father anyway in the hope that, being the mother, she will finally melt down; or a mother with no excuse refusing, in the hope that the poor father will somehow find the means to have the child fed elsewhere. Both are forbidden. It adds that the father may not compel her if she refuses for a genuine excuse — but if the child will not take another woman's milk, she is compelled to feed him. On wages it is even-handed: while she is his wife or within her ʿiddah, her maintenance already covers it, and asking more amounts to harming the father; once the ʿiddah has expired and maintenance has ended, a nursing wage she asks for must be paid, provided she asks no more than another woman would take — otherwise the father may engage a wet-nurse in her place.

**Weaning is a joint decision.** *"If they both decide on weaning, by mutual consent, and after due consultation, there is no sin on them."* Ibn Kathir: if the parents decide on weaning before the two years end, for a benefit they duly discuss and agree upon, there is no sin — and neither parent is allowed to make this kind of decision without duly consulting the other, as al-Thawrī stated. He calls that method of mutual consultation a protection of the child's interests and a mercy from Allah to His servants; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it plainly, that the child's welfare must be the paramount concern and that making the child a target-board of the parents' quarrels is undesirable. And if a wet-nurse is engaged, *"there is no sin on you, provided you pay (the mother) what you agreed (to give her) on a reasonable basis"* — the wages settled clearly in advance so there is no dispute later, and handed over at the appointed time with no postponement or evasion; if they are not paid as settled, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the sin rests with the parents.

## Living it

- **Reconciliation is not a tactic.** Take her back to live anew in good family relationship, with witnesses — never to hold her in captivity.
- **Endings have manners.** Housing during the ʿiddah, full sustenance, the dower as it is due, and a parting gift beyond that.
- **Wounded family pride is not a legal veto.** Maʿqil said "I hear and obey my Lord," gave his sister back in marriage, and paid the expiation for his oath.
- **Never route a fight through a child.** Not by withholding the milk he needs, not by seizing custody to wound the other parent.

Each of these ayat ends by turning your eyes to Allah's knowledge — *"Allah is All-Aware of everything," "Allah knows and you know not," "Allah is All-Seer of what you do"* — which, Ibn Kathir says, means none of your affairs or speech escapes His perfect Watch. That, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, is the Qur'an's way: it does not simply make a law, publish it, and leave whoever breaks it to his punishment; it persuades and warns, until a person keeps the law even where there is no chance at all of his being policed.

passages.title: Widows, proposals, and divorce before consummation
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat continue the Qur'an's law of marriage into two situations left open by the passage before them: the woman whose husband has **died**, and the woman divorced **before the marriage was ever consummated**. What holds them together is one question — when a marriage ends, what does the woman still hold, and what does the man still owe? Ayah 234 gives the widow a fixed term of waiting; ayah 235 governs how a man may and may not speak to her during it; ayat 236–237 turn to a marriage that ended before it began, and settle the money.

Notice the refrain: "Allah is well-acquainted with what you do" (234), "Allah knows what is in your minds, so fear Him" (235), "Truly, Allah is All-Seer of what you do" (237). This law reaches into places no court could inspect — a man's unspoken intention, a widow's private conduct in her own home — and so each section closes by reminding the reader Who sees it.

---

## Four months and ten (ayah 234)

The ayah commands the wives of men who die to wait four months and ten nights before remarrying. Ibn Kathir notes that by the **consensus of the scholars** this covers both the marriage that was consummated and the one that was not — the wording of the ayah is general, and nothing narrows it.

That the ruling reaches even an unconsummated marriage is illustrated by a striking incident Ibn Kathir reports, recorded by **Imam Ahmad and the compilers of the Sunan**, and graded *Sahih* by **At-Tirmidhi**. Ibn Mas'ud was asked about a man who married a woman, died before consummating the marriage, and had never fixed a *mahr* (the dowry a husband owes his wife). They kept asking him until he said: "I shall give you my own opinion, and if it is correct then it is from Allah, while if it is wrong it is because of my error and because of Satan. In this case, Allah and His Messenger are innocent of my opinion. She has her full *Mahr*." In another narration he specified a dowry like that of women of her status, "without stinginess or extravagance," and added, "She has to spend the '*Iddah* and has a right to the inheritance." Then Ma'qil bin Yasar Ashja'i stood and said he had heard Allah's Messenger ﷺ issue a similar judgment for Barwa' bint Washiq — and Ibn Mas'ud was delighted to hear it. In another narration, several men of the tribe of Ashja' stood and testified to the same. It is a small window onto how the early community reasoned: a scholar's careful *ijtihad*, offered with visible fear of getting it wrong, then confirmed by a Sunnah he had not known of.

**The pregnant widow is the exception.** Ibn Kathir explains that her '*iddah* ends the moment she gives birth, even if that is an instant after her husband's death, on the strength of Allah's words, *"And for those who are pregnant, their 'Iddah is until they lay down their burden"* (65:4). He cites the hadith of Subay'ah Al-Aslamiyah, in **the Two Sahihs** through various chains. Her husband Sa'd bin Khawlah died while she was pregnant; she gave birth a few nights later, and when her postnatal period ended she beautified herself for those who might seek to marry her. Abu Sanabil bin Ba'kak came and said, "Why do I see you beautified yourself, do you wish to marry? By Allah! You will not marry until the four months and ten nights have passed." She says: "When he said that to me, I collected my garments when night fell and went to Allah's Messenger ﷺ and asked him about this matter. He said that my '*Iddah* had finished when I gave birth and allowed me to get married if I wished." A woman who did not know went straight to the source rather than accept a confident man's verdict.

**Why this length?** Sa'id bin Musayyib and Abu Al-'Aliyah said the wisdom is that the womb may contain a child; when she waits this period, it becomes evident whether she is pregnant. Ibn Kathir links this to the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud in **the Two Sahihs**: a human being is put together in his mother's womb for forty days as a seed, then a clot of thick blood for a similar period, then a morsel of flesh for a similar period, and then Allah sends an angel who is ordered to breathe life into the fetus. That is four months; the extra ten days are to be sure, since some months are less than thirty days, and by then the fetus begins to show signs of life. Ibn Kathir closes the point with "Allah knows best."

**Calculating it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a detail most people are not aware of: if the husband dies on the night of the new moon, the months are completed according to the lunar calendar, whether each runs 29 or 30 days. If he died after the night of the new moon, each month is reckoned at 30 days — 130 days in all — and the '*iddah* ends when that period expires and the same time of day at which the death occurred comes round.

**Mourning, not merely waiting**

The '*iddah* is not an empty pause. Ibn Kathir draws from the second half of the ayah — *"then when they have fulfilled their term, there is no sin on you if they dispose of themselves in an honorable manner"* — the indication that **mourning for the dead husband is required until the term is finished**, since the permission only begins afterwards. In **the Two Sahihs**, Umm Habibah and Zaynab bint Jahsh narrated that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said: "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to mourn for more than three days for any dead person except her husband, for whom she mourns for four months and ten days."

Also in **the Two Sahihs**, Umm Salamah reported that a woman said, "O Messenger of Allah! My daughter's husband died and she is complaining about her eye, should we administer kohl in her eye?" He ﷺ said "No" several times as she repeated the question, then said: "It is four months and ten! During the *Jahiliyyah*, one of you would mourn for an entire year."

That last sentence is the key to the whole ruling, and Zaynab the daughter of Umm Salamah described what the pre-Islamic practice was. When a woman's husband died she would go into seclusion in the worst clothes she had, refraining from perfume and every adornment, until a year passed. She would then be brought out and given dung to throw; an animal would be brought — a donkey, a sheep, or a bird — and some blood drained from it, usually resulting in its death. Against that, four months and ten days is not a burden imposed on the widow but a **release**: a dignified, bounded period replacing a year of degradation and superstition.

What the mourning actually involves, Ibn Kathir summarises as not using beautification aids — perfume, and the clothes and jewellery that encourage men to seek marriage from the woman. He notes that all widows must observe it, whether young or old, free or servant, Muslim or disbeliever, as the general meaning of the ayah indicates. (He also records, from Imam Ahmad, 'Amr bin Al-'As saying: "Do not confuse the Sunnah of our Prophet for us. The '*Iddah* of the mother, who is also a servant, when her master dies, is four months and ten nights.")

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the practical picture and grounds it in the Arabic. The phrase is *yatarabbaṣna bi anfusihinna* — "they keep **themselves** waiting." That wording, it says, hints towards the avoidances: no perfume, make-up, kohl or hair oil, no unnecessary beauty treatment, no henna or gaudy dress; no talking about a second marriage in clear and unambiguous words (which is exactly what ayah 235 comes to regulate); and no staying overnight in a home other than her own. The same injunction applies, it adds, to a woman who has received an irrevocable divorce — and in her case it is not right for her to leave the house even during the daytime unless there is extreme compulsion.

**"There is no sin on you."** Whom does "you" address? Az-Zuhri said it means her *wali* — her guardian. Ad-Dahhak and Ar-Rabi' bin Anas explained *"when they have fulfilled their term"* as the finishing of the '*iddah*. And what she may then do "in an honorable manner" (*bil-ma'rūf*) is, said Ibn 'Abbas as reported by Al-'Awfi, that she beautifies herself so that she becomes ready for marriage proposals; Muqatil bin Hayyan was reported to give the same explanation. Mujahid — through Ibn Jurayj — glossed it as "allowed and pure marriage," and Al-Hasan, Az-Zuhri and As-Suddi are reported to have said the same. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that *bil-ma'rūf* means the marriage solemnised must be correct and permissible in the Shari'ah, with all its conditions of lawfulness observed; and it draws from "there is no sin **on you**" a further duty — that those who have the ability or power to stop someone acting against the Shari'ah are obliged to do so, and otherwise become sinners themselves.

---

## What may be said, and what may not (ayah 235)

Ayah 234 ended by lifting blame from those around the widow once her term is over. Ayah 235 turns to what may be said while it is still running. The concession is precise: no blame for a **hint** of betrothal, or for concealing the intention in yourself.

Ibn 'Abbas — narrated by Ath-Thawri, Shu'bah and Jarir — gave examples of the permitted hint: "I want to marry and I am looking for a woman whose qualities are such and such," talking to her in general terms in a way that is better; or, in another narration, "I wish that Allah endows me with a wife" — but no direct marriage proposal. **Al-Bukhari** reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the ayah means a man may say, "I wish to marry," "I desire a wife," or "I wish I could find a good wife." Ibn Kathir lists a long line of the Salaf and the Imams who permitted such indirect mention to a woman whose husband died: Mujahid, Tawus, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id bin Jubayr, Ibrahim An-Nakha'i, Ash-Sha'bi, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Az-Zuhri, Yazid bin Qusayt, Muqatil bin Hayyan, Al-Qasim bin Muhammad and several others. The same is allowed to a woman who has gone through final, irrevocable divorce — evidenced, Ibn Kathir says, by the Prophet ﷺ ordering Fatimah bint Qays to keep her '*iddah* in the house of Ibn Umm Maktum when her husband Abu 'Amr bin Hafs divorced her for the third time, telling her, "Inform me when your '*Iddah* term ends." When she finished it, Usamah bin Zayd asked to marry her, and the Prophet ﷺ married her to him. For the divorced wife who is **not** irrevocably divorced, Ibn Kathir reports there is no disagreement: it is not allowed for anyone other than her husband to mention marriage proposals to her, directly or indirectly, before the '*iddah* finishes.

**"Or conceal it in yourself."** Allah permits the private intention and then says *"Allah knows that you will remember them."* Ibn Kathir reads this as meaning: He knows these thoughts will be in your hearts, so He made it easy for you rather than criminalising an inward pull. He places it beside *"And your Lord knows what their breasts conceal, and what they reveal"* (28:69) and *"while I am All-Aware of what you conceal and what you reveal"* (60:1).

**The line that must not be crossed** is the "promise in secret." Ibn 'Abbas — through 'Ali bin Abu Talhah — said it means not saying to her, "I am in love with you," or "Promise me you will not marry someone else." Sa'id bin Jubayr, Ash-Sha'bi, 'Ikrimah, Abu Ad-Duha, Ad-Dahhak, Az-Zuhri, Mujahid and Ath-Thawri all understood it as taking the woman's promise not to marry anyone else. Only *"an honorable saying"* is left open — which Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id bin Jubayr, As-Suddi, Ath-Thawri and Ibn Zayd took as the indirect reference to marriage, such as "I desire someone like you." Muhammad bin Sirin asked 'Ubaydah about it, and he said it is to say **to her guardian**: "Do not give her away in marriage until you inform me first" — a statement narrated by Ibn Abu Hatim. Interest is routed openly through the proper channel instead of turned into a commitment extracted from her before she is free to choose.

**No contract until the term ends.** Ibn Kathir gathers Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ash-Sha'bi, Qatadah, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas, Abu Malik, Zayd bin Aslam, Muqatil bin Hayyan, Az-Zuhri, 'Ata' Al-Khurasani, As-Suddi, Ath-Thawri and Ad-Dahhak on this, and states that **the scholars agree marriage contracts during the '*iddah* are invalid**.

Then the closing: *"And know that Allah knows what is in your minds, so fear Him. And know that Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Forbearing."* Ibn Kathir reads the warning as aimed at the ideas men conceal in their hearts about women — directing them to think good about them rather than evil — and reads the ending as Allah not letting them despair of His mercy. Allah knows the inner life exactly as it is: that is a warning and a comfort at once.

## When the marriage ends before it begins (ayat 236–237)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out the full grid. Keeping dower and consummation in view, divorce falls into four situations: (1) no dower fixed and no consummation; (2) dower fixed, no consummation; (3) dower fixed and consummation — the fixed dower must be paid in full, an injunction stated elsewhere in the Qur'an; (4) no dower pre-fixed but divorce after consummation — a dower like that customarily given in the woman's immediate family (*mahr al-mithl*) is due, also taken up in another verse. **Ayat 236 and 237 handle the first two.**

**Case one — ayah 236.** No dower was fixed and the marriage was not consummated. Ibn 'Abbas, Tawus, Ibrahim and Al-Hasan Al-Basri said that "touched" means sexual intercourse. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah allowed divorce after the marriage contract and before consummation, and that the husband may divorce before consummating or before giving the dowry if it was deferred. But he must not simply walk away: Allah commands a *mut'ah*, a gift of a reasonable amount, "the rich according to his means and the poor according to his means," which Ibn Kathir explains is to compensate her for her loss. Under this same ruling Ibn Kathir cites **Al-Bukhari**, who reported in his *Sahih* from Sahl bin Sa'd and Abu Usayd that Allah's Messenger ﷺ married Umaymah bint Sharahil; when she was brought to him he extended his hand to her, but she did not like that, and the Prophet ﷺ then ordered Abu Usayd to provide provisions for her along with a gift of two garments. The marriage did not proceed — and she still left with provision and clothing.

The Qur'an fixes no amount for this gift, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the wording indicating the affluent should give according to their capacity carries an element of persuasion for the man of means not to behave tight-fisted in an act of grace. From Qurtubi it records that Sayyidnā Hasan, in such a case, gave a divorced woman twenty thousand dirhams, and Qadi Shurayh five hundred, while Sayyidnā Ibn 'Abbas said the lowest degree here is to give one set of clothes. The floor is low; the ceiling is your generosity.

**Case two — ayah 237.** A dower **was** fixed and the marriage was not consummated: he pays **half**. Ibn Kathir is careful here — this honourable ayah is not a continuation of the *mut'ah* of the previous ayah but a distinct requirement to relinquish half of the appointed *mahr*, and he notes that giving away half of the bridal-money in this case is the agreed practice according to the scholars.

Then the ayah opens two exits from the halfway line: *"unless they agree to remit it, or he in whose hands is the marriage tie agrees to remit it."* The first is the woman forfeiting her right, relieving the husband of further financial responsibility — so Ibn 'Abbas, as As-Suddi reported from Abu Salih; and Ibn Abu Hatim reported the like from Shurayh, Sa'id bin Musayyib, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, Ash-Sha'bi, Al-Hasan, Nafi', Qatadah, Jabir bin Zayd, 'Ata' Al-Khurasani, Ad-Dahhak, Az-Zuhri, Muqatil bin Hayyan, Ibn Sirin, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas and As-Suddi.

**Who holds "the marriage tie"?** Ibn Kathir reports, on the authority of Ibn Abu Hatim, that 'Amr bin Shu'ayb said that his grandfather narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said, "The husband is he who has the marriage tie." Ibn Marduwyah also reported this hadith, and it is the view chosen by Ibn Jarir. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, records that this hadith appears in *Darqutni*, narrated by 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb from his father on the authority of his grandfather, and also from Sayyidnā 'Ali and Sayyidnā Ibn 'Abbas, with the wording that the husband is the *wali* — the guardian — of the bond of marriage.) The husband genuinely holds the knot in his hand, says Ibn Kathir, since it is up to him to go on with the marriage or end it. He adds the sharp corollary — the wife's *wali* is **not** allowed to give away any of her rightful dues without her permission, especially the dowry. Only the person whose right it is may forgive it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a nuance on the word *ya'fū* ("forgives") being used for the husband too, since he is owed nothing. It suggests, tentatively, that this perhaps reflects the customary Arab practice of paying the dower at the time of marriage: after a pre-consummation divorce he would be entitled to take half of it **back**, so if he yields voluntarily and does not take his half, that too is virtually an act of forgiving. On authority over the bond, it states that this proves the power to continue or terminate the marriage rests with the husband — it is he who pronounces *talaq*.

**"And to remit is nearer to taqwa"**

The passage does not end with the arithmetic. Ibn Jarir said that some scholars held this statement is directed at **both** men and women; Ibn 'Abbas said it indicates that the one who forgives is nearer to *taqwā* — the sense of being answerable to Allah, commonly rendered piety or righteousness for want of an exact equivalent — and a similar statement was made by Ash-Sha'bi and several other scholars. Mujahid, An-Nakha'i, Ad-Dahhak, Muqatil bin Hayyan, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas and Ath-Thawri stated that the "liberality" you must not forget refers to the woman giving away her half *mahr*, or the man giving away the full *mahr*; Sa'id glossed it simply as kindness or generosity. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the point out: this forgiveness symbolically indicates that the severance of the marriage bond was also done with magnanimity and good grace, which is the objective of the Shari'ah — and it does not matter whether it comes from the woman or from the man.

Then: *"Truly, Allah is All-Seer of what you do."* Ibn Kathir: none of your affairs ever escapes His perfect watch, and He will reward each according to his deeds. The generosity may be invisible to everyone else. It is not invisible to Allah.

## Living it

Read together, the four ayat set a **floor of law and a ceiling of character**, and expect a believer to live somewhere above the floor.

- The widow's term is a protection and a dignity, and — measured against the year of seclusion and blood that preceded it — a mercy. Her mourning is a real obligation, not a formality.
- A man's private hope is not a sin, and Allah says so explicitly. What is forbidden is the promise in secret: the declaration of love, the commitment extracted from a woman who is not yet free. Interest goes to the guardian, openly, in words that leave her free.
- A marriage that ends before consummation still costs the man something. Where no dower was fixed he owes a gift he is not allowed to skip; where one was fixed he owes half. And the ayah's last word is not the half — it is *"do not forget liberality between yourselves."*
- All of it sits under Allah's knowledge of hearts. Which is why ayah 235 pairs the warning with *"Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Forbearing"* — the same knowledge that exposes you is the knowledge that forgives you.
